News.title: Gran refuses to sell patch of garden to save ancient oak from £45,000,000 Hereford Bypass
News.content:
Gran refuses to sell patch of garden to save ancient oak from £45,000,000 Hereford Bypass

A 500-year-old oak tree in Hereford could be cut down to make way for a £45,000,000 bypass, but the owner of a property in the way has refused to sell a patch of her garden

View 3 Images Jean Harris has refused to sell the patch in her garden (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

A gran is refusing to sell a patch of her garden to developers behind a £45million road scheme - in a bid to protect a 500-year-old oak tree.

‌



Jean Harris fears the ancient oak, believed to date back about 500 years to the reign of Henry VIII, will be destroyed to make way for the planned Southern Link Road near Hereford. The 79-year-old woman, a retired school secretary and piano teacher, said she is determined to protect not only the tree, but the wildlife which has thrived around it for generations.

‌



Jean has declined to sell any of her land. The elderly widow said: “It’s very old, about 500 years or so, and in perfect condition. Why would you want to ruin that? You can see it from the roads and it is definitely a landmark for us around here.”

‌



View 3 Images The ancient oak dates back about 500 years ago (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club READ MORE :

Jean, a mum of two, has lived in the three-bedroom bungalow in Allensmore, Hereford, since 2003. She believes losing the oak would devastate the area’s wildlife, with bats and owls regularly seen around her home.

She said: “We get lots of bats and owls, there’s lots of wildlife around here. It’s a key area for all wildlife and to lose it would be catastrophic.”

‌



The proposed two-mile Southern Link Road is designed to reroute the A49 around Hereford in a bid to ease congestion in the city centre. The scheme was first approved in 2015, but Jean argued planning rules have changed since then and believes building a 60mph road at the bottom of her garden is no longer the right solution.

She said: “It’s been called the Southern Link road, but it doesn’t do anything to alleviate heavy traffic in Hereford. All I will hear 24 hours a day is road noise. It’ll be an absolute nightmare.

“Lorries or big vehicles will create lots of loud noises, and the vibration will be horrible. It will be horrendous. There will be an embankment of the road where the end of the garden would be, so it’d effectively be right next to the house.”

‌



View 3 Images Jean has lived at the Herefordshire home since 2003 (Image: Emma Trimble / SWNS)

Jean feared the development would also leave her £575,000 home virtually impossible to sell. She said: “I am quite concerned about that. We bought it 23 years ago for £175,000. I had my eye on it for a long time before we bought it; it was our dream home. The family all love it.

“I have no plans to sell up, and it’s just as well because who would want to buy a property right next to a busy bypass?”

‌



Her determination to stay became even stronger following the death of her husband, Michael, whom she shared the property with. Although the section of land needed for the scheme has been valued at more than £58,000, Jean says she flatly refused to enter negotiations with Herefordshire Council.

The authority says most landowners affected by the scheme have either agreed terms or are close to reaching an agreement, but confirmed it has begun compulsory purchase proceedings where necessary.

A spokesperson said: “Most landowners have either agreed terms for the sale of their land or are close to reaching an agreement. In one case, discussions were paused by agreement to allow the landowner additional time, and we remain committed to working constructively to reach a voluntary agreement. Alongside these discussions, the council has begun the compulsory purchase process where required.

Article continues below

“This is a normal part of delivering major infrastructure projects and ensures the land needed for the scheme can be secured if voluntary agreements cannot be reached."

News.title: Police manhunt launched after 'loving' father shot in the head in Bradford
News.content:
Police manhunt launched after 'loving' father shot in the head in Bradford

Nine people have been arrested in connection with the investigation, four on suspicion of attempted murder and five on suspicion of assisting an offender

View 2 Images The family of Mohammed Hasan said he was a loving husband, father, son and brother who would go out of his way to help others (Image: West Yorkshire Police)

A manhunt has been launched after a “loving father” died after being shot in the head in Bradford.

The heartbroken family of Mohammed Hasan, 28, have asked for anyone who has any information to come forward after he died of his injuries on Sunday.

Cops are now searching for 24-year-old Luqman Khan from Bradford who is wanted in connection with the investigation. West Yorkshire Police said Khan is believed to have travelled to Suffolk and was thought to be in the Ipswich or Felixstowe areas.

In a statement following his death, Mohammed Hasan’s family said: “Hasan was a loving husband, father, son and brother. He would go out of his way to help other people. He was the life and soul of every room he’d walk into.

“He will be missed by all his family and the community. Life is often overlooked and communities need to come together to make sure nothing like this happens again."

View 2 Images Cops are hunting 24-year-old Luqman Khan from Bradford (Image: West Yorkshire Police)

“The family urge anyone who has any information to provide this to West Yorkshire Police.”

The force said officers responded to reports that a man had suffered a gunshot wound to the head on Bradford’s Gaythorne Road just before 11pm on July 8.

A total of nine people have now been arrested in connection with this investigation, four on suspicion of attempted murder and five on suspicion of assisting an offender. Eight of those arrested have been released on conditional bail with Hasnain Akhter aged 21 of Tichborne Road charged with attempted murder and remanded in custody.

Senior Investigating Officer, Detective Chief Inspector Dan Bates said: “Sadly, Mohammed Hasan was left with unsurvivable injuries from this horrific act of violence. We are determined to get justice for him and his family and need people to put aside any misplaced loyalties and think about how they would feel if it was their husband, their son, their brother.

“I would like to personally thank those who have already come forward with information. We continue to urge anyone who has information about Luqman Khan’s whereabouts or who has any other information about what has taken place and those involved to please report it.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact HMET via 101 or use the Live Chat option at www.westyorkshire.police.uk/livechat quoting reference 13260388729

Article continues below

Information can also be given anonymously to the independent Crimestoppers charity on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club
News.content:
Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club

Nathan Davies, of Bury, Greater Manchester, had gone from winning £98,000 on ITV's The 1% Club to claiming a Guinness World Record title after eating 15 fish fingers in just 60 seconds

View 2 Images Nathan can now add a Guinness World Record title to his £98,000 win (Image: Guinness World Records)

A defiant dad who vowed to break a world record after a big win on ITV’s The 1% Club has kept true to his word.

‌



Nathan Davies has become a Guinness World Records holder after making good on a promise he made live on national television. The 32-year-old project manager claimed the title for eating the most fish fingers in one minute after managing to wolf down 15 in just 60 seconds.

‌



Nathan, a dad of two, first revealed his ambition while appearing on ITV’s The 1% Club, where he walked away with a life-changing £98,000 prize after impressing viewers on the hit quiz show hosted by Lee Mack.

‌



Determined to turn his words into action, he later set his sights on a Guinness World Records title. He chose fish fingers for the challenge because they’re a staple in his household thanks to his two young sons.

View 2 Images Nathan believes he could have eaten more fish fingers (Image: Guinness World Records)

Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever READ MORE :

The quizzer, of Bury, Greater Manchester, said: “I decided fish fingers was achievable given that I’ve got a few less formal eating records so it’s up my street.”

‌



Before attempting the record, Nathan tested how quickly he could eat four fish fingers and decided the challenge was within reach. He later completed the official attempt by eating 15 fish fingers in just one minute.

Despite officially earning a place in the Guinness World Records books, Nathan admitted the achievement still feels a little surreal. He told Guinness World Record: “A bit strange, very proud to have a world record, but less proud when it’s fish finger related!”

‌



The father of two also believes he could have pushed himself even further had the fish fingers cooled down a little more before the attempt.

He said: “I think I could have done more if I had let them cool down longer, but just happy to have the record.”

Nathan’s latest achievement comes just months after celebrating his huge cash win on The 1% Club , where he told host Lee Mack he wanted to break a world record. Having now followed through on that promise, he can add a Guinness World Records title to his growing list of achievements.

Article continues below

Whether he’ll be chasing another unusual record anytime soon, however, remains to be unanswered. When asked if he had hoped to break any more. He joked: “Not if my wife has any say!”

News.title: Ofcom drops legal action against suicide forum linked to death of over 160 Brits
News.content:
Ofcom drops legal action against suicide forum linked to death of over 160 Brits

Ofcom investigators found illegal suicide content on the forum including instructional guides and threads detailing different methods of suicide

View 2 Images The Molly Rose Foundation which works to prevent suicide said online forum had been linked to 164 UK deaths (file photo) (Image: Getty Images)

No further action will be taken against an online suicide forum linked the deaths of more than 160 people in the UK, Ofcom has said.

‌



The watchdog said the forum provider, based in the US, had blocked access from the UK to the harmful content. This was the “the fullest extent of what can be achieved under the Online Safety Act,” Ofcom said.

‌



Speaking today the government body admitted that any further changes to the site “would impact global users, which is beyond UK jurisdiction,” and therefore “all possible legal routes under the Act have now been exhausted”.

‌



As the provider had voluntarily blocked access to UK users, there were no legal grounds to ask a court to “require internet service providers to block UK access to the site,” Ofcom explained.

The Molly Rose Foundation, which advocates for safer online environments and works to prevent suicide said the “nihilistic pro-suicide forum” had been linked to 164 UK deaths.

View 2 Images (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The group said families and survivors had been “left devastated by this incomprehensible decision that means more vulnerable people will continue to be groomed on the site and which will ultimately result in more lost lives”.

The suicide forum, which had been cited in multiple coroners’ in reports into the deaths of UK citizens, was the first target to be investigated by Ofcom under the new UK online safety laws last year.

Ofcom said its investigators found illegal suicide content on the forum including instructional guides and threads detailing different methods of suicides with some of them left up on the site for years.

‌



The forum’s operator was fined £950,000 in May for failing to comply with duties under the Online Safety Act. Ofcom told those behind the forum they had until June 12 to pay up - but the watchdog has still not received payment.

Ofcom confirms investigation into Married At First Sight UK READ MORE :

Sky News slapped with Ofcom complaints over Ann Widdecombe 'spinster' comments READ MORE :

The US-based operator of the site has previously disputed that it falls under UK jurisdiction, raising questions over whether the fine can be enforced. Ofcom previously said it would not identify the forum or its provider because of the nature of the content involved.

A spokesperson for Ofcom said: “The suicide forum’s provider is based in the US, and we have initiated work regarding the pursuit of this debt, as we have done with all companies that have not paid their fines by their deadlines.”

‌



Ofcom said it would review its powers relating to “business disruption measures” – through which the watchdog can apply for a court order requiring internet service providers to block access to a site in the UK.

Ofcom said since being fined, the forum made a further change to its geoblock which addressed an issue whereby registered UK users could still log in without a VPN.

The watchdog said this meant “the vast majority of UK users who do not use a VPN to mask their country location are now no longer able to access the site”.

‌



Ofcom said it recognised that geoblocks “do not fully eliminate all risk of harm, especially for individuals who choose to access sites through VPNs and use them to mask their country location”.

It added it was aware of a “very small number of existing registered users of the forum who, for technical reasons that do not appear linked to the provider’s implementation of the geoblock, are still able to access the site from the UK without using a VPN”.

The watchdog said it would closely monitor the forum to check the “geoblock remains in place”. Ofcom said it did not have the legal powers to apply for a business disruption order for failure to pay a fine alone.

‌



It added that it considered applying for a “conditional order” – essentially a pre-emptive court order that would become effective automatically in the event a site removes its geoblock – but the Act does not provide a mechanism to do so.

A spokesperson for Ofcom said: “While, in a narrow set of circumstances, failure to comply with obligations in the Act can give rise to criminal liability, this is not one of them and we cannot pursue criminal proceedings in this case.

“This means all possible legal routes under the Act have now been exhausted.”

‌



Ofcom said major search engines removed links to the forum following its investigation.

Suzanne Cater, director of enforcement at Ofcom, said: “This nihilistic suicide forum, and the predators who use it to prey on some of the most vulnerable people in our society, have devastated lives and inflicted immeasurable heartbreak.

“We’ve used the powers we’ve been granted to the fullest extent possible, which has resulted in blocking this site for the vast majority of users in the UK.

‌



“We recognise this may not bring closure for bereaved families but it will help protect people in the UK in the future.”

Andy Burrows, chief executive of Molly Rose Foundation, said: “It has taken Ofcom 468 days since launching its investigation to decide not to seek to block a nihilistic, pro-suicide forum responsible for at least 164 deaths, after having to be pushed every step to continue investigating by bereaved families.

“Families and survivors have been left devastated by this incomprehensible decision that means more vulnerable people will continue to be groomed on the site and which will ultimately result in more lost lives.

‌



“Deciding to bury this bad news on the day a new prime minister is announced demonstrates an utter lack of moral courage and shows why bereaved families are right to think Melanie Dawes has no place continuing to lead the internet safety regulator.”

Sarah Ruane, director of policy, practice and influencing at Samaritans, said: “We are extremely disappointed by today’s announcement from Ofcom.

“After months of investigating this suicide forum, and over three years since the Online Safety Act was passed, we are yet to see meaningful action against some of the most harmful sites online.

‌



“Online platforms must know that any breach of the act will be heavily punished and this is a missed opportunity to hammer that message home.

“All today’s announcement does is raise serious questions about whether the Online Safety Act is fit for purpose.

“Under the new PM’s leadership, we need to see a strong commitment to ensuring Ofcom has the powers it needs to take decisive action.”

Article continues below

David Parfett, of Families and Survivors to Prevent Online Suicide Harms, said: “We continue to see suicides where victims have found information on methods online, and often have been encouraged to self-harm.

“This continues what we’ve seen for years; vulnerable people being able to easily find information and communities online which would be illegal in the real-world.

“The Online Safety Act in Ofcom’s hands is not working and that’s starkly measured in continued avoidable loss of life.”

News.title: Ann Widdecombe suspect Joshua Kerry charged with murdering ex-Tory MP
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe suspect Joshua Kerry charged with murdering ex-Tory MP

Joshua Kerry, 28, was originally detained on suspicion of Ann Widdecombe's murder, before being re-arrested two days later on suspicion of commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism

View 7 Images Joshua Kerry has been charged with murder

A man has tonight been charged with the murder of former Tory minister Ann Widdecombe.

‌



Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, South Yorkshire, is set to appear in Westminster Magistrates Court on Tuesday accused of attacking the Conservative turned Reform UK spokeswoman in her Devon home.

‌



Kerry was originally arrested on suspicion of murder on Saturday, July 11, before being re-arrested two days later on suspicion of commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

‌



Frank Ferguson, Chief Crown Prosecutor of the CPS Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: “We have decided to prosecute Joshua Kerry for murder following a police investigation into the death of Ann Widdecombe in Haytor, Dartmoor.

“Police enquiries into the defendant's motives are ongoing, including a potential political or terrorist connection.

“Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

‌



View 7 Images Ann Widdecombe was killed on July 8 (Image: Steve Taylor/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, added: “I would like to firstly offer my deepest condolences to the family of Ann Widdecombe, and to everyone who knew and loved her. The impact she had on public and political life in this country has been clear to see since her death on the 8th of July.

“I hope some of the tributes paid over the last week have been of comfort to her family, who are also being supported by our specialist family liaison officers. It remains the case that we are not looking for anyone else in connection with this incident.

‌



“I know there has been significant interest in this case – and rightly so. I want to make it very clear that our investigation into this individual, determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing.

“Given Ann Widdecombe’s profile and the targeted nature of the attack, determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation, remains an active avenue of investigation for our detectives.

“As with all murder investigations, understanding the ‘why’ is a key part of our enquiries. This has been, and remains, a particularly intensive and complex investigation.

‌



View 7 Images Police were at the suspect's home from Sunday (Image: Iconic Media Group / SWNS)

View 7 Images A mid-terrace home was under police cordon following an arrest at about 9pm on Saturday, July 11 (Image: Tom Maddick / SWNS)

“Over the last week, our teams have gathered a huge amount of information, leading to over 800 lines of enquiry. Each of those needs assessing, carefully and thoroughly, and I ask that we are given the time to do that.

‌



“Should Counter Terrorism Policing identify further offences, we will liaise with the Crown Prosecution Service and work to submit evidence where appropriate.

“As always, to ensure the best outcome for victims and their families, we must do this right, not just quickly. And I reiterate my ask for the support of the public in this.

“I know many have been understandably concerned about their own safety after this horrendous attack, particularly after hearing about the nature of the attack she endured, in her own home.

‌



“We are working closely with the Speaker of the House and the relevant authorities to ensure elected officials are aware of what we have in place to protect them.

“As criminal proceedings are now underway, and to avoid impeding the judicial process, we will not be making any further comment on the investigation unless absolutely appropriate.

“I would like to thank the public, the media, and those right across the political spectrum for their engagement and support whilst we progress this challenging investigation.

‌



“I ask for patience as our teams do their work, thank you for your support so far.”

View 7 Images Ann Widdecombe was found dead inside her home (Image: Getty Images)

Ms Widdecombe was killed in her house on Wednesday July 8, 30 minutes before she was set to appear via video call from home, on Channel 5's Matt Allwright show. The 78-year-old had last messaged a producer at 12.19pm but failed to respond to a text at 12.48pm.

‌



Devon and Cornwall Police believed she died at 12.30pm in the bungalow where she lived alone with her cat on the edge of Dartmoor National Park. Her body remained undiscovered for almost 24 hours before being found in the kitchen of the house at 11.40am the next day.

An inquest will be opened into the death of Ms Widdecombe on Tuesday morning.

Kerry is understood to have been unemployed since working as an office administrator up until two years ago.

‌



Ms Widdecombe was first elected a Conservative MP in Kent in 1987, then served as an MEP for the Brexit Party and spokeswoman for Reform UK. She also starred in Strictly Come Dancing and Celebrity Big Brother. Prime Minister Keir Starmer said he had spoken to his successor Andy Burnham, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK's Mr Farage to "urge everybody to come together at a moment like this".

Paying tribute to Ms Widdecombe, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said on Tuesday: "Ann Widdecombe dedicated her life to politics and public service. For nearly 40 years, she was a fixture of our political life. She brought conviction to our politics, grounded in her profound Catholic faith. She was forthright in her opinions and argued courageously for the things she believed in. But, perhaps most of all, she brought an inimitable style to politics. She was forthright and fearless."

The Home Secretary added: "She was one of those rare politicians who was bigger than politics."

‌



7 View 7 Images The scene at a Rotherham address on Sunday (Image: Iconic Media Group / SWNS) 7 View 7 Images Officers were spotted searching bins and leaving the house with boltcutters (Image: Iconic Media Group / SWNS)

House of Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle also paid tribute to Ms Widdecombe in the chamber. He said: "Ann was a formidable politician, a prominent figure in public life. She was a member of Parliament for Maidstone for 23 years, holding a number of ministerial posts in the 1990s.

‌



"Ann was fierce and enjoyed robust political debate. Whether you agreed with her or not, she was principled, spoke her mind and was true to her beliefs, informed by a Christian faith. She was a friend in many ways. Politically we may not agree, but she was without doubt a courageous, principled politician and all our thoughts are with her family and her friends."

Sir Lindsay has previously spoken about his fears for MPs following the killings of Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016 and Conservative David Amess in 2021. He added: "Ann was a close friend to David Amess and both were animal lovers."

Counter Terrorism Policing took over the investigation into Ms Widdecombe's death after Devon and Cornwall Police initially said there was "nothing to suggest" the murder had been politically motivated.

Article continues below

Terrorism laws allow a suspect to be held for up to seven days in the first instance, with investigators permitted to apply for time extensions up to 14 days in total.

News.title: DARREN LEWIS: 'Burnham must get Black voters back on track'
News.content:
So just what is Andy Burnham going to do about Labour’s Black MP problem? Miatta Fahnbulleh is a start. She’s a key adviser to Burnham and has a wealth of experience developing and delivering policy to empower communities. We also know that she has worked hard to come up with new ideas to reshaping our economy inside government and out. But who else?

Glance at any of the selfies the UK’s new PM takes and the numbers of Black MPs in particular behind him are embarrassing. David Lammy has long since lost the confidence of his Tottenham constituency, near where I live in North London.

Dylan Law, the Green Party’s deputy mayor in Hackney Downs where I grew up, is the kind of fresh energy people want to get behind. Burnham talks a terrific game in his bid to fend off the rise of the Greens. But Zack Polanski’s disruptors champion Black political talent.

View 3 Images David Lammy at the the House of Commons (Image: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA Wire)

‌



Where will it be in this next Labour cabinet? Who is the next male cab off the rank to speak to the issues affecting millions of Black and Brown men and boys in this country?

Who will be their advocate around the table to address their over-representation in the criminal justice system, their high exclusion rates from school increasing their vulnerability to exploitation, their mental health disparities and stop and search?

Who is the female MP to fight for the Black women affected by the racism and discrimination endemic in NHS maternity care, leading to Black mothers being nearly three times as likely to die during childbirth compared to white women?

Who is the Black female Cabinet candidate to end the perception that Labour’s “regard” for Black voters is largely performative, per the treatment of Diane Abbott and Kate Osamor, under the regime of Sir Keir Starmer?

‌



Just a couple of months ago, Eunice O’Dame and Enid Mollyneux – two long-serving Black women councillors – were blocked by Labour from standing in one of its safest wards in Croydon, Bensham Manor. The seat was instead contested by Starmer’s niece, Ellie Sandover.

View 3 Images Dylan Law, the Green Party’s deputy mayor in Hackney Downs, is the kind of fresh energy people want to get behind (Image: Getty Images)

Nobody doubts Ellie’s ability to do the job and this is most certainly not about her as an individual. It is about Labour and their inability to read the room regarding Black candidates.

This is far from the first time this column has raised this issue. Labour simply cannot take our votes for granted. The UK is at its most febrile in terms of race relations since the vile Seventies and Eighties, with poisonous racism spouted unashamedly.

‌



The Windrush scandal continues to see the state waiting for claimants to die rather that meet its responsibilities. More fool us for believing things would change in that regard with the Tories out of power.

Then there’s the ongoing hostile environment, the empowerment and appeasement of those rejecting anti-racism and so much more. Burnham has a golden opportunity, to do better than Starmer whose government pretty much abandoned Black Britain.

Young, clued-up people want visionaries who looks like them, speak truth to power and understand their lives. A Dylan Law would probably never have made it on to a Labour shortlist, based on the patterns of many years.

And if Burnham wants to change his Cabinet, he needs to do better than Shabana Mahmood, who defended Starmer’s Island Of Strangers remarks.

‌



A woman who threw people of colour under the bus with her immigration policies and rhetoric. A woman whose left-wing principles disintegrated once she gained a whiff of high office. Us Black voters are waiting. Can Burnham rise to the challenge?

News.title: Organised crime cops help catch 1,393 'paedophiles and sex abusers'
News.content:
Organised crime cops help catch 1,393 'paedophiles and sex abusers'

Regional organised crime units who normally investigate gangland kingpins have been deployed on paedophiles and domestic abusers arresting 1,393 and safeguarding 1,351 children

View 3 Images Rhys Meikle, 31, was jailed for four years for a sex offence (Image: North West Regional Organised Crime Unit)

Specialist police fighting organised crime have helped catch more than one thousand suspected sexual predators, it has been revealed today.

‌



Tactics normally used to nail gangland kingpins have been deployed on paedophiles and domestic abusers leading to 1,393 arrests, safeguarding 1,351 children and securing 1,487 years of jail time.

‌



Regional organised crime units (ROCUs) continue to tackle drug dealers, serious violence, money laundering and firearms offending, but have become increasingly focused on protecting the most vulnerable people in society.

‌



Among those jailed were Declan Sains, 28, after talking online to an undercover police officer who he thought was a 14-year-old boy online.

Sains pleaded guilty to engaging in sexual communication with a child, making indecent images of children and inciting a boy to engage in sexual activity. He was sentenced to eight years and three months in prison at Teesside Crown Court.

Man planned to abuse young girl with her dad before police arrived at his home READ MORE :

View 3 Images Declan Sains, 28, was jailed for child sex offences (Image: NEROCU)

‌



Rhys Meikle, 31, was jailed last month for four years at Manchester Crown Court after he pleaded guilty to arranging or facilitating the commission of child sexual offences and making; and distributing indecent images of children.

Chief Constable Trevor Rodenhurst, the National Police Chiefs’ Council lead for ROCUs, said: "Organised crime continues to evolve rapidly, with offenders increasingly exploiting digital platforms and targeting vulnerable individuals in new ways. ROCUs are adapting alongside those threats, developing specialist skills, technology and intelligence capabilities to ensure communities remain protected.

"The ROCU network has evolved significantly since its creation and now plays a crucial role in tackling some of the most harmful threats facing our communities.

‌



"From disrupting organised crime groups involved in drugs and firearms, to protecting children from online predators, supporting victims of abuse and identifying hidden exploitation, our officers and staff are making a tangible difference every day.

"Organised crime is becoming increasingly complex, and ROCUs are needed more than ever."

View 3 Images Heroin seized by ROCU officers (Image: ROCU/West Midlands Police)

‌



'It is vital we recognise exploitation'

Deputy Chief constable Wendy Gunney, the NPCC lead for national SOC, added: "Today, vulnerability is a theme we recognise and see running throughout so many of our investigations because organised criminals are experts in exploitation and coercion. It’s vital that our officers recognise this and not only pursue dangerous offenders but identify and safeguard victims.

“The ROCU network has demonstrated that the tactics and capabilities they use to tackle SOC are highly effective and are confident they will greatly assist in the fight against violence against women and girls and online exploitation.”

Since their inception in 2013, ROCUs have grown into a national network of around 4,000 officers and staff.

Article continues below

Working alongside the National Crime Agency (NCA), officers are using advanced investigative methods to support local forces .

Over the past year, ROCUs have arrested 4,363 suspects, secured 7,242 years of prison sentences, protected 2,259 children and 823 adults and made 1,492 drug and firearms arrests.

The units have seized 95 firearms and 652 rounds of ammunition along with more than 1.5 tonnes of cocaine, 158 kg of heroin and 8.4 tonnes of cannabis.

News.title: Who's in the cabinet?
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has started building his new cabinet after taking office following the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer.

Tap or click on a cabinet member in our interactive guide below to learn more about them and their role in government. The guide will be updated as new appointments are made.

News.title: Faisal Islam: The new PM has big ideas - but what will they cost?
News.content:
Up until this point, the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described his policy changes with a broad brush. From today, he faces the constraints, trade offs, and realities of high national office.

For example, Burnham has said Tuesday's announcements on cost of living support would be paid for. In other words, it would mean a tax rise or spending cut, so we will see rather quickly what the new PM prioritises when push comes to shove.

Meanwhile, the markets seem to have already reacted to the suggestion he would be using some "flexibility" in his borrowing rules to help with new announcements.

The UK government's 10-year borrowing rose above 5% on Monday after falling in recent days. It has not gone up in this way in other European economies.

The move was not huge, but it shows the sensitivities at a moment when Burnham is overhauling his cabinet - including replacing Rachel Reeves as chancellor with former defence secretary John Healey.

The "flexibility" Burnham was talking about is, I understand, about the treatment of financial institutions. This has occurred in some green energy policies and essentially helps exempt certain types of borrowing from the measures of debt. There is scope for this model to extend to housing and other infrastructure.

It was not a general suggestion of, for example, using up the increased headroom against the government's borrowing rules.

All this shows how every tricky decision and trade off is being watched by the country and the markets at the same time.

News.title: Burnham promises help with your money. How could it affect you?
News.content:
In his first speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham has promised to give people more "breathing space" to help with the cost of living.

Policies will be announced on Tuesday - his first full day in the job. Although a few hours after taking office, the new prime minister confirmed he will be "looking at" the tax-free personal allowance ahead of his first Budget in the autumn.

Cost of living is a key issue for Burnham. Many people, he has previously said, can't go out for a pint on a Friday, can't take the kids out and can't go on holiday owing to the pressure on their finances.

The cost of living has dominated people's lives in recent years, and - to some extent - our politics too. Easing that pressure hasn't been easy.

So, if Burnham chooses to support people on issues such as energy bills and the cost of transport, allows people to earn more before being taxed, and makes care and somewhere to live more affordable - he'll face tough choices on funding those moves and managing the trade-offs that come with them.

And his new chancellor, John Healey, will be the one who has to deliver any changes, and outline how to pay for them.

News.title: Chancellor Healey will be under pressure to deliver for armed forces
News.content:
When Healey resigned last month, he had been offered only an extra Â£13.5bn - what amounted to a 0.08% increase in the defence budget.

At the time he made clear that was not enough to keep the country safe and to meet rising threats.

Those close to him said in reality the offer amounted only to an extra Â£10bn, with the rest what they called "Treasury Trickery".

Healey's resignation letter also expressed his frustration that the government had no clear timetable to meet its promise of increasing the UK's defence spending to 3% of GDP.

He wanted to reach that target by 2030, the year when many in Nato have said the alliance must be ready for conflict.

But under Sir Keir, the 3% pledge remained vague - some time in the next parliament. A further Nato pledge to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 appeared to be even more remote.

Now as Andy Burnham's chancellor, Healey will be under pressure to put his money where his mouth is.

But as chancellor he can't just focus on defence. There will be many competing demands.

And the extra spending he argued for as defence secretary is significant. According to calculations by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), reaching this 3% threshold will demand an additional Â£17.3bn per year by 2029â30. The overall defence budget would have to rise from more than Â£63bn a year to closer to Â£90bn by 2030.

Any increase in defence spending will increase the pressure for tax rises, though Healey has argued in the past for "creative funding options". That might suggest he has thought of other ways to fund the Ministry of Defence.

The Liberal Democrats have argued for defence bonds - though Sir Keir argued that was just another way of borrowing money.

But without extra funding, Healey has been clear Britain's armed forces will not be ready to meet rising threats. A revised DIP published following his resignation still had a Â£5bn black hole.

Key plans to transform the military with drones, and uncrewed warships and aircraft are still not fully funded. Defence chiefs have been emphasising the importance of learning the lessons from the war in Ukraine. But plans for new air defence systems and long-range weapons remain underfunded.

Now he's the chancellor, Healey will have the opportunity to set out a plan to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP himself.

If he is true to his word, it can only mean positive news for his successor as defence secretary.

News.title: Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM
News.content:
In his first speech in Downing Street, Burnham announced he would "end rough sleeping in our country".

This was swiftly followed by a No 10 press release promising an extra Â£340m for the task over the next five years.

He also promised a new 10-year plan for Britain - to be unveiled later this year - and to build a new economy, putting "life's essentials back under public control".

But arguing that people also needed "breathing space now", he said announcements on tackling the cost of living would start on Tuesday.

Other changes he promised included changing the education system to help young people into work, building more council homes, and honouring commitments to fund defence while sticking to the UK's spending and debt rules.

News.title: Man, 28, charged with murder of Ann Widdecombe
News.content:
A 28-year-old man has been charged with the murder of Ann Widdecombe, police and prosecutors have said.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing said "determining the motivation, including any possible political motivation" remains "an active avenue" of investigation.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

In a statement read outside New Scotland Yard, Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said: "I want to make it very clear that our investigation into [Kerry], determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing."

"As with all murder investigations, understanding the 'why' is a key part of our enquiries," he said, adding that it was "a particularly intensive and complex investigation".

Taylor said it remained the case that investigators were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

He added that counter terrorism teams have gathered "a huge amount of information" over the last week, leading to more than 800 lines of enquiry.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been lead by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)'s special crime and counter terrorism division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial," Ferguson said.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

News.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool footballer who managed England and Newcastle United, dies aged 75
News.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75, seven weeks after he revealed he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, his family have confirmed.

One of English football's most decorated players, Keegan enjoyed spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career.

He later went on to manage Newcastle, Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Keegan revealed he had stage four cancer in June, which is the most advanced stage of cancer and means the disease has spread to other parts of the body.

His family initially disclosed he was battling the disease in January, after he had "further evaluation of ongoing abdominal symptoms" in hospital.

A statement on behalf of the Keegan family said he was "surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments".

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather," it continued.

"The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Newcastle United paid tribute, describing Keegan as "one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history".

The club statement added: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him."

Liverpool, for whom Keegan played for between 1971 and 1977, said Keegan's "indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on".

Hamburg said football had lost one of its "defining figures" and they would always "cherish" his memory, while Fulham said Keegan "forged a strong connection" with the fans, who would "forever hold wonderful memories" of his short time at the club.

England and Manchester City both offered their condolences to the Keegan family, with the latter describing him as "one of the most iconic and fondly remembered figures in English football".

The Three Lions will celebrate Keegan's life when they host Spain in a Uefa Nations League match at Wembley on 26 September.

News.title: Ofcom launches investigation into Married at First Sight UK
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK is facing renewed pressure after the broadcast regulator launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 reality TV show.

In a statement on Monday, Ofcom said it was investigating "a fairness and privacy complaint" about the prime-time show.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Ryanair profits drop as Iran war puts off passengers and lifts fuel costs
News.content:
Ryanair's profits have fallen sharply as war in the Middle East sent jet fuel prices soaring and customers reluctant to book flights.

The Irish airline's pre-tax profits dropped 34% to â¬593m (Â£503m) between April and June while sales were flat as the company was forced to cut fares to stimulate demand.

Ryanair also said it expects summer fares to be slightly lower than last year due to "consumer hesitancy" around air travel.

The price of fuelling a plane has jumped since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and while Ryanair said it had "hedged" or struck deals for the most future fuel costs, those not included in these arrangements had more than doubled.

Crude oil prices hit $90 (Â£67) a barrel for the first time in a month on Monday, before falling back slightly, after a weekend of intense exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz â an essential route for global oil and gas supplies â has ground to a halt.

An interim peace deal last month brought some respite to oil and energy prices, but they spiked again as negotiations broke down and fighting resumed.

The airline warned that its results for the year will be "highly sensitive" to external factors such as conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine as well as the price of unhedged jet fuel.

Fares for for the key summer period between July and September are on track to be "modestly" lower than last year, with many passengers booking closer to departure than normal.

The firm's finance chief, Neil Sorahan, said flights on its popular Mediterranean routes were still full. "People [are] as keen to get away as ever, albeit booking just a little bit later," he said.

Between April and June, Ryanair's revenue ticked up 1% to â¬4.4bn.

While passenger numbers rose 6% to 6.1 million- helped by the Easter holiday in April - fares fell by 6% as the airline reduced fares to entice flyers concerned about the Iran war.

Ryanair's share price fell 5% on Monday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Ryanair was in a better position than many of its rivals, but nonetheless "visibility is worse than San Francisco airport when the fog sets in".

"The renewed escalation in hostilities in the Middle East is unhelpful and without a lasting resolution, challenging times for the airline and travel space look set to continue."

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: 'Scrutiny' needed over baby's death, court hears
News.content:
Preston had been taken to Blackpool Victoria Hospital three times before his death and seen by a "battery of professionals" including medical staff, social workers and welfare officers from various bodies.

Wilson told the hearing an inquest had initially been opened shortly after Preston's death but was then suspended while police investigated, culminating in the trial and conviction of his adoptive parents.

Wilson said he had to consider whether an inquest should continue, given "relevant issues" had already been heard during the eight-week criminal trial.

However, while he said he would not make a final decision on Monday, subject to submissions from lawyers for other public bodies, it was "highly likely" one would take place, probably in the autumn of next year.

He said: "I feel there's sufficient reason to resume. There are acts and omissions of public authorities that need to be scrutinised in a public hearing in which Preston's family can participate.

"It's clearly going to be a wide-ranging inquiry."

The coroner said he was aware there had been calls for a public inquiry, but his role meant that was not a matter for himself to consider, but to proceed on the basis of whether or not to hold an inquest.

The court heard Oldham Safeguarding Children's Partnership, had resumed a review into Preston's death, following its suspension for the criminal trial to take place.

This review was likely only to be completed by January 2027, and the inquest cannot be held before then, the court heard.

Much of the hearing dealt with which people or public bodies should be legally represented at any inquest.

They included Preston's biological mother and grandmother, Sara and Debbie Davey, neither of whom were present for the hearing but were represented by lawyers in court.

Preston was born while his mother was in custody and a place in a mother and baby unit in prison was refused, the court heard.

Instead, he was taken from her by a court order from Oldham Council and placed with temporary adoptive parents before being adopted by Varley and McGowan.

News.title: Fire crews to remain at Arthur's Seat for days after blaze
News.content:
Firefighters are expected to remain at Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh "for a couple of days" following a large blaze on Sunday evening.

Small plumes of smoke could still be seen on Monday morning along Salisbury Crags and large swathes of vegetation below the cliff face had been burned black.

Six fire engines were sent to tackle the the grassfire on the slope between the Scottish Parliament and St Leonard's with crews working overnight to douse the flames and dampen hotspots.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said there were "no reported casualties" but Police Scotland said Queen's Drive, the road that encircles the Holyrood Park hills, remained closed to all vehicles.

It is the second fire in the last three months at the landmark, an ancient extinct volcano that offers panoramic views of the Scottish capital.

Edinburgh University student Mahek Jayantilial, who lives near Arthur's Seat, said she could see the fire from her window.

"I was a bit worried because I thought the fire would come this way, but thankfully there's enough concrete here to stop it," the 24-year-old said.

News.title: Prisons minister Lord Timpson quits government
News.content:
The prisons minister has resigned from the government, the BBC has been told.

Lord James Timpson was appointed to the role in July 2024 after leaving his job as CEO of the Timpson group, a business which provides key cutting and shoe repair services and employs hundreds of former prisoners.

His arrival in government was greeted with much fanfare by some in the Labour Party and described as "radical" and "innovative".

But in a departing statement on Monday, seen exclusively by the BBC, Lord Timpson said he was stepping down and it was an "honour" to serve in the post.

His statement did not give a specific reason for resigning, but it is understood he feels he has done as much as he can in the role.

Prisons in England and Wales were at crisis point, reaching almost full capacity, when he first entered Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He oversaw the controversial early release scheme which saw tens of thousands of inmates let out to create more space in jails.

His critics will argue prisons continue to be violent, drug infused and overcrowded, while probation officers still report being overworked and unable to cope.

But figures do show assaults against staff and self-harm in prisons are falling.

Lord Timpson said in his resignation statement that he had left "our prisons and probation service in a much healthier and happier state than two years ago".

He added: "I'm proud to have become the longest-serving minister in this role for 15 years. I'm also proud that 75% of prisons and 90% of probation teams are now performing better than when I started.

"Self-harm, violence and assaults on staff are all down, and fewer people are leaving prison without a home to go to, a measure of dignity I care about deeply."

He also pointed to the Women's Justice Board he established, saying he "believe[s] most women should not be in prison at all" and "diverting them away from custody, helping them with often chaotic, damaged, and addicted lives, is one of the changes I'm proud to have achieved".

His critics may question why he is leaving before the Sentencing Act 2026 is enacted in September, when more people are expected to be released early and further criminals will serve their sentences in the community.

A source in the Ministry of Justice told the BBC: "We're gutted he's going but the new person is going to have their work cut out to get their head round what's round the corner."

News.title: Pupil not guilty of trying to murder history teacher after stabbing her in the head
News.content:
A pupil has been found not guilty of attempted murder after stabbing his teacher in the head with a kitchen knife.

The boy, 16, followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School in Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his history work on 5 February.

He pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her. Williams told a jury at Swansea Crown Court she feared she would die.

On Monday, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent, and unlawful wounding. He will be sentenced on 3 September.

The boy had previously pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife on the school grounds.

Judge Paul Thomas KC accepted a majority verdict on the charge of wounding with intent, which meant at least 10 jurors agreed following four hours deliberation.

During the attack, Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She received injuries to her head, back and hands after the attack.

She said the look on the teenager's face was one of "pure hatred".

During a police interview, Williams said how the boy, who was 15 at the time and who cannot be named due to his age, came to her classroom "cool and collected" at the end of the school day to ask if his "work was correct".

She said that "got [her] confused" because he had "never seemed bothered before".

It was when he shut the door to the classroom, saying it was cold, that "alarm bells" began to ring in her head.

Williams said he was trying to "keep her talking" while he was "trying to find something in his bag".

"I ask him again, 'are you sure you're alright?' And then he pulls [the knife] out of the bag and lunges at me," she said.

The boy told the court Williams had seen him with the knife and "tried to grab it" from him. He said he "accidentally assaulted her" during the struggle.

She told the court she believed she was about to die, thinking: "I'm fearful that I am dying, I've seen the knife, I know I've been stabbed, all I'm thinking at that point is, 'I need help'."

Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere".

The Trump administration has gone after the phone records of journalists’ relatives in its investigation of reporting on the president’s gifted Qatari-gifted Air Force One plane, court documents show.

Subpoenas were issued to multiple journalists at The New York Times last week after the newspaper reported on security concerns about Donald Trump’s new jet in what the newspaper characterized as an “extraordinarily aggressive and unorthodox attempt to unearth confidential sources.”

Attorneys for the newspaper filed a motion to quash the subpoenas over the weekend after the administration sought the records of one reporter’s mother and two journalists’ spouses in relation to the probe, the lawyers said.

“The identifiers for which the Government seeks information include phone numbers used by one Journalist's mother and two Journalists' spouses,” they wrote. “The mother is a mental health professional with confidential client relationships. One of the two spouses is the general counsel of a major law firm.”

“The disclosure of additional subpoenas for confidential newsgathering information of the Journalists is deeply concerning, revealing yet another instance of the alarming pattern of conduct detailed in the Motion to Quash,” the lawyers added in the motion.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has gone after the phone records of journalists’ relatives in its leak investigation concerning the president’s gifted Qatari-gifted Air Force One plane, court documents show ( Getty )

Julian Barnes, Tyler Pager, Eric Schmitt and Eric Lipton are among the Times reporters who received subpoenas.

The Independent has contacted the Justice Department for comment.

Freedom of the Press Foundation chief of advocacy Seth Stern said that targeting reporters’ relatives has “nothing to do with national security and everything to do with chilling journalism.”

“Even the Mafia says families are off limits. It’s gross that the administration — in its never-ending effort to harass and intimidate reporters who reveal its incompetence — is going after the communications of journalists’ relatives,” Stern said in a statement.

“The administration’s own guidelines say pursuing journalists is a last resort. But instead, it’s looking for any excuse to snoop on reporters and their relatives.”

In a previous statement, the Justice Department justified the subpoenas by saying that “to be clear, reporters are not the targets, those leaking classified information are.”

The Times initially reported that the Qatari jet “lacks the same defensive countermeasures as the older model, including antimissile capabilities.”

Trump told reporters on Sunday that the gifted plane was being taken out of service so it could be “maxed out,” and appeared to confirm the newspaper’s reporting.

open image in gallery Subpoenas were issued to multiple journalists at The New York Times last week after the newspaper reported on security concerns about Donald Trump’s new jet in what the newspaper characterized as an ‘extraordinarily aggressive and unorthodox attempt to unearth confidential sources’ ( AFP/Getty )

“It has a lot of capability, but as I understand it, in about a month or so, they’re going to send it to have it be maxed out,” he told a reporter who asked why the president was flying on a plane that lacked antimissile defense systems.

The new Air Force One, a $400 million Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, lacks “some of the advanced security features of the older aircraft, including antimissile capabilities,” the Times reported.

The jet, an expensive gift that has raised ethics and security concerns among Democrats, was retrofitted by the Pentagon earlier this year and officially unveiled by Trump last month.

Trump said last week he would be flying the older aircraft out of Turkey “for old times’s sake.” He later denied that security concerns factored into the decision.

Before the Times published the article, an FBI official contacted the outlet and asked that it be held, citing national security concerns. The official also asked the newspaper to reveal its sources for the article, which the outlet declined to do.

Brendan Rascius contributed reporting

We need to be better,” the new prime minister told the nation. Well, in at least a few respects, Andy Burnham has already done better.

Without being unduly unkind to his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, even the now ex-prime minister might agree that he could have been better at presentation and projecting a sense of purpose for his administration. Indeed, in his twilight days, he himself sometimes pretty much admitted as much.

Undoubtedly, Mr Burnham is a fresh start in that respect. Speaking without notes, sans lectern, in a more modulated voice with a softer accent, the upgrade in style was immediately obvious. The new prime minister has a more confident demeanour, as well he should, and offered some of the vision that has been lacking recently.

There was some substance, too. The idea of a national 10-year plan may not be entirely novel (it was a dismal failure for the Wilson administration 60 years ago), but it is intriguing – and at least has the prospect of being better defined and understood than Sir Keir’s lamentable tangle of missions, priorities, targets and phases.

It signals a certain long-termism, too. Obviously, there was plenty of politico cliche in Mr Burnham’s performance, such as the promise of “new politics”, “common purpose” and “an end to point scoring” (they all say that); but unveiled without any prior hint, and with some drama, was an unequivocal pledge to “end rough sleeping in this country”.

Surprise! Britain managed to do it during the pandemic, and Mr Burnham points to his efforts in Manchester to prove that progress is possible. If achieved (no deadline was mentioned), it will prove to the public that its government can actually get something done. If reproduced elsewhere – and there have been improvements already in areas such as NHS waiting lists and migration – it might help dispel the depressing national conviction that “Britain is broken”.

If we can conquer rough sleeping, why not social care, another priority of Mr Burnham’s? Or reform of social security, and rebuilding the nation’s defences? Or the housing crisis? He didn’t mention climate change, Europe or economic growth in his inaugural address, but it may be presumed that he wishes to attract more investment and further rebuild Britain’s relationship with the EU.

Mr Burnham was wise to pledge allegiance to the fiscal rules, and the signs are that he and his advisers, such as Lord O’Neill, may have found a way to borrow to invest within those structures and without spooking financial markets. He offers “the biggest changes in the last 40 years… a new political model and a new economic model”.

A “circuit-breaker moment” indeed – but it would be irrational, to put it mildly, to think that all the liberalising reforms to the economy made since Margaret Thatcher came to power in 1979 must now be discarded. Mr Burnham does need to be wary of promising a better yesterday.

If former mayor Burnham can be forward-looking and actually get things done, as he did in Greater Manchester, then he deserves to succeed, and he will indeed, as he says, give the nation some much-needed hope. “Vibes”, his critics sneer, is all that Mr Burnham is about, but they may underestimate him – and, in any case, a better national mood would be a welcome change.

To achieve that, like any other leader, he needs a team with him. As his distant predecessor, William Gladstone, famously noted: “The first essential for a prime minister is to be a good butcher.” Thatcher called cabinet reshuffles the “worst job I ever have to do here”. On the evidence of his first cabinet appointments, Mr Burnham, a nice man in most settings, has shown himself quite willing to carve the joint.

During his leadership campaign, such as it was, Mr Burnham talked about his plans for his “top team” and said “you will see it ⁠reflects all parts of our party, all communities”. Not all are cooperating with Mr Burnham’s effort at inclusion. A few of Sir Keir’s most loyal colleagues, notably Rachel Reeves, were reportedly offered alternative jobs in cabinet, but rejected them and chose to resign instead.

Most were simply sacked in a purge of the Starmerites – David Lammy, Liz Kendall, Lord Hermer, Peter Kyle – in what one commentator quipped was a “night of the long eyelashes”. As one of the thus dispossessed, Steve Reed, hinted at in his resignation letter, not all will feel that much loyalty to the new leader.

Yet, on their merits, he seems to have exercised sound judgement in making most of the right senior appointments, both in the national interest as well as the more grubby business of managing oversized egos and party factions.

John Healey is an inspired choice for the Treasury. He is just the kind of principled, tough figure needed to steer the Treasury in the right direction, and will now be in a better position to find the money for increased military spending and challenge the “Treasury orthodoxy” he attacked when he quit as defence secretary. But he must also retain the confidence of the markets and the integrity of the fiscal rules – a daunting task.

The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, shouldn’t feel too short-changed by his new role, and Shabana Mahmood has succeeded in remaining at the Home Office to finish her immigration and asylum reforms.

On the whole, Mr Burnham has given the Labour government a new lease of life, a renewed sense of purpose, and undertaken some difficult trimming of the old cabinet’s membership. No doubt there will be a bump in the polls. As for completing the biggest changes to British economic and political life since the 1980s… well, it is only day one of the remaining three or so years before the next election. He’s ambitious all right, is Mr Burnham.

News.title: California city manager arrested on burglary charges after being on the job for less than three weeks
News.content:

A newly appointed California city official was arrested on burglary charges after being found on someone else’s yacht over the weekend, less than three weeks after taking over the municipality’s top administrative role.

Elaine Forbes, the 53-year-old city manager of Sausalito, was taken into custody shortly before 7 a.m. on Saturday by the Marin County Sheriff’s Office, the Marin Independent Journal first reported. Forbes, who previously spent nine years running the Port of San Francisco, faces felony charges following an incident at a local dock.

According to sheriff's deputies, Forbes allegedly boarded at least two vessels docked near a local restaurant, including a boat named the Lisa Marie.

A yacht captain, Bill Aubrey, was moored nearby and first noticed the disturbance when he heard a boat horn blaring at around 5:30 a.m., according to The San Francisco Standard. Aubrey said he had found Forbes inside the wheelhouse, where she looked at him and replied, “Good morning!” pleasantly, after he had boarded the vessel and told her to get off.

Investigators stated that she appeared to try to start one of the vessels by manipulating its switches and control levers. Authorities also noted that alcohol bottles on board the vessels had been opened and either consumed or poured out.

open image in gallery Elaine Forbes, the 53-year-old city manager of Sausalito, California, was arrested on Saturday after reportedly attempting to steal a yacht, fewer than three weeks after starting her role ( City of Sausalito )

Residents reported hearing a disturbance at the harbor early Saturday morning. Michael Lappert, a witness at the scene, told ABC7 San Francisco that a boat horn was sounded continuously for nearly two hours before police intervened.

“She was honking the horn, all these large yachts have a very loud horn because you’re out in the ocean and you gotta be heard so when you honk that thing I think most people have heard what those sound like,” Lappert said.

The arrest comes amid recent adjustments to Forbes’ employment status, as reported by the Los Angeles Times. On Thursday, the Sausalito City Council held a closed-door session and approved an immediate leave of absence for the city manager, though local officials declined to provide specific reasons for the decision at the time.

The Sausalito City Council voted unanimously in May to hire Forbes, according to a city news release. She officially started her job on July 1 with a base salary of $275,000, the LA Times reported.

“Elaine has proven to be a strong executive and it's important for this community to have a strong executive to help us sort through the many issues that we face,” Mayor Steven Woodside said at the time, according to the city news release.

“People from around the world save money and dream of coming to Sausalito for very good reasons. I'm incredibly honored to join this community,” Forbes said at the City Council meeting in which she was appointed.

Following her arrest, the City of Sausalito released a statement acknowledging the situation.

“This is a difficult development for our City staff and our community,” the statement read, adding that the municipality would withhold further comment due to the active criminal investigation.

A representative for Forbes’ family, public relations executive Sam Singer, issued a statement asking the public not to rush to judgment.

“Elaine is experiencing a mental health crisis,” Singer wrote. “As the facts become clearer and Elaine obtains legal and healthcare counsel in the coming hours and days, we hope people will respond with compassion, patience and respect for her and her family during an extraordinarily difficult time.”

Forbes remained in custody as of late Sunday afternoon, according to booking records.

News.title: A road trip through New England revealed the region’s vast cultural legacy
News.content:
