“It’s better to keep your mouth shut and appear stupid than to open it and remove all doubt,” my daughter Monica said, quoting a phrase often attributed to Mark Twain, as we stepped into the great novelist’s wonderfully eccentric Connecticut home on the second day of our father-daughter road trip through New England.

We had collected a black Subaru Forester from JFK airport and set off on an unusual 2,000-mile pilgrimage through the literary heart of New England. The idea was simple enough: visit the homes of America’s greatest writers, trace the landscapes that shaped them, and see whether genius leaves any trace in the places it once inhabited. It also doubled as a search for good food and long, uninterrupted conversations on the open road.

Mark Twain’s Hartford house is unlike any literary shrine. It looks as though a Mississippi steamboat has collided with a Victorian Gothic mansion and then been left to settle into something exuberantly American. Red brick, ornate chimneys and playful gables give it the air of a building that refuses to take itself too seriously.

open image in gallery Mark Twain’s house is defined by its red brick, ornate chimneys and playful gables ( Adams & Knight )

Inside, the guide referred to him exclusively as “Sam”, as though Samuel Clemens had simply stepped out for a moment. Monica happily discussed Huckleberry Finn while I quietly realised how much I had forgotten. Parents are supposed to know more than their children. Literary pilgrimages have a way of correcting such assumptions.

The house, built with the fortune of Twain’s heiress wife Olivia, was one of the first in America to have electricity and central heating. In 1881 they commissioned Louis Comfort Tiffany to transform the interiors into a theatrical blaze of embossed wallpaper, stencilled ceilings and deep reds and golds. It was spectacularly expensive and eventually helped drive Twain back onto the lecture circuit to repair the family finances.

Just a short walk away stands the more modest home of Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It is hard to imagine a more concentrated patch of American literary history. In the billiard room upstairs Twain wrote much of Huckleberry Finn, the novel often described as the foundation of modern American literature. Standing there, it was impossible not to see his journey – from riverboat pilot and penniless journalist to national figure – as a version of the American dream itself.

That first stop set the tone for everything that followed.

Over the next fortnight we crossed much of New England, tracing the lives of Herman Melville, Emily Dickinson, Louisa May Alcott, Edith Wharton, and the transcendentalists Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau. Between them came bass fishing, canoeing, long glacial lakes, strawberry fields, village greens and white-steepled churches. And everywhere, inevitably, lobster rolls and clam chowder.

The journey had been inspired partly by cinema. Paper Moon and On Golden Pond had long suggested that travel matters as much as arrival. (Fans of On Golden Pond should stay at the Von Horn Estate which is a country house hotel actually on the lake.) Our version was considerably calmer. The only recurring dispute was musical. I leaned towards Pink Floyd; Monica introduced Geese, whom she described as “the modern Bob Dylan”. We found as much agreement over books as playlists as we juggled from the Grateful Dead to Oasis.

open image in gallery Long hours in the car created a space for family conversations that ordinary life rarely allows ( The Independent )

As the miles accumulated, something subtle shifted. Long hours in the car created a space for conversation that ordinary life rarely allows. Books gave way to politics, music, careers and the strange pleasure of simply observing America unfold beyond the windscreen. New England itself became part of the dialogue: maple forests blazing green, empty highways, and towns where white clapboard houses still gathered around village greens as though time had paused.

New England contains both astonishing beauty and an extraordinary density of history. Here the first shots of the American Revolution were fired. Here a young nation began to imagine itself. Here writers would later find the landscapes that defined its literature. We stayed in a treehouse at The Winvian, a Connecticut country estate of cottages and seasonal delicacies in their restaurant. There were warnings to look out for wild bears, but the more obvious reality was charming bike rides in the nearby woods. Hotels are part of the American Dream.

By the time we left Hartford, the purpose of the journey had already begun to shift. We had set out in search of writers’ houses. What we were discovering instead was something less tangible but more enduring: the pleasure of uninterrupted time together, measured in miles rather than minutes.

open image in gallery The treehouse accommodation at at The Winvian in Connecticut ( The Independent )



In the Berkshires, Herman Melville’s house at Arrowhead sits quietly beneath the shadow of Mount Greylock. It is modest, almost understated, and all the more powerful for it. Here Moby Dick was written – an epic that failed on publication and would not find its audience for decades.

Looking out across the landscape, it was easy to imagine Melville wrestling with his creation while the world outside remained indifferent. Every literary house seemed to carry the same lesson: recognition and talent rarely arrive at the same time. A wonderful diversion from the driver's seat was staying at Prospect Berkshires on a lake with super stylish cabins and sauna huts, a zeitgeisty resort which leans into its stunning waterscape.

In Amherst, Emily Dickinson’s house offers a different kind of intensity. Small rooms, restrained light and a life deliberately narrowed to allow imagination to expand. She published almost nothing in her lifetime, yet her poetry now feels foundational to modern literature.

open image in gallery Emily Dickinson’s house has small rooms and restrained light ( Lynne Graves Photography )

A short drive away, Louisa May Alcott’s Orchard House tells another story entirely – one of family, imagination and quiet radicalism. Little Women was written here, drawing directly on domestic life yet reshaping it into something far more enduring. If Dickinson represents solitude, Alcott represents connection.

At Concord, Emerson and Thoreau’s world feels more conceptual than domestic. Walden Pond, in particular, where Thoreau lived in a wood hut for two years, two months and two days, resists cliché. It is smaller than expected, quieter, more ordinary – and yet it remains one of the most influential landscapes in American thought.

Here, nature was not scenery but philosophy. Simplicity was not aesthetic but moral. Walking the shoreline, it was easy to see how a new relationship between people and the natural world was once imagined here.

Between these lit-stops, New England revealed itself in less formal ways. Diners with creaking porches served eggs, hash browns and endless coffee. Coastal towns offered lobster rolls eaten at picnic tables overlooking grey Atlantic water. Lakes stretched long and still beneath impossible skies.

open image in gallery New England revealed itself to be at the forefront of Americana ( The Independent )

Standout in New Haven, Connecticut was a sessional family pizza restaurant Modern Apizza and an ocean side seafood restaurant Shell and Bones which has true piquancy and zest for utterly delicious seafood. Do not pass on the oysters. Another stunning food high spot was Woods Hill Table, a perfect local restaurant in Lexington, Massachusetts, with a sophisticated vibe.

New England has always been, we reminded ourselves, at the forefront of Americana: Jaws, The Stepford Wives, Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter and Arlo Guthrie’s plaintive anti- Vietnam tour de force “Alice’s Restaurant”.

At Lexington, Massachusetts, history becomes physical. On the village green where the first shots of the American Revolution were fired, Gerry Marrocco, a charismatic guide in period costume, recounted Paul Revere’s midnight ride, warning “the Brits are coming” with evangelical precision. It is easy to forget how recent this history is.

open image in gallery Guide Gerry Marrocco recounts Paul Revere’s midnight ride ( The Independent )

We stayed at the Inn at Hastings Park in Lexington, Massachusetts, which has been converted by its perfectionist owner Trisha Keneally to be a beacon of high American cuisine. It is on the old Boston coach road and worth any diversion.

Nearby, architecture tells a different story of reinvention. The Bauhaus-inspired house designed by Walter Gropius in Massachusetts feels like a clean break from the past – precise, modern, almost radical in its simplicity. New England is rarely one thing for long. Gropius’s house is enchanting and revolutionary.

Somewhere along these roads, another journey was taking place.

Monica and I shared driving, music and long stretches of silence punctuated by argument and laughter. We disagreed over playlists, agreed over food and slowly accumulated a shared map of references that belonged only to us.

The landscape itself seemed to encourage it. Maple-lined roads, sudden glimpses of lake, and towns with names that echoed American history – Concord, Salem, Lexington, New Haven – created a rhythm that made conversation inevitable. New ventures reflect the entrepreneurial as well as the indulgent.

The Lake Estate on Winnisquam is a £100m dream vacation spot created by Patty and Ed Rocco. It’s straight out of a Robert Redford idyll, Arcadian and ambitious. It seems to whisper from their side of the pond: eat your heart out Lake Como. What began as a literary pilgrimage had become something else, a reminder that time together is not an incidental benefit of travel, but its real purpose.

open image in gallery The beautiful Lake Estate on Winnisquam ( The Lake Estate on Winnisquam )

By the end of 2,000 miles, we had visited writers who shaped a nation’s imagination and landscapes that shaped theirs. But the most lasting impression was not literary at all. It was the sense that journeys rarely deliver what they promise– and often deliver something better instead.

We set out to understand America through its greatest writers. We ended up understanding something simpler: that travel changes not only what you see, but how you talk to the person beside you. Twain believed that travel is fatal to prejudice. He might also have added that it is remarkably good for families.

How to do it

Journeyscape offers a 14-day Classic New England package, including visits to Boston, Plymouth, Cape Cod and the islands, Acadia National Park, the Berkshires, New Hampshire Lakes, Connecticut, Woodstock, Portland and more. From £4,180pp per person, excluding flights.

News.title: Maine Democrats have found Graham Platner’s replacement. Can he win control of the Senate seat?
News.content:

After the implosion of Graham Platner, many Maine Democrats feared they were lost in the wilderness.

On Monday, it was clear: Troy Jackson is the man they believe will lead them out.

Jackson ended the weekend with the committed support of roughly two-thirds of the delegates in the state who are set to gather this coming weekend and formally nominate a replacement for Platner, whose Senate campaign ended after his support dissolved in the wake of a sexual assault allegation from an ex-girlfriend, which he denied. Three of his rivals for the nomination have already dropped out of the race.

Barring a major shake-up, he’s poised to walk into that convention as the overwhelming favorite.

Now, he has to win the general election against incumbent and Republican Susan Collins - and if he does it could help flip control of the entire Senate to Democrats.

open image in gallery Troy Jackson has now secured a majority of the delegates he'll need to become the nominee as the Democrat in the Maine race for Senate ( Reuters )

Jackson’s apparent victory was cheered on by members of the left-wing faction that has challenged numerous Democratic incumbents this cycle and sought to push the party towards a more aggressive populist, working-class centric platform: The Democratic Socialists of America. The DSA, which counts new Democratic primary victors Melat Kiros and Darializa Avila Chevalier among its members, endorsed Jackson as he ran for governor this year in a ranked-choice Democratic primary.

Jackson was defeated in that race, but with the rumors around Platner already swirling by the June primary, one of his supporters presciently suggested on Twitter: “I now want Troy Jackson to not win the governor race and finish 2nd so he’ll most likely be the backup Senate nominee if Platner drops out.”

A DSA-endorsed progressive and former state director for Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaign in 2016, Jackson’s victory represents a major coup for a progressive left wing that took a rhetorical battering in the press after Platner’s withdrawal.

Accusations of poor vetting and an insufficient focus on the voices of women in the party were leveled at not just Platner but his senior advisers and wider campaign staff, many of whom rallied behind Jackson after the collapse of the Platner bid.

open image in gallery Graham Platner’s collapse in Maine led to his supporters facing calls for their exclusion from party politics going forward ( Reuters )

Many of those same progressives were adamant, in the face of that criticism, that Maine voters had spoken clearly and chosen a progressive over the party establishment’s hand-picked candidate, incumbent Maine Gov. Janet Mills, to represent the party in November against Collins.

Many of Platner’s supporters argued that winning the seat in November would be an impossible and fruitless goal should national Democratic Party figures be allowed to select a candidate to run in his stead.

Barring something major happening, Jackson has seemingly lined up overwhelming support within the state part for his bid. His campaign is now well-positioned to scoop up the existing infrastructure already in place powering Platner’s impressive victory over Mills last month. The question is: Can he recapture the same voter enthusiasm that accompanied Platner’s win?

On paper, Jackson checks all the boxes. As his endorsements (which also included Bernie Sanders in his gubernatorial bid, and the Maine AFL-CIO) would suggest, Jackson is a dyed-in-the-wool progressive, supporting Medicare for All, the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and an end to American support of Israel’s assault on Gaza, which he’s referred to as a genocide.

Like Platner, he also hails from a working-class background, having previously worked as a logger before joining Maine’s state senate, and later serving as its majority leader.

Whether Jackson can translate his similarities into the same momentum against Collins is an open question, though, as he came in third place in the Maine gubernatorial primary this year despite his list of powerful endorsements. Supporters argued that he built an impressive ground game and fared well against politicians with better name recognition, but some are still skeptical about his path forward.

Some fans of Platner and other Democratic observers questioned whether Jackson had the same charisma that led Platner to pack town hall events to capacity for months ahead of his primary victory in June.

open image in gallery Susan Collins has kept out of the discussions over the replacement for Graham Platner, but is expected to aggressively defend her seat against Jackson ( Getty )

Collins, meanwhile, has nearly faded into the background amid her onetime opponent’s self-destruction.

Much as the Trump campaign did in 2024, Collins’s campaign has largely stayed out of the fray as Democrats rushed to replace Platner — the incumbent senator, 73, is taking a more passive approach to campaigning as she holds on to advantages in name recognition, her reputation as a moderate in the Senate and a massive war chest supported by Senate GOP leadership which is waiting to flood the airwaves with more than $100 million in reserved advertising space through November.

The reality for Jackson is stark: His quick collection of the delegates necessary to win the Senate nomination was only the first battle he’ll face, with a much tougher one coming down the pipes.

He’s stepping into a race where the comparisons to Kamala Harris’s doomed 2024 bid are widely apparent, banking on the notion that a unified Democratic Party and dissatisfaction for the Trump administration and the Republican Congress will be enough to take a jump-started campaign over the finish line against potentially the hardest target for Democrats to beat of this entire cycle.

The federal investigation into a multi-state outbreak of the diarrhea-causing infection cyclosporiasis got even more confusing Monday.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration confirmed a Taylor Farms lettuce recall related to the outbreak, despite the agency announcing a “false positive test.”

“It’s important to note that the reevaluation of the sample does not alter the data supporting the outbreak advisory that prompted the current voluntary recall,” Donald Prater, the Acting Deputy Commissioner for Food, said Monday. “False positives are not common.”

The initial detection of the cyclospora parasite that causes the disease was traced to shredded iceberg lettuce from central Mexico. The FDA had informed Taylor Farms of that detection Saturday and the California company issued a voluntary recall of all affected lettuce.

On Sunday, the FDA said the test “should be considered a false positive,” and Taylor Farms said the FDA had “apologized.” On Monday, the FDA denied apologizing to Taylor Farms.

open image in gallery The FDA denied apologizing to Taylor Farms after the health agency linked the cyclospora parasite to a lettuce sample from the California company. The FDA said it was a 'false positive' ( Getty Images )

The Independent has asked Taylor Farms for comment.

In an X post Monday, the FDA also wrote: “To clarify, this false-positive lab sample DOES NOT change the basis for FDA’s ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.”

There are currently no confirmed positive product samples for cyclospora from Taylor Farms or other companies.

Cases of cyclosporiasis — which can cause “explosive” diarrhea — have risen sharply across the country in recent weeks, with health officials unable to identify a definitive source.

Federal officials had previously said fast-food chain Taco Bell — which stopped serving lettuce at some Michigan locations — was under investigation, resulting in at least one lawsuit.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also said Saturday that the outbreak had been linked to iceberg lettuce in five states.

The CDC is investigating nearly 7,000 confirmed and suspected cases nationwide as of July 13. By comparison, this time last year, there were less than 250 cases, according to The Hill.

State data, however, points to an even broader outbreak, with Michigan alone reporting more than 5,000 cases, alongside over 500 in New York and more than 300 in Illinois.

Part of the reason for the discrepancy between federal and state data is that states may report both confirmed and probable cases, while the CDC does not include unconfirmed cases in its tally.

Federal health officials have also come under scrutiny after the CDC removed cyclospora from a key foodborne illness monitoring program known as FoodNet last summer.

Dan Jernigan, former head of the CDC’s Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, downplayed the move’s immediate impact, telling The Washington Post that excluding cyclospora from FoodNet likely did little to hinder the current response.

open image in gallery The illness is caused by consumption of the cyclospora parasite , and symptoms can take over two weeks to manifest, officials say.

But other public health experts argue the issue runs deeper. They pointed to Trump administration staffing and funding cuts that have slowed the agency’s ability to detect and contain outbreaks.

“The response is being hampered by the loss of specialized staff and the loss of hands-on-deck needed to identify the source of the outbreaks,” Dr. Joel Barratt, who previously led a federal lab focused on parasitic diseases, told CNN.

Though rarely life-threatening, cyclosporiasis can lead to a nasty array of symptoms, including what officials describe as “explosive bowel movements,” as well as fatigue, low-grade fever, nausea and vomiting. Most cases resolve without treatment, though people experiencing symptoms are encouraged to seek medical attention, according to the CDC.

The illness, spread through food or water contaminated with fecal matter, can take more than two weeks to manifest symptoms — complicating efforts to trace its origins.

While infections occur year-round, particularly during the summer months, the latest outbreak appears unusually large. According to CNBC, only a handful of outbreaks over the past two decades have surpassed 1,000 reported cases, placing the current surge among the more significant in recent memory. Past outbreaks have been linked to contaminated produce, including cilantro and basil.

To reduce risk, public health experts recommend a battery of precautions: thoroughly washing hands with soap before handling produce, scrubbing fruits and vegetables, peeling outer layers when possible and cooking them where feasible. Bananas, kiwis, avocados and potatoes are considered safer bets for those worried about the illness.

It’s unclear when exactly consumers can expect the current outbreak to subside.

“What's different this year is the unusually high number of cases and the fact that investigators still haven't identified a specific source," Dr. Suraj Saggar, chief of infectious diseases at Holy Name Medical Center in New Jersey, told USA Today.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

News.title: How to have the perfect holiday in France’s gastronomic capital
News.content:
Calling all bon vivants. This is your city. Within seconds of tucking into a traditional andouillette (tripe sausage) or modern vegetarian cuisine in a jam-packed bistro, admiring fine art in a Renaissance abbey, or getting delightfully lost in a traboule (secret passageway) used by 19th-century silk weavers, you’ll quickly realise that Lyon is a city that knows how to live well.

Enthralling, cinematic and richly storied, after living here for 10 years, I still find myself being surprised by a walled garden I never knew, a fresque (wall mural) suddenly popping up on a riverfront wall, a new museum or river boat route.

Street-smart Romans first spotted the city’s extraordinary topography, founding Lugdunum (Lyon’s predecessor) in 43BC on the sunny slopes of Fourvière. And to this day, this basilica-crowned hill above Lyon’s quaint Unesco-listed Old Town (Vieux Lyon) is the perfect perch for clocking the mighty Rhône and Saône rivers that wend their way so gracefully through the centre.

The city’s quays, landscaped with peaceful water gardens and floating bars, buzz night and day – while culture lovers can explore a bounty of museums. Then there’s the gastronomy: among France’s finest, thanks to the unfaltering creativity and sass of city chefs, both past and present.

News.title: The 16 best things to do in Lyon
News.content:
Few dedicated foodies make the pilgrimage to Lyon without dining once chez Paul Bocuse, be it at the late chef’s mythical, out-of-town gastronomic temple in Collonges-au-Mont d’Or (which lost one of its three stars in 2020, having held three since 1965) or at the more affordable Comptoir Paul Bocuse inside landmark covered market Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse. Across the street, admire a larger-than-life portrait of the iconic chef, frescoed onto the side of a building. Inside the market, the moules glacées (cold mussel ‘soup’) at oyster and shellfish specialist Maison Merle and a gooey round of Saint Marcellin cheese from Fromagerie La Mère Richard are other local legends. Avoid buying fruit and veg here unless you have to – weekly outdoor food markets elsewhere in the city are cheaper.

To sample future talent in the Lyonnais kitchen, mingle with students over lunch, dinner or drinks and live music at La Commune – an innovative food court that hosts chefs aspiring to open their own restaurant in Lyon. Resident chefs cook up a storm at La Commune for maximum six months, meaning an ever-changing rollcall of epicurean excitement at this unique culinary incubator.

To extend the experience further afield, consider a road trip along a section of the Vallée de la Gastronomie, stretching 620km (385 miles). In Lyon, the gourmet route delves into the secrets behind chef Joseph Viola’s award-winning duck foie gras and sweetbread pâté en croûte (think French-posh pork pie) and the city’s distinctive offal-based bouchon (Lyonnais bistro) cuisine.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi shows true colours with emotional message after World Cup final loss
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi shows true colours with emotional message after World Cup final loss

Argentina came up short in their bid to win back-to-back World Cups and their captain and talisman Lionel Messi has broken his silence following the defeat to Spain

View 2 Images Lionel Messi has spoken after Argentina's World Cup final loss (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

Lionel Messi has penned an open letter to Argentina supporters following their unsuccessful bid to become just the third team in history to win successive World Cups.

‌



Messi and Co went into Sunday's final with Spain as the defending champions after victory in Qatar back in 2022. But Argentina were very much second best against Luis de la Fuente's side, who dominated from start to finish. Ferran Torres plundered the only goal of the game in extra-time after Enzo Fernandez had been sent off for a moment of madness in the final minutes of regulation time.

‌



At 39 years of age, there is every chance Sunday's final in New Jersey was Messi's final World Cup appearance.

‌



The seven-time Ballon d'Or winner broke down after the game when he was serenaded by Argentina fans. Nearly 24 hours later, he has taken to social media to speak about the pain of said defeat, while also congratulating Spain on their win.

World Cup final LIVE: FIFA investigation launched after disgraceful Argentina throw punches at Spain stars READ MORE :

UEFA's five major issues with FIFA World Cup as president snub highlights divide READ MORE :

“The pain is immense, it will take time for this wound to heal. But I also choose to hold on to all the good things, all matches we turned around by giving everything and moments that will remain in our memories forever.

“I will always remember the support of an entire country that, together with the work and effort of this group, brought us back once again among the best teams in the world.

‌



“Today, it is difficult to appreciate what we achieved… but this group has really reached two consecutive World Cup finals. Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and every message. Once again, we managed to come together as a country and stand united, sharing the immense pride of being Argentine.

View 2 Images Messi was devastated after the final whistle (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

“I also want to congratulate Spain on winning World Cup.”

‌



The aftermath of the World Cup final was marred by ugly scenes as Nahuel Molina and Leandro Paredes both lashed out at opponents.

Wayne Rooney condemned their actions, saying: “Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this with Argentina before.

“It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round. That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them.”

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in
Sports.content:
It has been confirmed that Kevin Keegan, the Newcastle and Liverpool legend, has sadly died at the age of 75 after a battle with cancer

Kevin Keegan has sadly passed away at the age of 75 following a battle with cancer, his family have announced.

It was confirmed back in January that the legendary former Newcastle manager was being treated for cancer, with Keegan himself revealing the disease was at stage four last month during an appearance at a fan event.

A statement released by Keegan's family on Monday afternoon read: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

"Kevin, a double Ballon D’or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. "This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan was real-life Roy of the Rovers star who lived and breathed football
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan was real-life Roy of the Rovers star who lived and breathed football

Kevin Keegan was one of English football's all-time greats and the sport will never be the same after the desperately sad news of his death at the age of 75

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

After such a memorable England World Cup campaign, the news about Kevin Keegan feels particularly sad.

‌



King Kev will go down as one of the greatest players England has ever produced and his international career - both as player and manager - was unforgettable.

‌



Keegan was a two-time Ballon D’Or winner, a trailblazer after he joined Hamburg, hugely successful with Liverpool and Newcastle. He was a real Roy of the Rovers player who gave absolutely everything on the pitch and a household name thanks to his starring role on the 1970s TV show Superstars.

‌



He was an icon who was back page gold because of his huge ability, his personality and he was never short of opinion which is another reason we loved him quite apart from his football ability.

Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family, fans and former players pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in READ MORE :

There was the often forgotten bust-up with the late Sir Bobby Robson which ended his England career prematurely - and also saw him quit as a player at Newcastle aged 33.

Keegan quit as England manager in the toilets at Wembley in October 2000 after losing to Germany as he admitted he fell short of what was needed to manage his beloved country. That hurt him so much and, realistically, it scarred him because he scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England in an international career which lasted ten years from 1972 until 1982.

‌



Keegan deserved a better platform than England gave him. They did not qualify for the 1974 or 1978 World Cups when Keegan was among the best players in the world.

By 1982, Keegan was in his 30s but went to the World Cup even though he had a bad back. He drove from Spain to Germany in secret to get treatment with a trusted specialist. As England were chasing a game - they needed a result against Spain - they threw on Keegan and Trevor Brooking to search for a late winner. Keegan missed a header and little did he know then that would signal the end.

View 3 Images Keegan represented England over 60 times (Image: Peter Robinson/EMPICS Sport/PA Wire)

‌



Keegan was dropped by Robson after he took charge - but was furious after finding out second hand from then Newcastle boss Arthur Cox who heard it on the radio. “I’m finished with England. I’ll never kick a ball for my country again,” Keegan ranted after hearing the news. And his retirement from England duty hastened the end of his playing career.

It is a crying shame we never saw Keegan at his peak on the biggest stage because he deserved it. England will always be a source of regret.

Let’s not forget here that, after his amazing stint in charge at Newcastle and working wonders at Fulham, there was huge public clamour for him to be England boss. So the revisionism about his shortcomings - he was a motivator but a limited tactician - must be put into context. We all wanted him because we loved King Kev.

‌



Keegan’s relationship with the press was tested particularly with England. He hated criticism. I remember seeing him for an interview during that ill-fated reign and it quickly turned into an interrogation. Him questioning me rather than the other way round.

View 3 Images Keegan managed England for almost two years (Image: PA)

He was angry, bitter and upset at the criticism. What did I think? Was it fair? Over the top? Say the wrong thing and the interview was not going to happen. It did go ahead because fundamentally he was a nice man. But he really cared and was so sensitive.

‌



I remember seeing him in Doha years later. We’d watched some football. He was still wary. He’d had enough of us press lot. But we started chatting football - and he just forgot what I did.

He couldn’t help himself. If anyone shared his passion and love of the game then he’d just get carried away and lose himself all over again. We talked and talked.

That was the thing with Keegan. His love of football was pure. He was one of the most passionate people I’ve ever met. And that mix made him King Kev.

Sports.title: UEFA's five major issues with FIFA World Cup as president snub highlights divide
Sports.content:
UEFA's five major issues with FIFA World Cup as president snub highlights divide

UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin was not in attendance for Sunday's World Cup final after criticising the decision to defer a ban for the United States striker Folarin Balogun

View 2 Images UEFA president Alexander Ceferin (L) did not attend the World Cup final (Image: Masashi Hara, Getty Images)

The president of UEFA, Aleksander Ceferin, decided to boycott the World Cup final following a breakdown in relations between the organisation and FIFA.

‌



While the President of the United States, Donald Trump and a number of other high-profile figures attended Sunday's showpiece final, which Spain won 1-0, in New Jersey, Ceferin was absent despite the fact he is a FIFA vice-president. And the circumstances behind the 58-year-old's decision not to attend are now starting to emerge.

‌



As per a new report from The Times, Ceferin's absence was a byproduct of the Folarin Balogun saga, which saw FIFA defer a ban for the United States striker after he was sent off.

‌



Trump himself boasted that he had been in touch with Gianni Infantino, the president of FIFA, to recommend the striker's soft red card be reviewed.

World Cup final LIVE: FIFA investigation launched after disgraceful Argentina throw punches at Spain stars READ MORE :

Balogun was subsequently cleared to play in the United States' pivotal round of 16 meeting with Belgium, who record an emphatic 4-1 win. Their stars then mocked Trump with their post-match celebrations, mimicking the President's dance moves.

UEFA condemned the decision to defer Balogun's ban at the time, saying it was “unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable” and that FIFA had “crossed a red line” by choosing to do so.

‌



Political interference is not the only gripe UEFA is said to have with FIFA around the World Cup, though, with Ceferin criticising the astronomical cost of tickets back in May. They also stepped in to appoint Omar Artan, the Somalian referee who was prevented from entering the United States, for the Super Cup final between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa in August.

View 2 Images Donald Trump revealed he had urged Gianni Infantino to review Folarin Balogun's red card, sparking a World Cup scandal (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

There are also concerns within UEFA regarding some of the rule changes that were pushed through by FIFA ahead of the World Cup and have already confirmed they will not follow their lead in instructing referees to send off players who speak to an opponent while covering their mouth, among other new rules.

‌



Moving forward, UEFA are against proposals to expand the World Cup to a staggering 64 teams. That would represent another significant increase to the teams involved at the tournament, with the 2026 edition being the first to feature 48 teams rather than 32.

Speaking back in April, Ceferin said: "This proposal was maybe even more surprising for me than you.

"I think it is a bad idea."

Sports.title: 'I met my boyhood hero Kevin Keegan - I will never forget his honesty and sense of humour'
Sports.content:
They say that you should never meet your heroes.

Kevin Keegan, a legend of the game and a hero to millions, was the exception to that rule.

Growing up on Tyneside, he was my idol at school because of his exploits with Liverpool, England, Hamburg and then of course my beloved Newcastle United, where he was a player and then manager.

As a kid with black curly hair, I bought a full England kit and the red, white and blue wristbands worn by my hero back in the 1970s and 80s, when I was still at school.

‌



Keegan was ahead of his time, the first star of the modern era, promoting Brut on TV and competing on BBC's 'Superstars'.

When I started working for the Mirror in 1993, I met him when he managed England, and later when he was in club football at Fulham.

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan with his old Liverpool team mate, the late, great Ray Clemence (Image: Bob Thomas Sports Photography via Getty Images)

Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75 READ MORE :

Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in READ MORE :

Keegan made a point of coming to meet George Cohen when I accompanied the 1966 hero to his old club to discuss the sale of Cohen's World Cup medal.

‌



Fulham bought it for £80,000 and displayed it at the ground where Cohen had played with such distinction.

Keegan took care of George that day, making us both feel welcome while discussing playing for England and his memories of 1966.

I was always struck by his honesty, his friendliness even when times were hard - and his sense of humour.

I met 'King Kev', as he was known on Tyneside, for the last time there for the unveiling of Alan Shearer's statue in 2016.

‌



View 4 Images Kevin Keegan receives his OBE on November 9, 1982 (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

He gave a friendly hello, recognising me from our previous meetings and recalling his time with Shearer.

He had signed the Premier League's all-time top scorer for a then world-record £15m while he was manager.

Surrounded by fans at the unveiling, he never refused an autograph request, and was perfectly at ease with the public.

‌



In fact, he was in his element with supporters, talking about the game he loved.

Keegan had the common touch, which is why he remained such a hugely popular figure throughout his career, even when his stint as England boss came to an untimely end.

In his last public appearance on Tyneside, on May 31 at the New Tyne Theatre, he spoke openly of his cancer diagnosis with the courage which he had displayed throughout his playing career.

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan in 1982, when he played for England at the World Cup (Image: Bob Thomas Sports Photography via Getty Images)

‌



He had joked with his surgeon, a Liverpool fan, that he 'would never walk alone'.

No truer words were spoken; Kevin Keegan was loved by fans everywhere he went and never walked alone.

He told that last audience in Newcastle that he did not want a statue because he wanted to go back to St James' Park to see the supporters one last time.

Tragically, he was cruelly robbed of that return.

‌



But there may be a statue to him yet.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick issues next Man Utd transfer demand as Premier League stars targeted
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick issues next Man Utd transfer demand as Premier League stars targeted

Manchester United have already been busy in the transfer market ahead of Michael Carrick’s first summer at the helm and the Red Devils boss is clear on what he wants next

View 2 Images Michael Carrick wants more signings at Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

Michael Carrick remains determined to sign ANOTHER midfielder for Manchester United this summer. The Red Devils have already added to their options in the heart of the pitch over the past few weeks.

‌



Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos have arrived for a combined £85m from Aston Villa and Chelsea respectively. But it appears that Carrick is not totally satisfied yet.

‌



According to The Guardian, the United boss is still intent on signing a third midfielder to add to his options even further following the departuer of Casemiro. It remains to be seen who that man will be but it is unlikely to be be Atlanta’s Ederson.

‌



The Red Devils had agreed a deal for the Brazilian, only to pull the plug on a move. Away from midfield, United are also keen on adding to their defensive options, with a left-back a priority.

Every Premier League summer transfer as Man Utd, Arsenal and Liverpool splash the cash READ MORE :

Man Utd land £8m teenage star from Premier League rivals as they repeat transfer trick READ MORE :

Tyrell Malacia left the club at the end of his contract at the end of last season, leaving United needing more back-up. A couple of Premier League options have already been identified ahead of a potential move.

Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Fulham star Antonee Robinson are among those. Hall has impressed at St James’ Park since his move from Chelsea.

‌



But having lost Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon this summer, Newcastle will not be keen on selling another key player. He remains under contract until 2029.

Robinson in the meantime has shone for Fulham over recent campaigns but being 29, is slightly older than United’s preferred profile.

View 2 Images Man United are interested in a deal for Lewis Hall (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Speaking after United’s opening pre-season defeat against Wrexham, Carrick was full of his praise for one of his summer arrivals. He said: "There’s loads of little positives to take from the game. I thought Andrey and Mason [Mount] did some really good things and connected really well. I could see some positives there.

"[At the] top end of the pitch, just because it is a week in, those sharp little movements and bright moments that you are looking for, they come as you progress through the weeks of training. That is what it is. There were good signs from Andrey on his first one, he’s getting in the rhythm and feel of it again, so it was good to see him in a red shirt.”

Carrick added: "As I said before the game, the boys have only been back together for 10 days or so. It was just about getting through today, looking for some positives, looking for some good things and knowing that it wasn’t going to be perfect.

Article continues below

"That is only natural for the first one. I think the most important thing is that everyone came through it in good shape. No injuries, so we can move on and take the next step next week.”

Sports.title: Brundle: The Hamilton-Russell penalty call and Antonelli's class of one
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

The Kimi Antonelli show, also known as the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix, took place in remarkably sunny and dry conditions throughout, if occasionally interrupted by an actual safety car deployment on lap one to clear a beached car, and a few more virtual safety cars to clear up high-tech litter from the racing surface.

The Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps has been developed and polished beautifully in almost every respect, even if in time-honoured fashion getting into and moving around the venue seems to have new systems and rules every day. To be fair, there is a huge area and a great many fans to be controlled.

As usual I was out and about trackside on Friday during practice and the cars looked very fast and impressive in front of the numerous grandstands. I've been racing here for 45 years, and I couldn't quite believe my eyes on the scale of the crowd.

It was enjoyable to watch the drivers jockey an excess of power over grip through medium-speed chicane exits, but like Silverstone there was a hidden story alongside the trackside 'wow', and the drivers were very restrained through the event not to complain too much about it.

We long ago lost Eau Rouge and Raidillon as corners to refined high-downforce cars with grippy tyres and a manicured racetrack, meaning from the turn one La Source hairpin to the long haul up to the turn five Les Combes chicane is effectively a straight.

Image: Kimi Antonelli rounds La Source during the race

But with the need to charge the hybrid batteries on this fast track, the longest on the calendar, just as with Copse, Becketts, and Stowe at Silverstone, as the engine is used to charge those batteries the arrival speeds into corners like Pouhon at Spa are dulled such that the corner effectively becomes a bendy straight too.

On such circuits we have lost the driver-defining, and thrilling, high-speed corners. It was the same in Suzuka.

Luckily in Budapest this weekend it will not be a problem at all, and normal service will be resumed, although there are no high-speed corners worth their name.

We have known for a while about these issues, and they are being addressed where possible for 2027 and again in 2028, but the last two races have unequivocally confirmed that we need a major power unit philosophy change much sooner than later.

There were always going to be teething problems reliability-wise but as we hurtle towards the summer break the words 'deployment issues' and 'no battery' are rather too prominent.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle takes you behind the scenes to show you how he prepares for his iconic Sunday 'Grid Walk'!

Russell's Mercedes problems and the 'racing incident' debate

George Russell is clearly not a direct descendant of the Alessandro Volta, Michael Faraday, Thomas Edison or Nikola Tesla families because he never seems to have the right battery power at the moment.

Whether that is missing straight-line speed compared to his team-mate Antonelli in qualifying, for whatever mystery reasons, or climbing the hill to turn five on the opening lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Drama at the start of the Belgium GP as George Russell's title hopes take a huge blow.

Antonelli got away well at the start and Verstappen's Red Bull launched unusually nicely too. But Max appeared to pull a cunning move by powering past before Eau Rouge at the bottom of the hill, but his post-race comments say that his car had too much battery deployment suggesting he had nothing to do with that cunning plan…

Both Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell started the race with less battery charge than needed, and it particularly hurt Russell on the long climb to the critical turn five braking point, and he was mugged by three cars including Lewis Hamilton.

George braked impressively late trying to make up for his poor arrival speed and was on the outside of Lewis, leaving racing room. Lewis, close behind Max, slid a little wide and contacted George who spun into retirement, and at the same time taking a massive hit to his championship comeback chances.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

More referee leeway is given on the first lap with the pack inevitably in close company along with full fuel and sub-optimal brake and tyre temperatures. I called it a racing incident in commentary, unless the stewards were satisfied that Lewis had lost control of his car, which didn't appear to be the case.

George recovered to the pits by scooter and called it a racing incident whilst far more distraught about his ongoing power issues.

Ferrari called it a racing incident, I guess you could say they would, and most people I know agreed. But with whatever extra information the stewards had they applied a five-second penalty mitigated down from the standard 10 seconds. It perhaps cost Lewis a podium but that's speculative.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oscar Piastri takes to his McLaren team radio to complain about contact with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Later in the race, Charles Leclerc would squeeze Oscar Piastri in the T5 braking zone and there was contact which damaged Piastri's aero parts, to an extent. For me this was a clear movement in the braking zone which can mean anything from a warning flag to a full pit-lane drive through penalty in the guidelines.

The stewards, though, decided it was about relative front axle positions and who had the right to the corner. Leclerc's telling reaction when it was played out in the cooldown room tells us everything we need to know on that one.

The pit stops that did - and didn't - make the difference

Hamilton had a torrid weekend with an accident in practice, the five-second penalty with Russell, and nearly running one of his mechanics over in the pit stop through no fault of his own. That incident attracted a team fine rather than a race penalty and so Lewis was perhaps relieved to finish fourth, probably for the first time in his life.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Ferrari pit crew were unable to tweak Lewis Hamilton's front wing level as the British driver knocked over a mechanic after being given the green light.

Piastri drove a spirited race to fifth despite his car damage although he lacked the same pace, which threatened to make the podium early on, after he swapped onto the hard compound tyres on lap 20 of 44.

Lando Norris drove beautifully all weekend but had to start 13th due to needing power unit control electronics beyond the allowance in the regulations, which is designed to keep costs down so that wealthy teams can't just throw new parts at the car every weekend.

Curiously McLaren chose not to use the virtual safety cars, or indeed a straightforward pit stop, until Lando eventually pitted on lap 30 to get rid of his starting hard-compound tyres. This left him with too much to do to catch Isack Hadjar who started his Red Bull from the back row of the grid, also due to numerous power unit penalties, to finish an impressive sixth.

Red Bull pitted Hadjar on lap one, and then again on lap two to cycle through the mandatory use of two different tyre compounds under cover of the Russell safety car, and then again under a virtual safety car on lap 20. Nicely done.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes Kimi Antonelli discusses his Belgian GP win and admits he's in a 'good position' after opening up a 45-point gap in the drivers' standings.

That same lap 20 VSC played out beautifully for Leclerc in his Ferrari as the time loss is only around 11 seconds when your rivals are lapping at reduced speed. Antonelli had pitted on lap 18 under full green conditions as Mercedes were covering off Red Bull's pit stop for Verstappen on lap 17.

Through all this Leclerc leapfrogged the pair of them and was now effectively leading, albeit with the yet-to-stop Norris ahead of him. Antonelli would hunt him down but perhaps not as rapidly as expected, Leclerc was driving beautifully.

'What a difference a year makes'

Eventually, and frankly inevitably given his speed throughout the event, the Italian teenager would take the lead, but Leclerc still wouldn't give up, and he finished second just two seconds adrift.

Verstappen would finish a solid third, Leclerc's safety car good fortune denied him a shot at second.

The final points went to Gabriel Bortoleto and Audi in eighth, Arvid Lindblad and Racing Bulls in ninth, and Franco Colapinto for Alpine in 10th. The safety cars played a role for and against throughout.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard Alpine's Franco Colapinto as he pulls off an incredible double overtake on Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson at the Belgian GP.

What a difference a year makes. Antonelli never ran higher than 14th on his F1 debut here last year, but he was in a class of one this season.

Mercedes are on fire too, with their eighth victory of the season, which is one more than they won over the last four 'ground effect era' seasons combined. That combination will take some stopping from winning both championships in fine style.

Sports.title: 'He's got to get an answer!' - Russell 'knocked down' by mystery car problems
Sports.content:
George Russell says he has been "knocked down" but will "get back up" after the latest setbacks to his world championship challenge at the Belgian Grand Prix

Having cut his title deficit to Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli from 68 points to just 25 points over the previous three rounds, benefitting from two reliability problems on the Italian's car, Russell dropped 50 points behind on Sunday at Spa-Francorchamps when his race lasted just five corners before a collision with Lewis Hamilton.

But Russell's post-race frustration at his early exit, and difficult race weekend as a whole, was aimed not at his former team-mate but instead towards weekend-long power issues on his Mercedes car that he said had left him vulnerable to such an incident on the first lap.

The Briton has been searching for stronger form for several months amid a failure to match Antonelli's pace on a consistent basis but, in a social media post on Monday, he resolved to keep fighting on in the championship chase.

"Knocked down, we get back up," Russell wrote.

"No matter how many times.

"So many tough moments this year but I will not stop fighting,"

Wolff explains Russell's power problems

While Mercedes are still working to get to the bottom of the mysterious straight-line speed issues afflicting Russell's car, team principal Toto Wolff explained after Sunday's race how two separate problems contributed to the Briton's difficult weekend.

On the first deployment issue in the sessions before race day - which Russell had initially hoped would be corrected by driving style changes but was not the case - Wolff said this had compromised the Briton's speed in the final sector of the long Spa-Francorchamps lap relative to Antonelli.

"The power units are so complex, in the way you harvest, the way you deploy, the interaction from the driver," said Wolff of 2026's new engines which feature a near 50-50 split between electrical and traditional internal combustion output.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

"We have a super strong package - championship-winning chassis and power unit, but we're still trying to give it our best to fix the reliability issue.

"And sometimes a new regulation (irregularity) happens. With George, over the weekend, there was definitely something on the engine that we have identified that meant he only had less energy to deploy into Turn 18 - that was the most visible.

"It's good that we spotted it here because in Budapest, which is not energy starved, it would have been more difficult to identify.

"But it still doesn't make it better for him. And that probably accounted for half the gap or a little bit more that he had to Kimi."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard with George Russell as he crashes out of the Belgian GP after contact with Lewis Hamilton.

All eight of the grid's Mercedes-powered cars were then hampered by a separate and "new" boost problem out of Turn One at the start of Sunday's race.

Andrew Shovlin, the team's trackside engineering director, said Russell's problems on lap one had been "more extreme" and so he was an effective sitting duck on the Kemmel Straight as the two Ferraris moved past him, with the Briton eventually spun into instant retirement at Les Combes due to contact with Hamilton.

Wolff added: "All Mercedes engines had a lack of energy out of Turn One, so that wasn't only George. It affected him more than Kimi, but also Kimi had that issue to a certain degree.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell pointed to an issue with the car as a reason for his collision with Lewis Hamilton during the Belgian GP.

"And that meant that he didn't come out at the end of the straight in P3, but P5.

"So, he lost his two positions, and then obviously the accident with Lewis."

'He's got to get an answer' - what now for Russell heading to Hungary?

Speaking during Sky Sports F1's post-race show in Belgium, Karun Chandhok suggested that Russell would want concrete engineering explanations before this weekend's race in Hungary as to what exactly was causing the confusing straight-line speed problems.

"I think he's got to go back and try to get clear answers from an engineering sense," said Chandhok.

"We've all had conversations this weekend with people from Mercedes, and the sense we're getting is that they don't have a clear answer.

"They've got to go back, they've got to look at the data, have a couple of days to digest it between now and Budapest, because he can't go on to the next race weekend with a four-tenth deficit in straight-line speed.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch all of George Russell’s unlucky moments so far this 2026 Formula 1 season.

"You're taking a pencil to a sword fight, so there's no point doing that. He's got to get an answer, and if it means they have to change the power unit and take a penalty, then maybe they have to do that to try to clear away this doubt.

"Because as a racing driver, arriving at a weekend having doubt in the package or the car you've got and whether you've got a fair fight, is an awful place to be. He will be looking for clear engineering-led answers, I think."

Russell said in interviews after the race that, having also run into technical issues earlier in the season most notably in China and, when leading, in Canada, he was now "numb to the disappointment".

Asked how he could keep his driver's spirits up, Wolff said: "You have to understand that the driver is very emotional when these situations happen. But on the other side, as a Formula 1 driver, you're part of a very elite group.

"I think it's quite an honour to drive a Mercedes. Sometimes we let ourselves down. And it's just the driver, but it's also us.

"It's valuable constructor points that we lose in our fight against Ferrari. So, I hope the numb feeling goes away. We will try to help to recreate optimism and positivity."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

Wolff, who has known the 28-year-old Russell for over a decade, added: "I think all of the drivers, at least the ones that I have worked with, when they have difficult spells, and it happens to any sports person, you need to find a way of motivating or building up.

"George has his way, and I'm definitely trying to do that. I've known him for such a long time, I understand the frustrations, and the team is 100 per cent there."

Sports.title: Did DeChambeau attempt to involve Trump in Open rules controversy?
Sports.content:
Bryson DeChambeau has been accused of wanting to involve United States President Donald Trump during his rules controversy at The Open, multiple media reports have claimed.

The two-time major winner was handed a two-shot penalty late on Friday night after officials reviewed footage and decided he had improved the area of his backswing by flattening down some long grass on Royal Birkdale's fifth hole.

Multiple reports claim DeChambeau allegedly threatened to call Trump during lengthy discussions with the R&A regarding the penalty, which dropped him from second place and one off the lead on Friday to tied-fifth and three back.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Scottie Scheffler defended Ryder Cup teammate DeChambeau after he was given a two-shot penalty

Sky Sports News has contacted the R&A, the White House press office and DeChambeau's management team for comment.

DeChambeau is a friend of Trump, serving on the President's council on sports, fitness and nutrition, making his last White House appearance in May, and has played golf with him.

Trump asked football's world governing body FIFA to review the red card shown to US forward Folarin Balogun during the World Cup, with the player's one-match ban subsequently being suspended, and DeChambeau wanted a similar intervention.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sam Burns said that 'there was not enough evidence' to penalise DeChambeau

While the call did not take place at the time, it is not known whether DeChambeau made contact privately, but on Saturday R&A chief executive Mark Darbon was asked whether the President had been in touch.

"No, I have not received a call from President Trump," he told BBC Sport. "Irrespective of which player this affected, it is the same decision - from a rules perspective it was clear cut."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brandel Chamblee and Paul McGinley were critical of DeChambeau's actions in the rough on the fifth hole

Sky Sports News understands that DeChambeau visited Darbon in the championship office after his third round on Saturday, where his request to gain possession of his scorecard from the previous day was declined.

The R&A has also yet to comment on that issue. DeChambeau is next scheduled to feature at the LIV Golf League event in England, beginning at JCB Golf and Country Club on Thursday, although he is not listed for any pre-tournament media.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Weir delves into why DeChambeau was given a two-shot penalty

'A lot of ups and downs' - DeChambeau reflects on challenging week

DeChambeau making it through to the weekend ended a run of three consecutive major missed cuts and avoided the 'Bryson Slam' of missing all four in a season, eventually ending tied-14th and six strokes behind Ryan Fox.

The American refused to speak to the waiting media for the eighth successive major round, having also not given post-round interviews during his missed cuts at the PGA Championship and US Open.

"A lot of ups and downs this week, to say the least," DeChambeau said on Instagram. "But I'm proud of the way I fought through it.

"Thank you to all my supporters for carrying me through. Onwards and upwards from here. Congratulations to Ryan Fox on an incredible win!"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy spoke to the media after his third round of The Open and said he was not impressed with DeChambeau's actions

World No 1 Scheffler defended DeChambeau over the rules controversy, insisting his fellow American is "not a cheater", while Rory McIlroy described the incident as "performative".

"I won't pretend to be up here and defend Bryson," McIlroy said on Saturday. "I'm not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it's for attention.

"To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn't feel like it was a great look."

Sports.title: The trends that defined the World Cup
Sports.content:
The biggest World Cup in history produced numbers to match. Forty-eight teams, 104 games and three host countries delivered a record 308 goals before Spain were crowned champions.

But the expanded tournament was not just bigger. It was older, more geographically demanding and more uneven. The average gap between opponents in the FIFA rankings reached a tournament high, teams crossed mammoth distances between base camps and venues, and heat, humidity and altitude influenced how much sides could run.

From mismatches and marathon journeys to hydration breaks, penalty run-ups and substitute impact, the data reveals the trends that shaped an unprecedented World Cup.

More teams, more goals and bigger gaps?

The expanded World Cup generated a record-breaking number of goals. Even when factoring in the leap from a 64-game tournament, the goal ratio averaged at 2.96 per game - the second-highest at a World Cup since 1966, basically on par with 1970.

What the champions told us

Spain were not the tournament's most extreme team in any one category, and that may be the point. In a World Cup defined by longer journeys, wider mismatches, older squads, heat, altitude and tactical interruptions, the champions found balance.

They were not heavily reliant on set-pieces, avoided the penalty drama that shaped other contenders, and still had enough depth for a substitute to decide the final.

The expanded format created bigger numbers everywhere, but Spain's title was built on control rather than chaos - epitomised by conceding a record-low one goal throughout the tournament.
