Sports.title: Football world mourns Kevin Keegan: Heartbroken Alan Shearer pays tribute to his 'hero', Jamie Carragher hails 'one of the greatest players this country has ever produced', while Prince William says he 'inspired generations'
Sports.content:
Alan Shearer has led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan after he passed away at the age of 75 following a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

And following the tragic news, figures from across the footballing world were quick to pay their respects to Keegan, who represented Scunthorpe, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle and later managed the Magpies (twice), Fulham, England and Manchester City.

Newcastle legend Shearer said: 'My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.'

Alan Shearer and Jamie Carragher led the tributes to football legend Kevin Keegan (pictured after winning the European Cup with Liverpool in 1977) after he passed away

Keegan is one of the best ever English players and enjoyed a successful managerial career

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher added: 'RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

'One of the most important men in making @LFC what it is today.'

Prince William, the official patron of The FA, said: 'Incredibly saddened to hear of the passing of Kevin Keegan.

'A truly remarkable footballer and manager who inspired generations with his talent, passion and love of the game.

'Above all, he will be remembered as a kind and generous man. Our thoughts are with his family and all who knew him. W.'

Former England captain David Beckham posted: 'Such a sad day to hear the passing of Kevin Keegan.

'A man that was very kind to me and my family xx. Sending lots of love and thoughts to his family and friends.'

Several of Keegan's former clubs also shared their own tribute, including Newcastle.

Taking to social media, they said: 'We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club’s history.

'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.'

Liverpool shared their own heartfelt post which read: 'We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss.

'His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin. 1951-2026.'

Former Reds star John Aldridge said: 'I've just been passed the really sad news.

'The great Kevin Keegan has passed away! He gave me great joy in my teens as a huge LFC fan, and the saying says never meet your heroes?

'Well I did!! Roger Hunt and KK and they surpassed everything I thought they were as people. Our thoughts are with all his family. God bless Kevin YNWA.'

Keegan, a forward in his playing days, won 63 caps for England before he later managed the Three Lions.

And they also posted a tribute which said: 'We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away.

'Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the #ThreeLions from 1999 to 2000.

'Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs.'

Shearer pictured with then Newcastle boss Kevin Keegan after signing for the club in 1996

Heartfelt tributes poured in for Keegan from figures and clubs across the footballing world

Former Newcastle owner Mehrdad Ghodoussi added: 'Devastated to hear about Kevin Keegan. Growing up watching football, he was one of the names that defined an era, a double Ballon d’Or winner, European Cup champion, England captain, and one of the most exciting players the game has seen.

'But what he did at Newcastle was different. He turned belief into something you could feel in the stadium.

'King Kev wasn’t just admired, he was loved, because everything he did came from the heart. Rest in peace, Kevin. Thank you for everything you gave the game.'

During his managerial career, Keegan also took Fulham from the Second Division (now League One) to the First Division (now Championship).

And the Cottagers shared some words for the footballing legend as they said: 'We're incredibly sad to hear the news that our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away.

'A legend of the game, Keegan led Fulham to the Football League Second Division title in 1999. He left Craven Cottage at the end of that season to focus on his duties as England manager.

'Our thoughts are with his friends and family at this difficult time.'

Manchester City, another of the teams Keegan managed, added: 'Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75.

'Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

'The promotion campaign in 2001-02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin’s family and friends at this very difficult time.'

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan dead at 75: Football legend passes away following battle with cancer as devastated family pay heartbreaking tribute to England icon
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

'The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support.

'This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

Keegan leaves behind his wife, Jean, who he met on the waltzers at Doncaster fair in 1970 – he was 19 and she was 16. They married four years later and had two daughters, Laura, 48, and Sarah, 44.

Kevin Keegan in the England strip in 1981 (left) and playing for Newcastle United in 1983

The former England manager was diagnosed with stomach cancer in January this year

Keegan, who played for Hamburger SV in the late 1970s (pictured), was a formidable footballer and twice won the Ballon d'Or - football's most prestigious individual prize - during his career

He won 63 caps for England and scored 21 goals across his ten-year international career

As a Liverpool player, Keegan delivered European glory for the Anfield club in 1977

In the 1970s, Keegan was renowned for his 'poodle perm' hair

Keegan pictured with his wife, Jean, who was by his side when he died on Monday

At Buckingham Palace with Jean and three-year-old Laura after being awarded an OBE in 1982

In a statement, Newcastle FC said: 'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

'As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

'As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

'Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

'Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

'At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him.

'Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev.'

Liverpool added: 'Liverpool FC is deeply saddened and mourning the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan. Our "Mighty Mouse", his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history. Rest in peace, Kevin Keegan.'

In January, Keegan was admitted to hospital due to 'ongoing abdominal symptoms', a statement from his family said.

'These investigations have revealed a diagnosis of cancer, for which Kevin will undergo treatment,' it added.

However, he looked sprightly when he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis in June, at An Audience With Kevin Keegan in Newcastle. He told fans at the Tyne Theatre that he was responding well to treatment after joking that he 'was still alive'. He also said, 'We have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got'.

'He [the doctor] was a Liverpool supporter, so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn't be walking alone, if you know what I mean.'

Keegan began his playing career at Scunthorpe in 1968, before moving to Liverpool to play for Bill Shankly three years later.

Keegan negotiated a contract worth £50 a week – Shankly had originally offered him £45.

It marked the beginning of a glorious playing career where he won 63 caps for England – captaining the Three Lions on 31 occasions.

The attacker won the First Division three times, the European Cup once and the UEFA Cup twice during a six-year stint at Liverpool.

Keegan even made the Charity Shield memorable after Leeds United midfielder John Giles punched him in the face and was shown a yellow card. Keegan's reaction, however, after a series of aggressive tackles from the other team, saw him sent off when it sparked a brawl with Billy Bremner and they came to blows. Liverpool won the game on penalties.

🗣️ "I WILL LOVE IT IF WE BEAT THEM, LOVE IT!"



We have lost an English football legend today 😢💔 pic.twitter.com/YWo87RCnUV — The 44 ⚽️ (@The_Forty_Four) July 20, 2026

After retiring from football in 1985, Keegan turned to management and was at the helm of his beloved Newcastle United for five years (pictured with famous Geordies Ant and Dec in 1995)

In 1996, in his post-match interview, Keegan accused Manchester United of being ‘slanderous’ and screamed ‘I will love it if we beat them, love it’, a meltdown that saw his team's Premier League title charge fall apart

Keegan also managed England but handed in his resignation in the Wembley tunnel following the drab defeat to Germany in October 2000

KEEGAN'S ILLUSTRIOUS CAREER Years Club Appearances Goals 1968–1971 Scunthorpe 124 18 1971–1977 Liverpool 230 68 1977–1980 Hamburg 90 32 1980–1982 Southampton 68 37 1982–1984 Newcastle United 78 48 1985 Blacktown City 2 1 Honours: Liverpool Football League First Division: 1972–73, 1975–76, 1976–77 FA Cup: 1973–74; runner-up: 1976–77 FA Charity Shield: 1974, 1976 European Cup: 1976–77 UEFA Cup: 1972–73, 1975–76 Hamburg Bundesliga: 1978–79 European Cup runner-up: 1979–80 Individual: Ballon d'Or: 1978, 1979 FWA Footballer of the Year: 1975–76 PFA Players' Player of the Year: 1981–82 Years Club Win% 1992-97 Newcastle United 55 1998-99 Fulham 62 1999-00 England 39 2001-05 Manchester City 44 2008 Newcastle 32 Honours: Newcastle United Football League First Division: 1992–93 Fulham Football League Second Division: 1998–99 Manchester City Football League First Division: 2001–02 Individual Premier League Manager of the Month: November 1993, August 1994, February 1995, August 1995, September 1995

He then moved to Germany to play for Hamburg and was named European Footballer of the Year in both 1978 and 1979. He added to the trophy cabinet in Germany, too, winning the Bundesliga and reaching the 1980 European Cup final.

After three years in Germany, Doncaster-born Keegan returned home and spent time at Southampton and Newcastle – who he would later go on to manage.

He rounded off his playing days with two appearances for Australian semi-professional side Blacktown City.

Keegan scored 204 goals in 592 career appearances across six clubs in a stellar career.

Alongside being iconic on the pitch, he produced his fair share of legendary moments off it too.

While Newcastle boss in 1996, Keegan launched a tirade on Manchester United during the heat of the Premier League title race.

Newcastle had let a 12-point lead slip at the top of the table, with Man Utd moving six points clear after beating ten-man Leeds United 1-0 in April 1996.

Leeds played the majority of the game with defender Lucas Radebe in goal, which prompted Sir Alex Ferguson to question the Yorkshire side's integrity and whether they would show the same grit against Keegan’s Newcastle.

Newcastle responded by beating Leeds 1-0 to move three points behind Man Utd with a match in hand, and only two left to play.

But Keegan let the pressure of the title race get to him in his post-match interview, accusing United of being ‘slanderous’ and screaming ‘I will love it if we beat them, love it’.

His managerial career produced its fair share of bizarre moments.

In 1999, Keegan succeeded Glenn Hoddle as England boss, but a year later famously resigned in the tunnel at Wembley following the drab defeat to Germany in October 2000.

After a brutal reception from the England fans, he told his players in the dressing room that he was stepping down before confirming his resignation to FA director David Davies in a nearby stadium toilet cubicle.

He guided Newcastle to the Football League First Division title during the first of two stints at St James' Park and came close to lifting the Premier League, only to be pipped by Manchester United.

He would go on to oversee promotions to the top flight for both Fulham and City.

Sports.title: 'He became a superstar but never changed... to say he was a gentleman would be an understatement': GRAEME SOUNESS pays tribute to his friend KEVIN KEEGAN
Sports.content:
'He became a superstar but never changed... to say he was a gentleman would be an understatement': GRAEME SOUNESS pays tribute to his friend KEVIN KEEGAN

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Graeme Souness faced Kevin Keegan as a player and manager - they later became friends and golfing partners. Here, after the news of Keegan's death at the age of 75, he pays tribute...

If you ever wanted an example of a man who became a superstar but never changed as a man, Kevin Keegan would be top of that list.

For everything he achieved in the game - the trophies, two Ballon d'Or - his greatest quality was the humility he carried with him through every waking moment. He treated every person he met in the same way: with utmost respect.

To say he was an absolute gentleman seems an understatement. He was a class act.

This was a genuine superstar. If only you could bottle the attitude he had and sell it to the players today.

I was in a restaurant not so long ago when I witnessed a young player, a so-called star, refuse to do a selfie with a fan. That was the absolute polar opposite to Kevin.

Kevin Keegan was a genuinely humble man who recognised he had got lucky in life, but boy did he make the most out of his talent and work hard at it.

He left nothing on the table. He got the absolute best out of himself every time he went out and played football whether training or in a game. His workrate was phenomenal and his enthusiasm lifted everyone around him.

Liverpool captain Graeme Souness shakes hands with Newcastle's Kevin Keegan before Keegan's testimonial at St James's Park in 1984

From an early age he became the biggest star in English football. When I faced him for Liverpool against Southampton, there was no legal way of stopping him. He didn't take kindly to that and gave me a right mouthful. But like all the greats, he didn't shy away, he just came back for more.

But afterwards we became friends. I got to know him even better in recent years.

We used to play golf in Portugal together and he'd always make it competitive. He was full of mischief. England v Scotland he'd say. He was a delight to be around and no matter who asked for a photograph, he'd always stop and make them feel special.

One Friday, a guest speaker for my charity DEBRA had let me down. The dinner was on the Sunday at Prestonfield House in Edinburgh. I rang Kevin and asked if he could step in. He said, 'give me five minutes'.

He rang back in three and said, 'I'll do it.' I said, 'how much do you want?' and he said 'just my travel expenses please', because he liked to drive everywhere.

He turned up, enchanted the room, then stayed and listened to the families' stories. When I went to pay him, he refused and said, 'put it in the pot'. It was a mark of the man.

He used to say, 'I wish for you and your family what you would wish for yourself'.

My heart goes out to Jean and his family.

Sports.title: Revealed: Stroppy Bryson DeChambeau threatened to call Donald Trump during his meltdown at The Open
Sports.content:
Bryson DeChambeau threatened to call Donald Trump during the extraordinary rules row that broke out during The Open, it has emerged.

In a remarkable new twist to the episode, which saw the American docked two strokes in wild scenes on Friday, well-placed sources confirmed to Daily Mail Sport that the double US Open champion warned he might seek a presidential intervention at the height of the drama.

However, unlike the World Cup controversy involving USMNT striker Folarin Balogun, the White House did not get involved and the penalty was not overturned.

The detail that DeChambeau took the desperate step of playing the Trump card was first revealed by respected American course architect and author Geoff Shackelford late on Sunday, after Ryan Fox had won golf's oldest major. While Fox's win was a fine end to the tournament, the DeChambeau drama remained the dominant theme of the week.

Bryson DeChambeau reportedly tried to get US President Donald Trump involved in the dispute that saw him hit with a two-shot penalty at The Open

DeChambeau was hit with the penalty on the second day after 'inadvertently improving his lie'

The American was subsequently embroiled in a dramatic argument with officials at The Open

After appearing to trample the grass behind his ball in the second round, the 32-year-old was hit with a two-shot penalty by officials and demanded to be returned to the site of the incident, where he angrily protested his innocence. During his remonstrations, he threatened to withdraw before returning to the championship offices where he protested for a further half-hour - it was in the midst of this strop that the LIV rebel raised the possibility of calling Trump, a close friend.

In losing the argument, DeChambeau toppled from one shot off the 36-hole lead to three back, before sliding further down the leaderboard on Sunday.

While Scottie Scheffler insisted DeChambeau was not a 'cheat', Rory McIlroy was scathing of his rival's antics. Speaking on Saturday, the world No 2 said: 'I was up in the players' lounge watching it with a few other players and as soon as he made the step into the ball, we all sort of looked at each other and we were like, "That didn't seem right". Then when I heard that he was called in by the rules officials, it was pretty obvious for why.'

McIlroy added: 'I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it is for attention. To hold the tournament hostage like that and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn't feel like it was a great look.'

Such an incident would usually be laughed off, yet given Trump's interventions at the FIFA World Cup, it could have been a hugely contentious issue.

This came when the USA suffered a blow in their last-32 World Cup win over Bosnia and Herzegovina when star striker Folarin Balogun was sent off, meaning he was set to be banned from their last-16 clash against Belgium.

However, Balgoun's ban was suspended by FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a close confidante of Trump, after the US President personally called him and urged the football supremo to allow the striker to play.

Despite Trump's interventions, the US were thrashed 4-1 by Belgium, yet the 80-year-old has repeatedly boasted about his involvement, including claiming things 'worked out much better' when speaking ahead of Sunday's final, where he was booed by many as he walked out onto the pitch.

DeChambeau's plea comes after Trump intervened to have a red card awarded to USA striker Folarin Balogun overturned, allowing him to play in a last-16 game against Belgium

DeChambeau's request for Trump's help also takes on added significance given the pair are close and class each other as friends.

Back in 2024 when DeChambeau won the US Open, he celebrated his success with the President's family, while the golfer is also a member of Trump's Council on Sports, Fitness and Nutrition.

The penalty ultimately proved to be inconsequential as DeChambeau struggled on the final round to end at four under par, six shots behind eventual winner Ryan Fox.

DeChambeau's attempts to involve Trump also come after legendary golfer Tiger Woods was picked up on police bodycam footage telling officers that he was on the phone with the US President following his car crash in March.

Woods, who is dating Vanessa Trump, the ex-wife of the President's eldest child Donald Trump Jr, was arrested and charged with driving under the influence, something he pleaded not guilty to.

But in the footage, as Woods walked over to an officer at the crash scene, he could be heard to say: 'Thank you so much. All right. You got it. Bye. I was just talking to the President.'

Trump has previously described Woods as a 'very close friend' and an 'amazing man'.

Sports.title: FIFA launch investigation into Argentina's shocking World Cup final post-match behaviour... as new footage shows what really sparked final-whistle brawl
Sports.content:
FIFA will investigate the behavior of Argentina's bitter players after the World Cup final descended into violence following their defeat on Sunday.

The probe into the violent final-whistle scenes in New Jersey comes just as footage reveals the exact moment that sparked the ugly brawl.

The South Americans were outplayed by Spain in a drab encounter at MetLife Stadium, with Lionel Messi and his teammates unable to disrupt their rivals with the same aggressive, physical tactics that unsettled England in the semi-final.

Barcelona star Ferran Torres bagged the winning goal in extra time to seal Spain's second World Cup triumph – after first winning the trophy in 2010 – leaving Messi, 39, in tears at the final whistle.

However, the action continued following the final whistle as a brawl broke out between the two sides, resulting in a red card for Leandro Paredes.

The Argentina midfielder was sent off for grabbing Eric Garcia by the neck and punching Gavi in the face before pushing him to the ground in appalling scenes at full time.

FIFA is now set to open disciplinary proceedings into the red card issued to Paredes, with the role of other players and officials also set to be investigated, according to The Times.

Jaja, es Molina el que empieza todo pegando a Rodri. Hay que largar a todo el clan loser este ya, que encima de macarras, perdedores e insoportables, son malísimos. pic.twitter.com/Wk6C0fwABY — The Lion (@loloutlaw) July 19, 2026

FIFA is set to launch an investigation into the violent behavior of Leandro Paredes and other Argentina players after the World Cup final descended into violent scenes

The move came after ugly scenes at the end of the game which Spain won 1-0 after extra time

New footage has revealed that a punch landed on Spain captain Rodri sparked the brawl

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes and staff ran on to the pitch to celebrate their victory.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina hit Spain captain Rodri in the torso as he was running by, resulting in the midfielder squaring up to his rival.

That saw players from both teams pile into the melee, before Paredes threw punches.

Elsewhere, 53-year-old assistant coach Roberto Ayala was also caught landing a punch on Spain's Dani Olmo at full time.

In the aftermath of the ugly brawl, DAZN Spain claimed Argentina defender Nicolas Otamendi complained to Rodri about La Roja's pre-match comments alluding to officiating concerns ahead of the final.

The South Americans had benefitted from a series of questionable decisions heading into the showpiece event, with the Manchester City midfielder raising concerns before the final.

'You and [Spain team-mate Aymeric] Laporte. Both of you,' he said to Rodri.

'You spent the time crying and complaining about the referees, my friend. But you shouldn't have spoken before the match, you know that? Didn't you see what he said this week?'

Argentina were thuggish throughout the World Cup final, just as they had been when they beat England in the semis.

Torres's 106th-minute winner came after Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off in the 93rd minute following a reckless challenge on Pau Cubarsi – which summed up the South Americans' deplorable approach to the game.

por que el raton ayala le pegó una piña a dani olmo jajdjsjsjsj pic.twitter.com/ZNkBpPAcjU — Peñargrol (@CAPArgento__) July 20, 2026

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes celebrated the win

Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni tries to intervene as Paredes clashes with Eric Garcia

Spain shared fears of roughhouse tactics from Argentina, and their concerns came to fruition with Enzo Fernandez sent off for a shocking challenge on Pau Cubarsi

Astonishingly, Fernandez complained about his dismissal for a second yellow, before attempting to get Chelsea team-mate Marc Cucurella sent off for covering his face while talking to Messi.

New laws state that footballers who cover their mouths when speaking to a player from the opposing team must be sent off, but replays showed Cucurella was simply scratching his nose as he spoke to Argentina's captain.

Paredes was also fortunate not to be sent off for a second bookable offense in regular time for a foul on the edge of the box which presented Lamine Yamal with a last-gasp free-kick before extra-time.

Following the game, the 2022 champions collected their silver medals from FIFA boss Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump on the stage but opted not to watch as Spain lifted the trophy – despite it being customary in finals of major tournaments.

Instead, the Argentina players, coaching team and staff walked over to the end where the majority of their fans were sat and turned their backs as their rivals celebrated.

Footage shows Spain players holding the World Cup trophy aloft as gold confetti explodes behind them, with the Argentina team facing the other way.

Argentina only had two shots in the entire match, with the first one coming in the 117th minute.

There were an estimated 1.5 to 1.8 billion viewers tuning in to watch the summer tournament's showpiece finale, which saw Trump take center stage during the trophy lift.

Argentina players decided to turn their backs to Spain's World Cup trophy lift on Sunday

Donald Trump took center stage as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday afternoon

The President refused to step aside to allow the victorious Spaniards to have their moment in the spotlight.

Trump and Infantino handed out various awards to match officials and players, before officially welcoming the team up to the stage to lift the World Cup trophy.

The President presented the prestigious title to Spain captain Rodri, who took great pleasure in raising it aloft.

Much like when he presented the Club World Cup title last summer, Trump stood awkwardly alongside the Spain squad as they lifted the trophy and celebrated wildly.

It seemed as though, when Spain were about to perform the trophy lift, Infantino had attempted to usher Trump away from the players – though the President remained where he was.

He stood to the side of the team as the confetti cannons went off at MetLife Stadium, clapping and grinning while Infantino laughed off Trump's awkward cameo.

Loud boos had come from the stands when Infantino and Trump made their way onto the pitch, as fans made their feelings on the pair undoubtedly clear.

Fans noted that one Argentina star – Tottenham defender Cristian Romero – completely ignored the President as he collected his medal from Infantino.

It appeared as though Infantino attempted to usher Trump away – but the President remained where he was

In a video which swiftly went viral on social media, the Argentinian could be seen receiving his silverware from Infantino before waltzing past Trump on stage.

Meanwhile, the President also presented a trio of awards to Spain's stars, including the Young Player of the Tournament, the Golden Glove and the Golden Ball – which were claimed by Pau Cubarsi, Unai Simon and Rodri respectively.

There was a degree of irony in regard to Trump presenting Spain with the World Cup trophy, after previously launching a stinging attack on the country at a UN summit earlier in July for not contributing enough money to NATO.

'Spain is a terrible partner in NATO. They don’t participate. They don’t pay. I don’t want anything to do with Spain. Cut off all trade with Spain, please, including visits,' he said. 'Don’t even talk to them. They’re hopeless, bad people.'

Then, on his way back to the United States on Air Force One, Trump said Spain had tried to improve its standing with him.

'I did have issues, and ​I still do. But Spain, they came back all the way today. Spain was very generous today,' he said.

'They honored a request for lots of payments, and if they didn't, we wouldn't have even ⁠talked to them.'

Earlier in the day, Trump and his wife Melania were seen taking in the action inside a packed MetLife Stadium suite – alongside FIFA president Infantino, Canada's prime minister Mark Carney and Mexico's president Claudia Sheinbaum.

Wayne Rooney savaged the 2026 World Cup final halftime show as he described the performance as 'c**p' and said the 'best part was when it ended' live on BBC

The show delivered a spectacular mix of music, nostalgia and global star power, with the likes of Madonna, Justin Bieber, Shakira and the Muppets all performing under one roof

Trump also shook hands with Spain's prime minister Pedro Sanchez as Infantino stood beside them.

Spain's Queen Letizia and King Felipe VI also greeted the President. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, reportedly watched the game from home due to 'superstition,' The New York Times reported.

Trump also waved at the crowd from behind the glass.

Inside the private suite, Infantino posed for pictures with the President's son, Eric Trump, his wife, Lara, and their children. Barron Trump also showed up for the big game.

The World Cup final also saw a bizarre half-time show, with Madonna, Coldplay, Justin Bieber, The Muppets and Shakira performing during the 27-minute interval, which was derided by Wayne Rooney.

'To be honest, mine [his highlight] was when it finished. I like a lot of those artists but to be honest I thought it was c**p', he fumed.

'I did honestly. It just didn't get me going. I wanted the football to be back on. It was a bit flat. I like Burna Boy, I like Shakira, I like Bieber but that was too flat.'

Sports.title: The day Kevin Keegan hurtled down the autobahn at 100mph to get me to the airport on time - after our lunch of beefburgers and steins of pilsner to mark his move to Hamburg, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
When Kevin Keegan was on the foothills of his international career in 1972, Sir Alf Ramsey called him into an enlarged England squad.

To say that he was not best pleased when this country's only World Cup-winning manager designated him to the Under 23s match on the night before the senior game is something of an understatement.

Keegan packed his bags in anger and had to be stopped from storming out of the hotel by urgent warnings that he would be jeopardising his England future.

In common with most Fleet Street football reporters, I denounced his prima donna tantrum. A year or three of strained relations with the press ensued.

Once, upon the conclusion of a football awards dinner in London, I took a few of my guests on to the members' club Morton's for late-night drinks. The all-time greatest gossip columnist Nigel Dempster among us.

We were merrily ensconced in the bar overlooking Berkeley Square as Kevin arrived with a couple of his pals. When he saw I was there, he pulled over the manager and told him: 'I'm not comfortable with that journalist being here, invading my privacy.' The reply: 'I'm sorry Mr Keegan, but Mr Powell and Mr Dempster are founder members of this club so we won't be asking them to leave.'

Kevin Keegan was all heart in the end - brimming with energy, flooded with adrenalin, full of fun and an arch competitor

An hour or so later he departed, with a cursory nod in our direction. A thaw, then? Maybe. I was told he appreciated that both Nigel and myself refrained from embarrassing him in print about that awkward incident.

Fast forward to his transfer to Hamburg and to some surprise he agreed to an interview about his new life in Germany. Our lunch of the world's largest and purest beefburgers washed down by steins of pilsner lingered until it seemed likely I would miss my flight back to London. 'Don't worry,' said Kevin. 'I'll drive you.'

He called the restaurant valet to bring his racy German car, while the Mail settled the bill. We went bouncing down cobbled streets and then hurtled onto the autobahn at well over 100mph. Speed limits back then in the Fatherland were virtually non-existent.

A mile or two from the airport, a British Airways plane loomed into view a few hundred feet above us on a flight-path which tracked the motorway. Keegan rammed his foot even harder on the accelerator and we undertook the plane. After screeching to a halt in front of departures we jumped out of the car, laughing. High-fived as he said: 'Yes, we beat it here. That must be your return flight home. Looks like you made it.'

That was Kevin Keegan. Oh so feisty if he felt wronged. All heart in the end. Brimming with energy. Flooded with adrenalin. Full of fun. Arch competitor. Raging with ambition yet eager to help others. All of that. Off as well as on the pitch. How on earth has this irrepressible 5ft 8in human dynamo died so young at 75? Curses on the cancer which has taken Mighty Mouse, as he was affectionately nicknamed.

Mine was just one of many such rollercoaster experiences. At Wembley in the infamous 1974 Charity Shield game between Liverpool and Leeds, he and Billy Bremner were sent off for punching each other, in the brawl which followed him being hacked down by Johnny Giles. After the match, Keegan joined the hysterical criticism of Leeds as a brutal side urged into mischief by their genius manager Don Revie.

A few years later, Revie made Keegan the captain of England. Not only was all forgiven, but it was not long before Kevin hailed the Don as 'my mentor and like a second father to me'.

Actually, he should have said third father.

While he was a Liverpool legend, his England achievements took him to just one World Cup quarter-final

Of all the moves during his football lifetime, the one which launched him towards the football stratosphere was gifted unto him by the immortal Bill Shankly.

The founding father of Liverpool FC as we have known and loved that bastion of the game in recent decades was told about a little kid making waves at Scunthorpe United down in the depths of the old Fourth Division.

One cold wet midweek night in 1971, Shankly's idea of how best for him and his beloved wife to celebrate their wedding anniversary would be to make that tortuous 240-mile round-trip drive over the Pennines and back to watch the boy Keegan in action.

One £33,000 transfer, 323 matches, 100 goals, three English championships, one FA Cup, one European Cup, two UEFA Cups and six years later, Shanks said: 'Best wedding anniversary me and Nessie ever had.'

There would have been many more Liverpool goals had it not taken a while for Shankly to transform Keegan from an orthodox midfield player into a second striker. A quite passable imitation of Maradona in that free-rein role.

Hamburg were next to benefit from that transition with a ratio of more than a goal every three games (40 in 113) after signing in 1977. Thus Keegan led them to their first German championship in 19 years and their first European Cup final.

His additional personal reward for those efforts was to be voted into the pantheon of only 10 players ever to be voted European Footballer of the Year twice. To go with his English Footballer of the Year honour in his penultimate season at Anfield.

Then, at both Southampton (42 in 80 games) and Newcastle (49 in 85), he averaged better than a goal every two games. But the vibrant essence of the man ran even deeper than those impressive statistics. They were the product of that impulsive instinct for the game, the fizzing speed off the mark, the instant eye for the perfect space to sprint into, the defence-splitting pass recognised before all around him were aware, the non-stop stamina. The never-say-die optimism.

He admitted the England management job wasn't for him - but he was raging with ambition yet eager to help others

In the more rarified challenge presented to England he scored precisely once every three games – 21 in 63 – and the first England captain he played under articulated his value. Bobby Moore would say: 'Loved Kev. Terrific player and best of all he drove the opposition crazy.'

Circumstances, including injury and under-achievement by the national team, limited his World Cup impact to one quarter-final. Which starved him of much of the wider recognition his brilliance deserved. Perhaps his quirkiness, too. He simply did not care when that bizarre perming of his thick growth of hair invited comedians to do their worst.

Nor did he bother to respond to scurrilous rumours which followed him being set upon while caught sleeping in his Range-Rover on the side of the M25 in Surrey. Simply leaving it to his assailants to explain in court that they saw him as a potentially wealthy target to rob, without realising it was Keegan.

When retirement from playing led to management he became embroiled in heated rows with directors. Not that his start-stop first spell in charge at Newcastle ever cooled the adoration poured onto him by the second of two of the most passionate communities on the planet. First Merseyside, then Tyneside. An idol on both shores of the northern powerhouse of English football.

If anything the Geordies massed behind him all the more loudly when first-season promotion from the Second Division was followed by the losing of a 12-point lead over Manchester United and with it the title.

If anything they loved him all the more when the paramount manager in the history of English football, Sir Alex Ferguson, beat him at the mind games which characterised that race for glory. 'I will love it if we beat them. Love it.' That was not to be. Nor was success as manager of England.

When his one year as successor to Glenn Hoddle ended in a 1-0 home defeat by Germany which set up England for failure to qualify for the 2002 World Cup, he retreated into a lavatory in the Wembley dressing room. In that sanctuary he sadly and quietly told the FA's media chief David Davies that he was resigning immediately 'because I'm not right for this job'.

Keegan was lampooned for that by some critics, who preferred not to acknowledge the honesty within the personal anguish.

Wistful nostalgia surrounds the loss of idol Keegan - he is survived by devoted wife Jean and their two daughters

After retirement he shied away from public scrutiny, other than when boosting his several charities, and into the bosom of family life with devoted wife Jean and their two proud daughters. One consequence is that he is not recognised fully by new young football fans and partly neglected by forgetful older generations.

Wistful nostalgia always surrounds the loss like this of an idol. Personally, I for one regret not responding with alacrity on one of the occasions when I pondered organising a reunion in Berkeley Square. If it is any excuse, Mr Dempster also died too young and Morton's closed some time ago.

Sports.title: Golf news: Rory McIlroy lays out priorities as PGA Tour star takes break from sport
Sports.content:
Golf news: Rory McIlroy lays out priorities as PGA Tour star takes break from sport

The fallout from The Open Championship continues after a plenty of drama on Sunday, with Rory McIlroy continuing to attract attention

View 2 Images Rory McIlroy had a tough weekend at the Open (Image: AP Photo/Peter Morrison)

The golf world is reacting to Ryan Fox's eye-catching Open victory over the weekend but big names including Rory McIlroy have also hit the headlines. Reigning Masters champion McIlroy finished down in a tie for 40th at Royal Birkdale as Fox won his first ever major.

‌



"I didn't feel anything for the putt - everything was shaking that much," the New Zealander said after winning by one stroke. "It's not a very comfortable feeling. It's certainly very enjoyable when you see it go in."

‌



The weekend was full of drama, with Bryson DeChambeau's controversial penalty and McIlroy's continuing feud with the American capturing headlines. Now, though, it's time to look forward.

‌



We've got an update on McIlroy's future as well as news on another PGA star. Here are our latest lines.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Bryson DeChambeau shows true colours with response to Rory McIlroy taunts at The Open READ MORE :

Behind the scenes at Sky Sports Golf as plans for 2027 Open already put in place READ MORE :

McIlroy gets honest

Rory McIlroy has continued working on a reduced schedule this year, confirming he won't be present at the FedEx St. Jude Championship. The tournament is scheduled for August 13 in Tennessee and the Northern Irishman admitted his motivation for Tour events isn't as high as it has been in the past.

‌



"I think it just sort of ebbs and flows," he said. "There’s been years where I’ve given it maybe more of my attention and years that I haven’t. Yeah, I guess I’m just at a stage that I have other things that I prioritise.

“Again, the PGA Tour is in a lot of flux at the minute with a lot of their schedule and structure and everything like that. So I think the change where it doesn’t matter where you are in the top 30 going into the Tour Championship, it’s like I just need to be in the top 30 going in there to have a chance to win a FedExCup.

"So why would I care about the first two? I sort of came to that decision last year, and I’m just sort of doing the same thing.”

‌



Fitzpatrick ready for break

View 2 Images Alex Fitzpatrick fell away over the weekend at Royal Birkdale (Image: AP Photo/David Goldman)

Alex Fitzpatrick plans to take some time out to recharge after a frustrating weekend at The Open. The 27-year-old was in the top 10 at the halfway point but fell back dramatically after shooting 77 on Sunday.

"It was c***. No two ways about it. My putting was woeful," said Fitzpatrick, whose brother Matt missed the cut at Royal Birkdale.

Article continues below

"I thought some of the pins yesterday were terrible, just brutally honest. And, yeah, mixed with me not playing very good at all, that's what it is."

When asked if he was desperate to get back out on the course to return to form, he added: "No, I'm having two weeks off. I'm putting the clubs away and having a good reset and actually enjoy my life."

Sports.title: 'He was one of my best mates' - Mick Channon tribute to Kevin Keegan after death aged 75
Sports.content:
'He was one of my best mates' - Mick Channon tribute to Kevin Keegan after death aged 75

England and Liverpool legend Kevin Keegan, who has died at the age of 75 after a battle with stage four cancer, has been fondly remembered as a successful racehorse owner

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan (right) with Mick Channon at his stables (Image: Mike King)

Mick Channon described Kevin Keegan as 'one of my best mates' following the death of the former England and Liverpool legend aged 75. Channon, the former professional footballer turned racehorse trainer, led tributes from figures in the sport to Keegan, who also enjoyed success as a racehorse owner.

‌



It had recently been revealed that Keegan, a star of the all-conquering Liverpool side of the 1970s who also both played for and managed Newcastle United, amongst other clubs. had been receiving treatment for stage four cancer.

‌



Channon, a teammate of Keegan's for both England and Southampton following his high-profile switch from Hamburg in Germany, was amongst his closest companions, with the former trainer having ignited his passion for racing.

‌



Ascot makes King George the richest race in Britain by lifting 2027 value to £2.5 million READ MORE :

David Easterby wears lucky Sondad silks on latest leg of 326-mile charity bike ride READ MORE :

Channon claimed the Listed Washington Singer Stakes with Keegan's finest horse, Funfair Wane, who would famously go on to win the Ayr Gold Cup on two occasions after joining David 'Dandy' Nicholls' yard.

"It's very sad," Channon said. "He was one of my best mates and we've known for a little while this was coming.

"I think as you get older yourself things like this get tougher. We had a great time together – when we were fit, young and well and with Bally (Alan Ball) too, we had a wonderful time with some real characters.

‌



View 4 Images Kevin Keegan and Mick Channon: teammates at Southampton (Image: Getty Images)

"Kevin came to Southampton a Ballon d'Or winner, but you wouldn't have known, he had time for everyone and never once acted like the star that he was. Life was fun and football was part of it. I was the one who was mad into the racing but Kevin and Bally loved it too, racing was great fun for them and we did a lot of it.

"Kevin was just a smashing lad, a great human being. When you think of the profile he had, he never turned away any autograph or photo, he was a people person. We had some great fun all of us together, that's how I'll remember him.

‌



"Kevin and Jean (wife) even bred a few horses and that added to the fun and then he became England manager which got in the way a bit!".

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan with Frankie Dettori at the Shergar Cup (Image: PA)

"When you look back at his time with England he was one of the better ones really. He was a mate though, first and foremost. It's a very sad day, but the poor lad is at rest now."

‌



Jockey Adrian Nicholls, a proud Sunderland supporter, rode Funfair Wane — bred by Jean Keegan — to the first of his two Ayr Gold Cup triumphs back in 2002, and holds fond memories of Keegan.

"Winning an Ayr Gold Cup for him was special. I was just a middle-of-the-road jockey and he was such a high-profile footballer – we had some great conversations, especially with me being a Sunderland fan," said Nicholls.

View 4 Images Funfair Wane: winning the 2004 Ayr Gold Cup (Image: Press Association)

Article continues below

"He was such a cool guy to ride for, he never put you under any pressure. He could have got anybody to ride him but let me. To win one Ayr Gold Cup is hard enough but to win two was unbelievable.

"It's a very sad day as he was just a legend of a bloke.

"It was down to Mick Channon how Dandy got Funfair. Mick recommended Dandy after he started to lose his way a bit and as they say, the rest is history."

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan was an under-appreciated national treasure and a joy to be around
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan was an under-appreciated national treasure and a joy to be around

After his death aged 75, Mirror chief sports writer Andy Dunn pays tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon Kevin Keegan

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan, pictured during his time as England manager, as died aged 75 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

In my memory, there has been no character in football as irrepressible as Kevin Keegan. Simple as that. A joy to watch, a joy to be around. Infectious, funny, passionate and never one to take himself too seriously.

‌



Which - considering he twice won the Ballon D’Or and considering the proliferation of elite footballers who do take themselves so very seriously - deserved the highest praise.

‌



And as a player, Keegan really was truly elite. But it was hard to escape the feeling that, as odd as it sounds, Keegan’s contribution to football has been and remains slightly under-appreciated.

‌



He should have been a national treasure. For what he achieved as a player and for his warmth and generosity, he would have been knighted nowadays.

But to many of us, and to our parents, he WAS a national treasure. And he was an Anfield treasure, even though his place in Liverpool’s history books is nuanced.

Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in READ MORE :

He is one of the club’s greatest-ever players, that much is certain, but he left the club of his own accord, joining SV Hamburg in 1977 for a new challenge and a lucrative payday.

‌



Keegan did not just collect an array of medals during his time at Anfield - three league titles, two UEFA Cups, an FA Cup and a European Cup - he produced defining individual performances.

One of those was in the 1977 European Cup final when he destroyed Berti Vogts - acknowledged then as one of the world’s best defenders - in Liverpool’s 3-1 win over Borussia Mönchengladbach in Rome.

It was one of THE great displays in a European Cup final. Vogts would later pay tribute to the Machtig Maus, the Magic Mouse.

‌



View 3 Images Keegan has a nuanced place in Liverpool's history books (Image: Mirrorpix)

Ironically, another one of his great individual performances was in the 1974 FA Cup final against his beloved Newcastle United, when he scored twice in a 3-0 victory for Bill Shankly’s side. He was truly a talismanic player.

Can you imagine the fuss in this era if an English player won the Ballon D’Or twice in two years, as Keegan did in 1978 and 1979 when in Germany?

‌



Over half a decade, Keegan was the Lionel Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo of his time, but incredibly down to earth. He always had an amusing tale to tell us when the notepads were away and the voice recorders were switched off.

He told of the time when he was almost late for his Liverpool debut, a police officer not recognising the new £33,000 signing outside Anfield. He would laugh with is about the time he fell off his bike on the TV programme, Superstars.

Our relations with Keegan became strained during Euro 2000 when his relaxed regime at the squad's base in Belgium came under scrutiny, and when England failed to make it out of the group stage.

‌



But Keegan was that type of relaxed manager, a manager who treated his players to fish, chips and beer after a good win. But he never held our fierce criticism of England’s showing at the tournament against us.

View 3 Images Keegan was a brilliant player for England before later going on to manage his country (Image: Peter Robinson/EMPICS Sport/PA Wire)

And, of course, he gave the media a truly memorable moment with his ‘I’ll Love It’ rant at Sir Alex Ferguson in 1996 as his Newcastle United team surrendered a 12-point lead in the title race.

‌



Later generations of fans remember Keegan as much for that as they do for his brilliance on and off the field. And don’t forget, as Newcastle manager, Keegan moulded one of the most entertaining English club sides of recent decades.

He was a player and a manager who belonged - in a good way - to a bygone age. When football seemed a lot more fun.

Ahead of a schoolboy cup final, this correspondent felt compelled to get a curly perm, thanks to Keegan, who had been on Top of the Pops - yes, Top of the Pops - a few days earlier.

Article continues below

His song ‘Head Over Heels’ only made it to number 31 in the charts. For some time in English football, King Kev was number one, an irrepressible character who will be greatly missed.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75

Former England manager Kevin Keegan was a football icon for his achievements with Newcastle, Liverpool and beyond and he was well-known for his passion and good humour

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan made his final public appearance alongside Sam Allardyce (Image: INSTAGRAM)

Kevin Keegan was an inspiring figure on the pitch, in the dugout and away from football, and captured hearts across Yorkshire, Liverpool and Newcastle until the very end. His honesty, passion and good humour were standout traits for one of football's true icons.

‌



Keegan died aged 75 after being diagnosed with cancer, but was still active in the final months of his life. The former England boss is survived by his wife, Jean, and their children, Laura Jane and Sarah Marie.

‌



Even after being diagnosed with stage four cancer, Keegan made a number of public appearances, working alongside Peter Graves. It was his close friend who confirmed his passing.

‌



Graves wrote: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in READ MORE :

"Kevin, a double Ballon d’Or winner, was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

‌



Keegan took in an impressive England display during his final publish appearance. Working alongside Ray Parlour, David James and Sam Allardyce. In an Instagram post, Graves said that 'Keegan was a big fan of "Tuchel Ball"'.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Earlier in June, when Keegan revealed his cancer diagnosis publicly for the first time, he expressed his usual humour to deliver the tragic news.

‌



Speaking with Graves at the Tyne Theatre, Kevin revealed a discussion over his treatment. He said: "I was in a car accident and, through that, I had to have an operation. Whilst having the scan for the operation, they found out I had cancer.

"They said they had an absolute top doctor for fighting what you have got, which is stage four cancer. So I went to meet him. He’s a Liverpool supporter so I knew I wouldn't walk alone.

"He said, 'Kevin, this new treatment, I've got a tremendous strike rate'. I said, 'What's your strike rate?' He said, '33%'. I thought it would be 80%, 90%. 33%!? I'm still here at the moment.”

‌



Kevin Keegan: England and Liverpool legend dead aged 75

During another moment, Keegan revealed he also wanted to say farewell, having not had a proper opportunity during his second spell managing Newcastle. "I want to say goodbye. I didn't get the chance when I left last time…"

Tributes have poured in for the late Doncaster-born star. Alan Shearer posted on social media: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss [Crying emoji]."

‌



Jamie Carragher tweeted: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

"One of the most important men in making LFC [Liverpool Football Club] what it is today."

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan is a legendary figure on Tyneside (Image: Professional Sport/Popperfoto via Getty Images/Getty Images)

‌



Newcastle United offered a lengthy, heartfelt tribute. A club statement read: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager.

"He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters. As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

‌



View 3 Images Keegan was affectionately known as the Messiah at Newcastle (Image: Stu Forster/Getty Images)

"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

Article continues below

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him. Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev."

Sports.title: Argentina in fresh punch shame after World Cup final as new footage emerges
Sports.content:
Argentina in fresh punch shame after World Cup final as new footage emerges

Spain's World Cup triumph descended into chaos as Argentina players and staff were seen throwing punches following the full-time whistle at MetLife Stadium

View 2 Images Roberto Ayala clashed with Dani Olmo

Argentina coach Roberto Ayala appeared to throw a punch at Spain's Dani Olmo during the chaotic scenes that followed the World Cup final. The defending champions suffered a 1-0 extra-time loss in New Jersey after Ferran Torres struck in the 106th minute.

‌



But the result only told half of the story. Enzo Fernandez was sent off just before the additional period for a second yellow card, while there were unsavoury scenes at full-time involving Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina.

‌



And now Footage has emerged showing Ayala, who is one of Lionel Scaloni's assistant coaches, swinging his right arm towards Olmo as they clashed. To his credit, the Barcelona star didn't react and team-mate Eric Garcia stepped in to play the role of peacekeeper.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Former England goalkeeper Joe Hart labelled Argentina's behaviour 'disgusting'. He said: "There was one man on the pitch who did have class and that was Lionel Messi, who shook hands with every one of those Spanish players.

"The game's done. They could have absolutely no complaints about what happened today. Disgusting behaviour."

‌



Full list of Argentina's 27 dirty tricks in World Cup final as they ruin greatest match READ MORE :

Before he added: "Spain fully deserve it. They have been absolutely superb all tournament. They have dominated all game against a rigid, rugged Argentina. The best team has won this World Cup."

While fellow BBC pundit Wayne Rooney said: "Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me.

"We've seen this with Argentina before. It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round.

‌



"That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them."

View 2 Images Paredes was sent off for an angry clash with Eric Garcia (Image: Getty Images)

Paredes was also sent off following the whistle, while Molina also appeared to throw a punch after the match. The latter took a swing at Rodri, while Paredes was spotted kicking Eric Garcia to the floor before pushing him back with a hand around his neck when the Barcelona defender attempted to confront him.

‌



He was also spotted in an exchange with Gavi and former Chelsea midfielder Craig Burley fumed: "Argentina were a complete and utter disgrace today, both with their performance and their antics.

"We expected the antics, we expected the thuggery, we expected the off the ball stuff, but we also expected a lot more on the ball, a lot more purpose... they were an utter shambles, disgusting, disgraceful. I'm so pleased Spain won. It was a disgusting performance [from Argentina]."

Sports.title: Argentina media label team 'polite and respectful' as FIFA launch brawl investigation
Sports.content:
Argentina media label team 'polite and respectful' as FIFA launch brawl investigation

Argentina players have been widely criticised for their behaviour after the World Cup but it appears that some members of the South American media don’t totally agree

View 2 Images Argentina players have been slammed for their behaviour after the final whistle (Image: Getty Images)

Argentina have been labelled as ‘polite and respectful’ despite triggering an angry brawl that marred the World Cup final. The South American side were aiming to become the first side since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy as they took on Spain in New Jersey.

‌



But it did not go to plan for the reigning world champions, with Ferran Torres’ goal seeing them defeated. The behaviour of a host of the Argentinian players was also the target of criticism.

‌



Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina were both involved in post-match scuffles, the former having been sent off for his part. Enzo Fernandez was also dismissed during the game for a woeful challenge on Pau Cubarsi.

‌



Despite that, newspapers in the South American nation believe that the team behaved well. A report from Argentine paper Clarin read: “As never before, the Argentine team displayed, both on and off the field, a range of values that are rare these days. From the pitch and beyond, they gave several lessons and showed the face of a country that we would like to see away from the football pitch.

FIFA launch investigation into Argentina after 'disgusting' World Cup final scenes READ MORE :

“A team that was polite and respectful, despite a few unfortunate isolated incidents in the last match; that didn't speak ill of its rivals or try to justify its own mistakes by blaming others.”

The response to Argentina’s behaviour is very different when it comes to the UK media. Speaking after Paredes’ red card, Wayne Rooney said: "Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this with Argentina before.

‌



“It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round. That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them."

He added: "That's a reaction to them being outplayed, out-fought, out-thought on the football pitch, and then they resort to that at the end. It's poor from those two players."

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez was sent off for Argentina in extra time (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Alan Shearer said: “Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone’s face. He went for them. There is no place or space for that.

“We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible.”

Gary Neville also gave his take on the clash. He said: “They’re very competitive and I love that element of them, but (Paredes) has just been a disgrace for the last couple of games, and why the referees have allowed him to continue doing what he is doing…”

Sports.title: Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever
Sports.content:
Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever

Josh Kerr - the new fastest man over a mile - felt the financial reward he was given didn't reflect the magnitude of his achievement

View 2 Images Josh Kerr said he felt short-changed by the prize money he received (Image: British Athletics via Getty Images)

Josh Kerr criticised the $50,000 (£37.2k) bonus awarded to him for breaking the one-mile world record. Kerr's time of 3:42.66 was the quickest in 27 years, toppling previous holder Hicham El Guerrouj's by 0.47 seconds.

‌



The Scotsman sparked scenes of wild celebration in front of a sold-out crowd at the London Stadium. However, the financial reward didn't reflect the achievement in his eyes.

‌



He received the exact same sum from World Athletics as Moroccan El Guerrouj did in 1999. Once the dust had settled, Kerr called out the prize money situation.

‌



"It was a good day for me financially but $50,000 is a ridiculous number," he told The Times. "To get the same amount 27 years later is appalling, not to sound greedy.

"I know how much that took from investing in myself financially over the last eight years as a professional. I just feel like I’ve been a bit short-changed a little bit."

‌



World Athletics offer a $100k bonus (£74.5k) at flagship outdoor global championships but that sum is halved for Diamond League meetings. Kerr also admitted he had hoped to have "gone a little bit faster," although he was happy to have hit his goal.

View 2 Images Kerr smashed the 27-year world record (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

"It was just incredible, that last lap," he told the BBC. "It was just me, my shoes and the track. I was absolutely deaf in the last 110 metres. I didn't take my foot off the gas, but I started to glide and I was like, 'Oh, wow, this feels incredible.'

Article continues below

"It's incredible because I'm slowing down. So, I was like, 'I better get to the line.' So crossing the finish line, seeing 42-something - anything - was my goal, so it was great.

"I am surrounded by amazing people and was just able to stay consistent, put the work in, and I knew I had 3:42 in me. I nearly lost it there at the end, but I got over the line.

"If I'm to leave my mark on this sport as a British legend, with the legends behind me and following in their footsteps, I have to put in those performances."

Sports.title: Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in
Sports.content:
Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in

Tributes have poured in after the sad news of Kevin Keegan's death aged 75 after a short battle with cancer

View 3 Images Alan Shearer has paid an emotional tribute to Kevin Keegan following the sad news of his death. (Image: PA Wire)

Alan Shearer has led the tributes to 'hero' Kevin Keegan after the former England, Newcastle United and Liverpool boss died following a short battle with cancer. The 75-year-old was diagnosed with stage four cancer back in January and has sadly passed away.

‌



A statement from Keegan's family read: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments. A double Ballon d’Or winner, Kevin was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather.

‌



"The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

‌



Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Donald Trump brutally booed at World Cup final as Spain and Argentina fans unite READ MORE :

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Shearer, who worked under Keegan for both club and country, took to social media to share an emotional goodbye. The Magpies legend said: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss [Crying emoji]."

Keegan enjoyed an illustrious career as both a player and manager. His work at Newcastle United helped transform the Magpies into one of the best clubs in the country, and the Toon have also paid an emotional tribute.

‌



A club statement read: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters. As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

View 3 Images Keegan passed away after a short battle with cancer (Image: (Liverpool FC via Getty Images))

‌



"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him. Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev."

‌



King Kev would manage Fulham, England and Manchester City after leaving the Magpies, winning the Second Division with the Cottagers and the First Division with City.

"Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75," a City club statement read. "Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

"The promotion campaign in 2001/02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin’s family and friends at this very difficult time."

‌



View 3 Images Steve Heighway and Kevin Keegan (R) celebrate with the FA Cup after Liverpool defeated Newscatle United in 1974. (Image: Mirrorpix)

Keegan was not just a decorated manager, but a brilliant player, winning the Ballon d'Or twice during his playing career and claiming just about every trophy there is to win during his time at Liverpool.

The Reds also paid tribute to Keegan and said: "We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss.

‌



"His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin. 1951-2026."

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher, meanwhile, tweeted: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

"One of the most important men in making LFC [Liverpool} what it is today."

Article continues below

England's official channel also paid tribute to the former Three Lions boss: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away.

"Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the Three Lions from 1999 to 2000. Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
