World.title: Sask. Roughrider in fatal crash was driving on wrong side of divided highway: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Roughriders linebacker Jayden Dalke was driving the wrong way on the highway with alcohol and cannabis in his vehicle before the crash that killed him and another driver, RCMP say.

Saskatchewan RCMP sent a news release Monday morning saying officers responded to a crash Saturday night at 9 p.m. CST.

RCMP say investigation found Dalke had been driving a silver SUV northbound in the southbound lane on Highway 11 between Regina and Lumsden. The entire stretch of Highway 11 between Regina and Lumsden is divided, with two lanes in each direction.

Dalke's SUV collided with a black SUV. Both drivers died in the crash and both were the only ones in their vehicles.

Bhishma Rajyaguru, 22, of Regina was identified as the driver of the other vehicle.

Sask. RCMP say 22-year-old Bhishma Rajyaguru died in a fatal crash near Lumsden, Sask., on Saturday night. (Submitted by Dakshesh Raval)

The families of Rajyaguru and Dalke, 30, who was from Leduc, Alta., have both been notified.

RCMP spokeswoman Mandy Maier told reporters at a news conference Monday that no more details were available about the alcohol and cannabis found in Dalke's vehicle.

She asked people to be kind in their online comments.

"There's a lot of people who are grieving right now," Maier said. "There are two people deceased."

RCMP did not receive any reports about a vehicle travelling the wrong way on the highway prior to the crash, Maier said. However, she revealed that RCMP received a report at 8:27 p.m. CST about a silver SUV having left a gas station in Lumsden without paying for fuel, and that further investigation found it was the same SUV that was in the crash.

She also acknowledged the RCMP could have released information about the crash earlier. The information released was determined after "extensive consultation" to ensure the details were accurate.

"News travels fast on social media," Maier said.

Maier said she could not provide an estimate of when autopsies and toxicology tests will be completed. She said collision reconstruction investigations can take months.

RCMP do not usually reveal the names of those killed in crashes, Maier said, pointing to the public interest in this case.

She added that because both occupants were killed and there will be no court proceedings, some questions about the incident may remain unanswered.

"We may never know," Maier said. "We have nobody surviving from this collision."

Rajyaguru​'s friends have started an online fundraiser in the wake of his death.

"His parents in India are currently facing the nightmare that no parent should ever have to endure: the loss of their chil​d," the page for the campaign says.

​"We, his friends here in Canada, are coming together to ensure that Bhishma is transported back home so his family can hold him one last time and lay him to rest​."

The fundraiser organizers described Rajyaguru as a "beautiful soul, a best friend, and a beacon of light," and called the crash as "a senseless tragedy that has shattered the hearts of everyone who knew him.​"

Police have identified 22-year-old Bhishma Rajyaguru as a victim of the fatal crash near Lumsden, Sask., on Saturday night. In an online fundraiser, his friends say they have 'lost a beautiful soul, a best friend, and a beacon of light.' (Submitted by Dakshesh Raval)

RCMP say cannabis and alcohol were found in Dalke's vehicle, and that autopsies and toxicology reports will be conducted.

The Riders drafted Dalke in the sixth round of the CFL draft in 2022. Information on the Roughriders website says Dalke was returning to Regina after spending the team's bye week in Leduc.

Roughriders general manager Jeremy O'Day spoke to media about Dalke on Monday morning, before RCMP had released details of the crash.

"In football he was tough and reliable, accountable. Never wanted to let anyone down. He was someone that always wanted to do good for his teammates."

O'Day offered condolences on behalf of the CFL.

"To Jayden's family, his friends, anyone that that has come in touch with Jayden. You know, we're deeply saddened by this tragic event," said O'Day.

The Lumsden RCMP detachment is investigating the crash with the help of an RCMP collision reconstructionist.

World.title: Trump tells Carney to take action on wildfire smoke during World Cup chat
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. U.S. President Donald Trump personally told Prime Minister Mark Carney to stop poisoning American air and take action to put out wildfires burning across the country. Trump said he raised the issue of wildfire management with Carney when the two leaders appeared together to watch the World Cup Final between Argentina and Spain in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. "I told him, I mean, 'You got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,'" Trump said at Joint Base Andrews after the game. The U.S. president said he has a "good relationship" with Carney before reiterating his threat to impose financial penalties on his northern neighbour for the wildfires' impact on U.S. air quality. "If we can help them, we'll help them. But maybe they should pay some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs. But it was terrible," Trump said. "I mean you had businesses closing in particular Michigan." Carney's office issued a short statement on Monday saying that he spoke both with Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, but provided little detail on what was said. "The prime minister provided an update on the wildfire management and the comprehensive approach taken to ensure the safety of all Canadians and Americans," the statement said. Last week, cities in Michigan shut down beaches, splash pads, the Red Oaks water park and even indoor pools because of the toxic smoke that blanketed Michigan and other northern U.S. states. The Detroit Free Press reported that dozens of workers at Ford's Michigan assembly plant were taken to hospital after inhaling wildfire smoke inside non-air-conditioned plants. Trump's threats over wildfires Trump first threatened to make Canada pay for the cost of U.S. air quality in a Friday social media post when he joined some Republican House representatives' broad criticism of Canada's forest management practices calling them "wilful negligence." "We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air," the president wrote in a social media post on Friday. "This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying." This morning, I met with federal workers in Ottawa who are supporting the wildfire response efforts in Northwestern Ontario and across the country. This is one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history due to extreme heat waves and record-breaking dry conditions.… pic.twitter.com/ubS7Gupgam —MarkJCarney During a wildfire briefing in Toronto on Monday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford described Trump's comments as "disappointing to say the least." "With all the assets the U.S. has, he's sitting there complaining," Ford said. "Why don't you send up some water bombers? Why don't you start helping us, like we would help you in a heartbeat? "You should support your neighbours. That's my message to the president." On Friday, Ford reminded the U.S. president, and other Republican legislators, it was time to repay the efforts Canada undertook to restore electricity in the U.S. after Hurricane Helene in 2024 and the California wildfires last year. "If there's some politicians out there chirping away, well maybe what you should do rather than complain is send support, send help, because we have done the exact same thing for our American friends. That's what you're supposed to do," Ford said. The premier said he thinks Americans are good neighbours but need to start acting that way. U.S. senator proposes sanctions Last week, Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno promised to introduce new legislation to sanction Canada for what his office called the "wildfire pollution emergency." The text of that bill, the Canada Fire Act, posted on Moreno's website, gives Trump the power to declare if smoke originating from Canada over the last 12 months found its way into the U.S. WATCH | Ford on wildfire comments from U.S. officials: 'Rubbish': Ontario premier responds to Trump's wildfire tariff threat | Duration 3:51 U.S. President Donald Trump raised the possibility of imposing punitive tariffs over Canadian wildfire smoke crossing the border. Ontario Premier Doug Ford called Trump's words a 'bunch of rubbish,' and pointed to wildfires burning in the U.S. If so declared, the bill, which has yet to be introduced to the Senate, sets out stiff financial penalties for any Canadian official, from the prime minister to lower-level officials, involved in wildfire management. Those penalties include halting loans to entities owned or controlled by the Canadian government, stopping any imports to the U.S. of anything produced by a Canadian government-owned entity and banning any officials from entering the U.S. if they have a hand in the wildfire response. As an interim measure, the legislation asks U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to consider kicking out Canada's ambassador, chief of mission and more than a dozen other officials right down to the embassy spokesperson.

World.title: What we know about the Black teen found dead after Mississippi boat trip
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The death of Nolan Wells, a Black teenager whose body was located on an island off the Mississippi coast after he spent the Fourth of July there with three white friends, has drawn widespread attention amid an ongoing investigation and mounting unanswered questions.

Family and supporters of the 18-year-old gathered in a Mississippi church Monday to mourn and celebrate him.

Wells's death, which has prompted an outpouring of reactions online — largely fuelled by questions about race in the U.S. — captured national attention and prompted calls for an independent investigation. Here's what we know about the case and why it has garnered so much online attention:

Who is Nolan Wells?

Wells, described by his parents as having a big heart, would have turned 19 next month.

The ceremony on Monday began with tearful remarks from Wells's parents, who described their son as a warm and gentle presence, a gifted athlete and a role model to his younger siblings.

"He had a way of making people feel seen, welcomed and valued," said Christine Wonsley, the teenager's mother. "He could lift your confidence with just a few words and make you feel like you belong."

Wells's parents, Christine and Elmore Wonsley, attend a news conference in Manhattan on July 10. (David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters)

Wells attended Southwest Mississippi Community College, where he played wide receiver on the football team.

His father, Elmore Wonsley, described him as a "silent leader" among his teammates and friends, adding that he was able to make friends anywhere he went.

"He was focused on what he wanted. He wanted to make life better for his family," he told GMA. "He wanted to have his own family."

Prior to the funeral, relatives filed into at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs, Miss., for a visitation period on Monday, featuring gospel singers and a photo slideshow in which Wells was often grinning and decked out in football gear.

What do we know about his death?

Wells travelled to Horn Island with a group of friends on July 4 but failed to return with them when they left around 3 p.m.

Conflicting accounts have been given as to whether he planned to remain on Horn Island, about 11 kilometres offshore, or return with his friends.

The roughly 17-kilometre-long spit of land is near the Alabama state line. The island is uninhabited and accessible only by boat, officials said, and is popular for parties and gatherings.

His mother reported him missing shortly after midnight.

The next day, boat and rescue crews launched searches and his body was recovered in waters on the northwestern tip of Horn Island.

Wells poses with his parents in an undated photo. (Ben Crump Law/Handout/Reuters)

Authorities with the Jackson County Sheriff's Department and other agencies were quick to say they did not suspect foul play. Results of an official autopsy are still pending, and the investigation is continuing, officials say.

Sheriff John Ledbetter has said Wells's friends are co-operating with the investigation. He said initial interviews suggested Wells chose to stay on the island and that his friends believed he would get a ride with someone else.

Both the family's attorneys and sheriff's department investigators have asked witnesses or anyone with video from the island to come forward as they seek answers about the moments before his disappearance and death.

There are many troubling questions about the case, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said at a news conference on July 10 in New York with civil rights leader Rev. Al Sharpton and Wells's parents. Crump represents the family and is aiding an independent investigation, including a private autopsy.

The main question, according to Crump, is the discrepancy between what Wells's friends said and what a young woman they met on the island said.

The three friends who travelled with Wells to the island said Wells told them he wanted to stay there with the young woman when they left the afternoon of July 4, per Crump, but she has said that Wells got on the boat with the boys. Crump also said that videos circulating online allegedly show Wells in a heated argument with his friends.

Also raising suspicions, Crump said, is that Wells's phone was found not with his body, but in the possession of one of the young men who had accompanied him to Horn Island. Wells's mother tracked it down using Life360, a location-sharing app, and she said it appears that several social media messages had been deleted.

His parents said their son was an avid Snapchat user, but there were no posts or messages from the 24 hours or so before they retrieved it.

Why has his death received so much public attention?

For some Black Americans, the case has sparked painful discussions about navigating predominantly white spaces and racism, while civil rights leaders and others have renewed longstanding concerns about disparities in attention to missing persons cases involving Black victims.

Speculation and suspicion about the teen's death have been rampant online, as people grapple with the state's history of racial tension and what it means to be a Black person in a majority-white space.

Family and attorneys have said photos and videos of the Fourth of July celebration on the island, where nearly 200 people had gathered, suggest that Wells was one of very few Black people present.

The Congressional Black Caucus also echoed calls for an independent investigation into the death.

CBC News reached out, but did not receive further comment from the sheriff’s office.

Filmmaker and actor Spike Lee attends the July 10 news conference regarding Wells's death. (David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters)

Actor and producer Tyler Perry is helping pay for Wells's funeral. Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick is helping pay for an independent autopsy, and filmmaker Spike Lee attended a news conference last week in support of Wells's family.

In a fiery eulogy Monday, Sharpton promised a $50,000 US reward for any new information about the circumstances around Wells's death. He invoked the history of racist violence in Mississippi, including the lynching of Emmett Till and assassination of American civil rights leader Medgar Evers.

"The reason why a lot of people in the nation are looking at this Nolan situation is that we've looked at history in Mississippi. Some of us remember what happened in Mississippi," Sharpton said, to loud applause in the church.

"Before we can medicate and heal today, we've got to look at your history."

What happens next?

Wells’s family has launched its own investigation into his death and commissioned an independent autopsy, saying the information they have received from authorities doesn’t add up.

Crump said the family's attorneys agreed to work with the local district attorney investigating Wells's death to inspect the contents of his cellphone.

He added that the district attorney committed to presenting the investigation, which is separate from the family's independent investigation, to a grand jury once it's complete. A grand jury is typically comprised of 15 to 25 citizens who listen to the prosecutor's evidence and decide whether there is enough evidence for an indictment.

"The hope is when this is presented to the grand jury, all relevant witnesses and evidence will be presented to them, so we can have a fair and impartial investigation into the death of Nolan Wells," Crump said.

"Our lived experiences tell us that we must question everything, everybody's role, law enforcement's role. That is the lived experience as Black people in America."

World.title: Alberta government gives public libraries Jan. 1 deadline to comply with new restrictions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta government has given libraries around the province until the start of next year to introduce new policies restricting access to materials with sexually explicit images.

The province updated its Libraries Act earlier this month to set a Jan. 1 deadline for libraries to comply and ensure they're not allowing anyone 15 years old or younger to use or borrow materials containing a visual depiction of a sexual act, without a parent or guardian's authorization.

The new restriction applies to books, periodicals, comics and graphic novels, films, TV programs and video games.

Library boards also have until Jan. 1 to determine which materials should be restricted, how to regulate access to them, and where to store them separately from other resources.

Boards must also meet the same deadline to establish how to determine a person's age, and whether a parent or guardian has authorized their access to restricted materials.

The province is calling on boards to introduce policies about issuing library cards to people 15 years old or younger, and on allowing people in that age group to use library computers to access the internet or play video games.

Staff at the Calgary Public Library's Memorial Park branch are required by the Libraries Act to ensure people below the age of 16 cannot access library materials with sexually explicit images, beginning Jan. 1. (Zazak Bouarab/Radio-Canada)

Boards are also required to consider how the same age restrictions can be applied to digital resources like e-books.

The restrictions are a result of Bill 28, which was passed in May.

The Coalition of Alberta Public Libraries said this week it's still reviewing the new restrictions.

The Calgary and Edmonton public libraries said they are still reviewing the impact of the new restrictions, too.

Earlier this month, the Canadian Federation of Library Associations said it's working with colleagues across the country to address concerns other provincial governments could introduce similar restrictions.

Rules could put more stress on small libraries

Jack Alarie, press secretary for the Ministry of Municipal Affairs, said no content will be removed from libraries due to the new restrictions. Instead, he said the province wants to ensure libraries continue to be family-friendly, without affecting adults' access to them.

Bill 28 gives inspectors, appointed by the Municipal Affairs minister, the ability to look at any matter related to a library's management, administration or operation. Alarie said this is an expanded scope for inspectors, after they were previously limited to board records.

“It is reasonable that there be accountability for public institutions that are governed by provincial statute and funded by tax dollars,” said Alarie.

Rob Miyashiro, the Alberta NDP's shadow minister for municipal affairs, said the new rules are likely to cost more money for libraries and put extra stress on their staff. He highlighted that it will be especially difficult for small libraries with only a couple of employees.

WATCH | New rules introduced for Alberta's public libraries: Why the Alberta government is telling libraries to put some books out of sight | Duration 2:05 Alberta’s municipal affairs minister says new rules will require public libraries to move any material with graphic sexual content so it can't be accessed by children or young teens.

“It’s something that wasn’t necessary, and the libraries were never asking for this. In fact, the vast majority of public libraries in Alberta already had policies and practices that did what this government wants as an outcome,” said Miyashiro.

"Local decision-making is going to be minimized in favour of a centralized approach by this government."

New rules on library restrictions in schools

The province is also requiring library boards that operate a location inside a school to set up a process for the public to ask the board to review whether restrictions are needed on specific materials in these libraries.

Reviews can be asked for by students, parents or guardians, staff and school council members, other members of the public with a connection to the school, and library card holders.

Boards have until Jan. 1 to establish these processes, and must regularly review their resources to ensure they comply with the Libraries Act, and provide reports, on request, to the minister.

World.title: Meet Jimothy, the unusually round Seattle raccoon capturing hearts worldwide
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Just a few days after Norway soccer star Erling Haaland made headlines for bringing a taxidermy raccoon back home from the World Cup, a Seattle raccoon with an unusually short body has become an internet sensation after a video of it scampering across a field went viral.

The raccoon nicknamed Jimothy, which is thought to have short spine syndrome, is inspiring murals, art and even tattoos — and has become, for some, a symbol of resilience.

"I initially thought that he was a cat, and just got my phone out because I love cats. And then when he emerged from the car, I realized he definitely wasn't a cat," Kiana Hall, 33, told Reuters. Her video of the raccoon went viral after she caught him on camera July 13 in the Ballard neighborhood in northwest Seattle.

"I think he's just sort of round and a silly little guy, and people just sort of need something silly and fun in their life right now."

And people do seem to be having fun.

Jimothy was celebrated by the Seattle Mariners, the Seattle Art Museum and the Seattle Public Library on social media. The raccoon will be recognized by Seattle councillor Alexis Mercedes Rinck in a ceremony next week. The University of Washington jokingly awarded it an honourary degree.

But Jimothy isn't just a local celebrity. The story made the Manila Times in the Philippines, where Jimothy is described as an "odd-shaped raccoon." Australia's ABC News details the "cult following."

And U.K. charity The Stroke Foundation joked on Threads that seeing Jimothy relax can lower your blood pressure.

A person dressed as Jimothy races mascots during a baseball game between the Seattle Mariners and the San Francisco Giants on Saturday in Seattle. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

'He looks like a Jimothy'

When Hall first posted the video, she commented: "What am I looking at?"

"I was seeing some kind of gray, fluffy creature that was shaped sort of like an orb with really long legs," she told Reuters.

But after several commenters pointed out it appeared to a raccoon with a birth defect, she gave it a name.

"He looks like a Jimothy," Hall said.

The name stuck, and despite not knowing for sure whether Jimothy is male or female, so did the "he."

Since then, other Seattle residents have posted videos and photos of their own sightings, including one of the raccoon walking across a balcony, and a post of baby Jimothy from someone claiming the raccoon was born to a loving raccoon family in his neighbour's cedars.

"He was so small and clumsy but his mother and siblings were always so patient and caring, keeping him from falling and sometimes just carrying him," Ben Trammell wrote on Instagram.

"With all the pain in our timelines [right now], I'm really loving how connected so many people feel [with] this funny little creature."

Now, there are subreddits devoted to Jimothy fandom and websites that track its sightings. As of Monday, Hall's video had been viewed more than 18 million times on TikTok alone.

Is Jimothy OK?

Experts have said they believe Jimothy has a congenital condition that shortened its spine.

"It does look quite unusual, but it is a condition that happens in other mammals as well," veterinarian Carrie Schneider told Seattle's KIRO 7 News.

Marcie Logsdon, an associate professor at Washington State University’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital, told the Seattle Times that Jimothy's prognosis seems positive despite its short neck.

"The fact that he’s made it to this age tells me that he’s managing and that he’s adapting," Logsdon said. "I was surprised and honestly a little bit inspired that he’s that resilient."

But another expert, Brian Collins of the Cornell College of Veterinary Medicine, told the New York Post Jimothy might have a shortened life expectancy. Its malformation could make it harder to climb trees, forage for food and escape from predators, he said.

Regardless, the best thing people can do for Jimothy is let it be, a spokesperson for the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife told CBC News.

Feeding wildlife can cause animals to become habituated to humans, and can also lead to overcrowding, which can spread disease and parasites.

"We do encourage folks to leave the animal alone as it does appear to be getting around fine, unassisted, with [the] apparent congenital defect," the department said in a written statement.

"Feeding raccoons may create undesirable situations for you, your children, neighbours, pets, and the raccoons themselves."

World.title: Soccer fans divided over World Cup's first-ever halftime show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. The first-ever halftime show at the 2026 World Cup Final opened with Madonna singing, "Music makes the people come together." But online reaction to the 11-minute-43-second blur of superstar performances proved to be divided. Here’s a quick recap. On Sunday, the 67-year-old pop icon kicked off the Super Bowl-style show in vibrant colour, arriving in a jeep driven by Brazilian football legends Ronaldinho and Ronaldo before stepping onto the pitch alongside the pair. She then passed the mic over to the Muppets band, Electric Mayhem, who performed a version of The White Stripes’ iconic Seven Nation Army alongside Los Angeles Philharmonic conductor Gustavo Dudamel. Next came an explosive performance by K-pop superstars BTS, who lit up MetLife Stadium with their 2020 hit Dynamite. Shakira performs at halftime during the World Cup Final match in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. (Matt Slocum/The Associated Press) After the group danced across the field, the cameras cut to none other than Jason Sudeikis as his manager alter ego, Ted Lasso, and Brendan Hunt as Coach Beard. As they strolled across the field, the pair mused about calling in a substitute — someone who has "some heart" and "some soul" — before introducing Justin Bieber. The 32-year-old stripped the production back with an acoustic guitar performance of his 2025 hit Everything Hallelujah. Justin Bieber performs during the halftime show on Sunday. (Ashley Landis/The Associated Press) Shakira and her hips then brought the energy roaring back, teaming up with Burna Boy for their World Cup anthem Dai Dai. The show concluded on a heartfelt note with the PS22 Chorus, a choir made up of elementary school students from Staten Island, N.Y. They performed We Dance, backed by Dudamel and joined by Coldplay singer Chris Martin, who curated the entire performance, along with Shakira, the Muppets, Justin Bieber and other performers. In soccer, halftime is traditionally reserved strictly for player rest, and the rules set by the International Football Association Board limit the break to 15 minutes. Sunday's halftime break lasted a total of 27 minutes and 19 seconds — delaying the resumption of the blockbuster final between Argentina and Spain and leaving many fans and football purists less than impressed. Many viewers on X criticized both the concept and length of the show. One user wrote , "This is just embarrassing & so out of place at a football match. Half time *show*. At least surely it proves The World Cup should never be in America again. Completely killed the atmosphere of the game. We wait 4 years for THIS?" This is just embarrassing & so out of place at a football match. Half time *show*. 🥱 At least surely it proves The World Cup should never be in America again. Completely killed the atmosphere of the game. We wait 4 years for THIS? #ESPARG —MrsOblivious Another wrote , "Completely ruined the momentum of the game and it’s probably responsible for the fact that these two teams are still fighting for the first goal after 105 minutes." Others focused less on the delay than on the show’s dizzying, eclectic lineup. "I need Chris Martin to come to the front bc going from Dynamite to Everything Hallelujah at a halftime show is a choice," one user posted. Even Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher entered the chat, writing , "It’s a good job I’ve got my spiritual socks on or that halftime entertainment could’ve tipped me over the edge." Halftime show rating: 6.8/10

Very random collection of acts, prob should have just been Shakira running the show there bc she’s amazing.

Ted Lasso, vuvuzela & R9/Ronaldinho good touches. All for the kids & positivity at the end.

Didn’t need Biebs & 70% of it though lol —ryanhammer09 Not everyone was critical, however. One viewer wrote in part, "I happen to be from New York but I enjoyed the halftime show. What’s wrong with a little music to bring people together? These days everyone finds a reason to hate something." Another commented in part, "Madonna was the only one with production value befitting of a finale halftime show! She brought energy, football legends and a song with a unifying message!" One user even compared the show to its American counterpart: "World Cup Halftime Show from a performance standpoint is far superior to the Super Bowl’s in every way."

World.title: Paramount, Warner must pause merger for at least two weeks, judge says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A federal judge on Monday ordered Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery to halt their $81 billion US merger for at least two weeks, allowing states that are challenging the deal more time to see their case through in court.

Twelve states, led by California, sued to block Paramount’s pending buyout of Warner last week— alleging that such a combination would "extinguish competition" in Hollywood and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly moviegoers and cable customers across the U.S.

The states' top prosecutors called on Warner and Paramount to not close the transaction until after a court had time to "fully evaluate" their claims. And when the companies refused, they filed for a temporary restraining order — which is what District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted on Monday.

That opens the door to a potential preliminary injunction that the states are also seeking to effectively block the deal.

"This is a critical first win in our case to ensure this megamerger never sees the light of day," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement following Monday's order. "History tells the tale of what happens when a few people have great power over markets that are central to Americans' lives: fewer opportunities for more people, worse products and services for all people."

A CinemaCon attendee sports a pin expressing opposition to the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger during CinemaCon 2026, on April 14 at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. (Chris Pizzello/Invision/The Associated Press)

A Warner-Paramount tie-up would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood — as well as host of TV networks, titles filling streaming libraries and news operations.

That would include Warner's HBO Max, fan favourites like Harry Potter and even CNN coming under the same roof of Paramount-owned CBS, movies like Top Gun and the Paramount+ streaming service.

Paramount did not immediately comment on Monday's order. But the company, which was bought out by Skydance just last year, has vowed to "vigorously defend" its Warner acquisition. Paramount previously called the states' complaint "wrong on both the facts and the law," maintaining that a merger would instead strengthen competition against bigger entertainment rivals. And it touted regulatory greenlights the deal has received elsewhere, including from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last month.

The temporary restraining order granted Monday halts the deal from progressing for at least 14 days, although the pause could be extended for up to 28 days. The court has set Aug. 3 as a date for a hearing on the states' preliminary injunction motion, although that schedule could also be pushed back.

Many were previously bracing for Paramount and Warner to try closing their deal as soon as later this week. And ahead of Monday's decision, the companies proposed wrapping up a preliminary injunction hearing by the end of August, leaving time to make a possible appeal by Sept. 30 — a date on the top of Paramount's mind because it's pledged to pay shareholders added "ticking fee" compensation amounting to about $7 million US per day if the deal isn't closed by then.

But the states called such a timeline unprecedented and unfair. They maintain that money Paramount might have to incur after Sept. 30 was the risk of a decision the company made on its own — and argued in a hearing held Friday that commencing a trial in April 2027 would allow enough time to for discovery and presenting proper evidence.

Including billion of dollars in debt, Paramount's proposed purchase of Warner is currently valued at nearly $111 billion US based on outstanding shares.

Beyond California, states joining Monday's lawsuit include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington. And others — including the Writers Guild of America — are also suing to block the merger.

World.title: B.C. wants to seize 2 Metro Vancouver homes of alleged drug-smuggling gang boss
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. government wants to seize two properties of alleged drug-trafficking boss Ravinder Singh Dhanda, who was one of the lead targets of an international crackdown on three India-linked organized crime groups earlier this month.

The Director of Civil Forfeiture is going after Dhanda and his spouse Manjit Kaur Dhanda's White Rock and Surrey homes, according to a notice of claim in B.C. Supreme Court.

The claim said the defendants "did not have sufficient lawful employment, income and/or legitimate business income to acquire, finance, improve, maintain, or preserve" the properties.

The director alleged Dhanda and his associates "coordinated the storage, transport, smuggling and distribution of bulk quantities of methamphetamine, cocaine and other controlled substances over international borders, primarily between the United States and Canada, on a weekly basis."

According to the claim, Dhanda also co-ordinated the smuggling of bulk quantities of controlled substances to various organized crime groups throughout Canada and directed and conspired with others within his drug trafficking organization to assist.

"R. Dhanda directly or indirectly engaged in, facilitated, benefited from, conspired in, or was associated with unlawful activity, including but not limited to trafficking of controlled substances," said the claim.

It alleged that Ravinder Dhanda's spouse Manjit Dhanda "knew or ought to have known" how the properties were being used or "was willfully blind" to how they were used.

The claim said the properties are "proceeds and instruments of unlawful activity."

Dhanda and his spouse became the owners of the Surrey property in 2003, then became the owners of the White Rock property in 2021, according to the claim. Mortgages and liens are registered on both properties, the claim said.

A Surrey, B.C., property is involved in a civil forfeiture proceeding against Ravinder Singh Dhanda. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

The White Rock property is assessed at almost $3.7 million and the Surrey property is assessed at nearly $2.7 million.

The claim said the properties were used by the defendants "to engage in unlawful activities" that allegedly included laundering the proceeds of unlawful activity, providing or collecting property for terrorist activities and failing to declare taxable income.

Operation Hard Ball

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and the RCMP's federal policing Pacific region started a crackdown on "criminal activity, international drug trafficking, extortion, racketeering and violence" in 2023, according to the claim.

Called "Operation Hard Ball," the investigation led to 37 defendants being charged across three indictments, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Three defendants, including Dhanda, were arrested in B.C.

Dhanda remains in custody awaiting a bail hearing scheduled as part of extradition proceedings.

Unsealed indictments detail charges against three separate groups: the Bishnoi Organized Crime Group (OCG); a gang run by imprisoned Indian national, Jaggu Bhagwanpuria; and Dhanda's alleged drug trafficking operation.

In civil forfeiture proceedings, the director doesn't need to prove a charge or conviction against the defendants, but must establish that the property is either "the proceeds or an instrument of unlawful activity," according to the province.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky

The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance. While there is no scientific consensus on its effects, itâs commonly associated with heightened emotions, sleep disturbances, and symbolic transitions.

World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Scientists begin first study of whisky matured in Antarctica
World.content:
Scientists begin first study of whisky matured in Antarctica

20th Monday, July 2026 - 19:01 UTC Full article

Isla Marambio spent three years on the ice at an Argentine research station and is now one of eight single malts being analyzed to see how extreme climates shape whisky

A team of scientists has begun the first analysis of a whisky matured in Antarctica, aiming to determine what three years at temperatures as low as -35°C did to the spirit's maturation, chemistry and taste.

Isla Marambio, made by the Argentine distillery La Alazana, is billed as the world's first whisky matured in Antarctica. It was created for The 8 Continent Series, a collection of eight single malts —one from each continent— curated by Daniel Monk through Cask World. All eight will be analyzed over six months by Dr. Aline Bortoletto, a Brazilian food scientist specializing in the chemistry and sensory science of alcoholic beverages, and her team at INOVBEV in São Paulo.

The whisky was first matured for five years at La Alazana, in Andean Patagonia. Its casks were then flown south to Base Marambio, the Argentine research station on Marambio Island —known internationally as Seymour Island— aboard a military Hercules with support from Argentina's Armed Forces. Néstor Serenelli, who founded the distillery with his wife Lila, traveled with the casks and settled them into an uninsulated hut on the ice, where they stayed for three years in temperatures ranging from around -35°C to +10°C, with frost forming on the wood. Lila later made the journey south to bring the matured whisky home.

It is the coldest of the eight climates in the study, and the first time a whisky matured in Antarctica has been examined scientifically. According to Lila Serenelli, the deep cold appears to have drawn flavor from the wood while holding the spirit in and reducing evaporation, leaving a floral note she says she does not detect in the distillery's other whiskies.

What the study is looking for

Over six months, Dr. Bortoletto and her team will build a detailed chemical and sensory profile of each whisky, combining techniques such as gas chromatography with a trained sensory panel, then compare the results across the eight climates using statistical models. Titled Climate-Driven Maturation Signatures in Global Whisky: A Comparative Multi-Continental Chemical and Sensory Study, it is presented as the first scientific comparison of single malts matured across every continent.

The findings will be recorded in an international scientific report, which organizers say would be presented at food and beverage science conferences, with the aim of helping producers understand how their own climate and environment shape the spirit.

The Serenellis and La Alazana

La Alazana sits in Las Golondrinas, near Lago Puelo, in the Andean foothills of Patagonia. Lila and Néstor Serenelli founded it in 2011 as Argentina's first single malt producer, in a country far better known for its wine. They grow all their own barley and distill in copper pot stills of their own design. Lila trained at Scotland's Heriot-Watt University —the first Argentine to do so— before returning home to shape a distinctly Argentine whisky.

Separately from The 8 Continent Series, the Serenellis sent two other barrels to Base Belgrano II, an Antarctic station even farther south and colder than Marambio, where they will continue to mature for several more years.

The 8 Continent Series

The 8 Continent Series brings together eight distilleries, each with a whisky made on a different continent. The collection follows the eight-continent model, which includes Zealandia, the largely submerged landmass encompassing New Zealand that some geologists have recognized as the eighth continent since 2017.

Distillery Country / territory Continent La Alazana Argentina (Antarctic whisky) Antarctica Union Distillery Brazil South America Shelter Point Canada North America Penderyn Wales Europe Boplaas South Africa Africa Rampur India Asia Lawrenny Tasmania Australia Pokeno New Zealand Zealandia

The markedly different climates of each whisky are central to the study: all eight matured in conditions far removed from whisky's traditional homes in Scotland and Ireland.

How different climates shape whisky

Lila Serenelli, co-founder and head distiller at La Alazana, said: “We are a small family distillery in Patagonia, and to have made the first whisky ever matured in Antarctica is something we are enormously proud of. I trained in Scotland, but everything we do here is our own, shaped by our mountains, our water and our climate. Standing on the ice, looking out at the frozen sea and knowing our whisky had spent three whole years out there, brought tears to my eyes.”

Néstor Serenelli added: “Taking our casks to Antarctica on a military flight, and placing them on the ice myself, is something I will never forget. We did this as Argentines, doing what no one had done before, and we are not finished yet.”

Dr. Bortoletto said: “This is genuinely uncharted territory. No study has examined how single malt whisky matures across climates this different, from the heat of northern India to the freezing cold of Antarctica. By combining chemical and sensory analysis, we hope to give whisky lovers, and producers, a clearer picture of how much different climates and place shape what ends up in the glass.”

Daniel Monk, curator of The 8 Continent Series and founder of Cask World, said: “Lila and Néstor are the ones who made this possible. I had the idea when I dreamed of a collection with a whisky of every continent and found that Antarctica was difficult if not impossible, but they did the work, overcoming every challenge to mature whisky in Antarctica.”

He added that while Scotland and Ireland are the spiritual homes of whisky, the collection sets out to explore how far the spirit has traveled and how it is now made all over the world, in different climates. He said the study could provide useful data toward making whisky production more sustainable in the future, if producers learn to work better with their own climates.

World.title: Spain crowned world champions with 1-0 extra-time win over Argentina in the final
World.content:
Spain crowned world champions with 1-0 extra-time win over Argentina in the final

20th Monday, July 2026 - 00:47 UTC Full article

Photo: EPA/EFE/RONALD WITTEK

Spain were crowned world champions for the second time in their history by beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time in the final played on Sunday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The winning goal came in the 106th minute, after a cross from Pedro Porro that Nico Williams headed on and that, according to the match report, Ferran Torres finished to settle a game clearly dominated by the Spanish side.

The run of play reflected Spain's superiority, with 68% possession and twenty shots, eleven of them on target, against Argentina's three attempts, none on goal. The defending champions, who had reached the final hoping to repeat their Qatar 2022 triumph, barely troubled goalkeeper Unai Simón and sat back for much of the match.

The game had two decisive incidents. In the second half, the referee disallowed a Spanish goal for a foul flagged earlier in the move, with the score at 0-0. Near the end of regulation time, Argentina's Enzo Fernández was sent off for a second bookable offense after a hard challenge on Spanish defender Pau Cubarsí, leaving Argentina with ten players for extra time. The South American side finished the match with five bookings and one dismissal.

With this result, Spain claim their second World Cup, sixteen years after the one won in South Africa in 2010, when they beat the Netherlands, also in extra time, through a goal by Andrés Iniesta. The title adds to Euro 2024 and cements the generation led by coach Luis de la Fuente, who called for the achievement to be “valued.” Midfielder Rodri was named the tournament's best player.

“Destiny was written. Every final is difficult, we had Messi in front of us, but we have always relied on ourselves, playing our game,” Ferran Torres said after the match. For Argentina, the defeat dashed their bid to become the first national team to win two consecutive World Cups since Brazil, champions in 1958 and 1962.

The final closed a World Cup hosted by the United States, Mexico, and Canada, whose decisive stages were played on US soil. The tournament was marked, in its closing stretch, by the controversy surrounding Argentina, after its players displayed a banner about the Falklands following the semifinal against England, an episode FIFA is assessing for a possible breach of rules barring political messages. Argentina played the final while awaiting that decision.

World.title: Trump takes center stage at the World Cup final, presenting Spain's trophy and holding it beforehand
World.content:
Trump takes center stage at the World Cup final, presenting Spain's trophy and holding it beforehand

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 23:05 UTC Full article

The episode fits into the close relationship between Trump and Infantino, which has run through much of the tournament

US President Donald Trump was one of the central figures off the pitch at the 2026 World Cup final, co-hosting alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino the trophy presentation to Spain, champions after beating Argentina 1-0 in extra time at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Trump, who watched the match from the VIP box with his wife, Melania, also held the original trophy before kickoff, in images that circulated widely on social media.

Trump's role in the ceremony marked a change from the tournament's two previous editions. At Russia 2018 and Qatar 2022, Infantino presented the trophy alone. FIFA had announced before the final that the two would do so jointly. The handover by the host country's head of state is, however, a practice with historical precedent at the World Cup: Queen Elizabeth II presented the trophy to England captain Bobby Moore in 1966, and King Juan Carlos I did so with Italy's Dino Zoff in 1982.

Trump entregando la Copa del Mundial de Futbol del 2026 a la selección española. pic.twitter.com/u0IoU3LK6a — Orlando Avendaño (@OrlvndoA) July 19, 2026

Before the match, the trophy was brought up to the presidential box, where Trump took it and patted it before returning it to the area set aside for the ceremony. The scene drew attention for taking place outside the official on-field act, in which the cup is usually kept under guard until its presentation to the champions. While players from both teams walked past the trophy without touching it, following a football tradition, the president approached it.

The episode fits into the close relationship between Trump and Infantino, which has run through much of the tournament. During an earlier White House visit, Infantino had already let Trump hold the cup and told him the trophy is “for winners.” FIFA also opened an office in Trump Tower in New York, and at the 2025 Club World Cup final, played at the same stadium, Trump remained at the center of champions Chelsea's photograph.

The final closed a World Cup hosted by the United States, Mexico, and Canada, whose decisive stages were played on US soil and in which Trump's role was a recurring feature, from the build-up to the closing ceremony. The tournament also introduced other US-inspired novelties, such as a halftime show and the award of championship rings to the winning team. Spain won their second world title, sixteen years after the one achieved in South Africa in 2010.

World.title: ICE kills a Colombian and a Mexican in operations where they weren't the target, officials say
World.content:
ICE kills a Colombian and a Mexican in operations where they weren't the target, officials say

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 23:00 UTC Full article

Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, who had lived in Houston for three decades, had died on July 7, at a traffic stop in that city

Two Latin American migrants were shot dead by agents of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) within a week, in operations in which, as federal authorities and lawmakers acknowledged, neither was the intended target. The deaths revived protests and calls for accountability over President Donald Trump's immigration policy.

Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, died on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, when an agent fired at the vehicle he was driving. Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, who had lived in Houston for three decades, had died six days earlier, on July 7, at a traffic stop in that city. Migrant-rights groups said Durán Guerrero was authorized to work in the country; the embassies of Colombia and Mexico are providing consular assistance to the families.

The circumstances of the Maine death are the subject of conflicting accounts. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said the driver tried to flee and that, “fearing for public safety,” the agent fired. Senator Angus King, after speaking with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, gave shifting accounts of whether the man was the target of the operation, and noted that the agents were not wearing body cameras. In Houston, the Harris County District Attorney's Office opened its own investigation and issued nearly twenty subpoenas, saying the federal government was not sharing evidence.

Following the two shootings, Mullin suspended most ICE traffic stops, at the request of Republican Senator Susan Collins, who said the Biddeford case raised “critical questions.” The pause, however, lasted hours: border czar Tom Homan played it down, and the measure was reversed by government decision.

The deaths come amid a sharp increase in immigration arrests. Democratic lawmakers and former officials linked the incidents to pressure to meet arrest quotas. “When there is that relentless pressure to do more, more and more, agents make mistakes,” Deborah Fleischaker, a former ICE deputy policy director, told CNN. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticized the administration for deploying thousands of agents “without making sure they were trained.”

DHS has repeatedly defended its agents' conduct. Mullin said in May that agents “sacrifice” themselves for the country's safety and that ICE had been “demonized.” Approval of Trump's immigration policy has fallen: about 60% of Americans disapprove of it, according to an Ipsos and Washington Post poll. Various media tallies, in the absence of official figures, put at several dozen the number of people who have died in ICE shootings or in custody since the start of Trump's second term.

World.title: Lula asks Trump to explain 25% tariffs on Brazil, speaks of a "war of truth"
World.content:
Lula asks Trump to explain 25% tariffs on Brazil, speaks of a “war of truth”

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 17:43 UTC Full article

“The war I want to wage with him is a war of narrative, a war of truth. I want to show the world who is telling the truth in this tariff war between Brazil and the United States,” Lula said

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva publicly called on his US counterpart, Donald Trump, to explain the reasons behind the 25% tariffs he imposed on most Brazilian products, a measure Brasília attributes to political rather than commercial motives. The levies, announced on July 15 by the Office of the US Trade Representative, will take effect on July 22.

“The war I want to wage with him is a war of narrative, a war of truth. I want to show the world who is telling the truth in this tariff war between Brazil and the United States,” Lula said on Friday during a visit in Rio de Janeiro. The president, who is seeking reelection in the October 4 vote, said his country was “a peaceful people” and that Washington would not manage to deceive Brazilian society.

The tariffs are applied under Section 301 of US trade law, following a yearlong investigation that concluded Brazil engaged in unfair trade practices. Washington cited the treatment of US technology companies, barriers to ethanol, intellectual-property protection, the PIX payment system, and illegal deforestation linked to agribusiness. The measure includes broad exemptions, among them coffee, beef, oranges, some energy products, and aerospace parts. A parallel investigation into forced labor, concluding next week, could add a further 12.5%.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio blamed Lula for the outcome of the negotiations and said he had not negotiated “in good faith,” arguing that the president had put his “ego” ahead of a deal. Lula rejected Washington's arguments: he said his government has reduced deforestation, that 76% of the US products Brazil imports pay no duties, and defended his country's right to regulate digital platforms and to keep PIX, which he described as “a heritage” of the Brazilian people.

The dispute moved to the center of the election campaign. Lula's main rival, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, rejected the government's accusations that his family had promoted the levies in Washington and attributed the measure to Lula's own handling of the matter. He and his brother, former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, met with Trump at the White House in May.

The tariffs come on top of the 50% ones Trump had imposed in 2025, explicitly tied to the trial of former president Jair Bolsonaro — a Trump ally — sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat. Brazil's government estimates the new levies could affect 18% of its exports to the United States, some $7.4 billion, and is weighing reciprocity measures and support for affected sectors.

World.title: Andy Burnham is the Labour leader, third time lucky for the UK’s prime ministerinwaiting
World.content:
Andy Burnham is the Labour leader, third time lucky for the UK’s prime minister in waiting

19th Sunday, July 2026 - 01:35 UTC Full article

Andy Burnham sworn is as MP fom Makerfield

By Eric Shaw, Honorary Research Fellow in Politics, University of Stirling. Mr. Shaw is alzo a member of the Labour Party - A brief introduction, Andy Burnham officially becomes UK Prime Minister next Monday and can be expected to announce plans for new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, as reported by BBC.

However the Labour Party's 2024 manifesto - which the new leader said he would follow - had pledged to not issue new licenses but to honor existing ones.

At the heart of the debate are two oil and gas fields in Scotland - Rosebank and Jackdaw - which regulators approved in 2022 and 2023 under the then Conservative government, but were overturned in 2025 after a legal challenge..

The announcement will form part of a flurry of measures from Burnham including plans to take water and energy companies under public control and a new council house-building program.

He is also expected to outline new measures that will give “people breathing space on the cost of living” and intends to make a “dynamic start... focused on delivering tangible change to people's lives as soon as possible”.

However on oil and gas, BBC reports that a source close to the incoming PM said no final decisions in the area had yet been made and would be unveiled at a later date instead.

Andy Burnham has won on his third attempt to be Labor’s leader. In a wide-ranging speech to Labour MPs at a special conference in London, a jubilant Burnham pledged to “bring back hope” and promised to be a leader for all nations of the UK. But it has taken him well over a decade to get here. In 2010, as a rising star associated with the Blairite wing, he made his first bid for the leadership.

In truth, back then he had little prospect of success: he was merely placing a marker. Five years later, he stood again but could do little to derail the Jeremy Corbyn bandwagon. Yet fast-forward 11 years and his ascent seemed unstoppable. Next Monday, he will become the UK’s 59th prime minister.

To understand why and how this happened, the circumstances that created this opportunity for Burnham are key. In 2024 Labour returned to power with a thumping majority, but with little more than a third of the total vote. Within months the new government was lurching from crisis to crisis; its standing in the polls collapsed and Keir Starmer became the most unpopular Prime Minister since modern records began.

At the same time, the party faced powerful challenges from opposite ends of the political spectrum – the radical-right Reform UK and the left-wing Greens. Labor’s electorate was visibly disintegrating, its plight made stark by the disastrous local and devolved parliamentary elections of May 2026 when it shed huge numbers of local councillorsand los Wales for the first time in over a century. The message for the parliamentary Labour Party (PLP) was stark: virtually all of them were at risk of losing their seats.

In these circumstances speculation around a challenge to Starmer mounted. But why should a man twice rejected by the party so rapidly emerge as the sole contender for the crown? The key (though not sole) factors are Labor’s system for electing its leader, the balance of internal party alignments, the structure of competition and the personal factor.

In terms of the election procedures, in 2010 Labor’s leader was selected by an electoral college divided into three sections: MPs, party members and trade union political levy-payers.

This was replaced in 2013 by direct membership voting, with three categories of members – ordinary members, affiliated (trade union) members and registered supporters. (This is discussed in detail in my book, Order and Rebellion: Labor’s Managerial Politics from Miliband to Starmer, co-authored with Emmanuelle Avril.) This was the system in 2015 when Corbyn swept the board across all three categories.

But by 2026 there had been two significant changes. First, the class of registered supporters had been abolished. Second, the nominations threshold for leadership contenders had been raised from 12.5% to 20% of the PLP. It is unlikely the former had much effect but the latter certainly did, by effectively blocking anyone from the hard left from entering. This benefited the soft left, where Burnham positions himself.

Soft-left membership

There are no really reliable estimates of the shifting balance of alignments within Labor’s membership. Gauging this is difficult because of massive turnovers in membership between 2010 and 2026. Most observers would agree that membership shifted after 2015 and then to the right after 2020.

Paradoxically, the center of gravity among the rank and file did not change dramatically. Close observers of the party agreed that the mean party members tended to be soft left. This is why Starmer contested the 2020 race on a soft left platform (soon abandoned). If Burnham had done likewise in 2015, he might have won.

The structure of competition in Burnham’s three contests differed considerably. In 2010 he was not a serious contender, with the race effectively between the Miliband brothers Ed and David Ed and David. In 2015 there were four contestants: Burnham, Corbyn from the hard left, and Liz Kendall and Yvette Cooper from the right.

As a member of the shadow cabinet under Ed Miliband, Burnham had shifted to the left and was initially seen as the frontrunner. However, he made a fatal miscalculation in assuming that in response to the 2015 election defeat the party would move to the right and so he did so himself.

In fact, the party swung left and Corbyn was able to sweep up the leftwing vote – including those broadly on the soft left.

Burnham learned his lesson. After quitting parliament and winning the newly created post of mayor of Greater Manchester, he increasingly adopted a soft left posture. In the race to succeed Starmer, there were only three other plausible candidates: Angela Rayner and Ed Miliband from the soft left, and Wes Streeting from the right.

Here, chance intervened on Burnham’s side. The popular Rayner was forced to resign as deputy prime minister and deputy leader over a tax issue. Otherwise, she would probably have been in pole position. Like Rayner, Miliband, who worked closely with Burnham, was unwilling to stand against him since both shared his soft left stance. This left Streeting. His problem was simple: even if he mustered the 81 nominations he required, as a right-winger he had no chance of beating Burnham in a leadership contest. Streeting new this, so opted not to stand.

Finally, among Burnham’s personal qualities, two are worth noting. The first is his undoubted popularity among those who know him best – his Greater Manchester constituents. More broadly, he normally receives a better net rating than any other Labor politician.

The second is his willingness to take a major risk by standing for a constituency, Makerfield, that he could easily have lost. Every one of its wards were won bt Reform in the local elections and its demographics rendered it a top target for the party.

But Burnham’s unexpectedly decisive victory in the by-election demonstrated his mass appeal. For hundreds of beleaguered Labour MPs fearful of losing their seats, he was seen as their one and only lifeline. Burnham had staked his career on Makerfield and won.
