World.title: El agua que hace crecer la población de toda una comarca
World.content:
Las plantas de Bezoya en Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) son un ejemplo de cómo innovación, adaptación, sostenibilidad y responsabilidad empresarial consiguen retener a vecinos de toda la zona que quieren trabajar y vivir en el mismo lugar

Carla Pardo era una niña la primera vez que pisó la embotelladora en la que hoy trabaja; fue en una excusión escolar. Desde su pueblo, San Cristóbal de Segovia, se tardan apenas cinco minutos en coche hasta la fábrica, situada en Trescasas, y esa proximidad marca la diferencia en su día a día: “Es calidad de vida, un lujo que no se compensa con otras cosas”, confiesa esta joven de 32 años, responsable de Calidad de las dos plantas de Bezoya en la provincia de Segovia. La segunda también está cerca, a unos 25 kilómetros de distancia, en Ortigosa del Monte. La combinación ha supuesto que Pardo haya podido quedarse donde se ha criado; de hecho, acaba de comprarse una casa.

Pardo no es una excepción. La mayor parte de la plantilla de estas dos embotelladoras está formada por vecinos de la zona. Su compañero Sergio Moreno (Otero de Herreros, 41 años) entró en la de Ortigosa del Monte hace 10 años por una baja, pasó a tener un contrato indefinido y escaló: “Empecé aprendiendo a manejar distintas máquinas y carretillas”, recuerda. Actualmente es jefe del equipo de Producción. “Si respondes bien, puedes ir creciendo”, explica. “Fue la mejor decisión de mi vida a nivel profesional”. Él también es de los alrededores, vive tan solo a cuatro kilómetros de su puesto de trabajo. “He nacido aquí y no me iría ni a Segovia capital. La tranquilidad, la naturaleza y la cercanía con los vecinos son fundamentales para mí”.

Sergio Moreno, jefe del equipo de Producción, sujeta la botella de agua PI (de 3,14 litros), uno de los nuevos formatos de la marca. Santi Bur

Para Carla Pardo, “cada vez más personas pueden desarrollar una carrera profesional en un entorno rural gracias a la existencia de empresas con empleo sólido”. Su testimonio refleja una de las principales apuestas de Bebidas Bezoya, como subraya su director general, Sergio Bravo (Santander, 48 años): “Tenemos en las plantas 170 empleados y en la compañía somos 230 en total; es una plantilla muy estable a la que iremos incorporando más personas”. Los tres, Pardo, Moreno y Bravo, son el ejemplo de cómo el viaje del agua del manantial a los negocios o casas retiene el talento de los pueblos.

Diseños innovadores y más sostenibles

En embotelladoras como estas se necesitan, además, personas de muy distinta cualificación. Como afirman desde Bezoya, la empresa tiene dos objetivos: la sostenibilidad y la adaptación a las demandas de sus clientes. Como explica Bravo: “La sostenibilidad es un eje clave en Bezoya, y no solo la económica y social, también la medioambiental”. Esa gestión responsable está vinculada a la innovación y a crear nuevos productos, dos pilares que se refuerzan mutuamente. Por ejemplo, han renovado los formatos pequeños y medianos para que sean más ligeros, ergonómicos y sostenibles. Su opción de bag in box (una caja de cartón con dispensador) utiliza un 70% menos de plástico que una botella convencional de capacidad similar. Además, han lanzado la botella PI de 3,14 litros, diseñada con menos material que otras alternativas equivalentes. “Permite la comodidad de una garrafa, pero es fácil de almacenar, de servir y cabe en la nevera”, describe Bravo.

Pero el objetivo de ser más responsables medioambientalmente es transversal, y empieza por el origen. “Cuidamos la diversidad del entorno del manantial”, asegura su director general. Lo hacen de la mano la Red Natura 2000, fundamental para la conservación de la naturaleza en la Unión Europea, cuyo propósito es asegurar la supervivencia a largo plazo de las especies y los tipos de hábitat. Esta red asegura la compatibilidad entre las actividades humanas y el uso adecuado del territorio.

Las fábricas de Bezoya emplean energía 100% renovable. Además, valorizan más del 90% de residuos y compensan la diferencia con reforestación, según Bravo. Toda la flota comercial es híbrida o eléctrica y las botellas están hechas en su totalidad de otras botellas recicladas.

Para trabajar en estos propósitos de forma más eficiente, en febrero la empresa matriz, Pascual, lanzó el Proyecto Aura, una reorganización que ha convertido sus distintas áreas de negocio en cinco compañías especializadas (Lácteos, Café, Distribución e Internacional, además de Hidratación). Todas mantienen un gobierno común, pero cada una cuenta ahora con un equipo propio y una hoja de ruta para adaptarse mejor a su mercado. En el caso de Bezoya, “el objetivo es trascender el agua mineral sin gas y consolidarse como una compañía centrada en la hidratación saludable”, describe Bravo, al frente de esa unidad.

Sergio Bravo, director general de Bebidas Bezoya, posa desde la embotelladora de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) con la Sierra de Guadarrama de fondo. Santi Burgos

Un agua de calidad

El consumidor es cada vez más exigente. “Su preocupación van más allá del precio, pide productos que no solo le ayuden a cuidar su salud, también quiere impactar lo mínimo en el medioambiente”, afirma Bravo. Por eso, responden con “máxima coherencia” y con mineralización muy débil (’Para vivir muy fuerte’, dice su lema). Como apunta Pardo, esta tipología “puede generar en el organismo una especie de limpieza. Las células del torrente sanguíneo están cargadas con distintos minerales y, al tener el agua una mineralización muy baja, si esa concentración es alta, la arrastra”. En cambio, si el agua tiene una mineralización media, el equilibrio se mantiene y, si es alta, aporta más electrolitos y minerales, “lo que ayuda a recuperar las sales”.

Pardo, como responsable de Calidad, se asegura de que el producto llegue al consumidor con las mismas propiedades con las que emerge del manantial. “El agua viene así de la montaña: es buena y pura, con una composición estable químicamente”, explica. La travesía hasta que llega al envase da comienzo en la sierra de Guadarrama, en un perímetro de protección al que llaman la zona de captación. Allí, la pluviometría (la lluvia o la precipitación que cae) se filtra por un terreno granítico, un tipo de suelo que deja esa mineralización tan baja.

Carla Pardo, la responsable de Calidad de las plantas de Bezoya, en el laboratorio de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia). SANTI BURGOS

El alumbramiento, la primera vez que se ve el agua, es ya dentro de la botella. Después pasa por el etiquetado, el loteado y el empaquetado, y ya queda lista para que el consumidor la beba. En todo momento, su temperatura se mantiene fría. “En invierno es aproximadamente de 9 grados y en verano puede llegar hasta los 13″, indica la experta.

En la zona de captación “no hay absolutamente nada; ni pozos ni ninguna extracción externa, porque el agua nos llega por gravedad”, describe la segoviana. Tampoco realizan intervenciones en el entorno más allá de la construcción necesaria para la planta que, en los últimos años, se ha ampliado. Sergio Moreno ha sido testigo de esta evolución: “Me motiva haber llegado desde abajo y ser parte de estos cambios; la fábrica, la línea, la formatos... Todo se ha modernizado”. Una evolución que, más allá de la adaptación a las demandas de los clientes y a la sostenibilidad, permite que el trabajo perdure, los puestos se mantengan y la comarca logre una población estable.

A Moreno el trabajo en cadena le gusta; le permite ayudar al compañero que va antes y al que va después. “He podido coordinar equipos y conocerles de primera mano. Algunas veces ayudo a personas que ya estaban cuando entré, y noto cómo he crecido. Es muy bonito”, confiesa. También se enorgullece del resultado, del producto final: “Vas de vacaciones y ves botellas de Bezoya. Además, a la gente le encanta. Es muy gratificante”, resume.

World.title: Olimpia Coral Melo y Fernanda Medellín: “La violencia digital sexual es extraterritorial. No tiene fronteras”
World.content:
Las creadoras de la ‘Ley Olimpia’ exigen un tratado internacional que imponga un castigo económico a las grandes tecnológicas que “sustentan, agravan y monetizan” las agresiones en sus plataformas

“Es la primera vez que me pongo una blusa enseñando los hombros” es lo último que la mexicana Olimpia Coral Melo dice antes de despedirse el día de esta entrevista. ¿Por qué? “Fui muy pública, vi mi cuerpo desnudo por todas partes, me cuesta enseñar piel, como si fuese una vergüenza que perdura”. Ahora tiene 36 años, fue con 18 cuando su expareja publicó un video sexual suyo sin su consentimiento. “Esto me llevó a encarnar de viva voz y en carne propia lo que significa esta violencia”, afirma. Tanto que su trabajo desde aquel momento y el de la organización Defensoras Digitales consiguieron una norma contra esa violencia en México. Tanto que ese conjunto de reformas legislativas lleva su nombre, la Ley Olimpia.

Ella es una de las miles y miles de mujeres que cada año enfrentan esos ataques online. Según la ONU, alrededor del 40% de las mujeres y niñas han experimentado alguna forma de violencia digital. “Y cuando es sexual, es como si te violaran sin penetrar tu cuerpo”, añade Coral Melo. Recuerda que se burlaban cuando empezó a decir que lo que ocurre en la red es igual de real que la violencia física: “Olimpia, ¿vas a hacer cárceles virtuales o qué?”.

Prisiones online, no, pero sí una norma aprobada ya en todos los estados mexicanos y que traspasó a otros países. Fernanda Medellín, sentada enfrente de Coral Melo, repasa: “Hay ya 39 leyes en el mundo que nacen de alguna forma de la Ley Olimpia. Estamos para aprobar en Bolivia y Ecuador. Nos quedamos en el segundo debate en Colombia. Va a Honduras, a Guatemala”. Medellín (29 años, Ciudad de México) es directora de Comunicación y Vinculaciones de la Red Latinoamericana de Defensoras Digitales y miembro de Red Carolina, también portavoz del Movimiento #LeyOlimpia, que “un movimiento político organizado y articulado en toda América Latina”.

Ha sido la base de la Ley Modelo Interamericana contra esta violencia, aprobada por la Organización de los Estados Americanos (OEA), que la ONU reconoce como un hito. En Estados Unidos trabajaron durante dos años junto con The Believe Me Community, uno de los grupos que impulsó la Take It Down, la legislación integral que tipifica la difusión de contenido íntimo sin consentimiento y que se aprobó el pasado año.

Fernanda Medellín, en la redacción EL PAÍS, tras la entrevista. Moeh Atitar

Ambas quieren que se entienda eso. Coral Melo insiste: “Olimpia no es la víctima que contó su caso y a raíz de eso se hizo una ley, no. Nosotras hicimos esa ley, cada verbo rector, cada coma, cada punto está hecho y analizado. No éramos abogadas, nos hicimos. No éramos psicólogas, nos profesionalizamos. No éramos diputadas, pero hicimos aquello desde el saber situado, desde las víctimas y desde nuestros territorios”.

También desde ahí nació OlimpIA, una app que Defensoras Digitales creó junto a AuraChat.IA para atender consultas de víctimas de violencia digital 24 horas, siete días a la semana, en más de 50 idiomas; y están trabajando para incorporar la lengua de señas mexicana e incluir llamadas. Fue reconocida como uno de los 50 mejores proyectos de inteligencia artificial del mundo en el Ai Action Summit del pasado año.

“Las aborígenes, las patarrajadas, las indígenas, las del tercer mundo, esas hicimos esa IA. Llevamos desde 2013 haciendo un trabajo de pedagogía, legislativo y tecnológico cañón. Ca-ñón”. Y en revisión continua: “Somos críticas con nuestro propio trabajo, es la mejor y la única postura que se puede tener. Siempre hay cosas que cambiar según evolucionan las circunstancias: mañana, en cinco o en diez años”.

Los días que pasaron en Madrid, invitadas por la Fundación Carolina, participaron en el Curso de Verano de la Fundación, pero no solo. Se reunieron “con el Ministerio de Igualdad, el de Transformación Digital, con legisladores, colectivas, escritoras, activistas, defensoras y sobrevivientes”, relatan las dos. “No vinimos a hacer turismo sino incidencia política”, apunta Coral Melo.

Y se detiene un momento en eso: ”No había cruzado el charco jamás. Y al final del día, en una historia colonial, de subordinación, para alguien como yo, que viene de un pueblo, Huauchinango, en Puebla, es impresionante”. Ella, nombrada una de las 100 personas más influyentes del mundo por la revista Time en 2021, no lo dice solo como algo individual, sino plural. “El trabajo de las morras, vengan de donde vengan, llegando a todas partes”.

No “para exportar nada. La Ley Olimpia no es algo que se exporta, sino que se construye desde las víctimas y en cada territorio”, dice Coral Melo. Y, sigue Medellín, “es contra el algoritmo patriarcal, que tiene modelos de aprendizaje, que es una extensión de la violencia sistémica que vivimos en los espacios materiales”.

Añaden que las redes sociales dejaron hace tiempo de ser sociales y democráticas, y son espacios privados que, apunta Medellín, “sustentan, agravan y monetizan la violencia que se da en ellas”. El día que se aprobó la Ley Olimpia en Quintana Roo, “los bots empezaron a etiquetar a cada legislador con mi video sexual, y con un texto en el que preguntaban: ¿Cómo van a aprobar la ley de esta pinche puta que de puta se convirtió activista y ahora quiere tener una ley? Así las redes", dice Coral Melo. ¿Qué hizo? Siguió como si nada. Se aprobó la ley.

Y si hubiese querido hacer algo hubiese tenido el problema que tienen tantas, el acceso a la justicia: “Muchas veces ni puedes denunciar aunque quieras, porque las pruebas que necesitas por parte de las plataformas a veces ni siquiera caen en la cancha de los Estados donde pones esa denuncia. Esta violencia es, entre otras cosas, extraterritorial. No tiene fronteras”. Y que las plataformas “no se hagan responsables, viola los derechos humanos”.

Olimpia Coral Melo, en la redacción EL PAÍS, tras la entrevista. Moeh Atitar

Ante eso, vienen trabajando en algo que definen como “urgente e imprescindible, un tratado internacional, global, que exija a las plataformas no solo en lo político y en lo social, sino en lo económico”. Es parte de lo que han estado hablando los días que han pasado en España.

En las reuniones que han tenido han puesto sobre la mesa la posibilidad de un acuerdo entre ambos países en materia de violencia digital, y dos trabajos que ya han hecho en México: la creación de una Cartilla de Derechos de las Mujeres como la que el año pasado publicó el Gobierno del país latinoamericano, y de la que ya se han repartido más de 27 millones, desde escuelas a espacios comunitarios, a mujeres y a hombres, y traducida a 35 lenguas indígenas; y la guía EMA, un protocolo para saber cómo abordar la violencia digital en las escuelas. EMA por Ema Bondaruck, una adolescente argentina de 15 años que se suicidó en agosto de 2024 después de que un compañero compartiera sin consentimiento de ella un video de ambos manteniendo relaciones sexuales.

En México llevan tiempo insistiendo en un cambio al TMEC, el Tratado de Libre Comercio entre su país, Estados Unidos y Canadá, específicamente al artículo número 19, el que regula el comercio digital. Pero no parece muy viable por el momento. Sobre todo después de que el Gobierno de Estados Unidos anunciara el 1 de julio que no iba a renovar el TMEC “en su forma actual”, es decir, a 16 años, sino que se va a revisar de forma anual. Lo que complica aún más la situación.

“Pero, pero”, dice Coral Melo. “Nos levantamos desesperanzadas y jodidas a veces, cansadas también. Camino todos los días por la calle donde me violaron: las redes. Cada vez que abro mi celular vivo ansiedad. Pero hoy, cada vez que buscas mi nombre en internet, ya no soy Olimpia la puta, la zorra, la del video sexual. Soy la de la Ley Olimpia porque logramos cambiar el algoritmo”. Ambas aseguran que “independientemente del sistema político” que encuentren, van a seguir avanzando: “En cada pequeña cuestión que podamos. Y no vamos a soltar la toalla por un pacto digital global”.

World.title: Los homicidios suben de 5 a 9 en Barcelona por el crimen organizado, pero el resto de los delitos caen
World.content:
Un total de nueve homicidios se han cometido en la ciudad de Barcelona en los primeros seis meses de este 2026; tres de estos asesinatos están relacionados con el crimen organizado y hay un cuarto que también podría estarlo, aunque la investigación sigue abierta. Los datos de homicidios, que pasan de cinco a nueve, contrastan con el resto de las infracciones penales, que disminuyeron un 11,2%, durante el primer semestre, hasta situarse en 74.350 hechos delictivos denunciados. “Vamos por el buen camino. Es una disminución histórica de los delitos. Los hurtos han caído un 21%. Ante el ruido, presentamos resultados”, ha afirmado el alcalde advertido Jaume Collboni tras celebrarse este lunes en la Junta Local de Seguridad.

Pese a los buenos datos estadísticos, el incremento de homicidios, del 80%, preocupa y más teniendo en cuenta que, en el mismo periodo de 2025, la cifra ya era alta: cinco crímenes. La situación ha sido analizada en la Junta Local de Seguridad celebrada, este lunes, en el Ayuntamiento de Barcelona, donde los cuerpos policiales han advertido de una mayor presencia de armas de fuego incluso en los escalafones más bajos de las redes de narcotráfico. Además, a los reunidos no se les olvida que el tiroteo que acabó con la vida de un menor en el parque de la Pegaso no entra dentro de esta estadística. Cinco de los nueve homicidios cometidos este 2026 han sido resueltos policialmente con la detención de los presuntos autores.

Collboni ha pedido un aumento de penas por la tenencia de armas. “No queremos esta gentuza en la ciudad. No queremos que Barcelona sea el campo de batalla de estas bandas organizadas. Estamos a tiempo de frenar esta situación y que no vaya a más”.

¿A qué se debe el incremento de los homicidios? Los Mossos d’Esquadra señalan que las armas de fuego aparecen cada vez con mayor frecuencia en los escalones inferiores de las organizaciones dedicadas al tráfico de drogas. Según las investigaciones policiales, cada vez es más habitual la utilización de armas de fuego entre narcotraficantes, en especial entre organizaciones de la Europa del Este. Las emplean bien para evitar que otros grupos les roben los cargamentos de droga, bien para mantener o disputar el control de zonas. Son homicidios que, en algunas ocasiones, se encargan en el extranjero y los ejecutan sicarios que se desplazan hasta Barcelona y abandonan el territorio poco después.

De hecho, y al margen de las estadísticas de Barcelona, en medio año, seis personas han sido asesinadas a tiros en Cataluña. Son solo dos menos que en todo 2025. Los heridos por arma de fuego también han incrementado, con 18 hasta junio, frente a los 28 de todo el año anterior. Los analistas de los Mossos dibujan cuatro perfiles que se pertrechan con armas de fuego: los pocos que las usan para cometer robos, las agrupaciones no muy sofisticadas que se dedican a un amplio abanico delictivo, la persona con un estilo de vida desestructurado que decide armarse y los narcotraficantes.

Presidida por el alcalde Collboni, en la junta local de seguridad han participado la consejera de Interior, Núria Parlon; la subdelegada del Gobierno en Barcelona, Mari Carmen Garcia-Calvillo; así como representantes de los cuerpos policiales, de la judicatura y de la Fiscalía.

Las estadísticas destacan que los delitos relacionados con la multirreincidencia —robos y hurtos principalmente— han bajado un 15,9%. Los Mossos han identificado a 2.190 delincuentes activos con riesgo de persistencia. De ellos, 771 ya figuraban como multirreincidentes en el semestre anterior (se les atribuyen 3.372 robos o hurtos) y 1.419 son nuevas incorporaciones (se les atribuyen 2.904 actos delictivos). A todos ellos se les imputan 6.276 delitos patrimoniales cometidos en Cataluña. Según los datos policiales, otros 2.023 ladrones clasificados como multirreincidentes han dejado de actuar durante 2026 en la capital catalana.

El Ayuntamiento mantiene que parte de la reducción de estos delitos se debe a la oficina adscrita a la fiscalía de la Guardia Urbana que comenzó a funcionar en 2026. Durante sus primeros cuatro meses de actividad gestionó 72 expedientes. Los cuerpos policiales tuvieron conocimiento, en el primer semestre, de 74.350 infracciones penales cometidas en Barcelona, frente a las 83.705 registradas durante el mismo periodo de 2025. La reducción del 11,2% supera el descenso medio del 8,1% del conjunto de Cataluña.

La cifra de delitos es también un 12% inferior a la registrada hace diez años. El dato de este semestre se encuentra por debajo de la media de 83.356 infracciones de los primeros semestres del periodo comprendido entre 2017 y 2026. El número de detenciones disminuyó un 6,7%, al pasar de 18.596 a 17.359, y las personas investigadas bajaron un 8%, de 25.423 a 23.378. El índice de resolución se situó en el 38%, 1,7 puntos más que un año antes.

Los cuerpos policiales realizaron 378.480 actuaciones, un 0,4% más; movilizaron 135.887 dotaciones, un 4,1% menos; e impulsaron 3.291 dispositivos, un 2,2% más. Los agentes identificaron a 167.618 personas, un 13,9% menos, y tramitaron 59.858 infracciones administrativas, un 13% menos.

Los hurtos caen un 21,1%

Los delitos contra el patrimonio representan el 83,4% de todas las infracciones penales registradas en Barcelona. Durante el semestre disminuyeron un 13,5%, al pasar de 71.626 a 61.971. La mayor reducción se produjo en los hurtos, que continúan siendo el delito más habitual de la ciudad y representan el 47,2% del total. Entre enero y junio se registraron 35.092 hurtos, frente a los 44.449 del mismo periodo de 2025, lo que supone una caída del 21,1%. Las estafas disminuyeron un 5%, de 5.432 a 5.163; los daños, un 2,7%, de 4.814 a 4.686; y los robos o hurtos de uso de vehículos, un 6,6%, de 1.123 a 1.049.

Los principales indicadores relacionados con armas blancas disminuyeron durante el semestre. Los incidentes vinculados a estas armas bajaron un 20,9% y los robos violentos asociados, un 29,1%. Los delitos de odio aumentaron un 64,3% respecto al mismo periodo del año anterior.

Las denuncias por agresiones sexuales disminuyeron un 9,4% en términos globales. En el ámbito de la violencia de género se redujeron un 13,8%. La evolución fue distinta en la violencia doméstica. En este ámbito, las agresiones sexuales pasaron de 21 durante el primer semestre de 2025 a 32 en el mismo periodo de 2026, un aumento del 52,4%.

Dentro de la violencia doméstica también aumentaron los homicidios, pasando de uno a dos; los quebrantamientos, un 70,9%, de 79 a 135; y las coacciones, un 18,9%, de 37 a 44. Los malos tratos descendieron un 5,6%, de 550 a 519, y las amenazas bajaron un 12,2%, de 180 a 158.

Respecto al incivismo, la Guardia Urbana gestionó más de 51.000 incidencias. Las molestias en el espacio público representaron el 31% del total. Las incidencias más habituales fueron las molestias provocadas por personas en la vía pública, con 11.309 actuaciones; las relacionadas con ruidos o música, con 10.255; y las molestias procedentes del ruido de establecimientos, con 4.233. También se gestionaron 2.770 incidencias relacionadas con obras, 2.460 casos de animales heridos en el espacio público, 2.384 infracciones de ordenanzas municipales, 1.918 avisos por animales abandonados o extraviados y 1.249 actuaciones relacionadas con objetos perdidos. Las intervenciones por botellón aumentaron un 19,4%, mientras que las relacionadas con la venta ambulante crecieron un 14%.

Durante el primer semestre, los cuerpos policiales desactivaron 74 puntos de venta de drogas y se recuperaron 22 narcopisos.

Expulsados 126 multirreincidentes

Un total de 126 delincuentes multirreincidentes que fueron detenidos en Barcelona durante el primer trimestre de 2026 han sido expulsados de España, 45 de ellos mediante acuerdo judicial. El dato es prácticamente idéntico al del año pasado, cuando en la primera mitad de 2025 se ejecutaron 130 expulsiones.

Las operaciones policiales realizadas desde enero han permitido identificar a más de 7.330 personas y detener a 80 por infracciones de la legislación de extranjería, según los datos compartidos este lunes por la subdelegada del Gobierno en Barcelona, Mari Carmen García-Calvillo, en la Junta Local de Seguridad de Barcelona.

World.title: SpaceX se hunde un 46% desde sus máximos en Bolsa y sufre con el retraso del lanzamiento del Starship
World.content:
SpaceX vuelve a sufrir este lunes en Bolsa, con caídas, por momentos superiores al 3%. La firma se ha visto penalizada por el retraso en el lanzamiento del decimotercer vuelo de prueba de su cohete Starship, ahora reprogramado para este jueves 23 de julio. En este caso, un fallo en el encendido de un motor Raptor 3 ha obligado a abortar automáticamente el intento anterior. El cohete transportará 20 satélites Starlink V3 por primera vez.

Con este retroceso, las acciones de la compañía de servicios espaciales e inteligencia artificial (IA) controlada por Elon Musk se dejan cerca de un 46% desde su máximo histórico, por encima de 225 dólares, registrado tras su OPV, la mayor de la historia. Los títulos han llegado cotizar este lunes en 120,26 dólares, precio que supone una pérdida de valor de mercado desde el citado máximo histórico cercana a 1,4 billones de dólares. Su capitalización bursátil se ha situado por debajo de los 1,6 billones, tras haber coqueteado con los tres billones, cota que llevó a SpaceX a superar en valor de mercado a Microsoft y Amazon tras su estreno en la Bolsa.

Además, las acciones han caído por debajo del precio de ese debut, llevado a cabo el pasado 12 de junio, de 135 dólares.

Según Bloomberg, SpaceX está teniendo un rendimiento inferior al de la mayoría de las grandes OPV del Nasdaq, y es probable que continúe esta tendencia a medida que se disipe el impulso inicial. Sus acciones se dispararon casi un 50% al cierre de su primer día a mediados de junio, convirtiendo a Elon Musk en el primer billonario de la historia, pero la euforia se está desvaneciendo.

La empresa de Musk parece estar inmersa en la búsqueda de nuevos clientes para ampliar sus fuentes de ingresos. SpaceX está en conversaciones para vender capacidad de procesamiento al Departamento de Defensa de Estados Unidos, según publicó The Wall Street Journal el pasado viernes. De esta manera, SpaceX ampliaría sus acuerdos de infraestructura. El acuerdo, que podría alcanzar varios miles de millones de dólares, es similar a los contratos previos que SpaceX ha firmado con Alphabet y Anthropic PBC.

En junio, Google acordó pagar a SpaceX 920 millones de dólares al mes por capacidad de procesamiento como parte de un acuerdo de servicios en la nube que se extiende hasta mediados de 2029. Anthropic también acordó en mayo pasado pagar a la empresa de Musk un total de 1250 millones de dólares al mes por capacidad de procesamiento para dar soporte a su software de inteligencia artificial Claude.

Estas conversaciones surgen en un momento en que el ejército estadounidense busca construir centros de datos en sus instalaciones.

A pesar del citado descenso en Bolsa, los analistas de Wall Street siguen siendo mayoritariamente optimistas con respecto a la compañía. Parte de este optimismo se basa en la capacidad de Musk para cerrar acuerdos de infraestructura y expandir la filial de inteligencia artificial de SpaceX.

Así, Adam Jonas, analista de Morgan Stanley, ha otorgado un precio objetivo para SpaceX de 300 dólares por acción. El banco de inversión prevé que la empresa registre un crecimiento vertiginoso en el futuro previsible. El estudio parte de la base de que los ingresos de SpaceX pasarán de 18.700 millones de dólares en 2025 a 319.000 millones en 2030 y a 3,3 billones en 2040. La mayor parte de este crecimiento proviene de la inteligencia artificial, sector en el que Morgan Stanley confía en que SpaceX desarrolle infraestructura orbital para la conectividad global y la IA.

World.title: Ex-police officers seek recognition after apology to Moluccans
World.content:
A group of around 100 former police officers have asked for official recognition of what they went through during the violent confrontations with young Moluccans in the 1970s, a month after prime minister Rob Jetten apologised on behalf of the government for the treatment of the Moluccan community.

Four retired officers filed a petition with Assen city council and the police recognition foundation on behalf of the group, the Volkskrant reported. They argue that the government ordered them to enforce a hardline policy against the Moluccan community which made the situation worse, and which the state has now admitted was wrong.

“We want it recognised that the hard policy also caused suffering for the police,” retired officer Ed Jissink (76) told the paper, describing a period in which officers’ homes were firebombed and a patrol car was riddled with bullets in an ambush. Some colleagues later developed PTSD or took their own lives, he told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur.

Broken promises

Some 12,500 Moluccans – around 3,500 soldiers who had fought on the Dutch side in the Indonesian war of independence, together with their families – were brought to the Netherlands in 1951 and housed in camps, including the former concentration camps Westerbork and Vught, on the promise that their stay would be temporary.

When it became clear the Netherlands would not support an independent Moluccan republic, frustration among the second generation boiled over into violence, including the 1977 train hijacking at De Punt, in which two hostages and six hijackers died, and the 1978 hostage-taking at the provincial government building in Assen, which left two people dead.

Police recognition

Jissink said his own view began to change in 1974, when he saw how stateless Moluccans were treated. He later refused to take part in a training exercise practising live fire on demonstrators, which the police subsequently ended. He hopes the lesson will be remembered now that many politicians are again calling for tougher treatment of some migrant groups.

John Wattilete, president of the Moluccan government in exile, said the officers were right to raise the issue “without diminishing Moluccan suffering”, since they too had been used to manage what was really a political problem.

He is calling for a full investigation into the government’s role in the period. The national police force said the officers’ request deserved a serious response.

World.title: Picnic makes first operating profit in NL
World.content:
Online supermarket Picnic made a profit in the Netherlands for the first time last year, 10 years after its launch, according to annual figures published on Monday and reported by the Financieele Dagblad.

The Dutch arm booked an underlying operating profit of €4 million, but heavy spending on new distribution centres in Germany pushed the group as a whole to a net loss of €272 million, slightly more than the year before.

The number of customers across the Netherlands, Germany and France grew by 700,000 to 3.6 million.

Picnic, which delivers in three-quarters of the Netherlands, is still in dispute with unions FNV and CNV over which collective labour agreement should cover its delivery workers. It lost a court case last year over unpaid evening and weekend supplements and is negotiating a settlement while appealing to the Supreme Court.

World.title: Asylum agency claims €185m from hotel reception middleman
World.content:
The refugee settlement agency COA is claiming €184.7 million from René Derksen and his company LCHD, which arranged emergency accommodation for asylum seekers in hotels across the Netherlands, the Financieele Dagblad reported on Monday.

The agency has secured a claim against Derksen’s farmhouse in Didam, Gelderland, blocking any sale of the property. It is is one of the largest claims ever brought by a Dutch government body against a company.

COA confirmed to the paper it has started legal proceedings against LCHD and its directors over “a dispute about the execution of the assignment by LCHD and the termination of rental agreements”, but declined to comment further while the case is before the courts.

LCHD acted as COA’s exclusive intermediary for hotel accommodation from spring 2022, when the arrival of refugees from Ukraine left the agency scrambling for beds.

Over two and a half years, COA paid the company more than €500 million to book hotel rooms nationwide. FD reported earlier that Derksen paid himself more than €40 million in dividends over the period.

Derksen has been a suspect in a criminal investigation since 2023, alongside his former business partner Bob van der Valk, a member of the hotel family.

Prosecutors and the fiscal investigation service FIOD are looking into the two men’s cooperation and the money flows between them; both are suspected of, among other things, private-sector corruption.

Derksen has denied any wrongdoing, saying his prices were transparent and everyone involved knew LCHD was a commercial party making a “logical minimum margin”. LCHD has lodged a counter-claim against COA for what it calls unjustified breaches of contract.

The agency spent €2.5 billion on emergency accommodation in hotels and on cruise ships in 2024, against €1 billion on regular reception.

World.title: Major transport disruptions over A27 bridge safety warnings
World.content:
The Merwedebrug, which carries the A27 motorway over the river Merwede near Gorinchem, has been closed to all lorries since Saturday evening.

Roads agency Rijkswaterstaat said inspections found the bridge’s steel was weaker than expected in several places, and that it could no longer guarantee the structure would hold under heavy traffic.

Cars, vans, motorbikes, buses and emergency vehicles can still use it.

Lorries are being sent on long long detours as a result. It is not clear how long the closure will last.

Transport association TLN, which represents Dutch hauliers, said the impact was enormous. “Transport operators are already facing sharply rising costs,” the group said, pointing to a new lorry levy introduced on July 1 and higher diesel prices. “Extra detour kilometres only increase the financial pressure.”

The nearby Papendrechtsebrug closed last week for nine months of maintenance, cutting off one alternative route. The Merwedebrug was last shut to lorries in 2016, when cracks were found in its beams. That closure lasted nearly three months. A replacement bridge is due to be built starting this summer.

World.title: Drugs lab find forces evacuations in The Hague
World.content:
Up to 200 residents of a street in The Hague were allowed back into their homes at 11pm on Saturday, after police finished dismantling a drugs lab found in a house in the Segbroek district.

Residents of dozens of homes on the Meidoornstraat, along with their pets, were told to leave by 1pm on Saturday and were taken in at the district office on Fahrenheitstraat while the police and and a specialist firm removed the remaining chemicals.

The city council said on Sunday there was no longer any acute danger, and that the evacuation had been a precaution against exposure while the material was being taken away. Residents have been advised to keep their windows shut because of the smell.

Police were called to the house at around 1pm on Friday after a report of a strange smell, and found a lab still in operation. Officers shut down the production process by pumping out the chemicals. A 39-year-old man from The Hague who had come into contact with the liquids was taken to hospital and arrested.

A 34-year-old man from Voorburg was arrested at around 10pm on Friday. A 44-year-old from The Hague and a 71-year-old from Leiden were also held. Police are still investigating what type of lab it was and are canvassing the neighbourhood for witnesses and camera footage.

According to NOS, barrels holding thousands of litres of chemicals were found at the property, of which 500 to 750 litres were removed on Friday. A spokesman for the regional safety board told the broadcaster that a lab of that size would not normally be found in a residential area.

World.title: Music colleges draw internationals as Dutch student share falls
World.content:
Only around two in 10 students training as performing musicians in the Netherlands are Dutch, according to figures from education agency DUO obtained by public broadcaster NOS.

The Dutch share of students at conservatoires – the country’s higher music education colleges – has fallen from 52% to 22% over the past 20 years. Nine HBO colleges teach music at degree level and seven offer a master’s in performance. Of those master’s students, 78% come from abroad.

People in the sector blame 15 years of cuts to music teaching. “Far from all schools have structural music education, where children can get to know music,” said Jan van den Eijnden, senior adviser at cultural education body LKCA and a teacher at the Tilburg conservatoire. Music lessons outside school have become fragmented, with big differences in cost and availability, he said.

The arts council Raad voor Cultuur has calculated that the culture sector, which includes music education, has lost more than €500 million a year relative to other sectors since 2005.

Many music schools and arts centres have closed, and there is less room for one-to-one tuition. “That comes at the cost of developing talent,” Van den Eijnden said.

The drop is showing up in amateur music too. At the Wereld Muziek Concours in Kerkrade, a four-yearly wind music festival with orchestras from 28 countries, no Dutch orchestra entered the youth division this year.

Van den Eijnden and WMC artistic director Björn Bus both said the government should guarantee organised, affordable music tuition, pointing to Belgium, where lessons are far cheaper, and Luxembourg, where free tuition is written into law.

International student numbers in the Netherlands fell for the first time in two decades this academic year, a decline the government has sought as it works to limit recruitment.

World.title: Save yourselves while you still can: an assimilated introduction
World.content:
Our regular columnist Molly Quell is worried that she might have gone a bit too far with her inburgering process.

“They were fine, but…” I trailed off. I couldn’t quite put my finger on why I hadn’t enjoyed meeting my husband’s colleagues after we ran into them at a pub.

My (Dutch) husband and I were out with some (Dutch) friends when several of his (non-Dutch) work acquaintances happened by the bar where we were set up with beers and bitterballen.

The group was welcomed to join us, chairs were procured from nearby tables and another round of trips was ordered.

The colleagues were jolly, with conversation running from summer holiday plans to obscure folk traditions from their various homelands.

And yet, they irked me.

As he and I walked home, my husband asked the standard, post-social-engagement debrief questions. He probed about my hesitation over his colleagues.

“They didn’t introduce themselves,” I said, finally articulating what had bugged me.

The internationals, I realised, hadn’t engaged in the Dutch ritual of introducing themselves to everyone at the table, with a firm handshake and requisite eye contact.

Ten years ago, I would have told you with great confidence that this was a silly and awkward social interaction. That it is disruptive at parties and gatherings. That you forget everyone’s name immediately and then run the risk of not knowing their name if you get into real conversation later.

I’m not here to defend the practice. But I have now become so accustomed to it that it bothers me when it’s not done.

I’ve gone too far with my integration.

I’ve integrated a lot. I swim in canals. I happily go to the nude, mixed-gendered sauna. I’ve sold stuff on King’s Day and bought plates with Albert Heijn zegels.

Those are all defensible. Jumping in a canal is really keeping me cool this summer and I still use my plates.

But mandatory group introductions at social gatherings? I should self-deport and spend some time thinking about what I’ve become.

This is more or less how all human traditions come to pass. Enough people do something enough times, it becomes normalised, and now I’m congratulating 25 people sitting in a circle on someone else’s birthday.

In general I do like Dutch Introduction Culture. Dutch teenagers are much more comfortable interacting with adults than teenagers of other nationalities, in my experience. I assume this is because they have been forced from a young age to introduce themselves to everyone.

You say hello. You acknowledge that there is another person present. You do it in all facets of human interaction. At meetings and events and, goddammit, when you run into your colleague at the pub.

But to go so far as to look down upon lovely people who have no idea it is expected of them and therefore don’t do it? Next thing you know, I’ll be carrying a “Grenzen dicht” poster at a far-right rally.

When you live amongst people, you absorb their cultures and customs. I spend most of my time around Dutch people these days and my sense of reality has been warped.

Honestly I think it’s too late for me. I’m offended by the idea of putting on a bathing suit to go to a sauna. I grow increasingly frustrated with colleagues who cannot simply say directly what they want. A few weeks ago, I teased a friend for having a “luxurious” lunch.

Reader, it was a salad.

Save yourselves, get out while you still can. But make sure you firmly introduce yourself upon arrival.

World.content:

A password manager used by several Dutch organisations concealed its Russian origins, according to an investigation by OCCRP, the international journalists’ collective, with Dutch partners Investico, De Groene Amsterdammer and NU.nl.

Passwork, which lets employees store company passwords in a digital vault, presents itself as a European firm based in Spain.

In reality, the researchers say, the software was developed in Russia in 2014, and a Russian sister company is certified by the FSB security service – a process requiring source code to be reviewed by state-approved auditors.

Novar, one of the largest builders of solar parks in the Netherlands, stopped using the software within a day of being informed by Investico and reported the matter to the National Cyber Security Centre. Regional broadcaster RTV Noord said it would carry on using it.

The journalists found no evidence that passwords were stolen or data compromised. Passwork’s chief executive denied any relationship with the Russian firm, saying the products merely share a common codebase origin.

A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to sign an agreement granting them certain rights. The proposed law would have marked the first time that Poland had recognised same-sex relationships in domestic law. However, Nawrocki argued that such a move would threaten the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. The measures in question were approved by both houses of parliament in May and June with the support of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The proposed law would have allowed couples, both same-sex and opposite-sex, to enter into a new type of contract, signed before a notary and then submitted to the registry office. It would have granted them some of the rights available to married couples, including joint property and tax settlement, access to their partner’s medical information, exemption from inheritance and gift taxes, and the right to decide about their partner’s burial if they died. However, the two main opposition parties – the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) – voted against the legislation, and Nawrocki himself also made clear that he intended to veto it. The government’s majority in parliament has approved a bill that would grant same-sex partners some of the rights available to married couples. However, President Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has made clear he will veto the law https://t.co/hx8viUN6QH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 29, 2026 On Friday morning, the president confirmed he would not be signing into law the two bills passed by parliament that would have introduced the new system. He said that the measures would effectively “introduce civil partnerships through the back door”, and that such partnerships are “intended to replace or substitute the institution of marriage”. “As the guardian of the constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the special status of marriage defined in article 18 of the constitution as a union between a woman and a man, placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” he added. Nawrocki also argued that the proposed measures were contrary to the principles of social justice because they would have granted such couples some of the privileges of marriage but without all of the same obligations. He also noted that the proposed new type of contract could be terminated far more easily than a marriage. “Marriage, which best secures family stability, cannot become one of many equally valid options offered by the state administration,” declared the president. “The family is a community fundamental to the survival of the nation.” However, Nawrocki added that, as he has previously said, he remains open to legislation that would grant loved ones rights relating to healthcare and various administrative issues. But only if it “does not create an alternative to marriage” or “introduce ideological changes to family law”. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision was condemned by Tusk, who called it “an expression of contempt toward people and their right to happiness and a normal life”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, accused the president of “turning his back on the two million Poles living today in informal relationships”. However, she pledged that “the veto will not halt social change”. If such change “cannot go through the door, then [it will go] through the window”. Kotula noted that Poland has already begun legally recognising same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union member states, after being ordered to do so by the European Court of Justice. While “not all benefits are yet available” to such couples, “this is something that I intend to deliver”, she added. Prezydenckie weto to wyraz pogardy wobec ludzi i ich prawa do szczęścia i normalnego życia. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 However, the government’s ability and willingness to take such action, even when it cannot be vetoed by Nawrocki, is hampered by internal disagreements over the issue within Tusk’s coalition. The Left (Lewica), from which Kotula hails, and Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party are generally in favour of strengthening LGBT+ rights. But they have met with resistance from more conservative elements in the coalition, in particular the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). The measures vetoed today by Nawrocki were already a compromise within the government: earlier plans to introduce same-sex civil partnerships were watered down to instead simply allow same-sex couples to sign a contract granting them certain rights. However, opinion polls show that the Polish public itself is in mostly in favour of recognising same-sex relationships. State research agency CBOS last year found its highest-ever level of support for the introduction of civil partnerships, with 62% of Poles in favour. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. Over 62% are now in favour, up from 52% last year and just 25% in 2011, when the question was first asked https://t.co/Y9ydpbwsoU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukrainian teen indicted by Poland for working on behalf of Russia to stir historical tensions
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have indicted an 18-year-old Ukrainian accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tensions between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of slogans in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which massacred Poles during World War Two. Among the sites where he placed graffiti were a monument to Polish victims of those massacres (pictured above), as well as a memorial dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. If found guilty, the suspect could face up to life in prison. The history of the UPA has been at the heart of an ongoing diplomatic dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv. However, the actions in this particular case took place in 2024 and 2025, before the current crisis emerged. Prokurator z dolnośląskiego wydziału PZ PK skierował do Sądu Okręgowego we Wrocławiu akt oskarżenia przeciwko Illii K., któremu zarzucono popełnienie 47 przestępstw związanych z działalnością dywersyjną i sabotażową na rzecz obcego wywiadu. 45 zarzutów dotyczy umieszczania na… — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 16, 2026 The suspect in the case was detained in August 2025, shortly after graffiti glorifying the UPA had appeared on a monument in Poland honouring victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles. On Thursday, prosecutors announced that they have issued an indictment against the suspect, whom they named only as Illia K. under Polish privacy law. He is accused of 47 crimes in total. Of those, 45 are for “acts of subversion and sabotage for the benefit of foreign intelligence, consisting primarily of writing slogans in Ukrainian on the facades of buildings and in memorial sites with the text ‘Glory to the UPA’ and red-and-black flags attributed to the UPA “, prosecutors said. Those actions “were aimed at inciting hatred on national grounds, deepening antagonisms between Poles and Ukrainians, causing social unrest and creating a sense of helplessness of state authorities”. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. The issue has recently flared up again after President Volodymyr Zelensky in late May named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. Russia has also long sought to exploit such tensions, and Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) notes that Illia K.’s actions were carried out “at the request of the Russian security services”, which were seeking to “incite conflicts between the Polish and Ukrainian nations”. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 In addition, Illia K. also faces one charge of participation in an organised criminal group and another of preparing for an act of subversion or sabotage that would have involved flying a drone over Poland’s Armed Forces Day parade in Warsaw last year, which was attended by President Nawrocki. Prosecutors note that the accused “acted for financial, not ideological, reasons”. He was paid for his actions in cryptocurrencies. That is typical of the so-called “disposable agents” Russia increasingly uses, who are amateurs – often young Ukrainians or Belarusians – hired and paid through messaging service Telegram. The suspect has been held in pretrial detention since he was arrested by the ABW last year. If found guilty, he could face up to life in prison. Prosecutors say that, although Illia K. initially admitted to the charges against him, he later decided to change his stance and has pleaded not guilty while exercising his right to remain silent. The head of Poland's security services has appealed to Ukrainians, the country's largest immigrant group, not to be tempted to earn money by acting as Russian agents. Russia regularly recruits Ukrainians in Poland to carry out espionage and sabotage https://t.co/aa5UUWWBrx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2025 Poland has in recent years detained, charged and in some cases convicted dozens of agents accused of carrying out espionage, sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” on behalf of Russia and its ally Belarus. In March, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism (ICCT) reported that Poland is now the “primary focus of Russian activity” when it comes to sabotage. In June, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski warned that Moscow is “waging a full-scale cognitive war against us” and that there is a “Russian fifth column” operating in Poland. Russia is “waging a full-scale cognitive war against us”, Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has warned. He also said that there is a “Russian fifth column” operating in Poland https://t.co/wsmZSvYnzN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Volkswagen hires 100 sheep to cut grass at Polish solar farm as experiment in agrivoltaics
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Carmaker Volkswagen has deployed a herd of 100 sheep to keep grass under control at a solar farm that powers one of its factories in Poland, providing a greener alternative to mechanical mowing. The project, which is being run in partnership with a local university, will also contribute to research on agrivoltaics, the name given to the use of land for both solar generation and agriculture. Scientists will assess the impact of the practice on animal welfare and the wider ecosystem. In 2016, Volkswagen opened a major plant near Poznań, Poland’s fifth-largest city. The facility employs around 3,000 people and mainly produces VW’s Crafter van. In 2023, the company opened a solar farm next to the plant. On sunny days, its 31,000 photovoltaic panels can power the whole factory, though over the year as a whole it supplies around 25% of its electricity. Volkswagen has now announced that, earlier this year, it welcomed around 100 sheep to the solar farm. They are grazing on the 27 hectares of land around the panels as an alternative to mechanical mowing. “The animals adapted very well to the new conditions,” says Justyna Nowak-Gajek, the owner of the flock. She explains that the sheep are splitting into smaller groups and “grazing peacefully”, whereas herds that feel unsafe tend to stick closer together. Meanwhile, scientists from the Poznań University of Life Sciences (UPP) are studying the impact of the project on the animals’ welfare and behaviour, as well as the functioning of the entire ecosystem. “We are checking, among other things, whether shade created by the panels reduces heat stress in animals, improving their comfort and living conditions,” says Joanna Składanowska-Baryza from the university’s Faculty of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Sciences. “At the same time, we are analysing changes in the microclimate, vegetation and soil to identify solutions that facilitate the effective combination of energy production with agricultural activities.” Volkswagen has chosen Poland as the location for a new €1.7bn plant producing materials for electric vehicle batteries. The investment has been welcomed by the Polish government, which is providing €350 million in grants for the project https://t.co/xh0LuzHOyq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2023 The study is expected to inform the wider practice of agrivoltaics, which aims to “create [solar] installations that coexist with their surroundings and bring additional benefits to the environment and local communities”, says Quanta Energy, the firm that constructed Volkswagen’s solar farm. “The photovoltaic farm now produces more than just green energy,” adds Marzena Pillich-Grońska, director of the Volkswagen plant. “It has also become a place where we support biodiversity, local agriculture, and the development of scientific knowledge.” In recent years, a number of Polish cities, including Kraków and Katowice, have also recruited sheep and goats as a greener alternative to mechanical cutting of grass on municipal land. Various firms operating in Poland have been investing in renewables to supply themselves with energy. In 2024, the largest chocolate maker in Poland, Mondelez Polska, said it would spend $1 million (3.8 million zloty) on solar installations at its production sites in the country. Successive Polish governments have also been seeking to bolster green energy. Last year, the country generated 29.4% of its electricity from renewables, up from 9.4% a decade earlier. Onshore wind led the way with 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. However, in 2023, a group of business associations and international companies, including Google, Amazon, Mercedes and Ikea, warned the government that there must be more rapid development of green energy in order to attract continued investment in Poland. However, since then, figures show a period of stagnation, despite the current government pledging to accelerate Poland’s green transition after taking power from its conservative predecessor in 2023. World.title: Senior official under former Polish government detained over media campaign that attacked judges
