World.content:
London – Irish no-frills airline Ryanair on Monday said net profit slumped 34 percent in its first quarter as the Middle East conflict sent jet-fuel prices soaring and impacted ticket sales.

Profit after tax dropped to 538 million euros ($616 million) in the three months to the end of June, from 820 million euros one year earlier, the Dublin-based carrier said in a statement.

Ryanair, which is Europe’s biggest airline by passenger numbers and flies mainly across the continent, said the cost of fuel not subject to advance purchase agreements had soared owing to the US-Iran war.

“Operating costs rose 11 percent to 3.81 billion euros as the price of our 20-percent unhedged jet-fuel more than doubled” in the first quarter, chief executive Michael O’Leary said in the earnings statement.

While passenger traffic grew six percent, fares dropped six percent.

Fares “required stimulation as the Middle East conflict led to consumer hesitancy, concerns about EU jet-fuel shortages, economic uncertainty and later bookings”, O’Leary said.

He added that Ryanair’s net profit for the remainder of its financial year “remains highly sensitive to… conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine, the price of unhedged jet-fuel, macro-economic shocks” and European air traffic control strikes.

Ryanair’s share price slid nearly six percent in Dublin midday trading after investors reacted to the bigger-than-expected drop in profits.

The airline’s “results show just how quickly nervousness surrounding the war has seeped into booking patterns and operational costs”, noted Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

“It’s a sign that consumers are once again tightening their belts and delaying discretionary spending, leaving airlines exposed not just to soaring jet fuel costs but also the prospect of softer demand.”

World.title: Iraq leads Gulf oil exports growth despite Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq was one of the main drivers of the increase in crude oil exports from the Gulf region during the first half of July, according to shipping firms Kpler and Vortexa.

This development comes at a time when oil export levels from the region were at their peak since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in late February, despite reduced tankers’ movements in the Strait of Hormuz due to increased military operations.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Kuwait, and Iran increased by roughly 16 percent compared to June, hitting approximately 12 million barrels per day, according to Kpler, while Vortexa estimated the figure at 13.06 million barrels per day.

Iraq experienced the largest increase in oil shipments among the Gulf countries during that period, contributing significantly to the overall growth in crude exports alongside Saudi Arabia and Iran, according to Vortexa.

Despite this improvement, Reuters noted that oil shipments from the Gulf region are still approximately 32 percent below their pre-war level of 17.6 million barrels per day in February.

The number of oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz plummeted to three on a single day, the lowest level since May, raising fears about growing tensions and potential threats to Red Sea commerce, which might affect global oil flows.

World.title: Burnham becomes new UK PM after meeting king
World.content:
London – Andy Burnham became British prime minister Monday after meeting King Charles III at Buckingham Palace and was set to set out his vision for the country after taking over from Keir Starmer.

Starmer departed Downing Street on Monday morning, insisting in a farewell speech his two years in office had made Britain a better place.

The monarch met Starmer to accept his resignation and Burnham arrived next for the formal procedure in which the king asked him to form the next government and he accepted.

The 56-year-old is the sixth prime minister to enter Downing Street in the last 10 years.

“I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago,” Starmer told reporters in his farewell speech outside his central London office.

“I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved,” he added.

Burnham will face an in-tray overflowing with challenges with little time to make his mark.

In an interview with The Times published late Sunday, Burnham said he wanted to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil.

“What we’ve been doing hasn’t been working. That’s the way I see it,” he said.

“I am going to try and do things in a different way.”

In his first speech, Burnham will set out “priorities for restoring confidence in government and giving Britain more breathing room” amid the cost-of-living crisis, his team said.

Delivering growth and devolving power to regional communities are also expected to feature.

Also on Monday he is likely to announce his senior cabinet appointments, with all eyes on who will replace Rachel Reeves as finance minister.

The former mayor of Greater Manchester, nicknamed the “King of the North”, has been parachuted in by the Labour Party, after Starmer resigned last month, with MPs viewing him as the party’s best chance of reining in Nigel Farage’s anti-immigration Reform UK party.

– ‘Bigger, bolder’ –

Among Burnham’s most urgent challenges will be a tepid economy, high government borrowing costs, a ballooning welfare bill and irregular migrants arriving in small boats that have fuelled support for Reform.

Unpredictable energy prices due to the US-Iran war and a volatile American president in Donald Trump also threaten to buffet his premiership.

Burnham told The Times he would take a “different approach to public spending, and to running the economy — more focused on early investment, early intervention, setting people up for success, and much less paying for failure.”

He promised “early moves to help” with the cost of living, saying that while campaigning he heard the “pressure people feel around their finances”.

Starmer led Labour to power in July 2024 in a landslide election victory after 14 years of Conservative rule.

He announced that he would resign as prime minister and Labour Party leader in late June after a string of scandals, missteps and policy U-turns blighted his leadership.

But Burnham, who only returned as a member of parliament four weeks ago, has little room to manoeuvre amid sluggish economic growth, high public debt and strict financial rules requiring him to balance government spending against tax revenue.

– ‘Last chance’ –

Burnham was an MP between 2001 and 2017, serving as a minister in the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.

He has since reinvented himself as a man of the people, melding a relaxed, folksy style with slick social media videos.

But he has only three years to turn things around, with Reform leading in polls ahead of the next general election expected in 2029.

Burnham told supporters on Friday his Labour takeover was the “last chance” for the party to get things right.

Critics have accused Starmer’s government of being under-prepared for power when he was elected in July 2024.

Burnham has insisted he has a “plan”.

But his swift “coronation” as Labour leader has raised questions on how he will achieve his aims.

His first policy announcement came on Saturday when he scrapped Starmer’s flagship nationwide digital ID scheme, estimated to cost £1.8 billion over three years.

A spokesperson said the time and resources would be diverted “to where it’s most needed, such as helping with the cost of living”.

World.title: Boeing gets order for 100 737 MAX jets from leasing company SMBC
World.content:
Farnborough – US aircraft maker Boeing said Monday that it has received an order for 100 of its 737 MAX jets from leasing company SMBC Aviation Capital.

In the first major order to be announced at the Farnborough Air Show that opened in the UK on Monday.

The head of Boeing’s Commercial Airplanes division, Stephanie Pope, said that the order “reflects the strong demand we are seeing for the 737 MAX family’s efficiency, reliability and versatility”.

Following production quality issues, lawsuits, and an overhaul of its governance, the US company plans to stage a major comeback at Farnborough, just outside London.

The green light from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in October 2025 to lift the cap on production of the single-aisle 737 MAX, its best-selling aircraft, is seen as an important milestone.

It is also awaiting the certification — after several years of delays — of its three new aircraft.

SMBC’s order, the value of which has not been disclosed, covers 60 737-10 aircraft and 40 737-8 aircraft.

“Our partnership with Boeing goes back more than two decades, and this order reflects market momentum, as our airline and investor customers look to increase capacity with the 737-10,” said SMBC chief executive Peter Barrett.

“This order will support their growth ambitions well into the next decade and reflects our strong confidence in the Boeing 737 MAX and sustained demand for fuel-efficient, technologically advanced narrowbody aircraft,” he said.

The company, based in Dublin, Ireland, and described as the world’s leading aviation finance platform, manages a fleet of 1,700 aircraft for more than 170 airlines worldwide.

Boeing also announced Monday that Saudi carrier Riyadh Air is exercising options for 28 787 Dreamliners from an order placed in 2023, and will convert 20 options to the largest variant of this aircraft.

Riyadh Air has also “confirmed an order for six additional Airbus A350-1000s, bringing its firm commitment for this type of aircraft to 31,” said the European aircraft manufacturer, Boeing’s rival, in a separate statement.

World.title: Indus Water Treaty in present form no longer exists, Pak aiding terrorism: India
World.content: The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) with Pakistan will no longer function in its present form, the government has concluded hardening its position on the contentious water issue amid little indication of Islamabad discontinuing its covert backing of cross-border terrorism.India is not yet actively considering abandoning the World Bank-brokered 1960 Treaty â an option it still has on the table - but a source speaking on condition of anonymity said it's not in India's interest to remain a party to the Treaty anymore.India had formally sought a review and modification of the IWT citing demographic shifts, clean energy priorities and new climate realities, prior to putting the Treaty in "abeyance" last year in retaliation for the Pahalgam terrorist attack."It would be accurate to say that the IWT in its present form will not function at all. If provisions related to river water sharing have to be reactivated, they will have to be done in a different form. Not in the present form," said the source, adding India will await further developments before considering the maximalist option of withdrawing altogether from the IWT.The IWT does not have an exit clause, but it's of significance to India that Article 60 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT) states that a significant violation of a treaty by one party allows other affected parties to suspend the treaty in whole or in part.While India and Pakistan are both not party to the VCLT, India believes that if it invoked customary international law, then Pakistan's state sponsorship of terrorism could be considered such a breach of obligations.According to Indian authorities, as a sovereign state, India cannot be compelled to stay in a treaty that is demonstrably not in its interest. These assertions come in the middle of efforts by Pakistan to internationalise the IWT issue by citing "unilateral and unlawful" suspension of the Treaty and claiming it threatens the water security and livelihoods of its 240 million citizens. Outside of the Treaty framework, India continues to provide issue flood warnings to Pakistan to ensure protection of lives and property.India believes that Pakistan has created an elaborate victimhood narrative, ignoring the fact that more water of the Indus system is lost in Pakistan due to surface runoff than India's entire share under the Indus water stream. Sources also point to how Pakistan has since 1976 not built a single large-scale storage project or invested in modern water management, despite receiving nearly 80% of the Indus Basin waters under the Treaty. As far as India is concerned, Pakistan's problem is water management, and not water availability.Fow India though, the central issue remains Pakistan's support to cross-border terrorism. India maintains that there is no deadline for keeping the IWT in abeyance. "The Treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism. This is the threshold condition," said a source, adding that Pakistan continues to provide enabling platforms just across the LoC to terrorist groups and individuals banned by the UNSC 1267 Sanctions Committee."During this period, India will pursue the optimal utilisation of its legitimate rights through scientific basin management, modern engineering practices, infrastructure modernisation and responsible stewardship of water resources," said the source.

World.title: 'Power does not last forever': Rahul Gandhi's warning to police after tear gas, lathicharge on student protesters
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Monday warned police officers that 'power does not last forever' and 'accountability will certainly be enforced', saying the Constitution, not the government is their 'master'.

His remarks came after police used tear gas and lathi-charged protesters during the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) march towards Parliament over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak.

In a post on X, Rahul said peaceful protest was a fundamental right and warned officials against 'blindly following orders' to act against students.

Delhi Police used tear gas and mild force to disperse protesters who attempted to march from Jantar Mantar to Parliament on the opening day of the Monsoon Session.

The protest was organised by the CJP, which has been demanding accountability over the alleged examination irregularities and the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

In his post on X, Congress MP wrote, "Peaceful protest is an inviolable and fundamental right."

Addressing police personnel and government officials, he added, "Every police officer and government employee blindly following orders to attack India's innocent students should keep this in mind: The Constitution is your master.





Power does not last forever. Accountability will certainly be enforced."

Earlier in the day, Lok Sabha LoP also shared a video message in which he criticised the police action against the protesters and accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of being 'the most anti-youth Prime Minister in India's history.'

He said the students protesting in Delhi were not criminals but were demanding a fair and functioning education system.

"Tear-gassing students, lathi-charging students is not democratic. It's not India's way and it is not the way this should be done. They have legitimate demands. The prime minister should accept these demands and do something about it," Rahul said in the video.

He also alleged that repeated paper leaks had affected millions of students and claimed the government had failed to hold those responsible accountable.

The remarks came after police cleared the month-long protest site at Jantar Mantar by Monday evening following clashes during the march towards Parliament.

The stage, tents and other structures at the site were dismantled, while police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed in the area.

Despite the crackdown, protesters continued gathering on nearby roads and said the agitation would continue until their demands, including the resignation of the education minister, were met. Several protesters alleged they were injured in the police action, while others claimed they were briefly held inside Metro stations and faced restrictions on access to water during the protest.

The protest was launched by the CJP over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and examination irregularities. Thousands of demonstrators attempted to march towards Parliament on Monday, but security personnel stopped them near Parliament Street, leading to clashes and the use of tear gas and lathi-charge to disperse the crowd.

World.title: CJP march: Police say detained protesters 'not students'; more arrests likely
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

on Monday said the protesters detained during the Cockroach Janata Party's march to Parliament were not students and that their identities were being verified.

A senior officer, requesting anonymity, told news agency PTI that Delhi Police had initiated the process of registering FIRs in connection with the clashes, damage to police vehicles and destruction of public property during the protest.

According to officials, police are also investigating the motive behind the clashes. They added that even "outer side angles" would be probed.

This comes after clashes during which police claimed that stones were pelted at security personnel by the protesters, prompting a lathi-charge.

Police sources told PTI that more than 100 protesters were detained from different locations, including Parliament Street, Patel Chowk, Constitution Club, Shastri Bhawan and adjoining areas, and shifted to different police stations and temporary detention centres across Delhi.

Several videos showing police caning protesters in response to the alleged attack and preventing them from marching towards Parliament surfaced on social media.

According to the officer, the investigation has been intensified and teams are examining video footage, CCTV recordings and other evidence to identify those involved in the violence.

"Those found responsible for attacking police personnel, damaging police vehicles and public property will face strict legal action," the officer said.





Police sources said they were verifying the authenticity of all the videos and that appropriate legal action would be taken based on the findings.

The officer added that further arrests were likely as the probe progressed and more suspects were identified through technical and field investigations.

Police are also scrutinising social media videos and other digital evidence to establish the sequence of events and identify those who allegedly participated in the violence, the officer said.

Thousands of protesters converged on central Delhi despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which bars unlawful assemblies except at designated protest sites with prior permission.

The march coincided with the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, prompting one of the biggest security deployments in New and Central Delhi.

Police claimed that protesters repeatedly attempted to breach multilayered barricades erected around Parliament Street, Jantar Mantar and other sensitive locations, resulting in confrontations with security personnel.

World.title: 4 Indians killed, 1 critically injured after cargo ship attacked off Ukraine's Odesa coast
World.content:
Smoke rises from a vessel on fire, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine in Odesa.

Attack on Indian-crewed vessel

Black Sea tensions rise

NEW DELHI: At least four Indian nationals were killed and one was critically injured after the commercial vessel MV Golden Leo came under attack while departing Ukraine's port of Odesa on the evening of July 19, the ministry of external affairs said on Monday.In a statement, the MEA said there were 17 crew members on board the vessel, including five Indian nationals, when the attack took place."As per information available, four Indian nationals have tragically lost their lives, while one is hospitalized in a critical condition. Our Mission in Ukraine is closely monitoring the situation and is making every effort to extend all possible assistance to those affected," the ministry said.The MEA expressed its condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured Indian national a speedy recovery."We extend our deepest condolences to the families of the deceased Indian nationals and wish the injured Indian national a speedy and full recovery," it said.The ministry condemned the attack, saying commercial shipping and civilian crew members should not be targeted."India condemns such attacks and reiterates that targeting commercial shipping and endangering innocent civilian crew members, or otherwise impeding freedom of navigation and commerce, is deplorable and should be avoided," the ministry said.According to Ukrainian authorities, the MV Golden Leo, a Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship carrying corn, was struck by three Russian cruise missiles shortly after departing the port of Odesa on Sunday. The vessel was reportedly manned by a crew from India and Syria, according to Reuters.The strike triggered a fire on board and led to an overnight search-and-rescue operation. Ukrainian officials said several crew members were killed, while others were rescued. A Reuters witness in Odesa also reported seeing smoke billowing from the vessel off the coast.The vessel is owned by Mumbai-based Ocean Grace Shipping Ltd, according to LSEG data.The attack comes amid renewed fighting in the Black Sea, a crucial shipping route for Ukrainian grain exports. After commercial shipping resumed under arrangements aimed at easing global food supply concerns following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, both Russia and Ukraine have recently stepped up attacks on ports, cargo vessels and maritime infrastructure.Ukraine has accused Russia of intensifying strikes on its deepwater ports and commercial ships, while Russia says it has targeted fuel storage facilities and infrastructure linked to Ukraine's military operations. The renewed attacks have raised fresh concerns over the safety of commercial shipping and global grain supplies, as both countries remain among the world's leading grain exporters.

World.title: 'No prima facie case': HC rejects plea of Mamata Banerjee faction to operate TMC accounts worth Rs 440 crore
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Calcutta high court on Monday refused interim relief to the Mamata Banerjee-led faction of the

(TMC), rejecting its plea to operate three party bank accounts frozen by the

(ED).

Finding no prima facie case in favour of the petitioners, Justice Krishna Rao dismissed the request for interim relief.

The court directed the ED to file its affidavit-in-opposition within three weeks, after which the petitioners will have two weeks to submit their reply, if any. The matter will be heard again on August 26.

The ED had earlier frozen the three bank accounts, which collectively held Rs 440.42 crore, as part of a money laundering probe linked to an FIR registered by the West Bengal Police over alleged dishonest financial transactions, unlawful collection of funds, and suspected routing of money through certain party accounts.

Justice Rao also observed that the ED's freezing order, issued on July 7, was not brought to the notice of a coordinate bench headed by Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya. The court noted that neither the state nor the petitioners informed the bench about the order, as the central agency was not a party to the earlier proceedings.

On July 9, Justice Bhattacharyya had appointed a special officer to facilitate the operation of the three accounts by the Mamata Banerjee-led faction of the TMC for day-to-day and legal expenses.





The petitioners had approached the court challenging the ED's initiation of an Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR), the equivalent of an FIR, in the matter.

According to ED officials, the agency's preliminary investigation found that around Rs 160 crore was transferred from TMC bank accounts to Carewell Aviation India Pvt. Ltd. and its related entity between April 2023 and June 2026.

The company allegedly routed Rs 82.96 crore to another newly incorporated entity during the same period, officials claimed.

Investigators found that a "significant" amount was transferred to the entity, of which Rs 112 crore was allegedly used to purchase an Embraer Legacy 600 business jet and an AgustaWestland 109SP helicopter, officials added.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: Who will ask if you’re home? The economy growing around urban loneliness
World.content:
India is the second-loneliest country in the world, according to a study by JB.com. The ranking offers a stark lens through which to view a country that is also aging rapidly, urbanising quickly and watching its traditional social structures thin out.

In 2011, India had about 100 million people aged 60 and above. Projections by the Technical Group on Population Projections, cited in the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementationâs report Elderly in India 2021, show that this figure will more than double to roughly 230 million by 2036, around 15 per cent of the population. By 2050, UNFPAâs India Ageing Report 2023 estimates, nearly one in five Indians will be 60 or older.

But loneliness is not waiting for old age.

It is already present in the rented flats of young migrants, in the quiet of a single-person home, in weekends spent scrolling through other people's lives and in the small, almost invisible moments when there is no one to ask, âAre you home?â

For Minal, from Bihar and living alone in Pune, loneliness is âfeeling I donât belong anywhere and nobody cares about me.â She calls herself âpretty socialâ, but in her current city âhas only few people I know so I have phases when I go out alone.â





A typical weekend is split between âone day I go out to eat somewhere nice and one day I stay in, cook something and journal or watch a movie.â

At home, she spends â8â10 hoursâ on screens. After closing Instagram and seeing peers travelling or getting engaged, she says she feels âempty and restless and also shit about myselfâ.

Swadha, who spent years living alone in Noida for college and work, remembers the strange contradiction of returning home.

âThere is a sense of reliefâ¦ but then there is also a sense of silence and nobody is there to ask are you homeâ¦ nobody cares whether you entered with the shoe on or have you left the shoe outside.â

She placed a mirror at the entrance of her home. âSomebody has to look at me, right? I used to do that for myself.â

Living alone, she says, âmeans you have absolutely no one to talk to about your dayâ¦ that will hit you so hard that it will push you away from your loved ones whom you actually speak to on the calls.â

For Neha, from West Bengal and working in Delhi, loneliness is even simpler: âno person to go back to when you feel heavyâ¦ no one to ask where you areâ¦ how have you been.â

She says she has âno social lifeâ. Her weekends are spent âgrocery shoppingâ¦ cooking and cleaningâ¦â. When she returns home, her first thought is, âwhat should I eat now.â She estimates her screen time at 4â5 hours a day at home and says that after closing social apps, she feels, âIâm wasting my timeâ¦ I should do something productive.â

Their lives may seem far removed from the concerns of India's elderly. But the emotional patterns are strikingly similar.

A LASI-based study on later life reports that about 13.4 per cent of older Indians experience frequent loneliness. The odds are higher among those not in a marital union, those with more than two chronic conditions and those with small social networks or limited leisure activities. UNFPAâs 2023 report identifies social isolation and loneliness as key stressors on elderly mental health, aggravated by migration, urbanisation and weakening family support.

The country is aging into this crisis.

India's elderly population is not evenly distributed. Kerala's elderly share is projected to rise from about 13 per cent in 2011 to nearly 23 per cent by 2036, while Uttar Pradesh moves from roughly 7 per cent to 12 per cent. Southern states, Himachal Pradesh and Punjab already have above-average elderly proportions, creating pockets where ageing, and the risk of isolation, are much more intense than the national average.

The profile is also sharply gendered.

Using LASI data, government summaries note a sex ratio of roughly 1,065 females per 1,000 males among Indiaâs elderly, with women making up about 58 per cent of older persons. More than half of elderly women are widows. UNFPAâs ageing reports underline that older women are more likely to be widowed, have little personal income and live alone, increasing their vulnerability to economic insecurity and social isolation.

This is the demographic stage on which India's loneliness economy is emerging.

From joint family to flat

For generations, the family was India's first social safety net. That safety net has not disappeared, but it has changed shape.

Migration, urbanisation, nuclear families and precarious work have moved millions away from the people and communities that once filled everyday life. A home that once had several generations may now have one person, one phone and a delivery app.

The coping mechanisms are increasingly mediated by markets. Food delivery replaces the shared meal. OTT platforms fill the evening. Social media offers constant contact without necessarily providing companionship.

For younger Indians, these services are conveniences. For an ageing population, they are becoming part of a much larger ecosystem of care.

The silver economy

Policy has increasingly framed this demographic transition as an economic opportunity.

NITI Aayogâs report Senior Care Reforms in India and the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowermentâs schemes speak of a âsilver economyâ built around the needs of older adults.

Government estimates linked to the Senior Care Ageing Growth Engine (SAGE) initiative put the value of Indiaâs silver economy at around Rs 73,000 crore in 2024, with scope for multi-fold expansion as the elderly population grows.

The first pillar is financial security.

Atal Pension Yojana subscriptions rose from about 1.54 crore in March 2019 to 8.27 crore by October 2025, according to Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority data quoted in government briefs. Assets under management crossed Rs 49,000 crore.

The Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme reaches around 2.21 crore beneficiaries, offering Rs 200 a month to those aged 60â79 and Rs 500 to those 80 and above.

The amounts are modest, but they establish an income floor that can help with food, healthcare and basic services.

The second pillar is health protection.

Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY offers Rs 5 lakh a year in hospitalisation cover to vulnerable households. In October 2024, the government announced free treatment benefits of up to Rs 5 lakh annually for about 6 crore senior citizens aged 70 and above from 4.5 crore families, irrespective of socio-economic status.

More than 40 lakh seniors had enrolled by January 2025.

The National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly, meanwhile, now covers all 713 health districts, with geriatric OPDs, wards and physiotherapy services, according to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

The third pillar is care.

The SAGE portal invites start-ups to develop solutions in healthcare, housing, technology and social engagement, offering equity support of up to Rs 1 crore per project, with government equity capped at 49 per cent.

The Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens grants fund 696 senior citizen homes across 29 States and UTs, with 84 more selected for 2025â26.

A geriatric caregiver training scheme, run through 32 empanelled institutes, trained 36,785 caregivers in 2023â24.

None of these programmes is explicitly called a loneliness programme. Yet they address many of the conditions that make loneliness more likely: widowhood, frailty, financial insecurity and living alone.

The business of being heard

Technology is becoming another layer of this support system.

The government's e-Sanjeevani telemedicine platform has delivered nearly 14 crore tele-consultations nationwide, including more than 1 crore consultations involving senior citizens, according to a 2023 Press Information Bureau update and a national telemedicine assessment.

For an older person who cannot easily travel, a consultation through a screen can be a lifeline.

But the broader shift is significant too: an increasing number of needs, including emotional ones, are now being addressed through digital interfaces.

Elderline 14567 offers senior citizens a telephone channel for grievances, abuse and emotional support, connecting callers to local services and authorities.

The legal framework, meanwhile, continues to place responsibility on families. The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and its 2019 amendment bill expand the definition of âchildrenâ and âparentsâ, remove the Rs 10,000 cap on maintenance, mandate that seniors should live a âlife of dignityâ and require dedicated police units and geriatric facilities in hospitals.

The amendment widens âmaintenanceâ to include healthcare, safety and housing. It is an acknowledgement that neglect, isolation and abuse are not merely private tragedies.

But loneliness is not always about being physically alone.

Anandeshwar, a civil services aspirant from Uttar Pradesh now living in Delhi, describes it as ânot being understood or connected to the people around me, even when I am surrounded by others.â

He has âa big enough circle of friendsâ but meets them rarely. Deeper conversations happen âpine ke baadâ (after drinking). His ideal weekend is full: âwrite some good things, spend time with friends, participate in debating eventsâ. Reality is often different. He stays home, âwatch YT, Twitter, or just lay on the bed smoking,â joking that âevery day is weakened for an unemployed.â

The problem, then, is not simply the absence of people.

It is the absence of meaningful connection.

The small economies of a lonely weekend

Loneliness often reveals itself through small choices.

Cook or order in? Call someone or scroll? Go out or stay in bed?

Minal divides her weekend between eating out and cooking at home. Neha's ideal weekend is âreading, writing and cleaning the flatâ, even if reality is often errands and rest.

Yukta, a psychology student from Bengaluru living in Jaipur, describes a more connected version of the same urban life.

When she is not overwhelmed by work, weekends with her roommate mean âsleep, cooking and eating good food together, watching something fun on an OTT platform, orâ¦ a movie and cafe date! And shopping or just strolling through a bazaar for fun.â

âNow, it feels like âI am finally homeâ,â she says. âI can do whatever Iâd like, be whatever Iâd like and just exist in a space with only comfort to offer.â

LASI-based studies identify regular social contact, leisure activities, yoga or meditation and even moderate television or computer use as factors associated with better wellbeing among older adults.

The difference is that in cities such as Delhi, Pune, Hyderabad and Jaipur, these activities are increasingly curated through markets: OTT subscriptions, cafes, delivery services and paid experiences.

At the other end is Srabastee from West Bengal, living in Delhi for work.

âItâs feeling like no one really knows whatâs going on in your head, even when youâre surrounded by peopleâ¦ when you have something exciting or heartbreaking to share and canât think of anyone to call.â

She speaks to family and âtexts a few friends once in a whileâ, mostly sharing memes and reacting to stories. Weeks can pass before they meet.

After scrolling, she often feels âdrainedâ, comparing her routine weekends of laundry, shows and ordered food with peers who seem to be âgetting promoted, buying homes, getting married, travelling the world.â

The same platforms that offer entertainment and convenience also fuel comparison.

The same screens that connect people can deepen the feeling of being left behind.

Who will pay for connection?

NITI Aayog argues that senior care needs to be recognised as a distinct sector, with regulations, standards, public-private partnerships and dedicated financing. Its vision combines public programmes such as pensions, NPHCE, telehealth and senior homes with private start-ups and NGOs.

That is where the silver economy begins to overlap with the loneliness economy.

The forces making Minal, Neha and Srabastee feel alone, migration, nuclear families, precarious jobs and digital overload, are also creating demand for therapy platforms, senior-living communities, companion-care services and digital communities.

Some of these services may offer genuine support. Others may simply monetise a need that was once met by family, neighbours and community.

The question becomes sharper when viewed against India's place near the top of the global loneliness index.

A country ranked number two by JB.com is also preparing for a dramatic rise in its elderly population. By 2036, roughly 230 million Indians will be 60 or older. By 2050, nearly one in five will be.

The challenge is not only how to feed, house or medically care for this population. It is also how to ensure that people have someone to talk to, someone who notices when they do not come home, someone who asks how their day was.

India's loneliness economy is already taking shape, from pensions and senior homes to helplines, telehealth, therapy platforms, cafes, OTT subscriptions and delivery apps.

The question is whether connection will ultimately be treated as a public responsibility or sold as another subscription.

Because the people who today spend their Sundays between grocery stores and glowing screens will one day grow old. And the way India responds to their loneliness will reveal whether it sees the need to be seen, heard and remembered as a basic human need, or simply another market waiting to be tapped.

World.title: DS Group launches Pallu Protection PPE to shield women farmers from pesticide exposure
World.content:
DS Group has launched an initiative to reduce occupational health risks faced by women farmers from exposure to agricultural pesticides and chemicals, rolling out awareness activities and a culturally tailored protective solution in seven villages of Baghpat district.

The programme, part of the companyâs FarmHER initiative, is currently being implemented in Pali, Katha, Bandpur, Sunehra, Basi, Mavikala and Sankrodh. It combines community education, preventive health services and distribution of a practical protective product designed for women who commonly use saree pallus or dupattas while working in the fields.

As part of the campaign, DS Group introduced a washable nano-fibre filter â marketed as the Pallu Protection Equipment (PPE) filter â that can be stitched into a saree pallu or dupatta to act as a barrier against pesticide particles, dust, harmful chemicals and PM2.5 pollutants.

The filters will be made available free of charge through selected tailor shops, pesticide outlets and chemist stores across the seven villages.

The company said the intervention was informed by field research which found many women already use pallus or dupattas as informal protection, despite their limited effectiveness. A male version of the product, designed to be integrated into the traditional gamcha, has also been developed.





DS Groupâs outreach in the villages includes mobile awareness vans, traditional puppet shows, nukkad nataks (street plays), door-to-door education and free health camps. The health camps provide blood pressure and blood sugar screening, basic counselling and distribution of PPE masks. Women participating in the programme also receive mirrors and calendars bearing messages about safer farming practices.

âWomen farmers play a vital role in Indiaâs agricultural economy, yet awareness of the occupational health risks they face remains limited,â said Rajeev Jain, Senior Vice President, Corporate Marketing, DS Group. âOur field research revealed that the saree pallu and dupatta are often used as informal protective coverings during pesticide-intensive agricultural work, despite offering inadequate protection.

This highlights the urgent need for simple, practical and culturally appropriate solutions that women farmers can seamlessly adopt.â

DS Group said the initiative aims to bridge the gap between awareness and action by providing accessible, culturally relevant interventions to protect womenâs health and encourage safer, more sustainable farming practices as part of its broader FarmHER programme.

World.title: Trainee IPS officer, accused of sexual harassment by colleague, hospitalised after suspected suicide attempt
World.content:
Representative image

(With PTI inputs)

NEW DELHI: A trainee IPS officer, who was booked for allegedly stalking and sexually harassing a fellow trainee at the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy (SVPNPA) in Hyderabad, was hospitalised on Monday following a suspected suicide attempt, police said.According to a doctor who treated him, the trainee officer was brought to a private hospital in an unconscious state by his brother and friends, who suspected that he had consumed a harmful substance.The doctor added that a stomach wash was performed, but no "abnormal" substance was found.The trainee officer's blood and urine samples have been sent for tests, while his vital parameters remain stable.Although he was unconscious when brought to the hospital, he is now drowsy. The doctor added that further details would emerge after he regains full consciousness and the test reports are received.An alcohol bottle and a sanitizer bottle were found near his bed, according to the doctor, who cited the trainee officer's brother.The case stems from a complaint filed by a 30-year-old woman trainee IPS officer, who accused her fellow trainee of stalking and sexually harassing her. She alleged that he had been sending sexually abusive messages through an instant messaging app since June 23 and making derogatory remarks about her in front of her colleagues.The complainant claimed that the officer falsely accused her of having a relationship with another trainee and pressured her to admit to it, while using abusive language.She further alleged that on July 9, he restrained her, took her to his room by force, pulled her hair, attempted to strangle her, and held a knife to her neck, preventing her from leaving. She also accused him of assaulting her the following day.The woman alleged that the officer recorded a private video of her without consent and sent it to her husband in an attempt to blackmail her.Based on the complaint, a case was registered at Attapur police station on July 18 under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including charges related to assault or criminal force against a woman, sexual harassment, stalking, and insulting the modesty of a woman, along with provisions of the Information Technology Act, police said.The trainee IPS officer denied the allegations in a social media post, calling the complaint and rumours against him "baseless and untrue.""I fully trust the legal process and believe justice will prevail," he wrote.A police official said investigators would issue a notice asking him to appear in connection with the case.Following the registration of the case, the trainee officer left the academy, according to sources. He had earlier served as a constable in Andhra Pradesh.

World.title: Structural stability assessment of KWA reservoirs in Kochi begins
World.content:
The strength and structural stability assessment of Kerala Water Authority’s (KWA) reservoirs and infrastructure within the Kochi Corporation limits has begun. The French firm SUEZ, which took over the operation and maintenance of water distribution in Kochi a few months ago, began non-destructive testing of the water utility’s reservoirs, pump houses, and other infrastructure a week ago.

The assessment is under way on the infrastructure at the Thammanam pumping station.

“The tests are being carried out on all structures constructed more than five years ago. Most of these reservoirs are old, and their structural stability needs to be assessed. The tanks built under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) are excluded as they are new,” said a KWA source.

The exercise covers structures within the Kochi Corporation limits, he added. It is learnt that the entire process will take around two months to complete.

“A large percentage of the reservoirs are over 30 years old. It is crucial to carry out these tests to detect any leaks or cracks, especially in the wake of the Thammanam tank burst,” said another KWA source. The 1.35-crore-litre twin-chamber water tank of the KWA at Thammanam burst in November last year, disrupting water supply in the city for several days.

According to a senior functionary of the French firm, the tests will provide information on the condition of the tanks and help determine the measures needed to reinforce them or plan new structures, if required.

“The work at the Thammanam pumping station began a week ago. Our project focusses on building sustainable and self-reliant water supply infrastructure. We need to assess whether these structures are stable enough to last for the next 30 years. While the structures are old, we cannot reject them outright. We need to assess their structural stability, the demand they can meet and the pressure they can withstand before deciding whether new structures are required,” he said.

Multiple tests, including pulse velocity, rebound hammer and Resipod tests, are being carried out on KWA’s infrastructure, he said. The assessment is being conducted at six pumping stations, five overhead tanks and eight ground-level tanks of the KWA within the Kochi Corporation limits.

World.title: Operation Southern Readiness gets under way with focus on tackling non-traditional maritime threats
World.content:
The need for collaborative efforts among friendly nations to address emerging “non-traditional threats” was stressed as ‘Operation Southern Readiness 26-2’, a multinational maritime security training engagement, got under way at the Southern Naval Command in Kochi on Monday (July 20, 2026). Leaders of the participating naval forces underscored the importance of shared learning in tackling contemporary maritime security challenges.

“The oceans and the seas do not divide nations. They connect nations, and on many occasions, instabilities and insecurities on land translate into non-traditional threats in the maritime domain,” Rear Admiral Deepak Singhal, Chief Staff Officer (Training), Headquarters Southern Naval Command, who delivered the keynote address at the inauguration, said. The officer said the four-day event focusses on training personnel from multiple countries to address non-traditional threats.

Commodore Dan Thomas, Deputy Commander, Combined Maritime Forces (CMF), who inaugurated the event, said training has become absolutely fundamental to all that the forces do, now more than ever, amid the ongoing regional and global fluidity and upheavals.

Hosted by the Southern Naval Command, Operation Southern Readiness 26-2 is being conducted under the aegis of the Indian Navy-led Combined Task Force 154 (CTF 154), in partnership with the Combined Maritime Forces (CMF). The event has brought together 254 participants from 26 countries, supported by 74 facilitators, representatives of four international organisations, and subject experts.

The exercise marks the first edition of Operation Southern Readiness to be held in India and represents an important milestone in the growing engagement between the Indian Navy and the Combined Maritime Forces (CMF). CTF 154, the CMF’s dedicated Training Task Force, is currently commanded by the Indian Navy and focuses on strengthening the capacity, interoperability and professional readiness of CMF partner nations through multinational maritime training. Commodore Milind M. Mokashi, SC, Commander, CTF 154, also addressed the inaugural ceremony.

A session by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), which addressed maritime security threats in the Red Sea and the western Indian Ocean, was among the highlights of the opening day.

World.title: Former CorroHealth staff say compensation promise is a relief
World.content:
Former employees of CorroHealth, a US-based healthcare analytics company, who were laid-off, welcomed the decision to provide them gross salaries for five months as additional compensation.

The decision came following a government-level discussion with the company representatives held on Monday (July 20, 2026). Around 800 employees of the firm in its Kochi and Kozhikode units had lost their job. The company agreed to pay the compensation at a meeting convened by Labour Minister Bindu Krishna in Thiruvananthapuram.

“The company has agreed to pay gross salaries for five months, in addition to the full and final settlement amount paid to the employees earlier. The management has informed that the amount will be paid on July 26. The company has also agreed to issue all necessary documents, including relieving letters, without any adverse remarks to all the affected employees,” the Minister said. She added the government was committed to helping the affected workers.

Vishnu T.P., a representative of the employees, who attended the talks said the compensation package was the best available option for the affected workforce. “We were afraid that nothing positive would emerge from the discussions. At least we could get such a package,” Mr. Vishnu added.

Jazil Aboobacker, who was with the company’s Kozhikode unit and took part in the talks, said the compensation has come as a breathing space for those who lost their jobs. “We can look out for other jobs without worrying about next month’s salary now,” he said.

Ludhia Fernandez, who was in the Kochi unit, exuded happiness that the compensation package is much more than what many of them expected. She said the responses from most of her colleagues to the outcome of the talks was positive. “We were almost sure that the company will not reopen. All that we could hope was a fair compensation,” she said.

The Minister said though the company had proposed to relocate 12 per cent of the laid off employees, the workers were apprehensive of such a solution and had raised doubts about job security in the firm. Thrikkakara MLA Uma Thomas, Labour officials, and representatives of different trade unions attended the talks.

World.title: Defections affect moral sanctity of democracy
World.content:
Winston Churchill once said that, “some men change parties for the sake of their principles; others change principles for the sake of their party”. India, however, seems to have perfected a third category — politicians who abandon both party and principle for the sake of power.

The break-up of the Trinamool Congress and the Shiv Sena-UBT (Uddhav Bal Thackeray) are only the latest examples of a disturbing trend concerning elections. Leaders campaign bitterly, questioning each other’s integrity and commitment to the nation, with voters asked to choose between sharply contrasting visions for India’s future. Yet once the ballots are counted, many of those differences dissolve, and hitherto irreconcilable opponents become political partners. Principles give way to pragmatism, and power becomes the only enduring conviction.

The immediate consequences are political, with governments becoming stronger, and Opposition parties weaker. But the deeper casualty is something far more precious — the sanctity of the democratic mandate.

Far-reaching consequences

In a parliamentary democracy, citizens do not vote merely for individuals. They vote for an idea, a manifesto, and a political alternative. When an elected representative crosses over after winning on another party’s symbol, it is not simply a change of affiliation; it is a unilateral rewriting of the contract entered into with the voter. The mandate, which belongs to the electorate, now becomes the private property of the elected representative.

It also exposes the perverse incentives increasingly operating within Indian politics. Politicians facing investigations or legal troubles often appear to discover ideological compatibility with the party in power. Equally striking is the troubling public perception that investigative intensity frequently diminishes after such realignments. Democracies rely not only on fairness, but also on public confidence that institutions operate without political favour. Once that confidence erodes, the damage extends far beyond any single party or government.

The larger casualty is democratic competition itself. Every democracy requires an elected government as well as an Opposition capable of scrutinising, questioning, and presenting a credible alternative. Without that balance, elections risk becoming contests over access to power rather than contests of ideas.

Yet there is an even larger paradox. Prime Minister Narendra Modi continues to command the trust of a significant majority of Indian voters. Few leaders in independent India’s history have enjoyed such sustained popular support. The Bharatiya Janata Party has repeatedly demonstrated that it can win elections on its own political appeal. If the electorate has already bestowed such a powerful mandate, why must that mandate be reinforced through the steady migration of dubious legislators elected on rival party symbols?

History suggests that great democracies are distinguished not by governments that accumulate the greatest power, but by governments confident enough to allow a credible Opposition to survive and compete.

Aristotle argued more than two millennia ago that political systems cease to be virtuous when public office becomes an instrument of private advantage rather than public good. Kautilya’s wisdom was in knowing that a ruler’s legitimacy rested on the confidence of the people. Even Machiavelli, often caricatured as an apostle of raw power, warned that the destruction of all independent centres of influence ultimately weakens the state itself. The tragedy of modern democracies is that electoral mandates are increasingly treated not as solemn covenants of public trust, but as negotiable assets in the marketplace of power.

History offers sobering parallels. Italy’s post-war Transformismo saw politicians frequently switching allegiances and governments held together more by patronage than ideology. Brazil’s coalition presidentialism has often encouraged transactional politics. The Philippines has long struggled with a culture of political turncoatism. Though not identical, they share a common lesson: when political office becomes a tradable asset, institutional decay begins, with citizens losing faith in the system.

The voter’s loss

Perhaps, however, the hardest questions are not for politicians alone. Why do parties continue to nominate candidates whose convictions appear so negotiable? Why does mainstream media celebrate defections as strategic manoeuvres instead of condemning them as betrayals of the electorate? And why do voters so often forgive the very conduct they publicly denounce?

If opportunism is flourishing, it is because parties reward it and institutions fail to discourage it, with citizens gradually coming to accept it as normal.

The greatest victim of political defections is not the Opposition party that loses a legislator. It is the voter. The voter casts a ballot believing it represents a choice between competing visions for the country. When that representative later abandons the very platform on which the vote was sought, the voter is left dispossessed.

Perhaps history’s greatest lesson is not that democracies collapse when governments become too powerful. They weaken when citizens begin to believe that their vote is merely a stepping stone for politicians to negotiate a better bargain after the election.

India’s democracy is strong enough to produce decisive mandates. It must also be strong enough to preserve the sanctity of those mandates. A vote is not a transferable asset that belongs to the elected representative; it is a trust reposed by the citizen. When that trust can be traded for power, the real defector is not the politician — it is democracy itself.

Prabal Basu Roy is Sloan Fellow of the London Business School

World.title: Lokayukta takes suo motu cognisance of illegal sand extraction in Bagalkot, finds widespread violations
World.content:
Taking suo motu cognisance of alleged large-scale illegal sand extraction in Bagalkot district, the Lokayukta has ordered an inquiry after receiving reports of rampant unauthorised extraction and environmental degradation across the district.

Acting on the directions of the Lokayukta, the Bagalkot Lokayukta Police on Monday conducted inspections at 41 sand extraction sites across Hungund, Ilkal, Badami, and Mudhol taluks.

According to the inspection report, only nine sites were found to be operating with valid authorisation.

Based on the findings, 25 criminal cases have been registered at various police stations.

The Lokayukta report stated that illegal sand extraction was being carried out on riverbeds, streams and agricultural lands by excavating sand to depths of 15 to 20 feet. The report observed that the activity had caused extensive damage to river ecosystems, agricultural land and public roads.

The report further noted that the district-level task force constituted to prevent illegal sand extraction had failed.

To strengthen enforcement, the Lokayukta has recommended continuous surveillance of vulnerable areas, coordinated raids by the Mines and Geology, Police, Revenue, Forest and Transport Departments, increased day-and-night patrolling, strict verification of e-transit passes, and seizure of vehicles and machinery.

The report also called for greater use of technology, including drones, CCTV cameras and GPS tracking, to monitor extraction activity and transport routes.

It recommended the installation of live CCTV cameras at authorised sites, with real-time monitoring by district authorities, besides promoting the use of manufactured sand to reduce dependence on river sand.

The Lokayukta has further recommended stringent action against offenders under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, the Karnataka Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1994, the Water Act, the Environment Protection Act, the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, the Motor Vehicles Act, and other applicable laws.

World.title: Political rivalries clash over Karnataka’s Bidadi township project
World.content:
The escalating political duel between Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and Janata Dal (Secular) leader and Union Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy over the proposed Greater Bengaluru Integrated Township (GBIT), popularly known as the Bidadi township project, is much more than just a tussle about land acquisition. It reflects a broader contest for political dominance in Karnataka’s Old Mysore region, where both leaders are seeking to shape the political narrative ahead of the local body elections and the 2028 Assembly polls.

The immediate trigger has been the government’s decision to proceed with the township project on Bengaluru’s outskirts. The project envisages acquiring about 9,600 acres across 25 villages in the Bengaluru South district. Both leaders, who belong to the influential land-owning Vokkaliga community, have sought to position themselves as defenders of farmers and the region’s agrarian identity.

Mr. Shivakumar has pointed out repeatedly that it was Mr. Kumaraswamy who had conceived the township project during his tenure as Chief Minister in 2006, while the JD(S) leader has charged the Congress government with attempting to acquire fertile agricultural land.

However, the confrontation is rooted in a long-standing rivalry between the two principal Vokkaliga leaders, whose political fortunes are closely tied to the Old Mysore belt.

The region remains one of Karnataka’s most decisive electoral battlegrounds. Although the Congress made significant gains there in the 2023 Assembly election, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-JD(S) alliance continues to regard it as a JD(S) stronghold. Consequently, every major issue — from irrigation to land acquisition — assumes political significance as both parties compete for rural and semi-urban voters.

For the Congress, weakening the JD(S) in the region is critical to consolidating its electoral gains. For the JD(S), opposing the township is central to reinforcing its “pro-farmer” credentials. The agitation has expanded beyond landowners, with farmers’ organisations joining the protests, making it harder for the government to dismiss them as politically motivated.

Long-standing rivalry

Recognising the widening social and political dimensions of the agitation, Mr. Shivakumar has announced a committee to re-examine the project. The move appears to be a political balancing act — defusing public anger without abandoning what the government considers an important urban planning initiative. Although the Chief Minister has insisted that the township is “not my dream project”, he has continued to defend its planning rationale, arguing that Bengaluru requires orderly expansion.

The dispute has since led to personal attacks. Mr. Kumaraswamy has questioned the Chief Minister’s accumulation of wealth over the past two decades, while posters targeting the JD(S) leader and his family have appeared in the notified villages. Congress leaders have portrayed his opposition as stemming from political insecurity over the rise of another influential Vokkaliga leader.

Both sides have crafted competing narratives. Mr. Shivakumar has released official records to argue that the project has enjoyed continuity across successive governments and that the present opposition is politically selective. Mr. Kumaraswamy, however, maintains that the current government alone is accountable for the proposed acquisition and cannot evade responsibility by citing decisions of previous administrations. These positions allow each leader to appeal to different constituencies, one emphasising planned urbanisation, the other championing farmers’ rights.

The rivalry between Mr. Shivakumar and the family of former Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda stretches back across four decades. After losing to Mr. Gowda in the erstwhile Sathanur Assembly constituency in 1985, Mr. Shivakumar defeated Mr. Kumaraswamy there in 1999. Now, the renaming of Ramanagara as the Bengaluru South district, Mr. Shivakumar’s call to JD(S) workers to join the Congress, and the party’s recent setback in the Legislative Council elections have further sharpened the rivalry.

Can Karnataka balance economic growth and farmers' rights?

The BJP-JD(S) alliance’s decision to launch a padayatra against the GBIT before the State legislature’s monsoon session suggests that the rivalry is only likely to intensify.

World.title: CJP protest in Delhi LIVE: Dipke, protesters reclaim dismantled Jantar Mantar protest site, as CJP awaits Govt response to demands
World.content:
Police cracked down on a protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi on Monday (July 20, 2026). The police action on one of the largest protests in the national capital in recent years left several people injured. The police swung into action amid an internet shutdown in the New Delhi district, even as CJP representatives Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka met with Union Minister J.P. Nadda to formally seek Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk announced on Monday (July 20, 2026) that he would continue his indefinite hunger strike, saying the police action against protesters during the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) “ Sansad Chalo” march has prompted him to extend the fast until youth leaders are allowed to meet parliamentarians or he is permitted to do so from the hospital.

Also read: Neha, a prominent face of the CJP protests, presses on with hunger strike

The protests brought to the fore the growing discontent over the NEET paper leak and irregularities in the CBSE school examination process. Slogans of “Dharmendra Pradhan, isteefa do” (resign) boomed.

World.title: Police outnumbered, taken aback by number of protesters who reached Parliament’s doorstep
World.content:
Delhi Police and other security personnel were outnumbered and taken aback by thousands of protesters who arrived in and around Jantar Mantar on Monday (July 20, 2026), a senior government official said. In an unprecedented turn of events, despite multiple layers of barricades, deployment of around 3,000 security personnel and an Internet shutdown, large crowds comprising mostly students and young people were able to reach the doorsteps of Parliament before they were tear-gassed and charged with batons.

The “leaderless” protesters faced little resistance from police as they marched from Jantar Mantar towards Raisina Marg, which leads to Parliament, The Hindu witnessed. All radials leading to Parliament were teeming with protesters who brought down the barricades as they marched on, with the police using buses to block their movement, just 100 metres from the Parliament complex where the first day of the Monsoon session commenced on Monday (July 20).

Follow CJP protest in Delhi LIVE updates

The crowd had gathered based on a call given by the online youth group, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), to march to Parliament demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the recent NEET(UG) examination leak. The forcible removal of activist Sonam Wangchuk from the dais at Jantar Mantar where he had been sitting on a hunger strike for 20 days, in an early morning operation on July 18, likely gave a fillip to the protest as hundreds of people started pouring in in solidarity.

Swelling protest

On Sunday (July 19) evening, after intelligence sources conveyed to the government that the numbers were growing at the protest site, the Union government through Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi, Sachin Sharma reached out to the CJP members for the first time. “The DCP approached us first on Sunday (July 19) evening, offering a meeting with the district magistrate. After we declined, this morning they offered talks with Minister of State (Independent Charge) and subsequently a Union Secretary. When we refused, the DCP asked us what we want to do. We said a delegation will meet a Union Cabinet Minister. Then they asked us to give a list of names of possible Ministers and that is how Health Minister J.P. Nadda met us,” said Saurav Das of the CJP.

Seeing the intensity of the protests and as the protesters reached Parliament, the Union government deputed Health Minister Mr. Nadda to engage with members of the CJP. Posting on X after the meeting, the Minister said: “This morning, for the first time, a proposal came from the protesters to hold talks with the government, and our discussions have been ongoing since 11.50 a.m. The meeting took place in a cordial atmosphere. An initial verbal discussion was held in detail with their delegation and they submitted a written petition around 4 p.m. I have requested all those protesting to end their sit-in and assist the administration in restoring normalcy.”

Within Parliament too, senior Ministers of the NDA government went into a huddle with one meeting between Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan lasting nearly three-and-a-half hours. No briefing was done post the meeting but it is assumed that issues with regard to the leak of NEET question papers and the resulting protests were discussed.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal too met with Mr. Shah for a short time, but it is not clear whether it was on the same issue.

A government official told The Hindu that clear directions were given to the police to not use force against the protesters. However, when they broke barricades and marched towards Parliament, police personnel first fired tear gas shells as warning shots and then batoncharged them, injuring several protesters and police officials.

The official added that a large number of people were mobilised to the venue by political parties such as Chandrashekhar Azaad’s Azaad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram), Aam Aadmi Party, and the Samajwadi Party.

A large number of protesters came from outside Delhi, particularly the Shekhawati region in Rajasthan, the official said.

Nitish, a police aspirant, who arrived from Azamgarh in Uttar Pradesh on Monday (July 20) morning said: “Government should be held accountable for the paper leaks.” When asked how he could reach so close to Parliament and whether he was stopped by the police, Mr. Nitish said, “After the first barricade was breached, we just walked, no one stopped us.”

World.title: Stone pelted on India’s first hydrogen train? Indian Railways responds to viral video
World.content:
Stone pelting on India’s first hydrogen train: Indian Railways has issued a clarification after a video went viral on social media claiming that a stone-pelting incident had taken place on the country’s first hydrogen train. Flagged off by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on July 17, the train is operating between Jind and Sonipat in Haryana. The 89-km-long section is a part of Northern Railway’s Delhi Division.

In a statement, Northern Railway said the viral video is an old video and clarified that the train seen in the footage is not a hydrogen train. According to the railway zone, the train shown in the video is operated by a WAG-12 locomotive. It further said that the hydrogen train is running as per its scheduled timetable.

World.title: AAP govt to distribute 4 lakh schoolbags with Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s photo today
World.content:
The Punjab government is set to distribute 4 lakh schoolbags with the photo of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann printed on them.

The bags, designed and printed by the Punjab School Education Board (PSEB), reached schools Monday, and distribution will begin Tuesday, teachers said. According to the official letter received in districts, the bags have to be distributed to class 11 and 12 students only. In some districts, teachers have been unofficially told to call MLAs or local AAP leaders to distribute them.

The yellow colored bags, with Mann’s photograph, have the slogan of AAP’s school education reform “Punjab Sikhya Kranti” written on them.

While officials said that it was an initiative to help senior secondary students in carrying books, assignments etc, teachers have questioned the logic.

“Class 11 and 12 students do not need school bags, but notebooks, registers etc. They are being given these bags with CM’s images as they are politically aware. The teenagers are being targeted for this political publicity as they are potential voters. Many in class 12 are already 18+ and registered as voters. If they really wanted to help class 11 and 12 students, then the right approach was to reduce the exam registration fee. The students even pay to get detailed marksheets,” said Dharamjit Singh, state secretary, Lecturer Cadre Union, Punjab.



Vikram Dev, state president, Democratic Teachers Front, said, “They are doing this for their campaigning but for a child, it is hurting his dignity. You are making him realize that even the bag he will carry to the school daily has been given free of cost by the government.”

Rajwinder Singh, a teacher, said, “This government has made it a routine to do politics in the name of education. Earlier they distributed government schemes pamphlets on Parent Teacher meetings, then books were distributed in polybags which had CM’s photo and now these bags. No one is a fool to not understand why these are being given to class 11 and 12 students only. They are potential voters and any effort to influence them will also reach their parents.”



When contacted, PSEB chiarman Amarpal Singh said, “We have only done the printing job as told by the education department. We have printed 4 lakh bags on their order and they have paid us for the job. We have not decided on its design.”

Sakatar Singh Bal, director of secondary education in Punjab, said, “Bags are being given to senior secondary students on a pilot basis. We will expand to other classes if required. The PSEB has designed the bags.”

Punjab education secretary Sonali Giri said, “In primary classes, we do not encourage heavy bags. So it is the senior students who require them as they have to carry books, worksheets, notebooks etc. PSEB had formed a committee to decide on the design of the bag. So it was probably their call to put up the CM’s photo.”



While Punjab education minister Harjot Singh Bains did not respond to calls and messages, his OSD Dapinder Singh said: “Bains is in Delhi where he participated in the protest at Jantar Mantar against paper leaks.”

AAP Punjab spokesperson Neel Garg said, “The CM’s photo on schoolbags should not be a point of discussion. Rather, the discussion should be on how AAP has transformed Punjab’s government schools. We used to criticize Badals for putting their images on everything because under them, schools and every other government facility were in pathetic state. AAP has revolutionized everything so there’s nothing wrong in putting photos of our leader. For children and their parents, CM Mann is an inspirational figure.”

World.title: Messi posts after losing World Cup final: Will take time for this wound to heal
World.content:
Argentine legend Lionel Messi said that the pain of losing the World Cup final to Spain will take time to heal while also thanking his teammates and everyone who supported the team throughout the tournament. He also congratulated Spain for winning the World Cup.

“The pain is immense, it will take time for this wound to heal. But I also choose to hold on to all the good things, all matches we turned around by giving everything and moments that will remain in our memories forever. I will always remember the support of an entire country that, together with the work and effort of this group, brought us back once again among the best teams in the world,” messi posted on Instagram on Monday.

World.title: Trump says Netanyahu won’t be arrested in US as Mamdani weighs legal options
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has announced that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will not be arrested while visiting the United States. This comes as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani had said that he was still considering arresting the Israeli prime minister when he visits America.

Without referring to Mayor Mamdani, Trump, in a post on Truth Social, wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America.” The US President credited Netanyahu for helping America in the war against Iran.

The New York City mayor, in an interview telecast on Saturday, had said that the city’s legal department ⁠is actively considering ⁠what the law allows it to do.



“I believe that Prime ⁠Minister ‌Netanyahu belongs in The Hague. He’s ​a war criminal who has ‌been charged by the International Criminal Court,” Mamdani told a New York Times video podcast.

Trump, while praising Netanyahu, said, “He is fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran, which recently killed 52,000 innocent protestors, and has spent the last 47 years killing American Soldiers, and others.”

Traditionally, Netanyahu travels to New York every year in September for the session at the United Nations General Assembly, where world leaders gather annually.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has issued an arrest warrant against Netanyahu for allegedly committing war crimes during the war with the Hamas militant group in Gaza. However, the Israeli government has denied the war crimes allegations and rejected the court’s jurisdiction.



Calling the ICC a “Kangaroo court” and the arrest warrant against Netanyahu “bogus”, Israel said, “Mamdani appears interested in diverting public attention from his follies and attacking the leader of the Jewish ‌state and the only ​democracy in the ​Middle East,” Reuters reported.

Notably, the ICC was established in 2002, but the United States and Israel are not members of the court.

World.title: Ferran Torres’s path to FIFA World Cup-winning goal goes through Navi Mumbai
World.content:
As Ferran Torres scored the winning goal for Spain in the FIFA World Cup final in the 106th minute, it brought back memories for Vijay Patil, watching from the stands at New Jersey’s Metlife Stadium.

Torres’ footballing journey had gone through India and Navi Mumbai, when he was part of the Spanish squad for the 2017 FIFA U-17 World Cup held in India.



One of his teammates in the current senior squad, Eric Garcia, also played at Navi Mumbai’s DY Patil Stadium.

Vijay Patil owner of DY Patil Stadium during FIFA World Cup final. Torres played at DY Patil Stadium in 2017. (Special Arrangement) Vijay Patil owner of DY Patil Stadium during FIFA World Cup final. Torres played at DY Patil Stadium in 2017. (Special Arrangement)

“Torres and Garcia came with the under-17 team and played at my ground. To see him scoring a goal in the World Cup final was an amazing experience and a memory to cherish. I had seen him in Navi Mumbai as a young boy and like most of their players, he too was looked at as one to watch out for,” Patil told The Indian Express from the USA.

World.title: Russia-Ukraine war: 4 Indian sailors among 10 killed as missile hits ship
World.content:
In the first deaths of Indian seafarers in the Russia-Ukraine war, four Indians were among 10 killed in a Russian missile strike on a merchant vessel departing Ukraine’s southern port of Odesa on Sunday.

India was quick to condemn the attack, without directly blaming Russia.

According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces launched three Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles during the attack. One missile struck the starboard side of the Golden Leo, a Turkish-owned merchant vessel sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau, igniting a fire.



“On the evening of 19 July 2026, the vessel MV Golden Leo was attacked while departing the port of Odesa. At the time of the incident, there were 17 crew members on board, including five Indian nationals,” the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said in a statement.

World.title: Sohail Khan says he feels ‘lovely’ meeting ex-wife Seema Sajdeh; expert on healthy healing
World.content:
Sohail Khan, who met ex-wife Seema Sajdeh on the reality show Alliance recently, shared that it is always “lovely” to see her. “Lovely. I have lived with this beautiful lady for 25 years, and let me admit on national television if there has been any mistake between us, I take the ownership….that responsibility,” he said in a promo of the reality show in response to host Kunal Kemmu’s question.

In a world where separations often become public blame games and social media encourages people to choose sides, his response offered something far more powerful: dignity, reflected psychotherapist and life coach Delnna Rrajesh.
