World.title: Joyce defends Hanson's controversial meeting as dog interrupts interview
World.content:
One Nation senator Barnaby Joyce has defended Pauline Hanson's meeting with far-right British activist Tommy Robinson during a television interview that was twice interrupted by his dog.

On ABC's 7.30 on Monday, Mr Joyce rejected suggestions the One Nation leader had crossed a "red line" by meeting with Robinson, who has a lengthy criminal record and has been condemned by British authorities over his role in encouraging anti-immigration demonstrations.

Hanson 'not backing away' from controversial far-right interview The One Nation leader was a guest on the podcast of controversial far-right UK figure Tommy Robinson, where she lamented the end of the White Australia policy.

Mr Joyce disputed claims that Ms Hanson had actively sought the interview, instead arguing it was arranged as part of a television production.

"I don't believe that it was a carte blanche case that One Nation wanted that meeting," he said.

"I think it was basically suggested by [Channel Seven's] Spotlight, agreed to by One Nation."

Presenter Sarah Ferguson challenged that account, saying Channel Seven had told the ABC the meeting had been arranged before the broadcaster became involved.

Mr Joyce said he had "read the emails" and maintained a different view.

The exchange centred on Ms Hanson's recent trip to Europe, where she attended a right-wing conference before recording a podcast and filming with Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

Robinson has been convicted of contempt of court, using a false passport, fraud, assault, and has been jailed.

He was a member of the extreme-right British National Party, and he was behind the now-defunct English Defence League, an anti-Islamic protest organisation.

Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, has multiple criminal convictions. (Supplied: The Karl Stefanovic Show)

Asked whether Ms Hanson should have known Robinson's background before agreeing to the interview, Mr Joyce said she had not travelled to Britain "with a bio of everything that Tommy Robinson had done".

He acknowledged Robinson had committed criminal offences, but said that did not mean Ms Hanson endorsed his actions.

Instead, Mr Joyce argued Robinson's prominence reflected broader tensions in British society.

"Tommy Robinson would not exist if there was not such a fracture … within English society that has given support to Tommy Robinson," he said.

Ms Ferguson repeatedly redirected the discussion to Ms Hanson's own actions and comments during the trip, including footage of her driving through predominantly Muslim neighbourhoods in Britain and criticising what she saw.

The ABC presenter asked Mr Joyce whether he agreed with Ms Hanson's characterisation of Muslims after Ms Hanson said in the program: "Muslims breed, and the taxpayer pays".

Mr Joyce responded by saying problems arose when communities failed to assimilate, arguing "Balkanisation" created divisions that were "at odds with the egalitarian ethos of Australia".

Dog halts interview twice

As Ms Ferguson pressed him on whether he had set limits on defending Ms Hanson, Mr Joyce looked off-camera and yelled "sit down!"

"Sorry … it's the dog," he said with a laugh.

Later, as Ms Ferguson questioned One Nation's policy on identifying visa overstayers through the health system, the dog interrupted the interview again.

"I have to apologise for this dog," Mr Joyce said.

When Ferguson encouraged him to continue answering the question, Mr Joyce replied: "Don't be rude. Otherwise, this interview will come to a grinding halt, Sarah."

Stefanovic-Robinson interview taken offline Today show host-turned-podcaster Karl Stefanovic has had his interview with far-right extremist Tommy Robinson taken down from social media and podcast platforms.

After the brief distraction, Mr Joyce denied One Nation would require doctors or hospitals to report visa overstayers, calling the suggestion "ridiculous", while maintaining people in Australia unlawfully should be removed from the country.

The interview concluded with questions about mining billionaire Gina Rinehart's relationship with One Nation and whether she had funded parts of Ms Hanson's European trip.

Mr Joyce said he did not know who had paid for the travel and suggested any support would ultimately be disclosed through parliamentary transparency requirements.

As the interview ended, Ms Ferguson assured Mr Joyce the dog had been "no problem".

World.title: Underwater gardening helping to restore Tasmania's lost kelp forests
World.content:
Linnea Bird has travelled from across the Pacific to help restore Tasmania's fast-disappearing giant kelp forests.

The 25-year-old Masters student from the United States is one of six participants taking part in a live-in internship program run by the Eaglehawk Dive Centre, an hour's drive south of Hobart.

Linnea Bird felt drawn to the Tasmanian reforestation project. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"Growing up in California and seeing the kelp forests there, it's always been something that I've been interested in," Ms Bird said.

"Being able to go across the world and see very similar ecosystems, but also just different biodiversity, has really drawn me to Tasmania."

Tasmania's giant kelp forests have been rapidly deteriorating since the 1940s.

Warming waters and overgrazing by invading sea urchins have led to the decline of what were once abundant marine forests.

The restoration project takes places at selected sites around the Tasman Peninsula. (Supplied: Ocean Imaging/Stefan Andrews)

Dive instructor Pauline Nuttens heads up the centre's newly established internship program, which is part of the larger Tasmanian Giant Kelp Restoration Project.

"The loss of the kelp has a massive impact on our ecosystem. For people who understand that, and want to do something about it, that's great," Ms Nuttens said.

" The ecosystem behind a kelp forest is huge. It's habitat protection, provides food and is a nursery as well for many, many marine species. "

Pauline Nuttens says she witnessed first-hand the decline of the marine forests. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Nuttens said that in 2015, she worked as a dive instructor at the centre, guiding groups through the giant kelp forests.

When she returned the following summer, she said the area's kelp was gone.

"It was gone in less than a year, a big forest … that was a big shock to me. This is when I realised how catastrophic this was," she said.

Pauline Nuttens manages the dive centre's live-in interns. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Reforesting under the waves

The technique used by the interns to restore the kelp forest was developed by Scott Ling from the University of Tasmania's Institute of Marine and Antarctic Science (IMAS).

Kelp forests provide much-needed habitat for many marine creatures. (Supplied: Ocean Imaging/Stefan Andrews)

The kelp spores are grown in a laboratory on a spool, which the divers then wrap around the base of existing seaweed at protected sites off the Tasman Peninsula.

Scott Bennett is a marine ecologist at IMAS and co-founder of the national marine charity Great Southern Reef Foundation.

"Our best estimates are that we've lost about 95 per cent of giant kelp forests across Tasmania, and those numbers are probably even higher now," he said.

Scott Bennett is leading the IMAS project to grow healthy pockets of giant kelp forests. (ABC iview: Back Roads)

Dr Bennett said the internship program was an opportunity to access more hands for restoration work.

"They can train these people up to a really professional standard, and that just increases our capacity to plant kelp and help look after the reefs," he said.

Dr Bennett said results from the project have been a "mixed bag" due to changing conditions in Tasmanian waters.

"When conditions are right, you can regrow a forest within a year," he said.

The tragedy of Tasmania's underwater kelp forests As a young man, Puck Vaughan would catch fish among the giant underwater kelp forests along Tasmania's south-east coast. He later landed a job in a kelp processing factory, but then the underwater forests began to disappear.

"Often we'll get hit by warm summer temperatures or a kind of herbivorous fish that moves in and finds the kelp really tasty, or big storm events, and all these things just really knock the restored patches around."

The current focus has been on choosing the right sites to restore.

"Increasingly, we're realising that site selection and picking the places that really are still amenable to giant kelp forest growth is really crucial to the ongoing success of restoration, as well as just looking after the remnant forests that we do still have in Tassie," Dr Bennett said.

The kelp spores are grown in a laboratory on a spool, before being transferred to the seabed. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Cold water plunge for interns

The internship takes place over Tasmania's winter months, which is the optimal time to plant the kelp spores.

'Hope' for giant kelp forests Tucked away in a picturesque bay on the Tasman Peninsula is a precious underwater field of giant kelp that's thriving thanks to a team of determined scientists.

Ms Nuttens said over their month of diving, the interns are trained to handle the cold water.

"Diving in Tasmania can be a bit challenging," she said.

"Because of the cold water, we need to use thick wetsuits and that changes the buoyancy control, the techniques."

Ms Bird said it was a shock coming from the warm waters of California to the chilly Tasman Peninsula.

"In between dives, we'll pour a thermos of boiling hot water into our booties, and that helps tremendously," she said.

The first groups of interns have come from across the world to take part in the program. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The program fee covers the cost of board, food and diving equipment for a month. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Immersive experience

To take part in the program, interns pay about $3,000, which covers board, food and dives for the month.

"I think the fact that they come and live in the dive centre, it is really immersive," Ms Nuttens said.

" You wake up, you dream kelp. You wake up, you dive kelp … the only thing that we talk about the entire month is kelp. "

For the program's first intake, six participants took part over two months, with three interns in June, and another three in July.

Two groups of three interns were selected for the 2026 program. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

As well as Ms Bird, the July interns included 27-year-old Hugo from Sweden and 20-year-old Paige from Perth.

Ms Bird said giant kelp was the subject of her master's project, so being able to participate in hands-on restoration was a great opportunity.

"We also do something called underwater gardening, which is a great term, and it was super fun," she said.

"We're basically cutting around the kelp restoration sites, so where we're out planting the juvenile giant kelp, we're cutting about a metre around all of the other kelp that could out-compete the juveniles."

For Ms Nuttens, she said she hoped the internship would allow more people to contribute to the restoration project, while giving young people valuable diving time and experience in the water.

World.title: Firebombed synagogue community to address royal commission
World.content:
The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion will today hear evidence from the community of a Melbourne synagogue gutted in a firebombing that Australia's spy agency alleges was orchestrated by the Iranian government.

Early-morning worshippers fled the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne's inner-south-east when the deliberately lit fire tore through the building in December 2024.

Three people have since been charged over the fire, which the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) alleges was ordered by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

This week, the royal commission hearings in Melbourne have primarily focused on security arrangements for the Jewish community.

Today, the Adass Israel Synagogue community is expected to give evidence to the commission on the impact of the firebombing on the community.

The synagogue is not expected to reopen for years as a result of the significant damage done to the building by the fire, which also damaged priceless Torah scrolls.

Torah scrolls were damaged in the arson attack on the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne's south-east in December 2024. (Supplied)

The scrolls were contained in a fireproof safe, which was installed after an arson attack on the same synagogue in 1995.

While the safe offered some protection during the 2024 blaze, radiant heat and water from dousing the fire caused damage to the delicate parchment.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the royal commission in January following Australia's worst terror attack in which 15 people were killed at a Hanukkah event on Bondi Beach in December 2025.

Security arrangements in the spotlight

This week, the royal commission is focusing on security arrangements for the Jewish community, the role of law enforcement agencies and emergency preparedness.

Much of yesterday's hearing focused on Jewish security organisation Community Security Group, which told the commission the cost of its operations had tripled amid a rise in antisemitic incidents after October 2023.

A representative of the group said he had major concerns about the sustainability of the operation, which works closely with police but was funded mainly through philanthropic and community support.

"The pressure has been immense on all our staff and our volunteers," he said.

"We ask more of them now than we ever have."

Jason Steinberg from the Queensland Jewish Board of Deputies told the inquiry that identifying what did and did not count as antisemitism had been a challenge for police in his state before recent changes around hate speech laws.

"It's easy to understand right-wing extremism: it's a Nazi salute, it's a swastika," he said.

Jason Steinberg is on the Jewish Board of Deputies and established the Queensland Holocaust Museum. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"But without that, the other levels of antisemitism of attacking Queenslanders as being genocidal terrorists, for example, in public, is not so easy to identify for police.

"Our community has felt vulnerable because the police haven't been acting on that."

The inquiry is expected to hear from police agencies in several states, a counterterrorism expert and a senior bureaucrat from the Department of Home Affairs as hearings continue this week.

World.title: Why Albanese would 'have a disagreement' with his younger self now
World.content:
Anthony Albanese has distanced himself from his left-wing roots, praised former Liberal prime minister John Howard and says he got some things about immigration policy wrong early in his career.

The prime minister acknowledged that if he encountered his younger self today the pair would be "having a disagreement … no question about that".

But, he said, over a long career in politics "you learn, and you can change your position". Albanese's Labor government now embraces the strict border measures he argued against in the 2000s, and as recently as 2015.

"If you want to run a migration system that's respectful of the contribution that migrants make, it has to be orderly," the prime minister told the ABC's Kitchen Cabinet with Annabel Crabb.

"And that's the lesson that the British Labor government is dealing with at the moment. It's a lesson that the US Democrats should have learnt but didn't. And it's something that we [the Australian Labor Party] have."

But Mr Albanese insisted that their immigration policy is always "respectful".

"Some of the positions are completely consistent, which is always to seek to bring people together," he said.

" We haven't used people, like during 'children overboard', which was just an attempt to divide people by saying things that were not true. "

In a wide-ranging and candid interview marking 30 years in federal politics, Mr Albanese nominated Mr Howard and Tim Fischer's defiance of their own constituencies to enact gun reform as an act of "courageous" leadership he had witnessed.

Anthony Albanese was a driving force in a protest against the abolition of a left-wing uni course. (Supplied: Frank Stilwell)

Before entering parliament, Mr Albanese cut his teeth in politics while attending the University of Sydney. As part of a protest over the proposed abolition of a left-wing university course, he scaled and defaced a clock tower and led a sit-in protest in a faculty staff common room.

Mr Albanese recalls that, after 10 days of being stuck in the same room with a collection of other activists, he felt like the group had lost sight of their original aims, and the act of protesting had become "the end in itself".

"It had to be consensus decision making, which meant nothing happened … it was an endless 24-hour meeting," he recalled.

So he brought in friends from the university Labor club, who banded together to force a vote to end the occupation.

Joking that if he hadn't forced an end to the protest, it would probably still be going, Mr Albanese acknowledges the incident as a key moment in his thinking about protest and change.

And it was just the start of a life in politics and protest for Mr Albanese. A leading figure of NSW Labor's minority Hard Left faction, he was elected to parliament on his birthday in 1996 — the day the Keating government suffered a crushing defeat.

Annabel Crabb met with Anthony Albanese at The Lodge in Canberra. (Supplied: ABC TV)

"I was excited to be elected, and you know, Paul Keating gave his last speech in the caucus room. You felt that sense of history," he said.

"But it was also a very significant defeat. We didn't just get beaten; We had, I think, around 48 or 49 seats in that election. It was time to be part of rebuilding.

"I felt that sense of an opportunity as well to be a part of that."

The prime minister still had a lot of losses to come. Three election defeats followed, and he wouldn't sit on government benches until Kevin Rudd's landslide election win in 2007.

But Mr Albanese thinks all that time in the political wilderness builds perspective.

One night Albanese would rather not relive

Asked to nominate the one day in politics he would least like to relive, Mr Albanese named the day of the 2010 Labor leadership challenge, in which prime minister Kevin Rudd was deposed by Julia Gillard.

"Many of the people who were behind the change of leader … were elected in 2007," he said.

"So, they didn't, in my view, value enough the difference of being in government and being in opposition.

" Being in government, every day, is better than being in opposition. I know because unfortunately I've experienced too long in opposition. "

All up, Mr Albanese has spent 20 of his 30 years in parliament in opposition and is now Labor's longest-serving caucus member.

Anthony Albanese and Julia Gillard on the opposition front bench in Canberra, 2005. (AAP: Alan Porritt)

He is only the second leader this century, behind Mr Howard, to serve a full term and be re-elected. Like Mr Howard, the Labor leader's prime ministership was the culmination of decades in parliament and coincided with the rise of Pauline Hanson.

Asked about the similarities between himself and the former Liberal leader, Mr Albanese expresses cordial respect for the opponent he was once given to lacerating in the parliament.

"John Howard understood his party. He had control of the caucus. Howard, as well, I think, understood that the 24-hour media cycle isn't what you have to be focused on. Credit where credit's due: it's a substantial achievement to govern for 11 years," he said.

Watch Kitchen Cabinet on ABC iview Join Annabel Crabb for a brand new season as she breaks bread with six of the federal parliament's most fascinating and powerful figures from across the political spectrum.

However, he does think the Liberal heavyweight "probably" stayed longer than he should have.

"I think if [Peter] Costello had have taken over in the lead up to 2007, it would have been tougher for us," he said.

A 'progressive' government occupying 'radical centre'

The size of the caucus, and the Coalition's poor polling numbers, mean Mr Albanese could be the first prime minister since Robert Menzies to retire on his own terms. But he wouldn't put a deadline on his departure.

A series of economic disruptions such as the pandemic and conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East have underscored Labor's years in government.

Mr Albanese pointed to that turbulence, paired with social media algorithms, as the driver of polarisation.

"It's a change in the way that discourse happens that's less respectful of others. And I've said so many times … turn the temperature down."

The prime minister described himself as a "traditionalist" and said his government was both "progressive" and occupied the "radical centre".

"I follow all of the protocols. All of that, I think is really important," he said.

Watch Kitchen Cabinet tonight on ABC TV at 8.30pm or on ABC iview.

World.title: Three graphs that show uncertainty in the property market
World.content:
Initial asking prices are falling and homes are sitting for longer as the housing market cools across Australia.

During a period of global economic instability, domestic tax reform and sustained higher interest rates, buyers and sellers in the Australian property market have been adjusting their approach to transactions.

"These cumulative effects over the last six or so months have dragged demand lower significantly," said Cotality's head of research, Gerard Burg.

To get a sense of how this uncertainty is playing out in the market, here is what four sets of data tell us.

Asking price over time

After decades of rapid growth, Australia's housing market is beginning to cool.

One piece of evidence that shows this is asking prices.

Buyers have been paying up to 3.6 per cent less than the original sale price for private treaty purchases across the combined capital cities in the past three months, according to data from Cotality.

That is up from 3 per cent in the March quarter.

What a fall in house prices would mean After decades of growth, Australian house prices are slowing. Here's what a fall could look like.

Mr Burg said he had seen a steady increase in the level of discounting since late last year.

"When there are fewer buyers, less competition and sales are taking longer to transact, that leads to a tendency towards larger discounts," he said.

Freedom Property sales agent Tomas Tonks-Foote said he believed Redland City, 30 minutes south-east of Brisbane, was looking at a 10 per cent decline in house prices.

"A few years ago I used to say, 'Whatever you think a house is worth, add another $100,000,'" Mr Tonks-Foote told the ABC.

"Now what I'm thinking is that, but in reverse."

Data from Homer, a property app that analyses agent sale trends to give more accurate price guides, also shows that vendors have lowered their prices.

More than a quarter (25.5 per cent) of the 144,772 listings the app tracks nationally have issued a second price guide that is lower than the first one.

The ACT has recorded the highest share of any state (37.3 per cent) when it comes to active listings with lowered price guides, followed by Queensland (27.3 per cent) and New South Wales (27.1 per cent).

Homer CEO Henry Pedersen said at the beginning of the year there were almost no price guide drops across Australia, but that has changed dramatically.

"It's a fantastic time for opportunistic buyers to find real value whilst confidence is low," Mr Pedersen said.

"With prices rolling back, it's never been more important to price in line with the market. Get it wrong, and you are left making painful reductions just to catch up."

Auction clearance rates and withdrawal sales

Another sign the market is shifting is the collapse in auction sales, leaving more homes on the market for longer.

In the four weeks to July 12, Australia's auction clearance rate was below 50 per cent, according to Cotality data.

Fearing their homes will not sell, 40 per cent of vendors are signing contracts before auction day.

Meanwhile, close to 20 per cent of scheduled auctions were withdrawn in the week to June 21. While this figure is volatile from week to week, the proportion of withdrawals has trended up since Labor unveiled its tax shake-up for investors.

A year ago only 11.5 per cent of would-be vendors pulled out of the auction process.

"The rate at which the market is slowing right now is faster than what a lot of potential vendors have been expecting," Mr Burg said.

"The trend towards selling prior is more just that unwillingness to take the risk that the auction might be unsuccessful and try to lock something a bit more guaranteed, even if it might be below what you were seeking."

Australia's auction clearance rates have dropped dramatically in the past couple of months. (ABC News: Charlie Mclean)

Time on market extending

Homer data shows the national median days on market in June was 42 days, up from 33 in May and 27 in November 2025.

Homes are taking longer to sell in every state in the past three months.

Western Australia recorded the largest jump in median days on market, nearly tripling between March and June.

Data from realestate.com also shows national median days on the market have extended in the past three months, albeit at a less inflated pace:

April: 30 days

30 days May: 32 days

32 days June: 36 days

REA Group senior economic analyst Megan Lieu said the numbers were showing a moderation in market activity, with buyers taking longer to transact.

"With new listings increasing in most capital cities and total listings up in both Sydney and Melbourne year on year, buyers may be benefiting from greater choice, reduced competition and increased negotiating power," Ms Lieu said.

"At the same time, we have seen buyer and seller expectations becoming less aligned.

"Over the next few months, vendors may become more responsive to slowing market conditions and reassess their pricing expectations."

Mr Tonks-Foote said homes in the Redlands were looking at a seven to 14-day sales timeline before the three rate rises and budget came into effect.

Now, he is telling his sellers that a six-week campaign to find a contract is the expectation.

"There used to be 15 groups on average coming through any open home," Mr Tonks-Foote said.

"But now we're seeing about five groups for the first open home and then between one and three for the weeks following.

"From 2013 right through to 2019 that was business as usual. So it's not that we're not meeting any buyers, we're just drawing back to a plateau."

Tomas Tonks-Foote is optimistic on how the market will fare towards the second half of 2026. (Supplied)

He said realestate.com enquiry traffic was down 50 per cent on pre-budget numbers.

"It shows that things are obviously going to take twice the time to sell when you're dealing with half the volume of buyers," Mr Tonks-Foote said.

What about the rest of 2026?

Some experts believe there is nothing significant that will turn around the weakness in demand.

The interest rate position is unlikely to change, rates will either remain on hold or increase, while the war in Iran is still bubbling away.

"I think the reality is we are now in a property downturn that is set to continue at least for the next six months or so," Mr Burg said.

HSBC's chief economist Paul Bloxham said the downturn was "just the beginning".

"As we see it, first home buyers and other owner-occupiers are unlikely to want to try to catch a falling knife," he said.

National housing market 'fully in decline' Australian home values record their biggest decline in more than three years as the housing market slowdown that began in Sydney and Melbourne spreads across the country.

But Mr Tonks-Foote is a little more optimistic on where the market is heading.

"From my past experience, every time there's an election, end of financial year, and budget and rate changes, everybody waits to see what that means for them," he said.

"And with the war in Iran and fuel crisis we've had bad news after bad news, which has led to so much negative sentiment in the market.

"But come September, October, I think we might be having a different conversation and see the market moving in the right direction again."

World.title: Tech wreck or tech correction? Why stocks are shuddering
World.content:
There was a certain inevitability that Elon Musk's latest adventure would disappoint.

Overhyped? Undoubtedly. Overpriced? Absolutely.

That it has taken just a month for its shares to descend below its float price doesn't augur well for the company or the future of the AI boom.

It is a boom that has sent Wall Street and lesser-known markets like South Korea's KOSPI to dizzying heights, fattening up Australian super funds along the way.

It also serves as a stinging rebuke to the army of investment banks and their analysts who promoted the company's prospects and bought into Musk's bizarre vision of the future.

And then there are the market operators at New York's Nasdaq, who rewrote the listing rules just to accommodate the world's first trillionaire.

Are wheels falling off AI boom? Overshadowing the tumult that is global politics has been a financial boom beyond almost anything witnessed before.

Finally, it has brought the US Securities and Exchange Commission into focus, since its decision last December to relax the rules — introduced after the dotcom crash — around stock analysts.

Almost all of us now own a slice of SpaceX, whether we like it or not.

Even if you're not directly exposed to it, the company has the capacity to influence global markets purely by virtue of its gargantuan valuation.

And, remarkably, it is a loss-making company totally dominated by one person; a man obsessed with becoming the richest person in history who, while undoubtedly brilliant as a salesman, routinely descends into bouts of extremely odd behaviour.

Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire with the SpaceX IPO. (Reuters: Joe Skipper)

For months, there have been concerns the mania surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) was on the brink of unravelling.

And then, over the weekend, another Chinese start-up, known as Moonshot, from out of nowhere, released an AI model that rivals and, on some measures, even outperforms the flagship versions from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Its new Kimi K3 model, developed at a fraction of the cost, has the potential to spark a price war for AI services that could jeopardise the huge expense racked up by the US tech giants in their race for domination.

It could also seriously dent their ambitions to raise more money.

Will Musk's ascent to the pinnacle be the defining moment in a bold new era? Or will it represent peak stupidity in the dying days of a boom?

Stock analysts or spruikers?

Almost every major investment bank on Wall Street had its fingers in the pie when SpaceX raised $US85 billion ($121 billion) last month through its initial public offering.

The fee frenzy generated about $US500 million.

You only need a glance at the analyst reports to realise they've, en masse, turned into disciples.

The verdict is almost unanimous.

SpaceX hit the Nasdaq to much fanfare in June. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

Of the 19 analysts now covering SpaceX, 18 have declared it a buy, with only one advising investors to hold. Not one denoted it a sell, even though the shares are now underwater.

Deutsche Bank described the company as "the apex of civilisational ambition" while JP Morgan claimed the company's "impact on humanity would be bigger than we've ever seen".

Another investment bank, Raymond James, proffered that, "just as railroads, electric grids and the internet reshaped prior economic eras, we believe SpaceX is building the foundational platform for the next generation of industrial capacity".

That may well come to pass because there is no doubt the technology works.

But it was an unfortunate comparison, given the investment mania surrounding both the railroad boom and the dotcom boom blew up in spectacular style, sending markets spiralling and bankrupting legions of investors.

Given SpaceX loses money, it is almost impossible to put a price tag on the shares. So, instead of profits, the analysts look at sales revenue.

And it's at this point that the analysis abandons any sense of logic.

How South Korea plans to cash in its AI chips South Korea is doubling down on its bid to lead in AI, unveiling plans last month to spend hundreds of billions on developing its chip manufacturing.

Goldman Sachs says the shares should rise to $US205 each within the next 12 months. Morgan Stanley says $US300.

That's 139 times the company's revenue. Not profit, revenue. In Morgan Stanley's case, it's 203 times the revenue.

On their own reckoning, it'll take between 139 and 203 years for the revenue to cover the cost of SpaceX stock. And that's only if it converts all that revenue into profit. Otherwise, it'll take far longer.

Spruiked as an AI company with plans to build data centres in space, SpaceX is a bit player in the field with just 3.5 per cent of the market.

It is a grab bag of businesses incorporating social media, with its X platform, a rocket launch business, satellite internet and AI.

Its huge ambitions, particularly regarding AI, come bound with a voracious appetite for funds.

Loading

A Seoul kind of feeling

It wasn't just the humidity in wet-season Seoul yesterday that had residents and onlookers across the globe in a sweat.

South Korea's stock market endured another punishing round of losses yesterday as its tech boom continued to unravel.

Once a niche market for international traders, in the past year the KOSPI has taken centre stage in a tech boom and bust that is threatening to go global.

The KOSPI boomed with the rush to AI and the demand for semiconductors built in South Korea. (Supplied: Trading Economics)

It dropped another 5 per cent yesterday as retail investors, many of whom had borrowed to cash in on the boom, were forced to surrender.

Since its peak in late June, the KOSPI has plunged almost 30 per cent, with the market operator forced on several occasions to suspend trading after losses exceeded 10 per cent.

Trading was halted for five minutes several times on Monday, as selling gathered pace after a Friday holiday, and as investors digested the latest developments in China's AI war with America.

For the past year, the stock prices of South Korean chipmakers specialising in AI have soared as demand for their chips has driven an earnings bonanza which helped treble the total market value.

Stocks in South Korean chipmakers have soared on the back of the AI boom but that boom has started to unravel. (Reuters: Angelina Katsanis)

Some of the world's biggest AI memory chipmakers, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, have been among the biggest beneficiaries but have since come under a wave of selling pressure.

The extreme action, however, hasn't dented the enthusiasm for some. Citi analysts reckon the market is still destined to head back towards 10,000.

That's a 50 per cent gain on current levels.

Moonshot to hit SpaceX?

This time next week, Moonshot will release an even bigger model of its new AI platform.

Given the 38 per cent slump in SpaceX's stock since its post-float peak, the timing couldn't be worse.

Anthropic and OpenAI, which have been neck and neck in the race for AI domination, were already facing significant challenges in their ambitions to list on the stock exchange.

That will now be far more difficult.

We want to hear your AI stories Most of us never chose to live in an artificial intelligence (AI) world. Yet over the past few years, it has become part of everyday life, changing how we think, learn and communicate.

Moonshot's new model reportedly costs around 40 per cent less than the two big US rivals. It too is looking to list but on the other side of the Pacific, in Hong Kong.

Like SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic have been valued at extraordinary levels, again based on revenue rather than earnings.

The two big US firms have signed a multitude of deals, both financial and service, with all the other major tech companies for the supply of chips, cloud services and computing power that ties them all together.

That creates a climate for potential contagion where problems at one operation flow through to the rest.

The huge investment in AI — estimated to total $US7.3 trillion by the end of the decade — was always going to be difficult to justify.

Why China, the US and South Korea all want to make computer chips Computer chips are needed to power everything from phones to cars to fridges and keep economies rolling. But a global shortage is sparking a battle between China and the US to make more of them and South Korea has been caught in the middle.

New Chinese players entering the field will undoubtedly grab market share.

With cheaper development costs, their AI services are likely to undercut those of the Wall Street titans, both taking market power and undercutting revenue streams, which will then flow back up the chain.

Maintaining those lofty valuations was always going to be a challenge, as Musk is discovering.

It is a lesson that could ricochet through financial markets soon. And one that all of us may learn.

World.title: Stubborn stigma fuelling shocking violence against sex workers in Australia
World.content:
As far as diplomatic missteps go, the United Nations' stumble was spectacular. In 2024, the Special Rapporteur on violence against women and girls invited civil society contributions to a report on the nexus between "prostitution and violence against women and girls".

Instead of responding with submissions, though, thousands of sex workers and their allies circulated a petition rejecting the very premise of the call.

The petitioners particularly objected to the use of the term "prostitution", which they believed conflated sex work with exploitative sex trafficking and failed to recognise sex work as a legitimate livelihood. A process built on such a disrespectful framework, they argued, could not possibly lead to the protection and fulfilment of sex workers' rights.

But rather than fizzle, as many petitions do, two years on it is being credited as one of the driving forces behind an inquiry into violence against sex workers in Australia and Thailand, which this week will hear testimonies from sex worker organisations about how different areas of law intersect with sex workers' lives, and what they see as priorities for legal reform.

The inquiry's organisers say the findings will inform the upcoming review of Victoria's Sex Work Decriminalisation Act, as well as support a grassroots campaign for decriminalisation in Thailand, which has gained momentum in recent weeks following the murder of teenager Tunchanok Donhomla, allegedly by Australian man Simon Carman. A citizen-sponsored bill giving adult sex workers labour rights and protections is now making its way through the Thai parliament.

Child exploitation 'hiding in plain sight' in Thailand's sex industry Thailand is struggling against a "hidden" world of child sexual exploitation that requires action from both the tourism industry and law enforcement agencies, according to NGOs.

Still, while decriminalisation in Australian jurisdictions like NSW, Victoria and Queensland has led to positive change, serious systemic problems and legal grey areas remain, including for Asian migrant sex workers and street-based sex workers who experts and advocacy groups say are particularly vulnerable to violence and exploitation.

"Even after decriminalisation, stigma remains one of the big issues," said inquiry organiser Debolina Dutta, research fellow at the Centre of Excellence for the Elimination of Violence Against Women (CEVAW) at Melbourne Law School. "Many sex workers talk about how they are often living a double life; that's how they deal with the stigma — you just don't tell anybody that you do sex work."

But that means sex work is "underground", Dr Dutta said, which can make sex workers more vulnerable to violence and more reluctant to report violent crimes like rape, assault or stealthing because they believe the criminal justice system won't take them seriously.

ABF raids a major focus

For some sex workers and anti-violence campaigners, the case of a man who killed two women within 24 hours in Melbourne in 2022 only confirmed their fears.

Advocates were outraged when Xiaozheng Lin was sentenced to a maximum of 14 years in prison for the manslaughter of Asian migrant sex workers Yuqi Luo and Hyun Sook Jeon, arguing it sent a message that the justice system did not value the lives of sex workers as highly as other victims of crime. (Lin was this year resentenced on appeal to a maximum of 18 years behind bars, with three judges agreeing his initial sentence had been "manifestly too low".)

Court increases jail sentence for remorseless sex worker killer Xiaozheng Lin will spend more time in prison for killing two sex workers in 2022, following an appeal by the prosecutor.

But stubborn stigma and sentencing decisions aren't the only problems migrant sex workers face. Mish Pony, chief executive of Scarlet Alliance, the national peak body for sex worker organisations, said their organisation's submission to the inquiry focused on Australian Border Force (ABF) raids on the workplaces of Asian migrant sex workers around the country since late 2022.

"They've been reported to us as being extremely aggressive and intimidatory," Pony said. "Migrant workers might have English as a second, third or fourth language, and that makes these interactions even more stressful and difficult."

Pony said Scarlet Alliance had obtained data via Freedom of Information applications and Senate estimates hearings showing the raids were detecting "very low numbers" of visa non-compliance and "virtually no" incidents of exploitation of migrant workers.

Scarlet Alliance chief executive Mish Pony. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

"If workers are facing workplace exploitation, it is well recognised domestically and internationally that raids are not the answer, that providing rights-based responses that allow workers to come forward and report exploitation to trusted services or agencies is a much safer mechanism of addressing this," they said.

"What these raids do is make migrant workers fearful of authorities, less likely to report exploitation, and push them into working in more hidden venues in order to avoid these harmful raids."

At a broader level, Pony said they were "very concerned" that sex workers were not being meaningfully consulted on the development of the Second Action Plan under the National Plan to End Violence Against Women and Children.

"There have been round tables that … have been happening but we haven't been invited to them," they said. "There is an open submission process, so we will be making a submission, but we will also be seeking to have some dedicated consultation as has been afforded to other communities."

Laws mark street sex workers 'a threat'

Gia Green, manager of the Victorian sex worker organisation Vixen, said her group had provided the inquiry with two submissions: one on ABF raids, and one about issues affecting street-based sex workers.

Although Victoria decriminalised sex work in 2022, street-based sex work near schools, childcare services and places of worship is a criminal offence between 6am and 7pm.

Vixen is advocating for sex work to be fully decriminalised. "Even if these laws around street-based sex work aren't enforced … they mark sex workers as a threat … to children and religious communities," Ms Green said, ultimately reinforcing harmful stigma. "We feel that this state-sanctioned stigma also emboldens perpetrators, violent clients, residents and members of the public who harass street-based sex workers as well."

Vixen manager Gia Green. (Supplied: Gia Green)

Another concern, Ms Green said, was the recent amendments to local laws in the City of Port Phillip, which empower the council to seize personal belongings in encampments in suburbs including St Kilda, South Melbourne and Port Melbourne. The council has insisted they are a "last resort" option to address anti-social behaviour, not an attack on homelessness.

But Ms Green said the changes were having an outsized impact on street-based sex workers, many of whom experience homelessness and housing insecurity.

"What we notice is when people are constantly having to chase up their belongings that have been impounded — that could include medications … and [supplies] to keep warm in cold Melbourne winters — it has a really big effect on the health, wellbeing, stability and safety of street-based sex workers," said Ms Green, who wants the amendment scrapped.

Violence and victim blaming

The inquiry is being heard by a panel of experts including former judge and academic Marcia Neave, Thai feminist lawyer Pranom Somwong, Melbourne University Professor Heather Douglas, and Christine Robinson, chief executive of the NSW Aboriginal women's legal centre Wirringa Baiya. The panellists will produce a final report with recommendations for law and policy reform, which will likely include decriminalisation in South Australia and Thailand.

"What we want the report for is really to make some noise about the right kinds of issues, for the right kinds of people to be visible, to be seen, to be able to speak and inform law reform, as well as policy advocacy," Dr Dutta said. "And … the Thai sex worker groups [Empower and SWING] … want to mobilise this event to help … fundraise — they want to showcase their work and their issues."

Panellist Fiona Patten, a former Victorian MP and former sex worker, said it was important for the inquiry to examine both the benefits and shortfalls of decriminalisation, which she said was never going to be a "silver bullet" for the stigma and discrimination many in the industry still experience.

"In jurisdictions where decriminalisation has been implemented there are still residual assumptions that affect sex workers," Ms Patten said. "These may present as sex workers being seen as morally suspect, unreliable, inherently vulnerable and … less deserving of protection." These assumptions affect how sex workers interact with authorities, she said, "but also whether sex workers are treated as ordinary workers and members of the community".

Inquiry panellist Fiona Patten is a former Victorian MP. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Ms Patten pointed to the case of Heros Hakopian, who in 1991 was convicted of the kidnap, aggravated indecent assault and aggravated rape of a St Kilda-based sex worker. The County Court judge who sentenced Hakopian to 16 months in prison said that because the victim was a sex worker, "the likely psychological effect" of the attack on her was "much less a factor" and "lessens the gravity of the offending".

One of the Supreme Court judges who increased Hakopian's sentence to 30 months on appeal agreed, pointing to a 1981 ruling which asserted sex workers suffered "little or no sense of shame or defilement" when raped, and that raping a sex worker was "not as heinous as when committed on a happily married woman", nor did it cause "a reaction of revulsion which it might cause in a chaste woman".

"I am fearful and suspect that that opinion still exists in our community," Ms Patten said — that violence against sex workers is seen as less serious, or that sex workers are to blame if they experience it. "I would argue it's actually more dangerous, it's actually worse … violence in the workplace should never, ever be accepted. But somehow, for sex workers, it does seem to be accepted."

To that end, the inquiry is an "extraordinary opportunity" to understand what else needs to be done to ensure people working in the industry are safe, she said: "I would hope it will assist other jurisdictions that haven't gone down a decriminalisation path with some tools and some evidence to further those campaigns."

World.title: How China's EV industry went from 'embarrassment' to the world's leader
World.content:
In some Chinese-made electric vehicles you can swap your empty battery for a new one in under five minutes.

It sounds too good to be true, but the process is simple: drive your car into a special swapping station, take your hands off the steering wheel, then let robots take out the old battery and pop in a fresh one.

The tech is just one example of how Chinese EV companies have pushed the boundaries of automotive invention on their path to electric worldwide domination.

Loading...

Other Chinese companies have developed super-fast EV chargers that can replenish a car's power to nearly 80 per cent in five minutes.

And finding a place to charge your car, a challenge in other parts of the world, is rarely a problem in China.

The country now boasts the largest EV charging network in the world with about one public charger for every 10 cars.

Australia, by comparison, has one public charger available for every 45 electric vehicles.

The extraordinary infrastructure and technology advancements have seen China largely overcome the problem of EV "range anxiety", the fear of not having enough power to complete a trip, and helped put China at the forefront of the world's electric vehicle revolution.

Chinese manufacturers are making cheap EVs with luxurious features. (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

China is now the undisputed global leader of the EV industry, producing almost 75 per cent of the world's EVs.

And it is not just production where China dominates.

The country is widely considered superior in all stages of the EV process: from conception and development through to manufacturing and exporting to the rest of the world.

But China's EV juggernaut did not happen by accident.

The grand EV plan

China's government decided to prioritise EVs in 2001 and developed a long-term plan that would eventually catapult the country to the forefront of the future automotive industry.

The government focused on bankrolling new EV companies, giving loans to and partnering with existing companies, funding research and development programs, providing buyer rebates and tax exemptions, and building the infrastructure needed to support an electric revolution.

More than $US230 billion ($328 billion) of state capital was invested into the emerging sector over a 15-year period to establish China's lead, and in the process transform China into an electric society.

EVs can be identified in China by their green numberplates. (Foreign Correspondent: Angus Llewellyn)

Global auto analyst Bill Russo, who has lived in China for more than 20 years, said China had won the EV race by achieving total self-reliance.

"[China wanted to] solve multiple problems at the same time: energy security, environmental pollution concerns and industrial competitiveness," he said.

"In order to get that different path to take root it invested in infrastructure, in tax incentives, put subsidies in early and then, over time, gradually removed them as the consumers started to accept the product."

Bill Russo says China's EV industry is "going global in a big way". (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Russo said that instead of trying to replicate what other countries were doing in the automotive space, China decided to transform the sector.

China worked on breaking its dependency on the part of the energy supply chain it did not control, oil and gas, by developing new technology and new ways of manufacturing, Mr Russo said.

Then the country re-imagined what a car could be.

"The entrepreneurial part of China said … 'We can be leaders — we don't have to catch up,'" Mr Russo said.

"Now they're introducing a whole new product configuration to the world which is the smart device on wheels.

"A moving living space with digital connectivity features. That's the really transformative innovation coming from China."

Luxury is the new standard — but cheap

Part of the success of China's EV grand plan was making cheap cars with the luxury trimmings usually reserved for higher-end brands.

China-based car reviewer Ethan Robertson said a standard EV in China now included TVs, fridges, massage chairs with zero gravity (that is, seats that recline to near-flat), surround-sound audio, and above all else, digital connectivity.

An EV with those features could be available for about $30,000 in China.

One of the best-selling EVs in China is priced at under $15,000 and is made by the world's biggest EV brand, Chinese-owned Build Your Dreams (BYD).

Close to 55 per cent of all new cars sold in China last year were electric.

Mr Robertson said China was now leading the pack when it came to the combination of technology, features and price — a mix he believed would leave many global competitors struggling to keep up.

Ethan Robertson is an American car reviewer who has been watching China's EV industry rapidly develop. (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

"It's a meme in China … if you don't have a big screen, a refrigerator that also heats things, and individual seats with heating, cooling, massage, zero gravity and everything else, you are uncompetitive," he said.

"These used to be stuff that you would have to pay thousands and thousands of dollars extra on cars from foreign manufacturers.

"But now that's the standard here."

Loading...

Mr Robertson said China could create the cheap but high-quality cars because it dominated the entire supply chain from conception through to the finished product.

"So long as these other manufacturers from other countries struggle to produce electric vehicles with the technology and the features and the price the consumers around the world want, I think they're going to lag behind the Chinese," he said.

One car every minute

The rapid advancement of automation and robotic development in China has redefined the speed at which cars can be produced.

Inside the manufacturing workshop of one of China's best-known EV brands, Nio, there is barely a person in sight.

Instead, robots on wheels carry car frames between stations, where other robots piece the rest of the vehicle together.

Yang Yi says the manufacturing of EVs in China has become "more and more smart". (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

Nio's promotional director Yang Yi said production technology had become so advanced in China his company was able to produce a car every minute.

That pace of development is known across the globe as "China speed".

"So in this factory there's over 1,200 robots [including] 300 to 400 AGV [automated guided vehicles] to transport the components," he said.

"In China, that's pretty much the standard now.

"This factory, it's amazing. It's becoming more and more smart."

Electric vehicles being built in the Nio manufacturing plant in Hefei, China. (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

At the Nio factory in Hefei an electric vehicle is manufactured every minute. (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

As a result of China's supply chain dominance, foreign car companies have flocked to the country to learn, develop and build cars there.

Even European brand Renault, which does not sell cars in China, has set up a top-level research and development lab in Shanghai to get the China advantage.

Renault's director of innovation technology Xiao Xing said the Chinese know-how was helping them develop cars three times quicker than ever before.

Xiao Xing works at Renault's research lab in Shanghai. (Foreign Correspondent: Angus Llewellyn)

Part of that, he said, was that China now had "the most mature" supply chain for EVs in the world, meaning that if a company wanted to design or build a car they did not need to leave China.

"China is the most competitive market in the world," he said.

"So you cannot run away, you cannot hide, you need to embrace it. Because if you don't embrace it, but your competitor embraces it, you will lose."

Security and trade collision

China's EV success and the wave of cheap cars flooding overseas markets has put the country on a collision course with other major manufacturers.

In recent years Chinese brands have increasingly looked to overseas markets to help sustain their profits and offset a slowdown in domestic spending.

In 2025, China exported about 2.5 million EVs to the rest of the world, double the previous year's figure.

Nearly 1 million of them were sold into the European Union (EU), the world's second-largest electric-car producing region and the home of major legacy car brands competing for survival against newer, cheaper Chinese alternatives.

European leaders fear the low-cost Chinese EVs, which can match European quality at a lower price, will hollow out local industries.

But despite additional EU tariffs of up to 35 per cent being imposed on Chinese EVs in 2024, Europeans' demand for Chinese cars continued to grow.

EU leaders are now threatening additional measures and signalling a possible trade war with Beijing unless China can rein in its export dominance.

China is edging ahead in the race for global electric vehicle dominance. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

One of the only markets in the world China has not penetrated is the United States.

In 2024, America introduced a 100 per cent tariff on all electric vehicles imported from China, and in 2025 banned all internet-connected vehicles from China.

At the time the US government said it was safeguarding the future of its manufacturing industry and responding to security concerns that people's data could be accessed by China.

Mr Russo said concerns about security were an ongoing issue that China would have to address through diplomacy.

"It's got certainly some data security risks associated with where and how information's being used," he said.

Last year China exported about 2.5 million EVs, double the previous year's figure. (Foreign Correspondent: Mitchell Woolnough)

But, he added, the world's view that China was "collecting data and targeting people with it" was "overblown".

"We shouldn't say lay down and let China control everything. We should compete with it," Mr Russo said.

"The global auto industry shouldn't block China. They should race at the speed of China."

The future is flying

Even though China's EV industry is dominating the world, the country is still innovating to keep its position at the top of the pack.

Car company Nio, which proudly boasts thousands of battery swap stations where EV drivers can swap over their battery in under five minutes, has started rolling out the technology internationally.

It is also in discussions to expand its operations to Australia, but the timeline remains unclear.

BYD, which claims its Megawatt Flash Charging System can charge an EV from 10 to 70 per cent in just five minutes, is reportedly rolling out an "even more powerful" generation of chargers.

The company has also revealed plans to become the world's number one car manufacturer and overtake Japanese company Toyota within the next five years.

Loading...

Multiple companies are also developing autonomous flying cars that will go on sale at the end of this year.

Mr Robertson said every year Chinese car brands were pushing the boundaries further and further.

He said they were backed by both the government and the public.

"Chinese brands have gone from something that frankly was an embarrassment for Chinese consumers … to a source of pride," he said.

"If you want to know what the pulse of the global car industry is you've got to be in Beijing."

World.title: They are now on the TV, but could these former athletes win today?
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV They are now on the TV, but could these former athletes win today? Nicole Elphick July 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Commonwealth Games will look a little different. After Victoria withdrew from hosting duties for the event in 2023, Glasgow stepped in as host for what will now be a streamlined version of the Games with 10 sports scheduled, instead of the 19 sports at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022. Former competitive swimmer Johanna Griggs, part of the hosting team covering the event for Seven, feels that despite the changes, the sporting community was mainly relieved the Games would go ahead, even in a scaled-back version. Johanna Griggs and Matt Shirvington are part of the team covering the Glasgow Commonwealth Games for Seven. Monique Westermann “To be perfectly honest, I think they’re over the moon that it got picked up,” says Griggs. “Everyone was a bit shocked when Melbourne made the announcement that they were going. I think there are a lot of people that wondered whether or not that would be the death knell for the Commonwealth Games, and there was a huge amount of relief – obviously the sports that miss out would be completely and utterly devastated – but I think we’ve just looked at it as, ‘Hey, the Games are on’.” The Glasgow Games are set to kick off on July 24 at 4.45am with the opening ceremony, with more than 3000 athletes from 74 nations and territories competing. Griggs, who won a bronze medal in the 100-metre backstroke at the 1990 event in Auckland, has a lot of fondness for the Games.



Related Article Australian TV Albanese and Taylor both said yes to Annabel Crabb, but one pollie is holding out “They have a really important place in sport,” says Griggs. “That started my swimming career. I’d just turned 16 when I went to the Comm Games and medalled there and then medalled at the world championships the following year and never got to an Olympics. So, of course, it holds a special place in my heart because it was some of the most extraordinary memories.” For fellow Glasgow Games host and former sprinter Matt Shirvington, the competition performs a crucial role particularly for up-and-coming sportspeople. “I love the Commonwealth Games,” says Shirvington, who competed in the 1998 and 2006 Games. “It is the ultimate stepping stone for any young athlete coming through. It’s almost like going to university for elite sports, it really teaches you so much. Any time wearing the green and gold is a proud moment, and particularly Commonwealth Games, when you think of the people that have gone before you. All the best Australian athletes – Ian Thorpe, Cathy Freeman – all of those iconic household names forged their path through the Commonwealth Games.” A young Johanna Griggs (right) at the 6th FINA World Swimming Championships in 1991 with (from left) Julie McDonald, Susie O’Neill, Nicole Livingston and Duncan Armstrong. Australian Broadcasting Corporation TV Publicity



Shirvington, who now co-hosts Sunrise, is also very positive about Australia’s chances at the upcoming Games, following a win in 2022 with 180 medals, closely followed by England with 176. “Yeah, we’ll top it again,” says Shirvington. “There’s 200 gold medals up for grabs at these Games and we will by far top the medal table. I think a lot of those medals will come both in track and field and in swimming. [But] it’s going to be a really competitive competition across the board.” Matt Shirvington celebrates after winning bronze in the men’s 100m final at the Goodwill Games in Brisbane in 2001. Vince Caligiuri When Griggs and Shirvington are asked about whether they would have been a match in their heyday for today’s athletes, they are candid. “I don’t think so,” says Griggs, laughing. “Look at that Australian team now, how different physically they are. It’s just extraordinary to watch how clever the sports have got and how much smarter they’ve got with their training.”



Related Article Tour de France ‘There’s no other race like it’: Caleb Ewan on why the Tour de France is so special Adds Shirvington: “No, they’re absolutely flying. This current crop of Australian sprinters is the best we have ever seen, hands down. Obviously, they haven’t broken Patrick Johnson’s national record yet, [but] I think that will go. We’ve just got great athletes, and they’re just pushing each other to go faster and faster.” With swimming and track and field experiencing a golden era for Aussie athletes, Griggs and Shirvington are hoping viewers will tune in to cheer on competitors across all disciplines. “Australian sport has never been in a better position,” says Shirvington. “Some of our youngest and brightest stars are coming through for the Commonwealth Games, let’s get behind them.” The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games will be broadcast from July 24 to August 3 on Seven and 7Plus.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street steadies; Judge pauses $157b Paramount-Warner Bros deal
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street steadies; Judge pauses $157b Paramount-Warner Bros deal Stan Choe July 21, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street is holding steadier, as stocks of chipmakers and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom trim some of their recent losses. The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent, coming off its first losing week in the last three and just its third since the end of March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 186 points, or 0.4 per cent,in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent higher. AI stocks recovered some of their heavy losses from Friday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to slide, with futures pointing to a loss of 39 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX dipped by 0.1 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.98¢ at 5.21am AEST. Nvidia added 0.9 per cent and helped the market recover some of its losses, swinging back upward after its drop on Friday was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Sandisk climbed 6.1 per cent after tumbling 29 per cent last week.



Advanced Micro Devices rose 3.5 per cent after announcing an expanded partnership where Microsoft will use its products for AI, including its new Helios product starting in the second half of the year. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street Trump’s company is failing. This is his shady plan to give it a lifeline Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such stocks have been under pressure for weeks on worries that their prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. On one hand, companies are making billions of dollars in revenue as customers pour money into AI chips and data centres. But all that spending may fizzle out if AI doesn’t produce as much profit and productivity as promised. Wall Street may get some hints on that soon as some of the biggest spenders on AI report their latest quarterly results. On Wednesday, Alphabet will tell investors how much it made during the spring and give updates on its AI efforts. All kinds of companies are under pressure to report strong growth in profit for the spring. They will need to in order to justify the big moves their stock prices have made. Indexes are near their records, even with the recent shakiness for AI stocks.



AMC Entertainment jumped 24.7 per cent after the movie-theatre operator reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also said some of its theatres in Los Angeles and other cities ran The Odyssey for more than 85 straight hours from Thursday through Sunday to meet demand. A federal judge temporarily paused Paramount Skydance’s $US110 billion ($157.1 billion) takeover of Warner Bros saying it “likely” violates antitrust law. US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland on Monday ordered the companies to hold off on consummating the deal for 14 days. Paramount and Warner Bros. hoped to close as soon as July 22. California and 11 other states sued to block the Hollywood mega-merger on July 13. The states allege the deal, which seeks to combine two of the five largest studios, would harm competition for film and cable TV distribution. The judge scheduled an August 3 hearing on whether to extend the hold for longer. The judge will decide whether to pause completion of the deal until after a trial to decide whether it is illegal under federal antitrust law. Paramount Skydance shares are 1 per cent lower while Warner Bros Discovery shed 3.4 per cent. Domino’s Pizza climbed 1.9 per cent after delivering stronger revenue for the spring than expected. CEO Russell Weiner said the company saw growth in orders for both its carryout and delivery businesses, even with the broad industry continuing “to face pressure on consumer demand.”



Another restaurant chain, Jersey Mike’s, is beginning its roadshow to raise interest in its stock, which it’s planning to sell on the New York Stock Exchange for between $US21 and $US25 per share in an initial public offering. Related Article Opinion

Mergers & acquisitions Coles’ backdown on $4 billion pet deal was a smart move. Private equity can’t have been pleased Elizabeth Knight Business columnist It and other businesses are facing pressure in selling to US households feeling crunched by still-high inflation, thanks in large part to high gasoline prices. The average cost for a gallon of gasoline in the United States is back above $US4. It’s been tracking the increase in crude oil prices. After dropping below $US72 early this month, roughly back to where it was before the war with Iran began, the price for a barrel of Brent crude has been jumping recently as fighting continues in the Middle East. On Monday, the price swung between roughly $US86 and $US91. It was most recently at $US88.90, up 0.9 per cent.



The war with Iran is keeping oil tankers from using the Strait of Hormuz to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf to customers, which pushes up oil’s price. S&P Global counted only 127 vessels crossing the strait during the week through Sunday, down nearly 50 per cent from the week before. Worries about expensive oil and high inflation have sent Treasury yields higher in the bond market, which threaten to slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.60 per cent from 4.55 per cent late Friday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran. Higher yields have already sent the average 30-year mortgage rate to its highest level in nearly a year. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe. The moves were sharper in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi fell 4.5 per cent. It’s been at the centre of the huge swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.



Stocks were stronger in China, where indexes rose 2.4 per cent in Hong Kong and 0.9 per cent in Shanghai. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: How a minister’s ‘signature move’ inspired this student’s portrait
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life How a minister’s ‘signature move’ inspired this student’s portrait Catherine Strohfeldt July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If his social media pages are anything to go by, Queensland’s education minister loves taking selfies. Now one has leapt off the screen, becoming the unlikely inspiration for a painting that young artist Angel Sadik hopes will soon appear in a Brisbane gallery. Dubbed The man behind the title, the circular painting of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek has been entered in the Brisbane Portrait Prize’s Next Gen category. Angel Sadik’s portrait of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek, dubbed The man behind the title. Morgan Roberts Sadik, the vice-captain at Corinda State High School, said she selected the selfie snapshot as an homage to the minister.



“He does this thing wherever he is … a 0.5x or whatever it is,” she said. Sadik is referring to the fish-eye-style selfie created by placing a phone camera on a 0.5x zoom setting – allowing more of the photographer’s surroundings to appear in the picture – which can frequently be seen on the long-standing Queensland MP’s social accounts. Langbroek has taken his “signature move” fish-eye selfies at Corinda SHS on multiple occasions. Facebook / Catherine Strohfeldt Langbroek’s happy snaps feature the grinning minister next to a range of people, from students to community figures and federal parliamentarians. “It’s just a nice way of bringing people together ... it’s like an inclusive signature move,” Sadik said.



Rendered in oil paints on sanded plywood, the portrait was a study on image, Sadik said. However, she said the viewer decided exactly whose image that was. Angel Sadik’s portrait of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Morgan Roberts “There are two cameras in the piece,” she said. “The circular canvas was like a camera lens, to represent how the outer society views him. “You can view it in this perspective … [that] you’re looking outwards at him.”



The second camera is the phone itself. “That’s more of a self representation, the way he views himself,” she said. “It’s just to do with how you view him as a person.” Related Article Art Brisbane muralist wins big with small portrait of fellow street artist The 17-year-old said she first considered Langbroek as a possible portrait subject when he visited her school in late October last year – stopping to take a few 0.5x ministerial selfies. The minister had called a press conference at the school, watched by the then incoming school vice captain Sadik and other members of Corinda’s student leadership team. Sadik said she was struck by the minister’s comfort in front of multiple news cameras, particularly when fielding questions about the state’s “best and final” pay offer, made to teachers that morning.



“He was just so composed and that really influenced me a lot … I wanted to represent him in a lens that really shows the man behind the camera,” Sadik said. When the minister again visited the school in February this year to sit for the portrait, she said she uncovered his “less intimidating” human side. Angel Sadik (right) and her art teacher, Pam Leech (left). Morgan Roberts Speaking to this masthead in February, Langbroek said he had been flattered by the offer, and felt it suited his ministerial portfolios of arts and education. “I’m interested to hear how Angel’s going to portray me, given that she doesn’t do what we’d call traditional works of art,” the minister said.



Sadik’s past entries, in year 10 and 11, included mixed media self-portraits using photography, acrylic paint and her own hair. She said her art teacher, Pam Leech, along with friends and family, had been huge supports as she created the piece. The Brisbane Portrait Prize will announce finalists for the main and Next Gen prizes on September 5 ahead of a gallery opening and unveiling of the winners later in the month.
