World.title: The secret to making failproof basmati rice –  no rice cooker required
World.content:
Tips & adviceRice The secret to making failproof basmati rice – no rice cooker required Sarina Kamini shares her tried-and-tested technique for perfect rice every time, including a simple but often overlooked step that makes all the difference. Sarina Kamini July 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rice in India is like tea in Japan. Different regions will have different endemic varietals best eaten with the masala, or spice mix, of that area. There are hundreds of varieties (though fewer now than previously), and each will require a different cook. Short grain. Tougher husks. More starch. Less starch. The common thread is that, no matter the variety, perfect rice is non-negotiable. Placing the colander of boiled rice into a lidded pot allows the grains to steam and separate. Patricia Niven So when I say perfect rice, I mean perfect basmati rice. Basmati is my jam, and part of my Kashmiri heritage. I love basmati and eat it most days. When I teach masala masterclasses, it’s the No. 1 point of interest. More than wanting to know how to cook a great rogan josh or a killer gobi sabji, folks want to know how to nail the rice. This is my analogue method. No rice cookers. No water measures. No Thermomix or electric pressure cookers. Just a large pot plus a bit of time and planning.



Soaking rice in water allows it to bloom and release its flavours. iStock The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Bloom it Rinsing and washing rice is – for the most part – a known step when it comes to cooking rice. But the soak takes it a step further. Soaking rice is the secret to unlocking its aroma and allowing its natural flavours to bloom. Without this crucial step, the fragrance remains trapped inside the hard grain. Think of it as the culinary equivalent of throwing a cold scotch fillet straight onto a hot barbecue – the sudden heat will cause it to seize, locking away the flavour rather than releasing it. Basmati rice requires the same patience. After rinsing thoroughly in three or four changes of cold water, submerge it in a fresh bowl of water to soak. When I’m on top of my planning, I set it to soak the night before. If I lose track of myself, I’ll give it whatever time I can. Even 30 minutes makes a difference.



Tip the pre-soaked basmati rice into boiling water. Patricia Niven Boil it Setting rice to cook on a rolling boil is the ultimate failsafe method – the perfect companion to a good soak. Set a large pot of water over high heat. Once boiling, drain the soaked rice and tip it into the bubbling water. Leave the pot lid off and stay close to the stove top. Because the rice has already been soaked, the grains have been partially hydrated, which means two things: It cooks incredibly fast: Once the water returns to a boil, pre-soaked rice needs as little as three or four minutes to cook through. The texture stays flawless: Because it spends less time tumbling in boiling water, the rice retains its distinct shape instead of getting mushy. And in the world of rice, better texture means better flavour. One last thing to keep in mind: if the rice looks translucent, it’s already overcooked. You’re aiming for a little bit of al dente resistance. Take a grain and taste it. That hint of texture is crucial for what comes next, as we head into our third and final step…



Steam it Once boiled, strain the rice through a large colander. Pop the rice-filled colander back into the empty pot, off the heat, and cover it with the pot lid. We’re now steaming the cooked rice. This second process dries off excess water, separates the rice grains and sets the aroma. It also finishes the cook, taking the rice from al dente to perfect without breaking down the texture. As kitchen techniques go, it’s akin to resting cooked meat. Rice can be steamed this way and kept warm for up to 30 minutes while you finish preparing the rest of the meal. Speckled with cumin seeds, jeera chawal is a delicious way to soak up rich curry sauces. iStock How to make jeera chawal (cumin seed rice)



This dish is the ultimate way to dress up fresh rice or transform leftovers. It isn’t so much a rigid recipe as a quick, three-step improvisation. Step 1: Melt a tablespoon of ghee (or to taste) in a small frying pan over medium heat. Step 2: Toss in a few generous pinches of cumin seeds, letting them sizzle in the hot ghee until fragrant and toasted. Step 3: Tip the aromatic ghee and seeds over your steamed rice, then gently fluff and toss the grains together using two forks. I like to add a few pinches of sea salt flakes to finish for a little extra pop of flavour. I love to eat this on its own when I’m feeling rundown. My second favourite is with rogan josh or a simple mutton or lamb curry.

World.title: AI is reshaping the economy, but good luck measuring how
World.content:
BusinessThe economyAI AI is reshaping the economy, but good luck measuring how Ben Casselman July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pretty much everyone agrees that artificial intelligence has the potential to reshape the economy in the coming decades. But no one is sure what effect the technology is having right now. According to some measures, AI is contributing to high unemployment rates among new graduates and might already have destroyed tens of thousands of jobs. Other sources suggest companies might actually be adding workers as a result of the technology. Researchers can’t even agree on basic questions like how many companies are using AI or which workers are most vulnerable to the disruptions it could cause. AI might be contributing to the US inflation problem, or be part of the solution to it. It might be responsible for a recent pickup in productivity growth, or might be playing virtually no role — or the productivity boom itself might be a mirage. Researchers can’t even agree on basic questions like how many companies are using AI or which workers are most vulnerable to the disruptions it could cause.



The conflicting signals partly reflect the challenge of detecting economic shifts in real time. Government statistics are inherently backward looking, and they are better at measuring broad trends than developments in specific sectors or regions. New technologies that might lead to the emergence of new products, jobs or entire industries can be particularly difficult to measure. Related Article AI AI models cheating and blackmailing in tests, minister says What makes AI different is the speed of its spread through the economy. It has taken less than four years for generative AI to go from a novelty useful mostly for writing limericks to a powerful tool adopted by the world’s largest corporations. Economists have become convinced that the technology will have profound implications for workers and the economy, even as they disagree about what those implications will be. By the time the data is clear, they warn, it could be too late for policymakers to figure out how to respond. “The stakes are super high,” said Nathan Goldschlag, director of research at the Economic Innovation Group, a think tank. “Getting the policy right is going to depend on getting the measurement right. You can’t get the policy right if you don’t know what’s happening.” Goldschlag has published a report documenting the challenge of AI measurement and proposing steps to improve it. He and other experts argue that the government and the private sector should be devoting more resources to the problem.



They are getting at least a hearing in Washington. In June, a bipartisan group of senators introduced a bill that would expand data collection and require the federal government to produce an annual report on AI’s effect on the labor force. “The government’s got to make some big decisions about AI and about the economy, and if you’re doing that in a vacuum, you’re going to make mistakes,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., one of the bill’s sponsors. “This affects millions of Americans’ lives and millions of businesses. And you can’t do this smartly without reliable data.” Mixed Signals Policymakers aren’t flying completely blind. Since 2023, the Census Bureau has asked companies about their AI use in a biweekly survey. It has also included questions about the technology in an annual business survey, although only intermittently. Researchers have developed several measures of “AI exposure,” many of which use a government database of job descriptions to assess which occupations will be most affected. Economists can use those measures to figure out whether the most exposed occupations are adding jobs more slowly, for example, or experiencing different rates of wage growth.



The trouble is that the sources often tell confusing or contradictory stories. Surveys reach wildly different estimates of companies’ AI use based on how questions are asked. AI exposure measures tell different stories about which jobs will be most affected. In one study, economists at Northwestern University and American University found that when they used different exposure measures, those could influence not just the scale of AI’s effect on jobs but the direction. AI was hurting employment according to some measures, and helping according to others. “I think it’s comparable to the Industrial Revolution in terms of how it’s going to affect the labor market.” Erik Brynjolfsson, director Stanford University Digital Economy Lab “It’s like going to the doctor and getting three different diagnoses for the same condition,” said Michelle Yin, a Northwestern University economist who was one of the study’s authors. Part of the problem is that the best-known measures of the economy were developed for an era before personal computers and the internet, let alone AI. The monthly jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, for example, provides breakdowns of job growth in manufacturing, retail and construction, but not in technology, which has adopted AI tools most aggressively. Instead, tech is spread across several categories, including information, a broad sector that also includes newspapers and film studios. Still, economists say that for all its shortcomings, government data will be crucial for understanding AI’s effect over time. Researchers at the Yale Budget Lab, for example, have begun publishing a monthly analysis based on government data that tracks “occupational churn,” how quickly the types of jobs that make up a given industry are changing. The measure is designed to be something of an early warning system for AI’s effects. As companies begin adopting the technology, the researchers theorize, they are likely to begin hiring for different roles even if their total number of employees doesn’t change right away.



“It’s easy to pick up case studies in retrospect,” said Martha Gimbel, executive director of the lab. “What makes this time different is we are actually trying to measure this and figure this out in real time.” Related Article Opinion

AI Think twice: Five key rules for using AI at work Tim Duggan Work columnist But those efforts could be hampered by a federal statistical system that has been plagued by falling response rates to government surveys. Shrinking budgets have made it hard for statistical agencies to fill the gaps. Erika McEntarfer, who led the Bureau of Labor Statistics until President Donald Trump fired her last year, said an additional $10 million a year in funding would allow the agency to expand the sample size of its monthly labor market survey so that it could do a better job of capturing economic shifts. “The data we’re currently using to understand AI’s impact on the labor market is in jeopardy because of funding shortfalls,” she said. “It would take only some very modest investments to shore them up.” Private data



Many economists aren’t waiting for the government to catch up. Several research teams have released AI measures based on private-sector data that is more detailed and more timely, albeit less comprehensive, than what is available from the government. The Stanford University Digital Economy Lab last month released a dashboard of AI indicators based partly on data from ADP, the payroll processor. That data shows that entry-level jobs have declined sharply in the most AI-exposed sectors since ChatGPT debuted in 2022. Erik Brynjolfsson, the lab’s director, called the trend a canary in the coal mine for AI-driven job losses. Economists have become convinced that the technology will have profound implications for workers and the economy, even as they disagree about what those implications will be. Peter Rae “I think it’s comparable to the Industrial Revolution in terms of how it’s going to affect the labor market,” Brynjolfsson said. “I wish the federal government was investing more in it. But meanwhile, there’s some great private data sources that we’re pulling together, and that’s what I think is helping to fill that gap.” But the private data is just as muddy as the government statistics. Research published last week by Ramp, an expense management company, and Revelio Labs, a labor market data firm, found that the companies using AI most intensely were adding jobs more quickly than those that had been slower to adopt the tools.



Related Article AI Slow down, save jobs: Labor senator leads call to protect workers from AI revolution Ramp has access to data on which AI tools its customers are buying and how much they are spending on them. That allows it to distinguish heavy users from more cautious adopters — a crucial distinction, because it takes time and investment for companies to figure out how to use the tools effectively, said Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp. “It’s difficult to measure AI’s impact on a business, because it requires sustained adoption,” he said. “It’s clear in our work that a simple chat subscription does not drive productivity for a firm.” Work in progress Researchers generally agree on one thing: AI’s effect on the broad economy has been limited so far.



That isn’t necessarily surprising. Brynjolfsson and other economists have found that technological innovations often follow a J-shaped pattern, in which companies initially become less productive as they experiment with new tools, then experience rapid gains once they figure out how to take advantage of them. The confusing economic evidence suggests that many companies are still on the downward part of the J. “The signals are mixed because, probably, the underlying economics are mixed, because we’re still in a period of experimentation,” said Goldschlag, the Economic Innovation Group economist. “The tools themselves are still becoming useful.” Over time, it should become easier for researchers to separate the effects of AI from other forces. But they still won’t be able to resolve the question that policymakers and everyday citizens want most to answer: What comes next? “What the data can almost never tell us is where we’re going to be in five to 10 years,” said McEntarfer, the former commissioner of labor statistics. “People are looking to data to answer that question, and it’s just too difficult.”



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: A dated business class on one of the few 747 jumbo jets still flying
World.content:
★★★½ Reviews & adviceAirline reviews A dated business class on one of the few 747 jumbo jets still flying Jennifer Johnston July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The airline: Lufthansa Route Frankfurt to Singapore Changi Airport, flight LH0780

Frankfurt to Singapore Changi Airport, flight LH0780 Frequency Daily on this aircraft; 16 weekly flights in all on this route

Daily on this aircraft; 16 weekly flights in all on this route Aircraft Boeing 747-400

Boeing 747-400 Class Business, seat 1K, window

Business, seat 1K, window Flight time 12 hours, 40 minutes (we are delayed 45 minutes on departure but land on time) Lufthansa is one of the few airlines still operating Boeing 747 jumbo jets. Checking in I flew into Frankfurt Airport from Portugal with my boarding pass ready for part two of three flights home to Australia. We board, then wait. Our departure delay is caused by a minor engineering issue, which requires documentation. “We used old-school pen and paper,” the captain’s voiceover explains with a chuckle. It feels appropriate for this old school aircraft. The first 747 took to the skies in 1969, and the 400 series flew commercially from 1989.



Baggage 



Inside the 747’s business class cabin. Lufthansa currently operates eight Boeing 747-400 aircraft, each configured to seat 371 passengers: 67 business class, 32 premium economy, and 272 economy seats. On the main deck, the 45 business lie-flat seats are forward-facing, angled and parallel in a 2-3-2 configuration. The upper deck has 22 seats in a 2-2 layout (more about that later). It’s a dated layout, as most major airlines now offer direct aisle access for all business-class passengers. The seats have a 64-inch (162cm) pitch, a 20-inch (50cm) width and 18-inch (46cm) depth. Arriving at my 1K seat in front of the bulkhead, I check my alarming thoughts, as I note the proximity of my very adjacent neighbour (a stranger). After dinner, I place my chair in lie-flat mode – 78 inches (198cm) in length – unroll my bed cover/mattress and blanket. The armrest frame provides some privacy, but fails to block my neighbour’s snoring. (Hooray for my ear plugs.) Entertainment + tech The seat and the screens, if you can reach them.



The 11.7-inch screen on the bulkhead feels distant (55cm from seat to the bulkhead.) After dinner, I plan to watch a movie, then sleep, but I’m bamboozled by the tech. My German neighbour assists, demonstrating how to use the remote integrated in my seat arm. Pressing a small button activates an arrow on the screen. Hovering, I navigate through the entertainment. Plenty of movies, but very few new releases. Over-ear headphones are located in a storage bin window side. Upon waking, my TV screen remains in slumber mode. My neighbour’s attempts to fix it fails. Laughing, he comments, “Old plane,” and offers his screen (while he uses a personal laptop). Related Article ★★

Airline reviews Airline review: Remember flying’s bad old days? After this flight, I do Service Before departure, a cabin attendant asks (initially in German, then English when I look blank) if I’d like an “Avionic aperitif” – a fruity drink with peach and citrus notes. A small paper bag on my arm rest sealed with a sticker stamped “Your welcome moment” contains salted almonds. Later, the flight attendant returns holding a small basket. Unsure of its contents, I copy my neighbour and take one – a long-sleeve T-shirt for sleeping, sans trousers. The attendant is pleasant throughout the flight. She also laughs when my neighbour explains my black screen. Food



Two meals are served during the flight. With three choices of appetiser, I opt for the burrata with tomatoes, basil and arugula. Three mains: corn-fed chicken breast in carrot cream with pickled shitake mushroom and broccolini; Halibut and prawn; or spinach and ricotta filled raviolini. I select the chicken, which is tasty with a crispy skin. Dessert is cheeses and fresh fruit. Despite the tempting wine list (German riesling, a fruity Austrian white, or a South African chardonnay), I request water, mindful that a toilet visit requires clambering past my neighbour, once his seat is in lie-flat mode. Before landing, breakfast is either farmer’s breakfast or kaiserschmarrn (sweet shredded pancakes with raisins, and a yoghurt with cherry and hazelnut). Sustainability Lufthansa’s website declares its commitment to a carbon-neutral footprint by 2050. Despite the 747-400 plane consuming more fuel than a modern twin-engine fuel-efficient aircraft, Lufthansa continues flying the “Queen of the Skies” (maybe for all the 747 fanatics). One more thing I was blissfully unaware of the 747’s upper deck – commonly referred to as the “bubble”. At our final destination, Singapore, a flight attendant notices me taking photos of our empty cabin. He asks if I have been upstairs. No! He escorts me up the internal staircase, where I spy the raised cockpit, unique to the 747. After commenting that the bubble feels very intimate, he replies: “Always book business seats numbered in the 80s.” A great tip for next time – unlikely, but a gal can dream.



The price From about $6200 return in business class, Frankfurt to Singapore. From Singapore, the airline has codeshare arrangements with Singapore Airlines for connections to Australian cities.** Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Qantas’ new ultra-long haul plane is about to arrive. I’d rather stick with the A380 Michael Gebicki The Tripologist The verdict These days it is rare to find an airline that flies a 747, so flying on a “Queen of the skies” before they retire (the eight remaining 747-400s are between 23 and 27 years old – Lufthansa retires its planes around the 30-year age) felt nostalgically special.



Our rating out of five ★★★½ *For more information about air travel and sustainability, see iata.org **Fares are based on those available for travel three months from the time of publication and subject to change. The writer flew at her own expense.

World.title: Europe’s most scenic train journey takes less than three hours
World.content:
InspirationTrain journeys Europe’s most scenic train journey takes less than three hours Andrew Bain July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Born out of a wartime escape, the true gold on Norway’s Golden Train is some of Europe’s finest mountain scenery. In Norway’s Romsdal Valley, the landscape is almost mythical in scale. Europe’s tallest vertical cliff towers overhead and the cairns of more than 100 Viking burials still furrow a section of the valley floor. Summit to write home about, with views across Andalsnes and the Romsdalsfjord to the mountains. Andrew Bain It’s a place connected to ancient tales of trolls, but the greatest story here is that of the Rauma Railway on which I’m travelling. Running for almost 50 kilometres from Andalsnes to Bjorli, the Rauma Railway was used by Norway during World War II to help smuggle 50 tonnes of gold out of the country when it was invaded by Nazi Germany. Under heavy bombing, the entirety of the gold, along with the Norwegian king, was successfully shipped to Britain.



Today, the train that travels along the line is known as the Golden Train and in 2022 it was named by Lonely Planet as Europe’s most scenic train journey. 



The most prominent of the mountain features is the Trollveggen – the Troll Wall – Europe’s loftiest rock face, rising more than 1000 metres above the train. Mount Everest was climbed 12 years before this imposing wall was conquered, while two local lads claimed to have climbed the equally daunting Romsdalshornet, which towers over the first stretch of valley, in 1828, but their boast was dismissed as drunken bravado. When it was finally summited by a Danish climber more than 50 years later, he found a cairn built by the pair atop it. Trollveggen, Europe’s tallest vertical cliff. iStock If the mountains were difficult to conquer, Rauma Railway’s course through the valley was no less problematic – opened in the 1920s, the line took 13 years and more than 600 men to build, and it ran 600 per cent over budget. The railway largely follows the line of the Rauma River through this valley, far deeper than it is wide. In winter, the sun is a stranger and the river lies frozen, more an ice floe now than a flowing stream. High up the valley, the railway makes a sweeping turn, crossing the river on the Kylling Bridge. With its high, graceful arch, it’s Norway’s most photographed bridge and a star of 2009’s Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, as well as Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One.



For all that, Kylling Bridge isn’t the Rauma Railway’s most impressive engineering achievement. As the line completes its horseshoe turn over the bridge, it swings almost immediately into another 180-degree turn, but this time inside a tunnel. The 1400-metre-long Stavem Tunnel was an extraordinarily ambitious and complex design feat that took nine years to complete. Related Article Train journeys The world’s 24 greatest railway experiences The valley finally widens and flattens as we approach the Golden Train’s turnaround point in Bjorli, where there’s a chance to alight, visit a display on the railway’s gold-smuggling moment and wander Bjorli’s few streets beneath slopes patterned with ski runs. With cruise passengers taking trains through the Romsdal Valley for more than a century, there was once a restaurant feeding 700 in tiny Bjorli, but it was bombed and destroyed during World War II and the best on offer now is takeaway coffee from a petrol station. As we’ve travelled the 50 kilometres inland from Andalsnes, the temperature has plunged by about five degrees – it’s now a frosty minus six – and Andalsnes’ snow-free streets have been replaced by a thick pelt of snow.



In the day’s late light, the train’s polished exterior glows as golden as its name. I’m quickly back aboard, ready for a second screening of this remarkable valley and its high peaks and cliffs. On The Golden Train, the journey is very much the destination. THE DETAILS RIDE

The Golden Train runs daily from Andalsnes, with round-trip tickets for the 2½-hour trip costing from $100. See thegoldentrain.com TRAVEL

Many of Hurtigruten’s Norwegian cruises, including the 15-day North Cape Line cruise, dock in Andalsnes, offering the Golden Train as a shore excursion. See hurtigruten.com MORE

visitnorway.com The writer travelled as a guest of Hurtigruten.

World.title: ‘Wellness’ is out. Relaxation holidays are now about extending your lifespan
World.content:
InspirationWellness holidays Opinion ‘Wellness’ is out. Relaxation holidays are now about extending your lifespan Lee Tulloch Travel columnist July 21, 2026 — 5:00am

July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Imagine if you could add 10 years to your life just by taking a holiday. No one is quite promising this yet, but the possibility might not be far away. Wellness retreats have hit a whole new level. Getty Images Travelling for longevity is the concept running hot through the travel industry right now. “Wellness” was the buzzword a decade ago, but now, being well in the moment is not enough. People are talking about having a “health span” as well as a lifespan – living longer in a state of optimum health for one’s age.



And the hospitality industry believes it is well-placed to provide a service to those willing to pay for the enhanced possibility of a healthy 100-year-old life. 



Preferred Hotels and Resorts, a collection of independent hotels, launched a worldwide wellness brand emphasising results-driven treatments that combine Eastern wellness philosophies with Western technologies such as biohacking, hydrothermal circuits and advanced skincare. It isn’t just about wellness, they emphasised, it’s longevity. The word popped up again and again. Even cruise companies realise that a relaxation massage might not be enough of an attraction for some guests. Regent Seven Seas Cruises announced a new Spotlight on Wellness & Longevity cruise starting in 2027. Longevity is the new travel buzzword. Getty Images For decades, Europeans have been booking into medical health clinics such as Clinique La Prairie in Montreux, Switzerland, for science-based medical treatments and cosmetic surgery along with their pampering massages and facials.



When I lived in France 20 years ago, you could get a prescription from your doctor for a free week at a medically based spa in Normandy or Brittany. In our part of the world, hospitality brands such as Six Senses, Kamalaya and Chiva-Som have been offering cutting-edge holistic treatments for many years. Biohacking, red-light therapy and sleep therapy programs are not new. What is new is an ageing population worrying about the prospect of a poor quality of life in their final decades, and constantly evolving medical advances, including diagnostic tools such as DNA analysis. Now, instead of a welcome drink when you arrive at your spa, you get an IV drip and live blood analysis. You can follow up with genetic DNA testing, cellular optimisation and 3D body mapping.



A growing number of spas are offering such medically integrated treatments, including RAKxa Integrative Wellness in Thailand, which partners with the VitalLife Scientific Wellness clinic of Bangkok’s respected Bumrungrad International Hospital. At SHA Wellness destinations in Spain, Mexico and the Emirates guests can book Advanced Longevity programs offering “biological ageing moderation”. The longevity program at Three Forks Ranch in Colorado, partnering with the Mayo Clinic, even offers early cancer detection. None of this comes cheap. At Palazzo Fiuggi Medical Concept, a five-star wellness retreat outside Rome, the base fee for a week of the longevity program starts at $18,000, including accommodation, meals, movement and wellness treatments and diagnostics. But for a discerning group of travellers – especially the wealthy, who can’t buy eternal life but can throw money at extending it – long-term results are the aim, not just the transitory warm and fuzzy feeling from a sound bath.



In Australia, many of these diagnostic tools are available if you’re sick, but the idea here is to get ahead of ageing, and incorporate beneficial treatments and healthy living practices well before age and illness set in. Related Article Thailand Diagnosed with severe stress, I managed to unwind thanks to this resort Interestingly, Generation Z and Millennials are the top spenders on wellness, so the hospitality industry clearly hopes it can mine a rich source of multi-generational angst about ageing. While it’s nice to be pampered, can longevity programs really deliver what they promise? The trusted keys to a long, healthy, well-lived life? Cultivate a strong sense of community. Travel by foot as much as you can. Incorporate exercise into your daily life. Have a good night’s sleep. Keep your mind engaged. Prioritise plant-based foods. Spend time in nature. Find time for yourself.



These are all free. The writer was a guest of ILTM.

World.title: They are now on the TV, but could these former athletes win today?
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV They are now on the TV, but could these former athletes win today? Nicole Elphick July 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Commonwealth Games will look a little different. After Victoria withdrew from hosting duties for the event in 2023, Glasgow stepped in as host for what will now be a streamlined version of the Games with 10 sports scheduled, instead of the 19 sports at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022. Former competitive swimmer Johanna Griggs, part of the hosting team covering the event for Seven, feels that despite the changes, the sporting community was mainly relieved the Games would go ahead, even in a scaled-back version. Johanna Griggs and Matt Shirvington are part of the team covering the Glasgow Commonwealth Games for Seven. Monique Westermann “To be perfectly honest, I think they’re over the moon that it got picked up,” says Griggs. “Everyone was a bit shocked when Melbourne made the announcement that they were going. I think there are a lot of people that wondered whether or not that would be the death knell for the Commonwealth Games, and there was a huge amount of relief – obviously the sports that miss out would be completely and utterly devastated – but I think we’ve just looked at it as, ‘Hey, the Games are on’.” The Glasgow Games are set to kick off on July 24 at 4.45am with the opening ceremony, with more than 3000 athletes from 74 nations and territories competing. Griggs, who won a bronze medal in the 100-metre backstroke at the 1990 event in Auckland, has a lot of fondness for the Games.



Related Article Australian TV Albanese and Taylor both said yes to Annabel Crabb, but one pollie is holding out “They have a really important place in sport,” says Griggs. “That started my swimming career. I’d just turned 16 when I went to the Comm Games and medalled there and then medalled at the world championships the following year and never got to an Olympics. So, of course, it holds a special place in my heart because it was some of the most extraordinary memories.” For fellow Glasgow Games host and former sprinter Matt Shirvington, the competition performs a crucial role particularly for up-and-coming sportspeople. “I love the Commonwealth Games,” says Shirvington, who competed in the 1998 and 2006 Games. “It is the ultimate stepping stone for any young athlete coming through. It’s almost like going to university for elite sports, it really teaches you so much. Any time wearing the green and gold is a proud moment, and particularly Commonwealth Games, when you think of the people that have gone before you. All the best Australian athletes – Ian Thorpe, Cathy Freeman – all of those iconic household names forged their path through the Commonwealth Games.” A young Johanna Griggs (right) at the 6th FINA World Swimming Championships in 1991 with (from left) Julie McDonald, Susie O’Neill, Nicole Livingston and Duncan Armstrong. Australian Broadcasting Corporation TV Publicity



Shirvington, who now co-hosts Sunrise, is also very positive about Australia’s chances at the upcoming Games, following a win in 2022 with 180 medals, closely followed by England with 176. “Yeah, we’ll top it again,” says Shirvington. “There’s 200 gold medals up for grabs at these Games and we will by far top the medal table. I think a lot of those medals will come both in track and field and in swimming. [But] it’s going to be a really competitive competition across the board.” Matt Shirvington celebrates after winning bronze in the men’s 100m final at the Goodwill Games in Brisbane in 2001. Vince Caligiuri When Griggs and Shirvington are asked about whether they would have been a match in their heyday for today’s athletes, they are candid. “I don’t think so,” says Griggs, laughing. “Look at that Australian team now, how different physically they are. It’s just extraordinary to watch how clever the sports have got and how much smarter they’ve got with their training.”



Related Article Tour de France ‘There’s no other race like it’: Caleb Ewan on why the Tour de France is so special Adds Shirvington: “No, they’re absolutely flying. This current crop of Australian sprinters is the best we have ever seen, hands down. Obviously, they haven’t broken Patrick Johnson’s national record yet, [but] I think that will go. We’ve just got great athletes, and they’re just pushing each other to go faster and faster.” With swimming and track and field experiencing a golden era for Aussie athletes, Griggs and Shirvington are hoping viewers will tune in to cheer on competitors across all disciplines. “Australian sport has never been in a better position,” says Shirvington. “Some of our youngest and brightest stars are coming through for the Commonwealth Games, let’s get behind them.” The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games will be broadcast from July 24 to August 3 on Seven and 7Plus.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street steadies; Judge pauses $157b Paramount-Warner Bros deal
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street steadies; Judge pauses $157b Paramount-Warner Bros deal Stan Choe July 21, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street is holding steadier, as stocks of chipmakers and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom trim some of their recent losses. The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent, coming off its first losing week in the last three and just its third since the end of March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 186 points, or 0.4 per cent,in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent higher. AI stocks recovered some of their heavy losses from Friday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to slide, with futures pointing to a loss of 39 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX dipped by 0.1 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.98¢ at 5.21am AEST. Nvidia added 0.9 per cent and helped the market recover some of its losses, swinging back upward after its drop on Friday was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Sandisk climbed 6.1 per cent after tumbling 29 per cent last week.



Advanced Micro Devices rose 3.5 per cent after announcing an expanded partnership where Microsoft will use its products for AI, including its new Helios product starting in the second half of the year. Related Article Opinion

Wall Street Trump’s company is failing. This is his shady plan to give it a lifeline Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such stocks have been under pressure for weeks on worries that their prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. On one hand, companies are making billions of dollars in revenue as customers pour money into AI chips and data centres. But all that spending may fizzle out if AI doesn’t produce as much profit and productivity as promised. Wall Street may get some hints on that soon as some of the biggest spenders on AI report their latest quarterly results. On Wednesday, Alphabet will tell investors how much it made during the spring and give updates on its AI efforts. All kinds of companies are under pressure to report strong growth in profit for the spring. They will need to in order to justify the big moves their stock prices have made. Indexes are near their records, even with the recent shakiness for AI stocks.



AMC Entertainment jumped 24.7 per cent after the movie-theatre operator reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also said some of its theatres in Los Angeles and other cities ran The Odyssey for more than 85 straight hours from Thursday through Sunday to meet demand. A federal judge temporarily paused Paramount Skydance’s $US110 billion ($157.1 billion) takeover of Warner Bros saying it “likely” violates antitrust law. US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland on Monday ordered the companies to hold off on consummating the deal for 14 days. Paramount and Warner Bros. hoped to close as soon as July 22. California and 11 other states sued to block the Hollywood mega-merger on July 13. The states allege the deal, which seeks to combine two of the five largest studios, would harm competition for film and cable TV distribution. The judge scheduled an August 3 hearing on whether to extend the hold for longer. The judge will decide whether to pause completion of the deal until after a trial to decide whether it is illegal under federal antitrust law. Paramount Skydance shares are 1 per cent lower while Warner Bros Discovery shed 3.4 per cent. Domino’s Pizza climbed 1.9 per cent after delivering stronger revenue for the spring than expected. CEO Russell Weiner said the company saw growth in orders for both its carryout and delivery businesses, even with the broad industry continuing “to face pressure on consumer demand.”



Another restaurant chain, Jersey Mike’s, is beginning its roadshow to raise interest in its stock, which it’s planning to sell on the New York Stock Exchange for between $US21 and $US25 per share in an initial public offering. Related Article Opinion

Mergers & acquisitions Coles’ backdown on $4 billion pet deal was a smart move. Private equity can’t have been pleased Elizabeth Knight Business columnist It and other businesses are facing pressure in selling to US households feeling crunched by still-high inflation, thanks in large part to high gasoline prices. The average cost for a gallon of gasoline in the United States is back above $US4. It’s been tracking the increase in crude oil prices. After dropping below $US72 early this month, roughly back to where it was before the war with Iran began, the price for a barrel of Brent crude has been jumping recently as fighting continues in the Middle East. On Monday, the price swung between roughly $US86 and $US91. It was most recently at $US88.90, up 0.9 per cent.



The war with Iran is keeping oil tankers from using the Strait of Hormuz to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf to customers, which pushes up oil’s price. S&P Global counted only 127 vessels crossing the strait during the week through Sunday, down nearly 50 per cent from the week before. Worries about expensive oil and high inflation have sent Treasury yields higher in the bond market, which threaten to slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.60 per cent from 4.55 per cent late Friday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran. Higher yields have already sent the average 30-year mortgage rate to its highest level in nearly a year. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe. The moves were sharper in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi fell 4.5 per cent. It’s been at the centre of the huge swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.



Stocks were stronger in China, where indexes rose 2.4 per cent in Hong Kong and 0.9 per cent in Shanghai. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: How a minister’s ‘signature move’ inspired this student’s portrait
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life How a minister’s ‘signature move’ inspired this student’s portrait Catherine Strohfeldt July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If his social media pages are anything to go by, Queensland’s education minister loves taking selfies. Now one has leapt off the screen, becoming the unlikely inspiration for a painting that young artist Angel Sadik hopes will soon appear in a Brisbane gallery. Dubbed The man behind the title, the circular painting of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek has been entered in the Brisbane Portrait Prize’s Next Gen category. Angel Sadik’s portrait of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek, dubbed The man behind the title. Morgan Roberts Sadik, the vice-captain at Corinda State High School, said she selected the selfie snapshot as an homage to the minister.



“He does this thing wherever he is … a 0.5x or whatever it is,” she said. Sadik is referring to the fish-eye-style selfie created by placing a phone camera on a 0.5x zoom setting – allowing more of the photographer’s surroundings to appear in the picture – which can frequently be seen on the long-standing Queensland MP’s social accounts. Langbroek has taken his “signature move” fish-eye selfies at Corinda SHS on multiple occasions. Facebook / Catherine Strohfeldt Langbroek’s happy snaps feature the grinning minister next to a range of people, from students to community figures and federal parliamentarians. “It’s just a nice way of bringing people together ... it’s like an inclusive signature move,” Sadik said.



Rendered in oil paints on sanded plywood, the portrait was a study on image, Sadik said. However, she said the viewer decided exactly whose image that was. Angel Sadik’s portrait of Education and Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Morgan Roberts “There are two cameras in the piece,” she said. “The circular canvas was like a camera lens, to represent how the outer society views him. “You can view it in this perspective … [that] you’re looking outwards at him.”



The second camera is the phone itself. “That’s more of a self representation, the way he views himself,” she said. “It’s just to do with how you view him as a person.” Related Article Art Brisbane muralist wins big with small portrait of fellow street artist The 17-year-old said she first considered Langbroek as a possible portrait subject when he visited her school in late October last year – stopping to take a few 0.5x ministerial selfies. The minister had called a press conference at the school, watched by the then incoming school vice captain Sadik and other members of Corinda’s student leadership team. Sadik said she was struck by the minister’s comfort in front of multiple news cameras, particularly when fielding questions about the state’s “best and final” pay offer, made to teachers that morning.



“He was just so composed and that really influenced me a lot … I wanted to represent him in a lens that really shows the man behind the camera,” Sadik said. When the minister again visited the school in February this year to sit for the portrait, she said she uncovered his “less intimidating” human side. Angel Sadik (right) and her art teacher, Pam Leech (left). Morgan Roberts Speaking to this masthead in February, Langbroek said he had been flattered by the offer, and felt it suited his ministerial portfolios of arts and education. “I’m interested to hear how Angel’s going to portray me, given that she doesn’t do what we’d call traditional works of art,” the minister said.



Sadik’s past entries, in year 10 and 11, included mixed media self-portraits using photography, acrylic paint and her own hair. She said her art teacher, Pam Leech, along with friends and family, had been huge supports as she created the piece. The Brisbane Portrait Prize will announce finalists for the main and Next Gen prizes on September 5 ahead of a gallery opening and unveiling of the winners later in the month. World.title: The secret to making failproof basmati rice –  no rice cooker required
World.content:
Tips & adviceRice The secret to making failproof basmati rice – no rice cooker required Sarina Kamini shares her tried-and-tested technique for perfect rice every time, including a simple but often overlooked step that makes all the difference. Sarina Kamini July 21, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rice in India is like tea in Japan. Different regions will have different endemic varietals best eaten with the masala, or spice mix, of that area. There are hundreds of varieties (though fewer now than previously), and each will require a different cook. Short grain. Tougher husks. More starch. Less starch. The common thread is that, no matter the variety, perfect rice is non-negotiable. Placing the colander of boiled rice into a lidded pot allows the grains to steam and separate. Patricia Niven So when I say perfect rice, I mean perfect basmati rice. Basmati is my jam, and part of my Kashmiri heritage. I love basmati and eat it most days. When I teach masala masterclasses, it’s the No. 1 point of interest. More than wanting to know how to cook a great rogan josh or a killer gobi sabji, folks want to know how to nail the rice. This is my analogue method. No rice cookers. No water measures. No Thermomix or electric pressure cookers. Just a large pot plus a bit of time and planning.



Soaking rice in water allows it to bloom and release its flavours. iStock The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Bloom it Rinsing and washing rice is – for the most part – a known step when it comes to cooking rice. But the soak takes it a step further. Soaking rice is the secret to unlocking its aroma and allowing its natural flavours to bloom. Without this crucial step, the fragrance remains trapped inside the hard grain. Think of it as the culinary equivalent of throwing a cold scotch fillet straight onto a hot barbecue – the sudden heat will cause it to seize, locking away the flavour rather than releasing it. Basmati rice requires the same patience. After rinsing thoroughly in three or four changes of cold water, submerge it in a fresh bowl of water to soak. When I’m on top of my planning, I set it to soak the night before. If I lose track of myself, I’ll give it whatever time I can. Even 30 minutes makes a difference.



Tip the pre-soaked basmati rice into boiling water. Patricia Niven Boil it Setting rice to cook on a rolling boil is the ultimate failsafe method – the perfect companion to a good soak. Set a large pot of water over high heat. Once boiling, drain the soaked rice and tip it into the bubbling water. Leave the pot lid off and stay close to the stove top. Because the rice has already been soaked, the grains have been partially hydrated, which means two things: It cooks incredibly fast: Once the water returns to a boil, pre-soaked rice needs as little as three or four minutes to cook through. The texture stays flawless: Because it spends less time tumbling in boiling water, the rice retains its distinct shape instead of getting mushy. And in the world of rice, better texture means better flavour. One last thing to keep in mind: if the rice looks translucent, it’s already overcooked. You’re aiming for a little bit of al dente resistance. Take a grain and taste it. That hint of texture is crucial for what comes next, as we head into our third and final step…



Steam it Once boiled, strain the rice through a large colander. Pop the rice-filled colander back into the empty pot, off the heat, and cover it with the pot lid. We’re now steaming the cooked rice. This second process dries off excess water, separates the rice grains and sets the aroma. It also finishes the cook, taking the rice from al dente to perfect without breaking down the texture. As kitchen techniques go, it’s akin to resting cooked meat. Rice can be steamed this way and kept warm for up to 30 minutes while you finish preparing the rest of the meal. Speckled with cumin seeds, jeera chawal is a delicious way to soak up rich curry sauces. iStock How to make jeera chawal (cumin seed rice)



This dish is the ultimate way to dress up fresh rice or transform leftovers. It isn’t so much a rigid recipe as a quick, three-step improvisation. Step 1: Melt a tablespoon of ghee (or to taste) in a small frying pan over medium heat. Step 2: Toss in a few generous pinches of cumin seeds, letting them sizzle in the hot ghee until fragrant and toasted. Step 3: Tip the aromatic ghee and seeds over your steamed rice, then gently fluff and toss the grains together using two forks. I like to add a few pinches of sea salt flakes to finish for a little extra pop of flavour. I love to eat this on its own when I’m feeling rundown. My second favourite is with rogan josh or a simple mutton or lamb curry.

World.title: AI is reshaping the economy, but good luck measuring how
World.content:
BusinessThe economyAI AI is reshaping the economy, but good luck measuring how Ben Casselman July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pretty much everyone agrees that artificial intelligence has the potential to reshape the economy in the coming decades. But no one is sure what effect the technology is having right now. According to some measures, AI is contributing to high unemployment rates among new graduates and might already have destroyed tens of thousands of jobs. Other sources suggest companies might actually be adding workers as a result of the technology. Researchers can’t even agree on basic questions like how many companies are using AI or which workers are most vulnerable to the disruptions it could cause. AI might be contributing to the US inflation problem, or be part of the solution to it. It might be responsible for a recent pickup in productivity growth, or might be playing virtually no role — or the productivity boom itself might be a mirage. Researchers can’t even agree on basic questions like how many companies are using AI or which workers are most vulnerable to the disruptions it could cause.



The conflicting signals partly reflect the challenge of detecting economic shifts in real time. Government statistics are inherently backward looking, and they are better at measuring broad trends than developments in specific sectors or regions. New technologies that might lead to the emergence of new products, jobs or entire industries can be particularly difficult to measure. Related Article AI AI models cheating and blackmailing in tests, minister says What makes AI different is the speed of its spread through the economy. It has taken less than four years for generative AI to go from a novelty useful mostly for writing limericks to a powerful tool adopted by the world’s largest corporations. Economists have become convinced that the technology will have profound implications for workers and the economy, even as they disagree about what those implications will be. By the time the data is clear, they warn, it could be too late for policymakers to figure out how to respond. “The stakes are super high,” said Nathan Goldschlag, director of research at the Economic Innovation Group, a think tank. “Getting the policy right is going to depend on getting the measurement right. You can’t get the policy right if you don’t know what’s happening.” Goldschlag has published a report documenting the challenge of AI measurement and proposing steps to improve it. He and other experts argue that the government and the private sector should be devoting more resources to the problem.



They are getting at least a hearing in Washington. In June, a bipartisan group of senators introduced a bill that would expand data collection and require the federal government to produce an annual report on AI’s effect on the labor force. “The government’s got to make some big decisions about AI and about the economy, and if you’re doing that in a vacuum, you’re going to make mistakes,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., one of the bill’s sponsors. “This affects millions of Americans’ lives and millions of businesses. And you can’t do this smartly without reliable data.” Mixed Signals Policymakers aren’t flying completely blind. Since 2023, the Census Bureau has asked companies about their AI use in a biweekly survey. It has also included questions about the technology in an annual business survey, although only intermittently. Researchers have developed several measures of “AI exposure,” many of which use a government database of job descriptions to assess which occupations will be most affected. Economists can use those measures to figure out whether the most exposed occupations are adding jobs more slowly, for example, or experiencing different rates of wage growth.



The trouble is that the sources often tell confusing or contradictory stories. Surveys reach wildly different estimates of companies’ AI use based on how questions are asked. AI exposure measures tell different stories about which jobs will be most affected. In one study, economists at Northwestern University and American University found that when they used different exposure measures, those could influence not just the scale of AI’s effect on jobs but the direction. AI was hurting employment according to some measures, and helping according to others. “I think it’s comparable to the Industrial Revolution in terms of how it’s going to affect the labor market.” Erik Brynjolfsson, director Stanford University Digital Economy Lab “It’s like going to the doctor and getting three different diagnoses for the same condition,” said Michelle Yin, a Northwestern University economist who was one of the study’s authors. Part of the problem is that the best-known measures of the economy were developed for an era before personal computers and the internet, let alone AI. The monthly jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, for example, provides breakdowns of job growth in manufacturing, retail and construction, but not in technology, which has adopted AI tools most aggressively. Instead, tech is spread across several categories, including information, a broad sector that also includes newspapers and film studios. Still, economists say that for all its shortcomings, government data will be crucial for understanding AI’s effect over time. Researchers at the Yale Budget Lab, for example, have begun publishing a monthly analysis based on government data that tracks “occupational churn,” how quickly the types of jobs that make up a given industry are changing. The measure is designed to be something of an early warning system for AI’s effects. As companies begin adopting the technology, the researchers theorize, they are likely to begin hiring for different roles even if their total number of employees doesn’t change right away.



“It’s easy to pick up case studies in retrospect,” said Martha Gimbel, executive director of the lab. “What makes this time different is we are actually trying to measure this and figure this out in real time.” Related Article Opinion

AI Think twice: Five key rules for using AI at work Tim Duggan Work columnist But those efforts could be hampered by a federal statistical system that has been plagued by falling response rates to government surveys. Shrinking budgets have made it hard for statistical agencies to fill the gaps. Erika McEntarfer, who led the Bureau of Labor Statistics until President Donald Trump fired her last year, said an additional $10 million a year in funding would allow the agency to expand the sample size of its monthly labor market survey so that it could do a better job of capturing economic shifts. “The data we’re currently using to understand AI’s impact on the labor market is in jeopardy because of funding shortfalls,” she said. “It would take only some very modest investments to shore them up.” Private data



Many economists aren’t waiting for the government to catch up. Several research teams have released AI measures based on private-sector data that is more detailed and more timely, albeit less comprehensive, than what is available from the government. The Stanford University Digital Economy Lab last month released a dashboard of AI indicators based partly on data from ADP, the payroll processor. That data shows that entry-level jobs have declined sharply in the most AI-exposed sectors since ChatGPT debuted in 2022. Erik Brynjolfsson, the lab’s director, called the trend a canary in the coal mine for AI-driven job losses. Economists have become convinced that the technology will have profound implications for workers and the economy, even as they disagree about what those implications will be. Peter Rae “I think it’s comparable to the Industrial Revolution in terms of how it’s going to affect the labor market,” Brynjolfsson said. “I wish the federal government was investing more in it. But meanwhile, there’s some great private data sources that we’re pulling together, and that’s what I think is helping to fill that gap.” But the private data is just as muddy as the government statistics. Research published last week by Ramp, an expense management company, and Revelio Labs, a labor market data firm, found that the companies using AI most intensely were adding jobs more quickly than those that had been slower to adopt the tools.



Related Article AI Slow down, save jobs: Labor senator leads call to protect workers from AI revolution Ramp has access to data on which AI tools its customers are buying and how much they are spending on them. That allows it to distinguish heavy users from more cautious adopters — a crucial distinction, because it takes time and investment for companies to figure out how to use the tools effectively, said Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp. “It’s difficult to measure AI’s impact on a business, because it requires sustained adoption,” he said. “It’s clear in our work that a simple chat subscription does not drive productivity for a firm.” Work in progress Researchers generally agree on one thing: AI’s effect on the broad economy has been limited so far.



That isn’t necessarily surprising. Brynjolfsson and other economists have found that technological innovations often follow a J-shaped pattern, in which companies initially become less productive as they experiment with new tools, then experience rapid gains once they figure out how to take advantage of them. The confusing economic evidence suggests that many companies are still on the downward part of the J. “The signals are mixed because, probably, the underlying economics are mixed, because we’re still in a period of experimentation,” said Goldschlag, the Economic Innovation Group economist. “The tools themselves are still becoming useful.” Over time, it should become easier for researchers to separate the effects of AI from other forces. But they still won’t be able to resolve the question that policymakers and everyday citizens want most to answer: What comes next? “What the data can almost never tell us is where we’re going to be in five to 10 years,” said McEntarfer, the former commissioner of labor statistics. “People are looking to data to answer that question, and it’s just too difficult.”



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: A dated business class on one of the few 747 jumbo jets still flying
World.content:
★★★½ Reviews & adviceAirline reviews A dated business class on one of the few 747 jumbo jets still flying Jennifer Johnston July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The airline: Lufthansa Route Frankfurt to Singapore Changi Airport, flight LH0780

Frankfurt to Singapore Changi Airport, flight LH0780 Frequency Daily on this aircraft; 16 weekly flights in all on this route

Daily on this aircraft; 16 weekly flights in all on this route Aircraft Boeing 747-400

Boeing 747-400 Class Business, seat 1K, window

Business, seat 1K, window Flight time 12 hours, 40 minutes (we are delayed 45 minutes on departure but land on time) Lufthansa is one of the few airlines still operating Boeing 747 jumbo jets. Checking in I flew into Frankfurt Airport from Portugal with my boarding pass ready for part two of three flights home to Australia. We board, then wait. Our departure delay is caused by a minor engineering issue, which requires documentation. “We used old-school pen and paper,” the captain’s voiceover explains with a chuckle. It feels appropriate for this old school aircraft. The first 747 took to the skies in 1969, and the 400 series flew commercially from 1989.



Baggage 



Inside the 747’s business class cabin. Lufthansa currently operates eight Boeing 747-400 aircraft, each configured to seat 371 passengers: 67 business class, 32 premium economy, and 272 economy seats. On the main deck, the 45 business lie-flat seats are forward-facing, angled and parallel in a 2-3-2 configuration. The upper deck has 22 seats in a 2-2 layout (more about that later). It’s a dated layout, as most major airlines now offer direct aisle access for all business-class passengers. The seats have a 64-inch (162cm) pitch, a 20-inch (50cm) width and 18-inch (46cm) depth. Arriving at my 1K seat in front of the bulkhead, I check my alarming thoughts, as I note the proximity of my very adjacent neighbour (a stranger). After dinner, I place my chair in lie-flat mode – 78 inches (198cm) in length – unroll my bed cover/mattress and blanket. The armrest frame provides some privacy, but fails to block my neighbour’s snoring. (Hooray for my ear plugs.) Entertainment + tech The seat and the screens, if you can reach them.



The 11.7-inch screen on the bulkhead feels distant (55cm from seat to the bulkhead.) After dinner, I plan to watch a movie, then sleep, but I’m bamboozled by the tech. My German neighbour assists, demonstrating how to use the remote integrated in my seat arm. Pressing a small button activates an arrow on the screen. Hovering, I navigate through the entertainment. Plenty of movies, but very few new releases. Over-ear headphones are located in a storage bin window side. Upon waking, my TV screen remains in slumber mode. My neighbour’s attempts to fix it fails. Laughing, he comments, “Old plane,” and offers his screen (while he uses a personal laptop). Related Article ★★

Airline reviews Airline review: Remember flying’s bad old days? After this flight, I do Service Before departure, a cabin attendant asks (initially in German, then English when I look blank) if I’d like an “Avionic aperitif” – a fruity drink with peach and citrus notes. A small paper bag on my arm rest sealed with a sticker stamped “Your welcome moment” contains salted almonds. Later, the flight attendant returns holding a small basket. Unsure of its contents, I copy my neighbour and take one – a long-sleeve T-shirt for sleeping, sans trousers. The attendant is pleasant throughout the flight. She also laughs when my neighbour explains my black screen. Food



Two meals are served during the flight. With three choices of appetiser, I opt for the burrata with tomatoes, basil and arugula. Three mains: corn-fed chicken breast in carrot cream with pickled shitake mushroom and broccolini; Halibut and prawn; or spinach and ricotta filled raviolini. I select the chicken, which is tasty with a crispy skin. Dessert is cheeses and fresh fruit. Despite the tempting wine list (German riesling, a fruity Austrian white, or a South African chardonnay), I request water, mindful that a toilet visit requires clambering past my neighbour, once his seat is in lie-flat mode. Before landing, breakfast is either farmer’s breakfast or kaiserschmarrn (sweet shredded pancakes with raisins, and a yoghurt with cherry and hazelnut). Sustainability Lufthansa’s website declares its commitment to a carbon-neutral footprint by 2050. Despite the 747-400 plane consuming more fuel than a modern twin-engine fuel-efficient aircraft, Lufthansa continues flying the “Queen of the Skies” (maybe for all the 747 fanatics). One more thing I was blissfully unaware of the 747’s upper deck – commonly referred to as the “bubble”. At our final destination, Singapore, a flight attendant notices me taking photos of our empty cabin. He asks if I have been upstairs. No! He escorts me up the internal staircase, where I spy the raised cockpit, unique to the 747. After commenting that the bubble feels very intimate, he replies: “Always book business seats numbered in the 80s.” A great tip for next time – unlikely, but a gal can dream.



The price From about $6200 return in business class, Frankfurt to Singapore. From Singapore, the airline has codeshare arrangements with Singapore Airlines for connections to Australian cities.** Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Qantas’ new ultra-long haul plane is about to arrive. I’d rather stick with the A380 Michael Gebicki The Tripologist The verdict These days it is rare to find an airline that flies a 747, so flying on a “Queen of the skies” before they retire (the eight remaining 747-400s are between 23 and 27 years old – Lufthansa retires its planes around the 30-year age) felt nostalgically special.



Our rating out of five ★★★½ *For more information about air travel and sustainability, see iata.org **Fares are based on those available for travel three months from the time of publication and subject to change. The writer flew at her own expense.

World.title: Europe’s most scenic train journey takes less than three hours
World.content:
InspirationTrain journeys Europe’s most scenic train journey takes less than three hours Andrew Bain July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Born out of a wartime escape, the true gold on Norway’s Golden Train is some of Europe’s finest mountain scenery. In Norway’s Romsdal Valley, the landscape is almost mythical in scale. Europe’s tallest vertical cliff towers overhead and the cairns of more than 100 Viking burials still furrow a section of the valley floor. Summit to write home about, with views across Andalsnes and the Romsdalsfjord to the mountains. Andrew Bain It’s a place connected to ancient tales of trolls, but the greatest story here is that of the Rauma Railway on which I’m travelling. Running for almost 50 kilometres from Andalsnes to Bjorli, the Rauma Railway was used by Norway during World War II to help smuggle 50 tonnes of gold out of the country when it was invaded by Nazi Germany. Under heavy bombing, the entirety of the gold, along with the Norwegian king, was successfully shipped to Britain.



Today, the train that travels along the line is known as the Golden Train and in 2022 it was named by Lonely Planet as Europe’s most scenic train journey. 



The most prominent of the mountain features is the Trollveggen – the Troll Wall – Europe’s loftiest rock face, rising more than 1000 metres above the train. Mount Everest was climbed 12 years before this imposing wall was conquered, while two local lads claimed to have climbed the equally daunting Romsdalshornet, which towers over the first stretch of valley, in 1828, but their boast was dismissed as drunken bravado. When it was finally summited by a Danish climber more than 50 years later, he found a cairn built by the pair atop it. Trollveggen, Europe’s tallest vertical cliff. iStock If the mountains were difficult to conquer, Rauma Railway’s course through the valley was no less problematic – opened in the 1920s, the line took 13 years and more than 600 men to build, and it ran 600 per cent over budget. The railway largely follows the line of the Rauma River through this valley, far deeper than it is wide. In winter, the sun is a stranger and the river lies frozen, more an ice floe now than a flowing stream. High up the valley, the railway makes a sweeping turn, crossing the river on the Kylling Bridge. With its high, graceful arch, it’s Norway’s most photographed bridge and a star of 2009’s Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, as well as Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One.



For all that, Kylling Bridge isn’t the Rauma Railway’s most impressive engineering achievement. As the line completes its horseshoe turn over the bridge, it swings almost immediately into another 180-degree turn, but this time inside a tunnel. The 1400-metre-long Stavem Tunnel was an extraordinarily ambitious and complex design feat that took nine years to complete. Related Article Train journeys The world’s 24 greatest railway experiences The valley finally widens and flattens as we approach the Golden Train’s turnaround point in Bjorli, where there’s a chance to alight, visit a display on the railway’s gold-smuggling moment and wander Bjorli’s few streets beneath slopes patterned with ski runs. With cruise passengers taking trains through the Romsdal Valley for more than a century, there was once a restaurant feeding 700 in tiny Bjorli, but it was bombed and destroyed during World War II and the best on offer now is takeaway coffee from a petrol station. As we’ve travelled the 50 kilometres inland from Andalsnes, the temperature has plunged by about five degrees – it’s now a frosty minus six – and Andalsnes’ snow-free streets have been replaced by a thick pelt of snow.



In the day’s late light, the train’s polished exterior glows as golden as its name. I’m quickly back aboard, ready for a second screening of this remarkable valley and its high peaks and cliffs. On The Golden Train, the journey is very much the destination. THE DETAILS RIDE

The Golden Train runs daily from Andalsnes, with round-trip tickets for the 2½-hour trip costing from $100. See thegoldentrain.com TRAVEL

Many of Hurtigruten’s Norwegian cruises, including the 15-day North Cape Line cruise, dock in Andalsnes, offering the Golden Train as a shore excursion. See hurtigruten.com MORE
