World.title: ‘Wellness’ is out. Relaxation holidays are now about extending your lifespan
World.content:
InspirationWellness holidays Opinion ‘Wellness’ is out. Relaxation holidays are now about extending your lifespan Lee Tulloch Travel columnist July 21, 2026 — 5:00am

July 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Imagine if you could add 10 years to your life just by taking a holiday. No one is quite promising this yet, but the possibility might not be far away. Wellness retreats have hit a whole new level. Getty Images Travelling for longevity is the concept running hot through the travel industry right now. “Wellness” was the buzzword a decade ago, but now, being well in the moment is not enough. People are talking about having a “health span” as well as a lifespan – living longer in a state of optimum health for one’s age.



And the hospitality industry believes it is well-placed to provide a service to those willing to pay for the enhanced possibility of a healthy 100-year-old life. 



Preferred Hotels and Resorts, a collection of independent hotels, launched a worldwide wellness brand emphasising results-driven treatments that combine Eastern wellness philosophies with Western technologies such as biohacking, hydrothermal circuits and advanced skincare. It isn’t just about wellness, they emphasised, it’s longevity. The word popped up again and again. Even cruise companies realise that a relaxation massage might not be enough of an attraction for some guests. Regent Seven Seas Cruises announced a new Spotlight on Wellness & Longevity cruise starting in 2027. Longevity is the new travel buzzword. Getty Images For decades, Europeans have been booking into medical health clinics such as Clinique La Prairie in Montreux, Switzerland, for science-based medical treatments and cosmetic surgery along with their pampering massages and facials.



When I lived in France 20 years ago, you could get a prescription from your doctor for a free week at a medically based spa in Normandy or Brittany. In our part of the world, hospitality brands such as Six Senses, Kamalaya and Chiva-Som have been offering cutting-edge holistic treatments for many years. Biohacking, red-light therapy and sleep therapy programs are not new. What is new is an ageing population worrying about the prospect of a poor quality of life in their final decades, and constantly evolving medical advances, including diagnostic tools such as DNA analysis. Now, instead of a welcome drink when you arrive at your spa, you get an IV drip and live blood analysis. You can follow up with genetic DNA testing, cellular optimisation and 3D body mapping.



A growing number of spas are offering such medically integrated treatments, including RAKxa Integrative Wellness in Thailand, which partners with the VitalLife Scientific Wellness clinic of Bangkok’s respected Bumrungrad International Hospital. At SHA Wellness destinations in Spain, Mexico and the Emirates guests can book Advanced Longevity programs offering “biological ageing moderation”. The longevity program at Three Forks Ranch in Colorado, partnering with the Mayo Clinic, even offers early cancer detection. None of this comes cheap. At Palazzo Fiuggi Medical Concept, a five-star wellness retreat outside Rome, the base fee for a week of the longevity program starts at $18,000, including accommodation, meals, movement and wellness treatments and diagnostics. But for a discerning group of travellers – especially the wealthy, who can’t buy eternal life but can throw money at extending it – long-term results are the aim, not just the transitory warm and fuzzy feeling from a sound bath.



In Australia, many of these diagnostic tools are available if you’re sick, but the idea here is to get ahead of ageing, and incorporate beneficial treatments and healthy living practices well before age and illness set in. Related Article Thailand Diagnosed with severe stress, I managed to unwind thanks to this resort Interestingly, Generation Z and Millennials are the top spenders on wellness, so the hospitality industry clearly hopes it can mine a rich source of multi-generational angst about ageing. While it’s nice to be pampered, can longevity programs really deliver what they promise? The trusted keys to a long, healthy, well-lived life? Cultivate a strong sense of community. Travel by foot as much as you can. Incorporate exercise into your daily life. Have a good night’s sleep. Keep your mind engaged. Prioritise plant-based foods. Spend time in nature. Find time for yourself.



These are all free. The writer was a guest of ILTM.

World.title: 'It's absolutely devastating': Ruahine Animal Rescue evicted from council site
World.content:
Animal rescue faces closure after council eviction Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Central Hawke's Bay's only animal rescue is facing closure because the local council is evicting the charity from its premises.

Ruahine Animal Rescue is based in Waipukurau where the SPCA was located for 30 years, but the land was sold to the council when the SPCA closed down in 2022. The area is currently used by both the animal rescue and the dog pound.

The council has given Ruahine Animal Rescue until 13 December to move out, which volunteer Grace White said is a huge shock.

"It's absolutely devastating. We've poured our blood sweat and tears in... we're all volunteers and we just don't want to give up.

"We can't see a future without a rescue in place," she said.

The animal rescue is funded by donations from the community and entirely run by volunteers. Grace White said it's about so much more than just animals.

"I started off with the inability to walk properly and through work here I'm now without a walker, you know it just gets better and better - we see and meet people from all walks of life as well," she said.

Grace White and Labrador Gary. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The council told RNZ it reviewed its dog pound operation in June and found there wasn't enough capacity, so it needed to use the extra space currently occupied by the animal rescue.

But Ruahine Animal Rescue Chair Carma Anderson said that didn't add up.

"From what we see on a daily basis we don't notice their kennels are full. No one has ever come to us saying they are at capacity and can they utilise some of our kennel space," she said.

However, the council's community safety and compliance manager Logan McKay told RNZ it's not just about kennel space and the pound needed three separate areas for rehoming, isolation and dogs with an unknown status.

"It may sound selfish, but it's not about the Ruahine Animal Rescue - it's about our ability to provide a pound, a safe space for the animals we take in and our staff," he said.

Ruahine Animal Rescue has rehomed 261 animals since it opened in December 2024. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The council couldn't provide RNZ with figures showing how many dogs it impounded each year, but said the data could be requested through the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act.

Instead it pointed to information collected about the number of 'dog related complaints' recieved every year, which had risen from 861 in 2022/23 to 1126 in 2024/25. The complaints were broken into categories such as attacks on people or other animals, barking, fouling, wandering and/or impounded.

"Every metric we are measuring has increased so we need to make sure we have a modern pound fit for purpose," said McKay.

The dog pound. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Since Ruahine Animal Rescue opened in 2024 it had rehomed 261 animals, and Carma Anderson said the charity was now desperately trying to figure out its future so it could continue to save animals.

She has launched a campaign to 'rescue the rescue' and was trying to raise enough funds to buy a property for the animal shelter.

"If I had a magic wand I would purchase an existing building and modify it for purpose and keep it in the community forever.

"It doesn't just provide services for animals, it fosters the spirit of voluntary service and provides opportunities for youth and connections for the elderly," said Anderson.

Public challenges the mayor over council decision

A heated discussion about the future of the rescue took place at a public meeting in Waipukurau on Sunday. Locals demanded answers from mayor Will Foley about why the council was evicting the animal rescue.

Mayor Will Foley answers the public's questions. RNZ / Alexa Cook

One man questioned the council's decision.

"I would like to know ... if you can't help animals you can't help anyone. I need a reason why they want them out of there because I want to help," he said.

The mayor replied, promising he was taking their concerns seriously. "I'm here today to listen and learn and help as much as we can," said Foley.

Among the dozens of people attending were Nancy Neal and her friend Maureen James.

"I'm a ratepayer therefore I have a share in that property along with these people sitting next to me and we want to see Ruahine Animal Resuce stay there so our first question is why are you having to move?" said Neal.

"Why are they having to shift out of what is absolutely suitable spot and set up well for them," queried James.

Nancy Neal (L) and her friend Maureen James. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Lisa Bennett was also worried.

"There's a real need for it in the community. So many animals get abused and thrown away like garbage, and they don't deserve it," she said.

Carma Anderson said Sunday's meeting resulted in a surge of public support.

"The community did not disappoint. They feel given the history of this piece of land it is right that Ruahine would continue to occupy it and are prepared to have their voices heard at the council.

"They [are] even asking the question about whether it'd be suitable for the council to vacate this premise and find somewhere else ... so it's ongoing, we will see," she said.

When asked if there was any hope that the animal rescue may be able to stay put, the council said that was unlikely.

"We had the conversation this morning, but from our chief executive and from Will ... It is about safety. Safety of animals we care for, safety of people that work in this space and the safety of our community when we do remove those dogs.

World.title: Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale arrives in US for high-level talks
World.content:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale has arrived in Washington for a series of high-level talks with US officials this week, his office says.

Wale's official overseas travel since taking office on 15 May this year now spans four separate diplomatic tours across six countries. These include Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and his current official visits to the United States and Japan official.

As part of his official programme in the US, Wale is expected to meet with Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

The prime minister will also hold meetings with senior officials from the Development Finance Corporation, the Millennium Challenge Corporation and the Peace Corps.

A statement from his office said these talks will focus on strengthening development cooperation, expanding economic opportunities and advancing shared priorities.

"Upon arrival in Washington, DC, the prime minister convened a briefing with his delegation to outline key objectives and align priorities ahead of the scheduled meetings," the statement said.

"The visit emphasises the government's commitment to deepening international partnerships and pursuing opportunities that support national development and the well-being of all Solomon Islanders."

World.title: 'A very high-risk way to spend $1 billion': Experts on NZ First's oil and gas policy
World.content:
New Zealand First's oil and gas exploration policy is "a very high-risk way to spend $1 billion", a resources law expert says.

Another researcher in the field says the policy is unlikely to achieve the party's aim of shoring up domestic fuel supply.

At the party's campaign launch on Sunday, leader Winston Peters announced New Zealand First would invest $1 billion in a 'National Subsurface Development Survey', to identify and create a single dataset across oil, gas, geothermal and carbon dioxide storage sites.

Peters said New Zealand potentially held Norway-scale energy prospects beneath the seafloor and the odds of a major commercial discovery were "well above 90 percent".

"If we identify those reserves in our basins, we will have the ability to utilise the natural resources we have to make our country secure, prosperous and to build real resilience."

University of Waikato energy and natural resources law professor Barry Barton said he did not know where Peters got the 90 percent figure from.

"And in a situation like this, even to use the word 'reserves' is dangerous. The best you can hope for is you find something that may be a resource."

Barton said what the party was proposing investing in was "not investment-grade stuff", but a first step that might yield nothing at all.

University of Waikato energy and natural resources law professor Barry Barton. Supplied / University of Waikato

"The challenges of taking geophysical survey data further, to work it up to be a prospect that would actually justify drilling and exploration wells, is considerable," he said.

"It's a very high-risk way to spend a billion dollars, isn't it?"

Even a significant find somewhere like the Great South Basin - one of the areas Peters singled out - might not necessarily be useable.

"Many New Zealand fields have turned out to be gas-rich and light on oil. If that was to happen again, if you've got a big gas discovery near the Auckland Islands or something, the challenge of bringing it ashore and then what you're going to do with it when you bring it ashore is very considerable," Barton said.

New Zealand not 'energy-poor'

Peters said surveying would take two years, and within six years, the country could have a pathway to own and control its own supply of energy, through a Norwegian-style sovereign fund.

Energy Resources Aotearoa chief executive John Carnegie backed that timeframe, saying the Pohukura field, offshore from Taranaki, took just six years to get up and running.

But Pohukura was not a good example, Barton said.

"Bear in mind that the platform is within plain sight from the highway ... and indeed, some of the reservoir is exploited from onshore wells, which are far cheaper and far easier to get up and running."

$1 billion would be far better spent on funding home insulation to make energy use more efficient, or accelerating the growth of renewable energy.

"Home insulation sounds incredibly boring, but you can ... get better homes for people, it can happen quickly, it employs a lot of people, and the results are pretty much guaranteed."

The country's abundance of renewable sources, and new firming options like biomass, made New Zealand energy-rich without the need for fossil fuels, he said.

"We have to stop telling ourselves that we're energy-poor."

Energy Resources Aotearoa chief executive John Carnegie. Supplied / Rob Tucker

Policy ignores 'structural issues'

University of Canterbury civil engineering professor David Dempsey said government-sponsored exploration surveying had been a good thing for New Zealand in the past.

However, there were "structural issues" that would likely prevent the policy from achieving its aims of providing domestic fuel security and revitalising the domestic fossil fuel industry, he said.

"For a start, we don't really have bipartisan agreement.

"That creates an enormous amount of risk for companies who would ... need to be pretty well convinced that they have freedom to operate for a long period of time."

New Zealand no longer had any refining capacity, which it would need to ensure true domestic security throughout the supply chain, Dempsey said.

In the meantime, parts of the economy were already transitioning away from oil and gas.

"Domestic transport, a lot of that will end up on electric. Probably gas is being forced to transition away more than anything else, over timeframes that are likely to be shorter than anything they can promise."

Some fuel types - such as diesel and aviation gas - would take longer to transition away from.

"It would be nice, I suppose, to do those domestically, but whether or not we could afford to or convince others to come down and do it affordably, that's where I see more of the challenge."

University of Canterbury civil engineering professor David Dempsey. Supplied/ University of Canterbury

Potential for geothermal, CO2 storage

Dempsey was pleased to see the inclusion of geothermal energy and carbon dioxide storage in the policy, though.

"Those are both things that we could potentially use more of in the future," he said.

"They're already doing a lot on the supercritical geothermal, but there's plenty of low temperature distributed [geothermal] resources that could also be looked at."

Barton said there was already "a fair bit" of survey data available on the country's geothermal resources but New Zealand First had a point that surveying techniques had advanced since that work was done.

The range of uses for geothermal had also expanded, even at relatively low temperatures.

"We have got other ways to look at geothermal as well, relatively low temperature resources, for example.

"Groundwater doesn't have to be all that hot to be useful for a greenhouse, for example - electricity generation is only one way to use geothermal."

It also made sense to gather additional data about underground reservoirs and other natural formations where carbon dioxide could be stored permanently, he said.

World.title: Scrapping council-iwi agreements will see existing Treaty settlements relitigated - Labour
World.content:
Labour says the government scrapping council agreements with local Māori will mean "a lot" of relitigating existing Treaty settlements.

The opposition party has stopped short of promising to repeal and replace the legislation, instead vowing to produce ahead of the November election a reworked bill setting out in detail what it would change.

The government says scrapping the Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements is necessary to ensure all other New Zealanders are treated equally.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop announced the move alongside Prime Minister Christopher Luxon on Monday after the weekly Cabinet meeting, saying only eight of the agreements were in place late last year until his Resource Management reforms were announced.

The reforms initially would have allowed existing Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements so long as they were completed before the legislation passed, but Bishop said the coalition had become concerned that "several dozen more" had been completed or begun since the announcement.

"Instead, councils will have the option of entering into new narrowly scoped iwi participation agreements to record how iwi authorities will participate in statutory planning processes and processes required to give effect to Treaty settlement redress. Clear guardrails will be included in the legislation to prevent scope creep."

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said there would "certainly be some changes" to that if Labour won power at the coming election.

"We're not proposing to continue to go through a repeal and replace cycle because that takes three years and ultimately we're comfortable, broadly, with the structure of it. But there are clearly areas that are off the table for us."

He said he had asked his environment and RMA reform spokesperson Rachel Brooking to draft up what Labour was proposing to change "in some detail, so that we can set that out, so everyone knows exactly ... the two versions that they would be voting for".

Brooking told RNZ such changes would include changing the goals and purpose statements, adding stronger environmental safeguards with firm limits, greater efficiency, removing the regulatory takings provisions, and reversing what she said was a degradation of Māori rights.

"We'd start at the start of the legislation," she said.

She said the government's decision to scrap the Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements at this stage in the process would lead to relitigation of Treaty settlements.

"It is just astounding that the government would put in a bill, have its a full select committee process on it - a bill that already degrades Māori rights and interests and participation rights - and then at the bequest of the Taxpayers' Union on the day that we report back after months and months of deliberation and a lot of work that they just completely flipflop on the one thing that was protecting some Māori participation rights.

"It's extraordinary, but what we have come to expect from this government."

Labour's environment and RMA reform spokesperson Rachel Brooking. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

The agreements had already been negotiated between mana whenua and councils to set out an agreed approach on how they would work together, but she said that was done on the understanding that Māori would be involved in certain decisions.

"That is why we had countless submissions saying 'well, this means that our Treaty settlement is worth a whole lot less than it was when we signed it ... I'm sure there will be a lot of litigation around this point and that goes to the inefficiency of this new process."

ACT leader David Seymour said scrapping the agreements was "absolutely necessary".

"It's acting in good faith to all the other New Zealanders who expect to be treated as equals with equal rights before the law," he said.

"The idea that a council goes and cooks up an agreement with a small sector of their community to the exclusion of all other, that is bad faith and that is what's being removed."

He said it was disingenuous for certain councils and iwi to have tried to "cook up" the agreements "to beat the law change".

"I don't think that is acting in good faith, the government is restoring equal rights and democratic representation ... any future agreements should be restricted to the use of Māori land and Māori sites of significance to Māori, they shouldn't be for example a council declaring that Ngāpuhi never ceded sovereignty as happened in the Far North."

Seymour said the process for those iwi and hapū that had not yet settled was "totally separate".

ACT leader David Seymour. Marika Khabazi / RNZ

What else would Labour change?

Brooking also criticised the regulatory takings regime which would see councils pay out to landowners if their enjoyment of land was impacted, saying it would set up a "cottage industry" of valuers.

"The person whose property it is can claim for some sort of compensation, which can include monetary compensation for the burden that is on their land. And this is interesting because biodiversity has not always been considered to be part of the land," she said.

She said much of the detail on how that would work was not detailed within the legislation, but it would likely mean a person coming to look at a given property and determine how much a council should be paying.

"That will cost huge amounts. We had a report from Martin Jenkins that the government commissioned saying it could be up to $1.99 billion, but also we know that councils do not have a lot of money at the moment, and this government is also talking about a rates cap. So, if they can't afford to put in these protections or continue with these protections, then what's going to happen? There's going to be no protections."

Brooking said the previous approach of requiring development of land to avoid breaching environmental limits - like air or water quality - had been watered down with the legislation now including "all these workarounds, particularly for infrastructure, and then infrastructure has a very wide definition, and it's particularly where the minister approves".

World.title: FENZ spends $90k on PR and lawyer for inquiry into vehicle fleet
World.content:
Fire and Emergency (FENZ) has spent $90,000 on a PR person and lawyer for the inquiry into the state of their vehicle fleet.

MPs have demanded answers from FENZ leaders and the board's new chair over the spending.

They have appeared at the latest hearing of a four-month-long select subcommittee inquiry - triggered by firetruck breakdowns and MPs' anger over a series of convoluted answers about a seven-year process that has so far failed to put any of 30 new trucks on the road.

National MP Melissa Lee asked why chief executive Kerry Gregory had to look outside to get answers about operations where he was in charge.

"It's all operational questions," Lee said.

"And the fact that you had to hire outside a PR company and law firm to actually find answers for yourself and paying exorbitant amounts of money actually tells me that you really need to think about how your organisation is actually operating."

National MP Melissa Lee (file photo). RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Gregory responded that FENZ needed outside help to understand what the inquiry wanted and to get information out of old IT systems "to our fingertips". He said he did not know how much more they might spend this way.

"The thing is making sure that we had a good understanding of what the committee was after and being able to understand what the committee was looking for as far as the breadth of the review into fleet."

MPs repeatedly pushed Gregory on what had gone wrong since FENZ was set up nine years ago.

He repeatedly said: "We will do better", while saying the problems went back years.

"A long tail," he repeatedly called it.

The four-month-long select subcommittee inquiry was triggered by firetruck breakdowns. File photo. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

National MP Tim Costley widened the blame.

"The board appeared to be tracking nothing," he said.

Ex-Watercare head Raveen Jaduram - the new board chair installed just three weeks ago - sounded a warning note to management about accountability, adding he also expected the board to do their job.

But he added that he was too new in the position to know if they had been.

"It's not acceptable," Jaduram told the committee about the years of problems dragging on.

"It's disappointing."

The MPs heard the top two people in charge of the fleet - national manager Mike Moran and deputy chief executive Sarah Sinclair - had both just resigned.

Asked by Green MP Mike Davidson if they got any exit package, Gregory was not clear, but said Sinclair did not.

The professional firefighters' union on its website said: "FENZ's corporate structure is fracturing because they cannot answer for the crisis on the frontline."

As the long hearing went on, with MPs poring over an 80-page submission from FENZ that the PR person and lawyer had helped with, the list of admitted shortcomings admitted to grew:

Inadequate truck-buying (procurement) systems.

Inadequate contract management so that they could not hold suppliers to account.

Inadequate maintenance reporting systems using paper records of breakdowns that often did not even say if a problem had been fixed.

Inadequate IT and document systems.

The agency introduced a whole new procurement system in 2022, then a procurement "roadmap" in 2025.

Gregory admitted to "some inconsistency" in procurement, but added: "We've been on a procurement improvement roadmap that we've been applying over a number of years now, so making some good steps forward through there."

"Am I right in reading from your submission, it didn't work?" asked Costley. He was told that was correct.

"You implemented the solution at the start of it before you had the roadmap and knew what it looked like," said Costley." And now we've effectively got rid of that new model and we've gone back to business units?

"It feels like another example of sort of reactionary decision making."

He added there was no evidence the board had looked into the thorniest fleet issues, despite two years of questions.

Asked how the board and management talked about fleet defects, Gregory said: "It's been fragmented to have a look at the national level around what those things mean."

Davidson asked about the basics - whether 1.8 percent was enough to spend on the fleet out of revenue over nine years of $6.3 billion, and whether 10 large-ladder (aerial) trucks were enough for the whole country when the population had grown so much since 2017.

NZ First MP Andy Foster wanted to know why 10 new trucks were not being added each year as old ones retired, and instead it had taken nine years to get 10.

Gregory, his number two commander Megan Stiffler and corporate head Darryl Purdy defended this by citing the Future Operating Capability plan - underway since 2024 - or deflected questions by saying they would have to get more information.

File photo. NZ First MP Andy Foster. VNP / Phil Smith

The lightning rod issue - 30 so-called Type 3 quite large trucks first commissioned in 2017 - made in the UK, shipped over here, then shipped back for fixes, then back here - and still now being tested and modified, although out of warranty, was the one Gregory kept going back to.

It was the exception, a process that had lacked "rigour", but the agency had done well with other parts, such as replacing its many smaller Type 1 and 2 vehicles.

They were now stabilising the core fleet and the key going forward was not to buy trucks they had to customise to New Zealand conditions, but standard trucks, the chief executive said.

Foster said it looked like they were "'going backwards at great rate of knots".

Jaduram said he would be demanding better decisions from now on, with stronger contract and clear risk management, better visibility and reporting back to the board.

Costley said the committee had been misinformed if not misled and asked the new chair - who replaced Rebecca Keoghan when she was not reappointed by the minister Brooke van Velden: "Not to mention the other things that we've just covered now, like what more would it take for every other board member to resign?"

"Or where would the point come that you would not have confidence in the board that you are leading?"

Ex-Watercare head Raveen Jaduram was recently installed as new board chair. RNZ / Dan Cook

Jaduram said those were "profound questions".

"The public see the firefighters and the fire engines.

"The firefighters, they see whether the organisation behind them actually works, the engine works.

"And as chair, it's my job to make sure they both work.

World.title: Community newspaper The Akaroa Mail celebrates 150 years
World.content:
Newspapers in New Zealand and around the world are under increasing pressure with many businesses facing restructures, going digital or closing all together but a free newspaper on Banks Peninsula is celebrating its 150th anniversary.

The Akaroa Mail was first published on 21 July, 1876, and prints 10,000 paper copies every fortnight.

Owner and editor Michael de Hamel has been running The Akaroa Mail for the last 41 years, having started at a time when the local manual telephone exchange operator would get phone calls to him by ringing the local shops and asking if they had seen him.

"In the early days if someone wanted me on the phone and I was walking around Akaroa, someone would dash out of a shop and say, 'Hey Michael you're wanted on the phone'," he said.

de Hamel said he always aimed for stories focused on local issues and events, with the job providing constant surprises.

"I found on one occasion a World War Two German aeroplane in someone's basement here in Akaroa, it was a training glider admittedly, rather than a full aeroplane, but nevertheless there are things that happen which constantly raise the eyebrows," he said.

de Hamel is not the only long-lasting editor, with one of his predecessors Ethel Jacobson running the paper from 1903 to 1953 after taking over from her father Howard Jacobson.

In the early days the paper would cover visitors to Akaroa in details, with reports of who had arrived by ship or who was staying at the local hotel, and cases at the Akaroa magistrates' court.

To celebrate the 150th anniversary, the Akaroa Museum has put together an exhibition about the paper's history.

Museum collections manager Daniel Smith said the first edition on 21 July, 1876, looked quite different to modern versions.

Akaroa Museum collections manager Daniel Smith prepares a printing plate for the display at the Museum. Supplied / Akaroa Museum via Akaroa Mail

"There weren't a lot of headlines. The whole page was entirely full of advertising. The second page has a column introducing the newspaper and its endeavours to follow local issues and then page three and page four were principally full of advertising as well. It was very much a commercial newspaper in that respect but I think that has also been its value over the years as well, it has been a really important commercial directory," he said.

Smith said The Akaroa Mail had always played an important role in recording the goings-on and the people of Banks Peninsula.

"All the community organisations regularly get named and individuals get named. You know you are part of the community once your name has been in the Mail. It's a really important role in that way. It is part of the glue that keeps the community together," he said.

Smith said researchers regularly requested to look at old council documents and he often suggested they look at the related edition of The Akaroa Mail.

"The Akaroa Mail always has a fuller record of the meetings and includes what the debate is about. You get much more context for what happened," he said.

Auckland University of Technology head of journalism at Greg Treadwell said surviving 150 years was a triumph for any newspaper in New Zealand.

He said a good local newspaper could help to keep a community strong.

"I can't say enough how important it is for a community to have a reliable verified news organ. Community news hasn't translated to online particularly well, I'm not saying there aren't some successful start ups and some models that will work, but news deserts are a real thing and spreading rapidly in New Zealand so if you are a community with a paper like The Akaroa Mail count yourself lucky," he said.

People could pick up a paper copy of The Akaroa Mail at places like the library and local businesses or subscribers could get it by post.

World.title: Man killed in Lime scooter crash wasn't wearing helmet, had been drinking
World.content:
A 23-year-old who died after falling off a Lime e-scooter wasn't wearing a helmet and had been drinking.

Almost seven years after Toben Hunt's death in 2019, Coroner Alex Ho has released his report on the fatal scooter accident.

Hunt had attended a work function at Auckland's Viaduct on the 16th of September, 2019.

"Toby drank alcohol at the function. He left at around 6pm. He hired a Lime electric scooter and did not put on a helmet," Coroner Ho wrote.

"At about 6.10 pm, in daylight before sunset, he was riding the e-scooter on Westhaven Drive towards Herne Bay. He was travelling at around 25 kilometres per hour in the middle of the single westbound lane."

A witness driving behind Hunt said the 23-year-old turned and checked for traffic before losing control of the scooter.

"As he looked over his shoulder he started drifting to his right, towards the centreline of the two lane road," the witness said.

"As he got closer to the centreline, he came 'unstuck', by that I mean the rear wheel of the scooter lifted quickly and he went over the handle bars.

"[He] let go of the scooter and had performed a complete 180 degree turn in the air before he hit the ground."

Hunt was rushed to Auckland Hospital with brain bruising, bleeding and swelling.

He died four days later, on the 20th of September 2019.

Toben Hunt died after falling off a Lime e-scooter. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Coroner Ho said while Hunt's alcohol consumption may have contributed to the crash, he was "not in any way implying that Toby was primarily responsible for his own death or that he was operating the scooter in an unsafe manner."

He said speed was another factor, but stopped short of recommending a change to the maximum speed of e-scooters.

"Reducing the speed at which electric scooters can travel would certainly make it safer for both riders and pedestrians. However, just like for motor vehicles on roads, safety is not the only consideration," he said.

"Regulators must also take into account the utility of vehicles being able to get around in a reasonable time... The road toll would undoubtedly decrease if cars were restricted to travelling at 10 kilometres per hour, but this would come at a high time cost."

Ho recommended that anyone riding an electric scooter should wear a helmet, but noted they weren't mandatory.

"While helmets are not legally required for people riding e-scooters in New Zealand, [the Transport Agency] strongly recommends wearing a helmet. It emphasises that helmets can significantly reduce the risk of head injury," Ho wrote.

A spokesperson for the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport told RNZ further work would be required to weigh the safety benefits of mandating helmets on e-scooters.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop told RNZ he encouraged e-scooter users to "ride responsibly, wear helmets and be considerate of pedestrians," but didn't indicate any plans to reassess the law on helmets.

Instead, Bishop said he wanted to allow e-scooters in cycle lanes.

"Under current rules, e-scooters aren't permitted in cycle lanes. I think this is outdated and dangerous," he said.

"This will be updated by the end of 2026, meaning e-scooter users will be able to use cycle lanes instead of the footpath where a cycle lane is available."

In a statement, Lime said it had cooperated fully with the inquiry and accepted the Coroner's findings.

"We extend our deepest condolences to Toben's family and friends," a spokesperson said.

"We note the Coroner's comments on helmet use and encourage all riders to wear a helmet every time they ride."

Emergency medicine and paediatric emergency physician Dr Stuart Dalziel. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Helmets for escooter riders needs to be compulsory

Calls grow for mandatory e-scooter helmets Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Emergency medicine and paediatric emergency physician Dr Stuart Dalziel said Hunt's death was a tragedy and something that needed to be prevented from happening to someone else.

Speaking to Morning Report on Tuesday morning, Dalziel said medical professionals were seeing an "increasing" number of injuries in hospital due to escooters.

Last year, 4000 people were injured in escooter accidents - with half of that number either children or young people, he said.

It averaged out to about 10 people per day and was causing a "significant cost" to the economy.

Dalziel said types of injuries includes head injuries, broken bones, lacerations and sprains.

In his opinion, wearing a helmet while riding an escooter would create a "huge difference" in terms of the number of injuries seen.

It "doesn't make sense" for helmets to be compulsory for cyclists but not escooter riders when both are travelling at similar speeds.

"It's a gap that needs to be corrected."

Currently, Dalziel said it wasn't something the government was taking action on, although he said it needed to be made a priority and would be a "relatively simple piece of legislation".

World.title: Tribunal upholds three-match ban for Crows forward Darcy Fogarty
World.content:
The Crows have failed in their challenge to Darcy Fogarty's three-match striking ban at the AFL Tribunal, the panel finding Fogarty had time to decide to swing his arm at Sydney's Harry Cunningham.

Fogarty was charged after his high hit on Sydney's Harry Cunningham in the second quarter of Adelaide's game with the Swans at the SCG.

Cunningham jumped to try to get the ball deep inside Sydney's defensive 50, and Fogarty came in and caught the Swans player high.

Cunningham was ruled out of the game with concussion and will miss this week's match against cross-town rivals GWS.

The hit was assessed as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact.

The Crows argued that Fogarty's actions did not constitute a strike, and that even if they did it should be high, not severe impact.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, said the actions were careless and a breach of the duty of care. He said it was no surprise the incident resulted in a concussion.

The contact "was flush, it was direct, and it was on a player whose eyes were on the ball, so he was vulnerable in that moment".

"Cunningham goes to ground, he is visibly severely impacted," Woods said.

"He remains on the ground and requires the help of support staff to get up and exit the field."

After deliberating for less than 20 minutes, the panel returned and chair Jeff Gleeson said they were "comfortably satisfied" that Fogarty had indeed committed the offence of striking.

"Fogarty had time to consider how he would tackle Cunningham in those circumstances. He chose to do so by swinging his right arm forcibly in the direction of Cunningham's upper body and head," Gleeson said.

Fogarty will now miss Crows matches against Collingwood, Essendon and Richmond.

Look back at proceedings in our live blog.

World.title: Electric Tiwi football final sees back-to-back victory for Imalu Tigers
World.content:
Just minutes into the men's Tiwi Islands football grand final, black-and-yellow-clad supporters jumped the sideline fence and started storming the field prematurely, caught up in the excitement of their first goal.

The Imalu Tigers had not yet won the flag, but their devoted supporters never gave them a reason to doubt their hopes of securing back-to-back premiership glory.

Some Tigers fans were so passionate, they ran onto the field each time their team scored. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For the thousands of people living on the Tiwi Islands, Aussie Rules is much more than a friendly sport. It's a religion, and it all culminates on grand final day.

And for the many visitors attending the grand final game at Wurrumiyanga Oval on Bathurst Island, about 80 kilometres north of Darwin, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Tapalinga Super Stars players and supporters hug after their win in the women's grand final match. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Each year, hundreds of tourists charter planes and catch ferries across to the Tiwi Islands to watch some of Australia's most promising upcoming AFL players battle it out in front of their home crowds.

This year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was one of them, becoming the first Australian leader to attend the game while in office.

The Tigers' opponents, the Ranku Eagles, also had plenty of supporters. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Victory for Imalu Tigers, Tapalinga Super Stars

Despite the opposing team, the Ranku Eagles, having the home-ground advantage, Melville Island's Imalu Tigers had the real upper hand, with droves of loyal supporters dominating the fence lines.

With reigning premiers Imalu only having lost a single game this season, it was always going to be a David-and-Goliath battle.

The men's grand final game was close early on before the Tigers pulled away. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

At half-time, it appeared the Eagles stood a chance, with the Tigers only narrowly in front by 12 points.

But in the third quarter, Imalu doubled their lead and soon became unstoppable.

For the second time in as many years, the Tigers took home the premiership cup, claiming victory in a thrilling 11.9 (75) to 7.8 (50) win against Ranku.

The winning Tigers team lifts the cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

One young Tigers fan told the ABC he hopes to be playing alongside his male relatives next season.

"It's the sport we grew up with and we just love playing it," he said.

"We love to beat people in it. It can get a bit rough, but yeah, we love it."

The Imalu Tigers had a dominant season in the lead-up to the final. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In the women's division, it was a tight contest until the end between the Tapalinga Super Stars and the Jikilarruwu.

It was tit-for-tat for much of the first half of the game between the two sides, before Tapalinga created some distance in the third quarter, leaving Jikilarruwu trailing by 10 points.

As the final siren sounded, cheers were met with tears as the Super Stars won the game, defeating Jikilarruwu Thunder & Lightning 8.9 (57) to 4.8 (32).

Player with the Tapalinga Super Stars pose with the premiership cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Huge day of art trade

Grand final day is the largest social event on the Tiwi Islands' social calendar, attracting hundreds of tourists to the community from around the country.

With art centres open amid the influx of visitors, for the islands' artists, the event also doubles as their biggest day of trade and an opportunity to pour money back into the local economy.

Artist Romolo Kantilla said it was also an important time to share their culture.

Romolo Kantilla says the grand final is an opportunity for Tiwi Islands people to share their culture through art. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's a very special day for Tiwi people, it's a big day and we get everyone from the mainland and it's a good time to come see the art," he said.

"The art is based on creation stories, totem and country.

"Art is always part of us Tiwi people."

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking of 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as the underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his most recent singles title was at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu in 2018.

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

World.title: Tears streaming down his face, Messi leaves the World Cup stage a legend
World.content:
Lionel Messi had so desperately hoped his World Cup would end differently.

Tears running down his cheeks, a silver medal around his neck, his teammates in various states of depression, strewn around him like the detritus of some cataclysmic event as Spain roared amid garish golden confetti and an explosion of colour and joy.

Arguably the greatest player to ever grace a pitch was distraught.

It's impossible to know exactly what was going through his mind.

A decade earlier, on the same Metlife Stadium pitch where he was currently sobbing, Messi had tearfully decided to retire from international football after losing the Copa América final against enormous underdogs Chile.

The pain of that defeat was simply too much to bear for Messi, saddled with the expectation of a nation desperate to anoint him as Maradona's heir.

The world was the beneficiary as Messi reversed that decision.

Fans around the world have rejoiced at Messi's success. (Getty Images: Wang HE)

So too were Argentina, who claimed the 2021 Copa América title, the 2022 Finalissima and, most tellingly, the 2022 World Cup under Messi's leadership, cementing his legacy among his fellow countrymen for all time.

But once again in the New Jersey sunshine, Messi's tears were the defining feature for a generation of football fans.

Was this another tearful goodbye to the international stage?

Messi is 39 years old.

With 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí on the other side of the divide and winning for Spain, the next generation is not just arriving to force him out but has already arrived.

To play another World Cup in four years may be beyond even his mystic powers, even despite his impressive ability to adapt to the constraints his age has imposed on him.

The next generation, personified by Lamine Yamal, is snapping at Messi's aging heels. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

At this World Cup, Messi has walked for roughly half the time he was on the pitch, strolling and stalking for about 5 kilometres per game.

And yet, inarguably, no one player has had a greater role in his team's success than Messi has for Argentina.

His goals, eight of them, and his four assists dragged the defending champions through the group stage and the knockout rounds.

His ability to bend a game to his will, no matter the situation, made him seem nothing short of inevitable.

Despite all the walking, whenever Argentina threatened, the little magician was there in the heart of the action, conjuring and scheming and dragging his team home just when they needed him to.

His very presence seemed to inspire his teammates to feats beyond their capabilities, a totemic figure to rally around, his energy imbuing those around him with positivity and confidence and class.

Lionel Messi came close to lifting the World Cup for the second time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Tullio Puglia)

Against England in the semifinal, his two assists powered the Albiceleste to a famous victory in stoppage time.

Against Egypt, as his team faced elimination at 2-0 down, he provided the cross for the first and delivered the shot for its equaliser.

Against Spain in the final? It just didn't happen.

The fact that his tears only came after he had been given his silver medal was almost illustrative: No matter how late it got, Messi perhaps still had hope that he might somehow manage to influence the game in his favour.

He'd done it before, after all.

Only when Donald Trump laid the heavy silver slice of defeat around his neck did he realise there would be no more magic, that no amount of sorcery from his phenomenal feet could change history now.

Against Spain, the little master managed just 55 touches, none of which came in the Spain penalty area.

Lionel Messi was unable to stamp his authority on the contest. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

He was stifled as effectively as if Spain wrapped him in a blanket.

And his Argentina teammates simply couldn't back up their superstar when it mattered most.

Messi could not deliver the magical moment that his nation demanded.

It was telling that Argentina offered so little other than niggly fouls and angry words as opposed to the free-flowing football Spain occasionally managed when the mood took them.

Let's not beat around the bush: Argentina were woeful in this final.

Argentina didn't have a single shot on goal in the first 90 minutes of the game, the first time any team has failed to do so in a World Cup final.

Their first attempt on goal did not come until the 26th minute of extra time.

Lionel Messi had Argentina's first shot of the game, in the second half of extra time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

Their 25 total fouls resulted in seven yellow cards, one of which was a second that saw Enzo Fernández up-end Pau Cubarsí, making him the sixth player ever to be dismissed in a World Cup final.

Argentina's nefarious skulduggery was finally, belatedly, penalised by a referee brave enough not to stand for it.

Coach Lionel Scaloni said afterwards that his team "showed that we know how to lose" in his post-match press conference, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Argentines thoroughly disgraced themselves after the game's conclusion, Leandro Paredes lashing out and sparking a minor brawl that ended with him shown a red card after the final whistle.

Fractious barely covers it.

If this is to be his international swan song, the landscape post-Messi may as well be post-apocalyptic, so absent of joy and light does it appear to hold.

Claudio Tapia, the president of the Argentina Football Association, knows how important Messi is to the team. (Getty Images: Andrew Harnik)

It was not Messi's fault that he could not have the impact on the game he might have hoped for.

Spain were able to successfully nullify a far better team than Argentina in the semifinal with their Rodri-led midfield dominance suffocating their opponents' creativity.

Messi simply didn't have the space.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He was closed down as ominously and relentlessly as the ticking of the clock that will one day herald the end of his stellar career.

Messi couldn't muster the magic to help Argentina become the third men's team to win back-to-back World Cups.

It is not the finale that Messi might have envisaged.

But if this is to be his tearful sign off, fans will still look back at having been blessed by one of football's greatest of all time.

World.title: The 13 photos that summed up the chaos of the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
It was a tournament where the football was magical, the off-field antics were questionable, and ultimately, Spain left the United States as the champions of the world.

A day after the utter chaos of the third-placed playoff between France and England, where 10 goals were scored, Argentina and Spain played things a little more conservatively — right up until the game exploded into action.

Here are the 13 photos that tell the story of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

1. The Fresh Prince of Barcelona

Teenage superstar Lamine Yamal arrives at the stadium looking like the coolest dude on earth. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

While much of the tournament had been focused on the more established superstar names like Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, teenager Lamine Yamal had floated under the radar for the World Cup passers-by.

Coming to the final having never lost a match where he had started for Spain, expectations were high on the 19-year-old as he came into the stadium. Would he be the hero Spain needed to overcome the perceived might of Argentina?

Whatever the pressure, he arrived looking like the coolest dude on the planet; calm, collected and rocking a style straight out of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

2. Smoke and mirrors

Mark Carney greets Donald Trump ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

All eyes turned to the skies before kick-off as US President Donald Trump made his usual subtle entrance into the arena, coming in low and fast in the Marine One helicopter.

Once settled in prime position in a corporate box on the wings, Trump was afforded the questionable chance to give the trophy a little pat as FIFA boss Gianni Infantino brought the iconic gold statue to Trump's seat.

Before that, though, there was the potentially awkward meeting between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, just a couple of days after Trump accused Canada of being "filthy" and "polluted" over its wildfire smoke that had blanketed New York in the lead-up to the tournament.

All-in-all, things seemed reasonably diplomatic, given Mother Nature had done her job to send the smoke packing just in time for the game.

3. America makes a double Buff

American announcer Bruce Buffer turns the World Cup into a blood sport briefly with his iconic introduction. (Getty Images: Sebastian Widmann)

In the most American moment of this entire game, event organisers decided that what this little old soccer match needed was a double Buffer.

Bruce and Michael Buffer, to be exact, the legendary ring announcers from every blood sport imaginable.

Flipping from one brother to the next, the pair excitedly announced that the game was "ready to rumble", in scenes not far off that time that soccer came to Springfield in The Simpsons.

4. The GOAT meets the rising star

Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal share a laugh together early in the match. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Looking a little less cool than when he arrived, but still the picture of confidence, Yamal made a beeline for Lionel Messi before the match to wish arguably the greatest player in history some luck.

It was a full-circle moment for the pair, who originally met on a photo shoot in 2007 when Yamal's parents won a UNICEF raffle to have Yamal photographed for a calendar with the then rising star Messi.

This time around, Messi's hair was a little shorter and his face a little more wearied, while Yamal was a little less nude.

5. The World Cup's Mariah Carey

Shakira performs during the half-time show, a spectacle one England footballing legend would go on to call "crap". (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Shakira was rolled out for the half-time show, with the Colombian star fast becoming to the World Cup what Mariah Carey is to Christmas.

She's just always there.

While her performance was fantastic, the rest of it — from Justin Bieber to Madonna to BTS — left a little bit to be desired.

So much so that English footballing champion Wayne Rooney didn't hold back with what he thought.

"I thought it was crap," he said on the BBC coverage.

6. The spectacular red card

Enzo Fernandez fouls Spain's Pau Cubarsi, leading to the Argentinian's second yellow card and a send-off. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

As soon as we all saw it happen on the TV, we knew that the photos were going to be spectacular.

And veteran Getty photographer Al Bello didn't let us down.

Rising Spanish star Pau Cubarsí was sent flying by Argentina's Enzo Fernández, but it was made all the more spectacular by Cubarsí really leaning into the flip.

Had Fernández not already had a yellow, it's unlikely he would have been sent off at all, but the red card made it all the more dramatic as the scores stood at 0-0 heading into the death.

7. Hydration break goes to a new level

Spain's Dani Olmo takes the hydration break to the extreme as he utilises the sprinklers to cool down. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

Two things have been major talking points during this tournament: it's been bloody hot and the hydration breaks have been bloody irritating.

So it was fun to see the two come together in the final regular-time break of the tournament, as the Spanish players took advantage of the sprinklers to cool off.

Was it the trick that won them the World Cup? Who's to say. But almost certainly yes.

8. Free kick wipes a goal

Nico Williams reacts after his goal was marked off for a foul that was immediately obvious on the replays afterwards. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

In a moment of brilliance, Nico Williams looked to have won it for Spain when he slotted a goal past the keeper to make it 1-0 late.

But the referee called it back. There was a free kick somewhere in the mess of bodies in the box.

In live action it wasn't immediately clear where the free kick was. On replay, it still wasn't totally clear.

But on the fifth or sixth watch: yeah, no idea.

Williams was furious, and rightfully so.

9. Deadlock ends in headlock

Nico Williams gives Ferran Torres a little chokehold celebration after Torres scored the winning goal. (Getty Images: Nick Potts)

Go back to the very first photo at the top of this story and you can experience the majesty of the Ferran Torres goal that broke the game open.

Hair blowing in the breeze, his teammates running in behind him, the fans screaming and cheering in ecstasy.

And then Williams decided to choke Torres for some reason.

Angry that he wasn't the hero after his goal was wiped? An in-joke that we don't know about?

Who knows. But it made for an odd scene in an incredible moment.

10. Tears of a legend

Lionel Messi slumps to the ground after the final whistle, in what will likely be the football legend's last World Cup game. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Small in stature but grand in legacy, Messi cut a forlorn figure after the final whistle.

His tiny body huddled in the middle of the massive stadium was enough to make anyone feel sorry for the attacking superstar.

His place as the greatest player the game has ever seen would have been secured had he managed to drag his teammates to victory, but even Messi couldn't get his countrymen through the incredible defensive wall that Spain had built.

11. Infantino chases after Trump

Rodri prepares to lift trophy as Gianni Infantino attempts to move Donald Trump out of frame. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

Trump had made headlines this time last year when he joined Chelsea on stage for the celebrations in the Club World Cup final, despite the apparent confusion of the players.

This time there was surely no way that Trump would be caught right in the middle of the pack as the Spanish players lifted the most coveted trophy in world sport, right?

Well, kind of. This time Trump wandered right across stage as Infantino pivoted left, leaving the FIFA boss to scramble after the US president, with the pair awkwardly caught in the team celebration photos.

On the broadcast, you could hear someone say "they'll crop him out" in an unexpected, but funny, hot mic moment.

12. Utter heartache for Argentina

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez shows his dejection as the ceremony for the winners gets into full swing. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez had been immense through the World Cup.

But as Spain lifted the trophy, the Aston Villa keeper let the emotions flow, caught by the camera as he sat on the sidelines thinking about what might have been.

It was a reminder of what this thing, this silly, epic, immense mess of a game, means to the people who play it.

13. The love of a mum

Lamine Yamal's mum races out onto the field to celebrate the victory with her son. (Getty Images: John Todd)

In the end, all we really want is the hug of a mum who's proud of you.

And that's what Yamal got as his mum, Sheila, ran onto the ground to give her son a big old cuddle.

Having given birth at just 16 years old as an immigrant from Equatorial Guinea, Sheila's story is the one that really captures the essence of the World Cup.

Not the championship rings or corporate boxes. Not the powerful men in powerful suits making powerful political moves.

A mum with a dream for her son to shine on the world stage.

This was the moment that really mattered.
